pros:
1. Learning and Growth Opportunities: Working at Morgan Stanley often provides extensive learning opportunities. Associates are exposed to diverse financial products and services, enabling them to gain comprehensive knowledge in the field.
2. Professional Environment: The firm is known for its professional culture, where associates work with experienced colleagues and industry experts, providing an excellent environment for professional development.
3. Networking Opportunities: As a global firm, Morgan Stanley offers vast networking opportunities both within the firm and with clients, which can be invaluable for career advancement.
4. Competitive Compensation: The company typically offers competitive salaries and benefits, including bonuses, which can be quite rewarding for high performers.
cons:
1. Work-Life Balance: Like many investment banks, the work can be demanding with long hours, which might impact work-life balance. Associates often report extended working hours, especially during critical project phases.
2. High Pressure Environment: The work environment can be highly pressurized, with tight deadlines and high expectations. This can lead to stress and can be challenging for some individuals.
3. Bureaucracy and Hierarchy: Being a large organization, Morgan Stanley may have layers of bureaucracy and a strict hierarchy, which can sometimes slow down decision-making processes or limit flexibility.
4. Intense Competition: The competitive environment within the firm can be intense, with high expectations for performance. This can create a highly competitive atmosphere that might not suit everyone.

summary: A year of facing extreme stress but also learning valuable skills
advice: Learn to treat your employees fairly and give them an opportunity for 1-1 feedback. I only had 1 session on this during the entire year I worked at Morgan Stanley which I had requested for multiple times. I should not have asked for that - that is management's responsibility. Every other team member received multiple opportunities for this. Also - despite working there for a year you never once bothered to give me an opportunity to be trained on different responsibilities and allowed other people instead to be trained on multiple categories. To my senior manager SC - I was not given any support during a difficult time due to personal reasons which I was facing. We were extremely understaffed that day and I was responsible for a full category myself which is far too much for one person to maintain during a busy period. Instead of reporting my chasers straight to the recruitment manager, I would've appreciated some support as to why I was falling behind - and when I had to take a full week off you still did not reach out. Also you did not once reach out during my time of leave thanking me for my hard work in bookings for the year. I was a number to you and I will now know never to be treated like that by toxic senior management like you in the future. Also to manager MH - During an IT system outage, I should not have been contacted at 8pm asking to log in when there was absolutely no clarity on when the system outage would be resolved earlier that day. It was also never mentioned who specifically should be staying behind and what specific time we can log out. The next day I was told off by you during a meeting for not staying on beyond 6:30pm and you tried to make me feel guilty for this. I am not a slave to be expected to stay logged in beyond 9-10pm like how everyone else was expected. This is not our responsibility. Overall, learn to make your employees to not feel like a number and bombard one person with a workload enough for 2-3 people and expect them to not fall behind and blame them for it when it's your responsibility that the team is understaffed and hardly trained on different categories. Furthermore, learn to train your team efficiently on different roles and categories so that when there's absences, nobody is facing extreme stress because they're stuck on a category which they've never been trained on. Do better and fix up on the toxic elements of your management structure and put yourself in an employees' shoes like I was. No young person coming straight into a graduate job should be facing that much stress and end up having to take sick days because of the vast pressure you force upon us without any support.

summary: Good for a few years experience, not long term
advice: The firm constantly talks about how its people make it what it is; it should value them more.
pros: The people there are genuinely good. There is a strong fit on bringing the right personalities in and that is reflected in a collegiate group of people who make a positive working environment. The benefits are such as private medical cover are good, and the firm is very flexible with parental leave which was really appreciated as a new parent. The firm tries to drive an inclusive culture where LGBTQ persons feel valued. It is a strong company to have on your CV.
cons:
For a firm that makes so much money, they are incredibly miserly. Make sure you negotiate a good salary when joining as year on year pay rises are poor. 2024 pay rises were very low (2.x% even for strong performers) with the narrative that it had been a challenging year for the firm. 2025 pay rises were worse (1.x% for some strong performers, with some colleagues not getting any raise), despite a significant focus on reducing costs in the last 12 months and the firm recording very strong results. Bonuses are OK but nothing great compared to market. It feels like the firm are happy to undervalue employees financially and take the risk on attrition than pay fair rises in the first place. Employees have been struggling through a period of double digit inflation and soaring costs while the C suite get double digit pay rises. Annual leave is very poor compared to European firms.

Within Legal and Compliance, employees are expected to provide their own equipment for working at home. No budget is given for this. Other departments in the building get an allowance for things like monitors. In recent years the Legal and Compliance department have also been expected to pay for their own Christmas party. Travel to the London office for non-officers is non-existent now and generally needs to be self funded if you do want to go. Even small things which generate goodwill, like letting employees log off early ahead of bank holiday weekends, are being scaled back. Investment in tech and improving systems is minimal and so many processes depend on smart people doing manual work.

While the department is currently working on a hybrid basis, there seems to be a general suspicion from senior management about working from home (maybe this is related to why there is no equipment budget; so as not to encourage it).

The promotions process, particularly to officer level, is difficult to navigate and without a clear pathway to achievement. There’s calls every so often to ‘demystify’ the process for people; if the process seems like a mystery, something isn’t right. Glasgow is heavily stacked with Directors looking to move up to Vice President so it feels like there’s a queue that isn’t moving along any time soon. And unlike a lot of other companies, you can’t get promoted by successfully applying for a job at the level above your current grade. You have to be nominated, and go through a process where senior people speak up for you, and feels like a lot of ‘playing the game’ instead of coming in, working hard and being good at your job. Even in the main locations, it’s often seen easier to leave, get a promotion at a peer firm and then come back as an officer than actually make it through the promotions process at MS.

The MS Glasgow office is what’s called a ‘Global Centre’ - that is, an outsourcing centre. It’s effectively regarded as Mumbai + and this is reflected in the fact a lot of the work done there isn’t particularly interesting or challenging and management feel isn’t valuable enough to merit being done in a main location. It feels like Glasgow supports London rather than working with London; that is perhaps the fact of it but it does give a two-tier vibe to how work is done, and the impression is that if you really want to work on interesting projects, make a good wage and progress your career, maybe you’d be better off in the London office (or somewhere else).

If you’re ambitious then, given the issues with pay, promotion and quality of work, it doesn’t feel like an environment to push and challenge yourself. But if you want to work with nice people, earn an OK wage and have a good work life balance, then it’s a pleasant working environment.

summary: Good work/life balance, good treatment of employees
pros:
Morgan Stanley in general will treat its employees fairly and well. There are of course obligatory training (compliance, diversity, Know-Your-Customer etc) and there is required approval process for any personal trading, but these both points are regulatory requirements to any front-desk facing job in banking, so cannot hold it against them.

The work environment is relatively relaxed compared to other banks and the managers are rather friendly. When I had trouble with my health (not preventing any work, but making commute rather inconvenient) they allowed work from home for extended time, until I got better. They do not like employees working crazy hours and seem to have checks (or at least, managers' good will) to prevent burn out. Also they have decent candidate selection  (and annual review, later one) process, meaning you are more likely to work with good developers than with poor ones.
cons: If you are a permie software developer, your base salary and bonus will be capped - no matter how good you are. This is common in banking, and one way out of this bracket is move to contracting. You are unlikely to be promoted, unless you have worked at the firm for many years.

advice:
Initiate a discussion with non-officers about simplifying the promotions at the bottom of the career ladder, maybe just two or three levels before VP, these may take more time to go through but I think that's ok. After all there are only three levels of officer.

Something like Analyst, Associate and Director could work well. It would distinguish between the most junior grads, those with a couple of years and individuals close to being an officer.

Or even just Analyst and Associate. I think the IB and trading floors had a simpler structure like this.
pros: A dynamic environment with lots of opportunities to develop. A collaborative environment with some of the best leadership in the business.
cons:
There is quite a rigid nature of promotions in the Legal & Compliance department that I felt was not ideal, particular at more junior levels. There is a formal annual process, combined with a lot of levels; Analyst, Associate, Manager, Director, VP, ED & MD.

Promotions are great and should be celebrated, but career progression in the form of going for a title change every year or two years isn't what most people want, and often at the junior levels the change in title doesn't meaningfully reflect a change in role.

advice: Drop the DIE nonsense. Focus on hiring good people no matter what their skin colour and/or gender. Box-ticking is only going to drive away your few remaining competent employees.
pros: MS used to be a pretty interesting place to work. My co-workers were bright and highly motivated, and there was a real culture of excellence and meritocracy. Unfortunately, all that has now been overturned in the pursuit of "equity" and leftist box-ticking. The recruitment and promo processes are now weighted against males and white people, and as a result MS is now on a slow slide to irrelevance and oblivion.
cons:
I worked at MS for nearly a decade. I left because of 2 main reasons :

(1) short-sighted cost-cutting mentality that focusses on hitting next year's financial targets at the extent of building a skilled and motivated workforce. I got sick of hiring and training good people only to see those same people fired a year or two later. This happened repeatedly during my decade at the firm.

(2) excessive pandering to left-wing "social justice" causes that prioritises certain demographics over others, regardless of job competency

To expand on the first point, many teams at MS are chronically understaffed. The firm has incredibly complex systems with decades of history, a huge backlog of important regulatory work - but not enough people to do it all. Rob Rooney (head of technology) made a series of deep cuts in late 2019 in a bid to hit profitability targets, which caused morale to plummet. The firm only started to hire again the start of 2021. The problem is that every single team is now in a mad bidding war and HR is struggling under the load. We're therefore forced to engage external consulting firms (aka bodyshops) in a desperate bid to get more people in before the gates close again.

There's another problem...

The location strategy. MS is pushing hard to cut costs in "metro locations" and hire cheap workers in India and East Europe. Many managers have been instructed not to make any more hires in London or New York. The problem is that we need people with a very specific set of skills, and those people simply don't exist in other locations (certainly not in the numbers we need). We also lack good senior managers in many of the locations that we're allowed to hire into. Quality control is becoming a serious problem. Result : an influx of new people with little finance experience, and often only passable tech skills. There are also language barriers that cause frequent confusion. 

Then there's also the whole "diversity and inclusion" agenda. You can't escape this stuff in a big org, but at MS it is out of control. MDs have been instructed to hire more females and minorities or "there will be consequences" (to quote from an older Rooney town-hall). The result has been a sharp decline in quality. There simply aren't enough good female engineers to go round, so what do we do to hit the target ? Lower the standards of course. I was hired after a gruelling 3 hour interview which tested my financial and IT knowledge to the limit. We're now making hires based on a thirty minute Zoom call. We're also passing over highly qualified males in a bid to hit targets. The inevitable result is a large influx of underqualified hires who are just going to drive out the few remaining talented people. 

The D&I agenda carries over into the promo process too. The process goes like this : first, a panel of peers interviews the relevant stakeholders and objectively ranks the promotion candidates based on their ability and achievements. Then, the list is passed on to an MD who shuffles people around to make sure we hit all the right "diversity" targets (and to ensure that his/her year-end bonus doesn't get cut). Result : perfectly good people get moved down the list because they're not the right gender and/or colour. Of course, they're never told why they got passed over, since that might expose the firm to legal action. Nice.

On a related topic : shortly before I left I was repeatedly nagged to attend training courses informing me about my "white privilege" and I have also been subjected to regular emails about the firm's commitment to social justice issues and (shudder) "racial equity". I can't begin to tell you how repellent I find this brainwashing. To have an investment bank, a bastion of free-market capitalism, peddling hard-left propaganda to its staff ? Please just leave me along and let me get on with my work. Personally, I'm thoroughly sick of being subjected to divisive political propaganda while I'm trying to earn a living. The barrage of woke drivel is getting unbearable and I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one who's fed up with it.

summary: Looks great from the outside, but.....
advice:
-Make an effort to retain talent and pay the market rate.  Success breeds success therefore makes no sense to lose experienced staff.
-Remove a layer of management.  Far too often, initiatives are middle management led, looking to enhance their bonus potential with little regard for how well their pet project is implemented...This is where a true headcount saving can be made.
-Invest in grassroots.  There's no point in running grad programmes but seeing nearly all members leave after a few years as that's just a waste of money.  This should be the basis of the future and senior leaders need to understand this.
-Transparency.  Being open and honest about compensation allays any concerns staff have, otherwise this causes suspicion, envy and concern as to what colleagues of a comparative level are earning.  The clearer you are on comp, the less likelihood employees have a wondering eye on joining another bank!

summary: Glasgow Operations run by weak line management and middle managers
advice:
Deeply ingrain in the bottom level managers a sense of responsibility and a duty of care to the ordinary worker drones. Also, do not make people who were only "good enough" line managers. These people are vindictive, bitter, and don't care about the firm or their work. They are only there for a paycheck and it shows. 

This also means that despite you pandering to new joiners about how much you love and need us to suggest improvements, your bottom managers (line management and the next level up), operate on the ostrich policy. They will never implement, never mind consider any change, be it to systems or processes, unless you, their manager, force them to do so. They don't care about how little risk control exists, how poor the timeliness of information is, or how awfully inefficient processes are. They only care about covering their backsides to guarantee their bonuses. They don't look beyond their own job security and bottom line, and are inherently selfish.
pros: Nice analyst group, collegiate, friendly.
cons:
Line managers are mostly embittered long-timers who have never been promoted in rank due to inadequate work morale, insufficient drive, and lacking motivation and ability to motivate. 

Their managers in turn are often too young, and too busy with machinating their next step up the career ladder than acting like good managers. Responsibility never lies with them and they always look to blame their direct reports for anything that goes wrong. The buck never stops with them. They are also generally unknowledgeable of the day-to-day work that goes on and the systems utilized, much to their own peril and thus they speak in ignorance readily and with great arrogance. They don't understand the limitations and flaws of the outdated and primitive systems in use, and rather than find solutions, or change what is flawed, they insist that it's always been so and if it ain't broke... (yeah, it's only technically not broken, in any self-respecting organization such primitive and contrived work-arounds to outdated garbage would be considered what they are: disasters in the making)
They are also often prone to contradictory orders and statements on policy/practice/regulations.

Support from bottom-end management is entirely lacking, and politics and a vicious blame-culture are palpable on a daily basis. Direct and clear communication is almost non-existent, and the passive-aggressive office culture means that verbal communication is rare and not valid, almost everything must be put in electronic form. Just don't expect it be to be clear or explicit. Instead, get used to having to read between lines and deduce information. 

Do not expect any support and orientation in a new role. You will not get it. Documentation is nonexistent. Most things are taught inadequately by being shown at lightning speed once and then corrected slowly as the inevitable mistakes are made.

Line managers will not grant you permission to stay later to complete work but they themselves will excuse themselves to show up late and leave early on a regular basis. This is what is called work-life balance.

The work itself across operations is for the most part tedious, monotonous, intellectually stultifying, and only difficult because of poor systems, inefficient work processes that are impervious to improvement and change, and the lack of support from management.

The organization at large is full of people at the lowest rank who have been there too long, have been beaten up and demotivated too much, and feel unappreciated and underpaid compared to the competition.

advice: Don't lose your nerve regarding your strategic IT initiatives-- their success will become a big part of what will help you recruit quality candidates in the future. Keep up the good work with establishing the collegial tone of the place; it engenders a lot of loyalty and goodwill. Dump the quintilling practice-- there's too much evidence out there that it poisons workplaces. Make the case for improving IT bonuses; the retention of institutional memory is worth it. Find some way to make the location strategy more effective; too much time is spent by senior people in NY and London managing people in the other locations.
pros:
These comments are specific to my time in Technology & Data in London.

I found a welcoming collegiality during my time at Morgan. Co-workers were realistic about the good and bad of the systems they were in charge of, and always seemed open to discussions about new approaches to improving them (and often acting on those discussions). This collegial aspect was reflected through the organization, with management setting the tone for those below them to follow. I generally found most people easy to work with.

There's lots of smart people in Morgan IT, both from a business as well as a technology perspective.

Morgan has evolved a substantial capability for remote work, and many managers are comfortable with people working from home on a regular basis (and they do it themselves). For the parts of the organization I'm familiar with, I would say that Morgan has less stress on perpetually working long hours that other places have. In general, I found work-life balance good, hampered the most through their inconvenient location in Canary Wharf, which often entails miserable commutes.

Promotions are available but aren't handed out willy-nilly. ED level promotions are taken quite seriously and a lot of review by a lot of people takes place. This results in getting pretty good people in senior roles.

One thing I really appreciated was the fact that Morgan has such a good culture but doesn't go around broadcasting it as a selling point. I've come to learn that the organizations that talk the most about how good their culture is often have lots of unattractive aspects to hide, but Morgan doesn't talk about it's own culture much at all-- they simply walk the walk. I'm starting to be convinced that this is a hallmark of a truly good culture.

Although some complain about it, I found Morgan's internal automation of IT to be pretty impressive. Most of the time software can be delivered with minimal fuss
cons:
Morgan is resource constrained, and IT finds much of its budget devoted to things it has to do rather than things that it feels are new and important to do, either for itself or for the business. Thus, new and interesting work, although available, isn't always easy to get involved with, so if that's important you may want to bear that in mind.

Morgan also has some fairly old systems that it has to live with due to the point above; some are better than others, although many are surprisingly robust and handle significant volumes on a daily basis. There's strategic work to lay the foundation for changing many of those, but that's going to take a good amount of time to achieve.

Some people complain that there's too much consensus building, and that it takes too long to reach decisions. I've heard stories about how people thought that a decision was reached, but when someone discovered they had been left out, the entire decision was scuttled and had to be discussed all over again. I never witnessed that specifically, and making significant decisions doesn't seem any more fraught than in any other big bank, but I have had that communicated to me by multiple people there.

While the rigorous promotion process yields quality results, Morgan is frugal with promotions, and there's a fair amount of competition, so if moving up rapidly in IT is important, you should bear this in mind.

As with other banks, Morgan pays above average for IT as a whole, but bonuses have suffered in recent years. Some MDs have told me their view is that since the days of big profits are probably not coming back, Morgan may be constrained structurally in how good bonuses will get.

Morgan's location strategy is to focus on building IT capacity in non-major metro areas, which includes Glasgow, Montreal, Budapest, and Shanghai. Often this leads management to conclude that London is ideally situated as it has significant time overlaps with all of these locations. If you're happy to spend the majority of your day on the phone in meetings with remote workers as they overlap with the UK business day, then this will be heaven for you, but if you want to actually get work done, the amount of communication you need to perform will be challenging to say the least.

Morgan uses a quintilling process (forced ranking) as part of the review cycle, and there's just too much evidence that this is actually a poisonous practice for organizations. Morgan seems to have so far managed to avoid its ill effects, but be aware that a ranking distribution must be met.

As with most banks, career opportunities dwindle as you move up in the org.

advice: A shift in mentality and behaviour is urgently needed. Not that my review will change anything, as from what I've said some people will pretend that nothing is going on. However, because I've met nice people in the firm too, I would like to address them and say that if you haven't left the firm yet and need to change something, then please notify the higher managers of what's happening and exercise enough pressure so as for them to stop ignore the real problems and issues. Money and profits is not everything. There are hard working people who are trying their best to get experiences and help the firm reach the point where it is just now. And these people need to feel that their work is appreciated. A "good job" and a pat on their back is not enough. They need material proof that this is happening. A good raise in salaries and bonuses would be a good first step, with others to follow.
pros: Looks good on the CV
cons:
Where to start?

-Extremely long working hours and OF COURSE, unpaid overtime. If you ever ask about overtime or any other forms of compensation for the crazy hours you have worked (e.g. an extra half day off), you will be told off at the best case. You are EXPECTED to stay late. If you try to leave sharp for whatever reason, people will most likely look at you with those annoyed faces.

-Extremely low compensation. Increase of barely 1.5-2% on a annual basis, the bonus being even lower than that. To be fair though, I heard that they raised the salaries in 2019, which is good, even though it took them almost 20 years to realise.

-Everything is about politics. It doesn't matter if you exercise crappy management, it doesn't matter if teams fall apart and clients leave because of you, at the end of the day you will get the promotion if you know the right people. On the other hand, it doesn't matter how well you perform, it doesn't matter how much time of your life are you investing, there's gonna be no promotion whatsoever, unless you are good in politics.

-The mentality about people who are high performers but don't want to get into the politics thing is more or less "rather than complaining, get on with your job. It's an honour for you that you are working here. And don't say much, because we can easily make you leave. There's 10 more people after you, looking for your role".

-From what you have understood so far (and from other reviews), management is poor. This, though, won't stop them from pretending that the problems are not there at all. They will pretend that everything is fine, that 11-12 hour shifts is something normal, that the salaries and bonuses are more than enough, that despite the attrition rate might reach 50% everything is excellent etc etc.

summary: Great at providing challenges, will look to underpay wherever they can get away with it

Stop cutting corners by trying to consistently under pay. 

Remuneration is a significant part of individuals feeling rewarded for the effort they put in. Trying to cut a few £1000 here and there on total comp uptick, may as a consolidate total across ops look impressive to the board, but will demotivate as a collective significantly enough for a material portion of workforce to ease off effort, or worse leave. 

Don’t worry though, you can make the retention numbers better by adjusting the figures you report to the board (“retention of high performers” magically changed from once reported “retention total”, which doesn’t adjust for where motivation has dropped and people are looking to move on). The same numbers can be made to report whatever story you’re hoping to support.

summary: How to waste two years of your life
advice: Recent firmwide announcements have suggested focus will be paid to increasing profitability. How about increasing employee happiness first?
pros: The graduate training scheme is unparalleled, a wonderful learning experience. For the first fifteen weeks of your career, you will feel like you made the right decision.
cons: A corporate policy of Morgan Stanley is that there can be no promotion until you have served a total of nine years in higher education and the financial industry. If you have a bachelors degree, you will spend six years without any appreciable increase in salary or rank. The average bonus for new hires now is below three thousand, and the average raise is close to zero. There is a split culture; those who arrived before the crisis, in the "good times", still brag about wealth and insist on the best Champagne. For new hires, however, that could not be further from the truth. It is a long standing open secret that Morgan Stanley has the worst graduate salary of any large investment bank; the expectation being with advancement comes significant monetary improvements. What is likely to take you by surprise is that until the first promotion (6 years), the expected raise is zero.

advice: Don't treat it like part of the armed forces.  Stop using fear as your primary motivational tool.
pros: Good place to get broad experience of investment banking, there isn't much that MS don't get involved with.
cons:
Glasgow is basically a big operations factory supporting the main sites in London, NY and far east.  The campus is run by a lot of ex armed forces people, who run it like the armed forces.  Head down, don't complain, get on with it until it's done.   Technocrats and process driven workaholics do well.  People with personality tend to leave.  Be part of the machine or don't.

The single biggest motivational lever used is fear.  Fear of a poor performance rating, fear of job losses, fear of falling behind your peers.  There is very little positive motivation or working to people's strengths.  Be warned - you are either part of the 'inner circle' or not.  Promotions at a senior levels (VP and above) are based on perception not performance.  The expectation to do more than your day job really means evenings and weekends. Performance reviews are based on a 1-5 quintile and staff are continuously pitted against each other using this system.

Pay is around mid-market and the old notion of 'total reward' rather falls down with the significant decrease in bonuses over the years.  Benefits package, esp pension, has been slowly eroded away as well.

Institutionalized workforce, they want to mould you to be a "Morgan Stanley" employee. With as little transferable skills as possible. Build everything in house to keep people from acquiring real skills (they even went far enough attempt to build their own programming language). Overall lack of motivation, no body cares about anything. All talk and no action. People have meetings about having meetings about other meetings and then they go home. Nothing gets done. And if by accident something is done, it is done in the absolutely the worst lacklustre way possible.

Actively hostile environment to software developers. Development environment crash constantly (i.e. Visual Studio and Eclipse) due to over-the-top restrictive access controls and antiquated OSs. C++ devs have it the best but only because they use Textpad or something even more primitive.

Computers are slow, software is slow, people are slow, EVERYTHING IS SLOW!

pros:
I really enjoyed my coworkers and management, always looking out for your best interest and being considerate of what you may not like, be good at, or have going on personally. At least that's from my experience. Others may not like their team which I feel like stems from not liking the job itself. Also, getting sponsored to take the SIE, Series 7, and Series 63 is pretty nice. You only get 1 chance to take the SIE, but 2 for the 7 and 63. 

Work life balance is pretty standard (9:00am - 5:00pm). No real reason to stay late unless you want more hours since you're hourly However, I should mention that lunch is not paid so whether you have a 30min, lunch or a 45min. lunch, that is just added time you have to stay there for your shift until you reach the designated hours.

Pretty decent vacay / sick package as well. Vacation and sick are both paid and I think you get 10 days (or 80 hours) of each if I recall. But that's all c changing next year. Not for anything worse though, just something that's man aged a bit differently
cons:
So essentially a Registered Client Service Representative is Stock Broker in a sense. At least it is if you pass your series 7 and Series 63 upon hiring. If not, then your pay goes down to about $21.00 / hr. but you still basically do the same work. You wont be able to call yourself a registered broker with you if you leave for other firms if you don't have these licenses. 

This job in every shape, level, or added license is a "Call center" so be prepared for that. A lot of us where confused during training as it was always alluded to the number of calls were taking, but we figured that that's just a part of it, But no, that's all it is really is. Even if you do pass the exams. It can be very tedious and daunting especially since you can expect to be talking non-stop throughout your entire shift aside from your breaks and lunch.

They also currently have an issue where jobs posted on there internal system are not actually interested in hiring anyone. They are just there to "gauge interest". Be mindful because this translate to the public careers postings as well. So a lot of what you are applying for there is literally going no where or to some folder to not be looked at.

To foster a healthier and more productive work environment, management should consider the following steps:

Promote Respectful Communication: Establish clear guidelines for communication that emphasize respect and professionalism. Training programs focused on constructive feedback can help managers understand the impact of their words.

Implement Accountability Measures: Establish consequences for unprofessional behavior. Holding managers accountable for their actions will encourage a culture of respect.
Invest in Employee Well-Being: Provide resources for mental health and stress management. A supportive environment promotes productivity and employee satisfaction.

advice:
Improve Role Clarity and Transparency in Hiring Process:

Candidates should fully understand the expectations, structure, and culture of the role during the hiring process. If the position involves high-call volumes and a focus on adherence to metrics, these aspects should be clearly outlined in both the job description and interview conversations.
Ensuring transparency from the outset can prevent future dissatisfaction and reduce turnover among employees who feel misled about job responsibilities.
Address Employee Mental Health and Job Satisfaction:

Regularly assess job roles that may be causing significant stress or affecting employees' mental health, and provide tailored support. While it's valuable to offer resources like counseling, sometimes a change in the environment, workflow, or expectations is necessary.
Managers should be proactive in recognizing signs of burnout or mental health issues due to job stress, especially in high-stress roles. A supportive conversation that explores feasible options, whether through job rotation, reasonable accommodation, or time off, can make a significant impact.
Provide Supportive Management and Flexibility on Metrics:

While it’s understandable that the role requires metrics to measure performance, creating a balance between accountability and employee wellbeing is essential. Messages and alerts for minor adherence infractions can create unnecessary pressure, making the work environment feel overly rigid and micromanaged.
Offering flexibility, such as a grace period on metrics or reducing penalties for minor issues, can make employees feel trusted and reduce stress. When feasible, flexibility in handling metrics for short, unintentional absences can go a long way in improving morale.
Regular Check-Ins and Career Development Support:

For employees seeking career growth, establish a structured plan for internal mobility, even if role changes cannot occur immediately. Managers could offer targeted development assignments, mentorship, or leadership training that helps employees develop skills aligned with their career goals while meeting role tenure requirements.
Managers can offer to set up regular check-ins to discuss progress on development plans or temporary role adjustments to address specific challenges within the job.
Clear, Compassionate Communication:

In sensitive conversations about role limitations or unmet expectations, managers should aim to actively listen, empathize, and clearly address employee concerns. Reframing feedback with empathy and validating employees’ feelings can help them feel heard and respected, even when a desired outcome isn’t achievable.
For employees expressing dissatisfaction, it’s essential to acknowledge their concerns as valid rather than framing them as misunderstandings. This fosters trust and may lead to employees feeling more satisfied despite challenges.

pros: Amazing colleagues, smart people, great technology, better work/life balance than other banks on the street. Clubs organised by employees to enjoy some bonding outside of work.
cons:
Apologies for the bloc of text but I needed to vent.

Promotion
=======
Opaque promotion process, bottleneck for promotion within the department. You first need to obtain a "ticket" from management to even be considered for the promotion process as one of the candidates. If luckily your management does not dismiss your "requests" for promotion, you get the ticket. You will then be presented as candidate by your manager who will defend your achievements in front of a committee. If your manager does not want to bother helping you in your career or is junior, forget about career advancement. If your manager is not good at defending or articulating thoughts, forget about promotion.
The promotion criteria are a moving target. Once you think you know them, you are told that last year they changed for your region. Of course, the official document containing the criteria is confidential and not readable by aspiring candidates.

Typical promotion topics responses from different people (when you manage to hold a career convo with someone):
"Maybe in 3-4 years we can come back to this conversation."

"You need sponsors in IT and business units to support your candidacy. Your achievements and experience alone are not enough." --> i.e. A big chunk of your time goes to networking and making friends with people for the sole purpose of checking this box.

"Look at X, they have been volunteering for months." --> i.e. Why don't you volunteer on top of your paid daily duties for free so maybe we can promote you? Why don't you start yet another useless meetup for people in the office to show your name around?

"You should know how well you perform against other people in your local team. I'm surprised you do not know." --> I am the only one in my location working on my project and do not interact with others in my department, yet they are a factor in the recognition I get from the company? Do they know how well they perform against me, a person that has nothing to do with them? Really?

"You are meeting expectations this year." "But I did XYZ on top of my daily duties, mentored people etc. and went above and beyond compared to others." "I summarised the feedback from your colleagues and mine in the improvement section for you. They are not all mine. I think you should focus on the first feedback first for this year." "Can you give me an example where that happened and how I should have behaved?" "No... recently it was good." --> Then why is it in my review?

Me in my 1:1 with manager: "Do you have any feedback for improvement?" "No." "How can I improve to get promoted?" "Let's wait. Let's not get ahead of ourselves."

--> It leaves me with a feeling that management wants to see me as a junior, like the other members of my team regardless of my experience. I need to fit their agenda of "my manager is the one that will help me grow and thanks to them I will get to the level where I can get promoted..." regardless of my actual situation.

Pay
===
Subpar pay compared to other banks on the street like GS. Feeling shared by other people I talked to in the office. The last global survey showed that ~50% of employees are not happy with their pay. We are talking about a top tier bank that "does business in a first class way".

Events are organised in the company but they kind of give a vibe of "bread and games!" to keep employees happy. I mean, I am probably exaggerating here given those are organised by genuine people that care, but I feel like it benefits upper management in that way.

People
=====
You meet amazing people but the common behaviour in my department has been to slap low quality code into the codebase. In the beginning in my previous projects, no one cared about unit tests, integration tests bits were copy pasted all over. People dismissed my arguments that adding tests would make our lives easier. There were patches everywhere, deployments into production from 10 different branches because it's too difficult to verify that all changes added on the master branch are safe for some specific environments.
My current team (last 2-3 years) cares much more about testing in general which is good, but still sometimes I need to fight on pull requests reviews to make devs review their design but sometimes I lose because "we'll change this later". Then X months later I need to code a feature and I need to pay the technical debt fee when I use/update their code.

No one in my current department bothers to update their coding setup proactively. I had to push to make them use linters for Python etc. so that people that have the tooling enabled on their side do not spend their time fixing syntax errors and code smells.

In some occasions I had to communicate very important things to senior management in situations that were quite scary for me. I never got a reply, even though I spent weeks on top of my work to investigate and prove that I had not done anything wrong.

Work location and remote
=================
We moved to a super limited "work from another location" that requires MD approval. I think it's a very small amount of days of remote work per trip in a location. I know Japanese companies that allow 1 months per year. Shouldn't we be at least as good as Japanese black companies?

Diversity and Inclusion
===============
Great push for D&I but it creates reverse discrimination against people that are not part of a minority or diverse (diverse meaning female in Japan). I applied for internal mobility and was told after 4 months that I had not been considered until then because they were considering diversity candidates instead of me. Great job at creating equal opportunities.

Conclusion
========
I have given up on promotion. It feels like swimming against the current. If I go above and beyond, I meet expectations. If I work at 60% I meet expectations. What's the point of slaving away for no reward?

Consequence is I do care less about some things now. I care less about how people see me in the team. Sometimes on Sunday nights I get insomnia because I replay frustrating things from work in my head. I don't need a free subscription to Headspace, I need objectivity at work and recognition. If you have no recognition to give me, then make me work on stuff to earn it and please stop the gaslighting.

I am looking around to find a better paying job and management that listens. The only thing keeping me there is how nice my close colleagues are. 

Seriously, my domestic partner is getting almost twice my pay at a competitor. They are laughing at my bonus and increase every year.
Go to a competitor if you want career progression. Some people here have been 10+ years in the business without getting to VP.

summary: Use ALL of your vacation before you quit!!
pros: Great bonus and perks from company paid lunch to overall benefits.
cons:
Not sure if the following is only applicable in Canada.

Morgan Stanley (MS) separated between vacation time and vacation pay. They will only pay the vacation based on the minimum 4% of your earned salary which is what's on the Employment Standard (ES) of where I live. That said, even though I still have an unused earned vacation balance, MS declined to pay the balance because the vacation that I have used is already more than 4% of my earned salary.

To make things worse, what MS did by separating vacation time and pay is not against the ES.

That said:
1. If by the time you quit (or maybe even when they fire you but I'm not sure on this one), you have yet used any of your vacations, then, MS will only pay up to 4% of your earned salary.
2. If by the time you quit, you already used more than 4%, but still have a remaining balance (which you have already earned), then, MS will NOT be paying you the balance.

Therefore, make sure that you use ALL of your earned vacation before you quit!!!

summary: Sometimes a fun job, sometimes rough
advice: Management could be a little more straightforward, but they’re likely just being very polite and professional on purpose.
pros:
The company will take care of you if you just keep working harder and smarter there. Great paid time off. Worked remote for a year 2021-2022 then returned to office/hybrid. WFO isn’t so bad, there are way fewer distractions. Ideally, you live close to the office/can minimize the commute. I would say many folks don’t try hard enough to get clients invested or bring over new assets. My recommendation to them is look up some sales videos and also learn the securities you’re recommending pretty well. You get paid well, so find the time whether at work or outside of work to improve yourself and the value you can bring to the clients, whether that’s in the form of a better experience or in the form of being able to get them better risk-adjusted returns.

You learn a lot on the job, especially when studying for the exams which they generously pay for. I recommend using Anki/spaced repetition flash cards, as well as simply taking lots of quizzes and tests to prepare for your Series 7 and 66 exams, as well as your SIE exam prior to onboarding.
cons:
Clients can be mean and discriminatory. The job also makes you realize how many people use other paid services as a proxy for getting therapy and having friends/someone to talk to.

Another con can be that being a financial advisor is in part a Sales job and they sometimes don’t make it out to be that way. They WANT clients to invest their money with you and incur commissions/management fees. They want more assets under management, just like a hedge fund. If you’re not ready to sell, dont become a financial advisor. Do be open to it though as it pays better than just being a customer representative (this doesn’t pay half-bad, though).

Another con is that you can’t do full-remote if you’re performing well. They should definitely let you WFH if you prove yourself to be competent. Likely some commercial real estate conflict of interest that is behind the CEO’s push for Work From Office.

advice:
Management is absolutely heartless when it comes to employees.  This past year I've been encouraged to avoid taking time off, micro-manage employees to an absurd degree, and utilize the stick over any carrots.

The biggest kick in the pants has been around the so called "volunteer" functions, such as Global Volunteer Month and the "Annual Appeal."  

These are far less volunteer initiatives, with the managing director making it clear that he expected 90% participation in both initiatives.  Frontline management was expected to do whatever was necessary in order to reach these numbers.  For those that do not know, the annual appeal is CHARITIBLE GIVING (cash contributions) that the Company Tracks and touts each year.  Rather than treating it as an optional, yet wonderful opportunity for those who were able to give back, hit hovered over our heads like the proverbial Sword of Damocles if our line of business didn't reach the arbitrary goal the MD selected.  We're talking about entry level call center employees live paycheck to paycheck being bullied into making cash contributions by management.  That is not charity, it's extortion.

Management should really look into the people they've put into power and how they operate their business, because it's heartless, and unethical.

-there is a yearly salary increase for pretty much everyone, which should be a given everywhere, but I know it’s not, so I guess you could call that a pro

 -there is a hierarchy, so it’s possible to climb the ladder, not a complete dead-end road career-wise (well, for some people it is)

I would not recommend accepting an offer if the contract is temporary, keep looking.

You could be working very hard, doing everything as you’re supposed to, and still not get noticed if you’re given the ‘wrong’ kinds of tasks. Someone else could walk in off the streets and be hired at a level that you’re supposed to be working hard to achieve..

-many things just simply don’t make sense, it’s extremely bureaucratic, but I guess that’s true for most multinationals.

summary: Good job to start a career, but management is out of touch and seems desperate
advice: Sometimes, I feel like I am in middle school at this job. Granted there are many VEA's who are a few years removed from college, but not every VEA is. The lead manager feels like a middle school principle, who appears like he wants to be feared. The way management speaks to us is often inappropriate and out of touch with needs of actual financial advisors and their practices. The metrics we are evaluated on other than bringing in money (which still is the responsibility of the FA), have nothing to do with the satisfaction of the people we work with or how well we are doing at out job. I find myself trying to balance expectations from management with my actual job of marketing for financial advisors, and appeasing management is a much more challenging and frustrating experience. I understand this is a bank, but it often feels like we are trying to make career long Financial Advisor's into slimy retail brokers, rather than helping them and their clients. Because we do not receive any incentive for bringing in more money other than a pat on the back or the occasional Pizza Party there is almost no reason to care about management's expectations, other than keeping your job. The relationships we foster with financial advisors are much more beneficial in terms of our future career prospects than reviews from management telling you you hit your metrics quota's for the quarter. So maybe they should take some constructive feedback and actually listen to us, instead of trying to scare us all the time.

advice: Understand that you need to enable advisors to operate more independently to stay competitive in the market. It takes time and is mentally draining to help someone navigate their finances- bogging advisors down with service calls and projects then penalizing them for not meeting the sales expectations or not abiding by the ridiculous phone metrics is a insult to the profession and severely hurts the product. Advising should be relational, not transactional.
pros: #1) Excellent Training for aspiring advisor with 0 experience. Its very uncomfortable to start because you have to learn the service work before you advise, but it’ll lay an excellent foundation to learn more later on through licensure and advising (which can take quite a while depending on advisor training schedule). #2) A few good managers that really care. #3) Nice facilities and a overall upbeat workplace considering the negative below.
cons: #1) They say its a “Call center like environment”. Don’t let them fool you, its a call center. Call metrics were very important to management, which some people dont vibe well with, including myself. #2) Staffing issues at the time I worked there made the service department very shorthanded, so as an advisor, who has sales expectations, will get very bogged down doing service work (which takes time off the phone), all while getting pinged by managers asking why youve been off the phone for a few minutes (enormously frustrating and micromanagy). #3) I wasn't a fan of the sales mentality and the value proposition presented to clients considering whats available outside of Morgan Stanley. Absolutely nothing unethical to be clear, but i just didn't feel like clients were getting much for how much they were paying (plus they pay a absolute premium, which I didn't like). A few more that I don’t want to get into, but they reveal themselves pretty shortly after you start.

You can use a few online learning sites (but only from within your VDI). Teams are forced to be Agile, if you have a good Scrum Master and PO that can work well. Company had mature IT infra 20 years ago, with inner CLI tools for basically everything (config management, distributed filesystem, process scheduler, pubsub system, web hosting, etc). Today we have better 3rd party industry standards for these, but typically you can't use those in practice, because migration effort is "costly and risky".
cons: Although going to cloud / modernization is an often cited company goal, in practice most legacy core components are bound to company's inner infra and custom tools, so those and hundreds of dependers can't go to public cloud. Partially some are trying to use on-prem on demand resources. Company likes to fire certain percentage of employees from time to time to save costs. For reasonable refactors (stabilization and modernization) there are not enough resources. Minimal teams are trying to keep the system's head above the water by desperately handling constant support issues, mandatory upgrades, critical bugfixes and urgent, short term business needs. Internal mobility is possible, but most projects are similar. Advancing in career is an unclear process with lots of fluid requirements. No one can explain, what you have to do exactly for being promoted (or just nominated at least). It's easier to leave the company and return later to a higher position than being promoted during years of committed work.

advice: There are a number of legitimate "star athletes" on teams that, for whatever reason, have not been offered the same types of opportunities afforded to others who may possess certain types of personalty or cultural traits that fit the pre-existing mold. Continue to listen to employee concerns and be empathetic. Too often mid and senior level managers can be dismissive and more concerned with providing excuses for why the perceived issues are not valid, as opposed to being understanding and using their position as a senior leader to support and help exceptional team members overcome the significant obstacles towards career progression. There is accountability on both sides where the individual needs to adapt and work towards self-promotion and marketing their achievements, but managers who recognize these talents also need to do their part in providing visible support and exposure to other senior leaders.
pros: Morgan Stanley's wealth management business is an incredible platform that stands head and shoulders above its peers, with bright minds providing insightful, well-informed and executable guidance and thought leadership. If given the opportunity, high-level performers can be in a position to really shine and exhibit the type of service, expertise, and quality of advice the firm is known for and has built a stellar reputation on.
cons: The opportunities for high-level performers, particularly at the mid-level stage, to display their expertise, capabilities and really add even more value to the business can be few and far between, especially for employees who don't naturally fit the mold and personality that could be a bit more old-school and dated (less a meritocracy, more a "popularity" contest). Morgan Stanley's efforts in ESG and diversity and inclusion have been remarkable and there has been significant progress, but there's still a long way to go (this is not just specific to the firm, but for the industry as a whole).

Any type of finance career you will have team and group meetings which feel mundane, yea it sucks but it's part of corporate America this is not a Morgan Stanley exclusive con -big company so other teams take care of different functions and sometimes you will have to hound them to take care of stuff/update information because the clients will be hounding you. This is most def by biggest complaint because everything is on a time crunch so if your client is calling/emailing/messaging/emailing your manager asking for an update on something you can not change is stressful, because you are waiting for a different team to update the information but they of course have their workload as well. Overall it's just a lot of moving pieces , and some people just don't care about their job and deadlines as much but that is at any place of work -the training can be light. Usually you have a few shadow sessions with a senior team member and then start with a light load after about 2-3 weeks of shadowing. overall you need to learn as you go and ask questions and take notes so you are not asking the same questions.

advice: I had high hopes in finishing my 2 weeks after I put in the notice of resignation— but didn’t return to the firm, even for that short remainder of time. Very stressful role due to lack of organization structure and/or training. After the initial 4-6 weeks, new hires are introduced to their designated role and then expected to overperform on a variety of different Morgan Stanley platforms that training was not received specifically on. I was expected to know things about certain services that were only briefly touched on. You’re told by one of your colleagues who meets with the Advisory Council “A lot of this is learned on the job, I had to do it” and to basically just get over the fact that you’re being overworked and not properly prepared. I understand the importance of hard work and comprehend the concept of learning/growth while on the job, but I don’t believe it’s efficient to cut cost or time for proper employee training. The strategy seems to be, overload your employees with as much information as you possibly can. It’s a sure fire way for offsetting cardiac arrest by your mid 30s. You stay obliviously in this cycle because you just want to be passionate about something and feed your family during times of uncertainty and economic fear. High turnover rates and lack of employee retention, in my opinion, is caused by these factors. My direct boss never had time to effectively communicate with me or constantly had to push back our meetings due to being busy. Busy interviewing candidates as we are hiring to fill in numerous empty spots— we were told it was growth and business expansion due to merging with E Trade and buying Solium Shareworks but I believe more importantly it’s just due to lack of employee retention. A new and improved process has to be in place for properly caring about your current employees. I believe we need a better way to optimize and refine the American working class— It’s deficit and obsolete

pros: Most people are great and it was a positive environment, never had any issues with my team on a day to day basis.
cons:
-Compensation was way below market averages unless you worked a lot of overtime. While you get a generous amount of PTO, the benefits were average, and commuter benefits were practically non existent as well (e.g. parking or gas stipend). 

-High turnover. As a result of low compensation, people were constantly leaving, causing teams to be short staffed continuously. This happened to my team and many other teams in my department. 

-Long hours. As a result of being short staffed, the hours were terrible. The OT pay was nice (1.5x), but working 50-60 hour weeks to only make the market average was not worth it. 

-Work flexibility was poor. While a lot of companies have moved to a hybrid environment as necessary, it felt forced at MS. My work could be done from home easily. I was personally less productive in office, but still was mandated to come in 3 times a week. In a world where you can easily find fully remote jobs and considering MS's shortcomings in the previously discussed items, this was not really acceptable to me. 

-Technology was extremely outdated. They didn't even give me a laptop when I had to work from home during COVID. You are expected to use your own computer. If that wasn't bad enough, the software we used was all very old, 32 bit, and applications constantly ran out of memory. This worsened productivity and caused more errors/problems. On top of that the technological tools I used were not transferable at all besides Excel; they need to use industry standards. 

-Difficulty in changing roles. I often heard it was possible to switch to a different team if you were interested in something else during my undergrad internship, but once I was hired on full time, it was clear that internal hiring is practically non existent. I never saw anyone successfully change roles, and it was never encouraged. However, when management felt like it they changed my role without me having any say. I liked my initial role and was moved, and was given a new manager twice. Seemed like internal changes only happened at management's discretion.

summary: High on functional domain knowledge, but lagging on tech innovation, HIPPO culture
advice: Wake up and smell the coffee. Morgan Stanley is no longer the preferred place to work for top engineering talent. When I look at how engineering works at product firm, tech at MS feels like existing in dinosaur age. With the booming tech startup sector, MS is not just competing with other Wall Street firms - it is competing with tech startups and new age technology firms.
pros:
Great people-centric work culture. Very professional and structured corporate environment. Mostly merit-driven but career progression may be slow. 
Great place to learn finance, accounting, working with global teams. One will build deep domain expertise if one stays long - will result in competitive advantage in financial services technology. Globalised exposure to markets, financial norms, and processes. 

Decent (not exciting or top tier) compensation compared to IT Services firms.
cons:
MS, about 15-20 years back was a leading technology firm on wall street (though it is a financial services org) - pioneering cutting edge technology infrastructure, tooling and processes. But since then, it has missed the technology evolution and innovation bus. Many of its systems and platforms are legacy over 15 years old, innovation is very slow. Risk taking in technology is discouraged and generally very difficult to bring in new technology stacks or experiment with new technology. 

Senior technology leadership is more focused on funcitonal domain knowledge and people/client/user perception management over technology innovation, risk taking and leap-frogging. There is a strong element of HIPPO (Highest Paid Person's Opinion counts) culture too - if you dont agree with your manager or super manager, it can lead to your career stalling. So it encourages conformance and rarely any disagreements will be taken lightly.

At one time, it used to be in top 10 percentile of compensation for technology based roles, priding itself as the best engineering shop on Wall street. But since the last decade of the software boom and after the 2008 financial crisis, it is not even in the top 25 percentile. Compensation is no longer exciting, growth is slow compared to new age startups and product technology firms such as FAANG. Even now, Cloud computing is a novelty and buzzword at MS and there is no definite roadmap for implementation. Teams in non-US locations are generally disempowered and not part of key ownership or decision making processes. Center of power continues to be NY and unless the users are in your location, you will be treated as second class corporate citizens. 
FOMO, and disempowerment drives Indian technologists to accommodate calls at unreasonable times and being deferential to less competent colleagues abroad. Due to global nature of work expect calls at odd times of days/late evenings to cover or work with colleagues in other timezones.

pros:
I have been working with Morgan Stanley Bangalore for 6+ months but below 1 year.

Sharing my experience as I joined Morgan Stanley from a Tech giant previously.

1. From a hiring standpoint the salary hike was competitive for the role.

2. Benefits are decent, nothing much to complaint, but don't expect more if you were working for a tech giant before who might have added additional benefits for fitness re-imbursement. I heard it is available but for people at a higher designation level.

3. For the office transportation facility the firm sets the expectation in the beginning that it is a shuttle service during 08:00 AM - 7:PM Login/ logout so no door to door pickup and drop, however if you login a bit late you will have just the door-door drop (Better than not having any thing from my stand point). I feel this should not be a problem unless any one has specific concerns.

4. Usually it is day shift here in which lot of people work. I have not yet heard or seen any one logging in during Night shift (Again I might be wrong as I have not see this.) which is good not to have night shifts.

5. Work culture: This depends on the team you are hired. I work for the technology division in Bangalore location India. The culture from my experience is really good. My manager chases me if he sees me extending my shift so, yes they seem to be concerned with work life balance.

6. Usually the managers for a employee here are employees working from other countries. In some cases you might have your manager located in India its self. Advantage of managers from different location is (again my thought), you do not have that typical Indian culture of manager. People out side the country probably would treat you better.

7. The firm and Management expect employees to be transparent in terms if any blunders done or any mistakes done during the job role so things can be corrected.

8. I have seen they encourage to take leaves as well, which is good. The leaves given are around 21-23 which look similar to other companies.

9. Usually Indian holidays are applicable, but I guess it depends on your team as well. Most Indian holidays are covered but NOT all.

10. The office premises has a cafeteria, decent snacks are available. Food is available currently as offices are open post COVID and the meal is free. But not sure until when this free meal will be applicable how is it going to be.

11. Colleagues are open to help if you are stuck with work related issues. In my experience and team, I have not seen any one being harsh for not knowing some thing.
cons:
1. Hiring process is a bit slow, could be good to see an Improvement.

2. Many employees were shocked to hear during the on-boarding that the firm expects you to close your existing trading accounts and transfer the shares to a new trading account which Morgan Stanley has tie-up with two banks and the conditions are:
A. Your new trading account will be monitored by Morgan Stanley.
B. You can't invest on all stocks and can invest on specific stocks ONLY.

Note - Your shares previously purchased can be still kept/ transferred to the new account or sold so this is available. You can't use them further or invest on stocks which are not allowed.

I don't trade so this did not effect me. But was shocking for people who trade. I guess this is why they pay more to hire due to this hidden condition which is disclosed after joining.

3. Officially from a dress code standpoint as per the HR documents in India, I did not see Jeans mentioned for India region. However I have seen folks wearing jeans including me and nobody has asked me about my dress. So would like to see this culture change with dressing. Based on my discussion with my manager from the other region it is not mandatory to be in formals, seems the India specific thing. Let us work remotely full time, we’ve proved it’s possible. Please limit the manager turnover. I had 4 in a period of 4 months. cons: Terrible onboarding and training experience. Terrible process for making sure employees have correct entitlements to perform their job duties. I can say this is not an isolated issue, as every person I’ve known that has switched roles (including manager level) has experienced issues with not being able to pull up certain accounts or not being able to access relevant applications. It’s not great pay but I accepted because I was desperate after a 2 year work hiatus, maybe I could of negotiated more. I think, fundamentally, the issue is that Morgan Stanley has acquired so many different companies/segments (E*Trade, solium, share works, whatever) without giving much thought on how to successfully integrate all of the new business units/segments/accounts. Not only from client perspective, but for the employees also. Finally, I feel like I might be at some sort of generational threshold between millennial and Gen z….honestly feels as if the younger crowd is doing the bare minimum and really couldn’t care less about client service. I try to help my colleagues out by leaving very detailed notes re: what actions need to be taken in the event the client calls in. More often than not, these notes are completely disregarded and in spite of our service model championing “1 call resolution” (which could of been achieved if my colleagues bothered to read my notes), poor client has to call in multiple times to get a standard request completed. The impression given is that you're there to advise clients, but actually there's an incentive to get their money invested (via metrics and bonuses), even if you have reason to believe cash will perform better and be less risky than most investments, after fees, in the short-term (1-2 years). summary: My experience working for Morgan Stanley at Work (aka ShareWorks)
advice: Provide more career paths that do not require leadership abilities. Allow employees to work from home more often.
pros: They provide extra days off over and above vacation time (i.e. your birthday off, three extra days in the summer)
cons:
There is a very large emphasis and pressure on becoming a leader in your team. You will be constantly pushed into participating in leadership extracurricular activities even if this does not suit your personality. All careers paths in the company lead to a role which requires leadership responsibilities even if you are a developer. The company seems to be trying to mold all employees into the same type of person (extraverted, outgoing, and leadership material).

They are forcing employees to come into the office 3 days a week. They cannot provide a good justification for this decision and have actually stated that they have seen that employees work very effectively and more efficiently from home. From my personal observations a large portion of the employees at Morgan Stanley at Work are unhappy with the orders to come into the office. Management has been struggling to get people to follow the orders (they are not seeing enough people come in each week). This makes me as an employee feel like Morgan Stanley does not care about what the majority of it's employees want.

There is no concept of a Software Development Lead who runs the Agile ceremonies. Instead there are Software Development Managers. All Software Developers have to run the Agile ceremonies themselves.

Note: This is only a con if you are not a fan of public speaking. Compared to other companies I have worked for and what I have heard from other Software Developers about their companies Morgan Stanley at Work requires a lot of presentations and demos from it's employees.

Bonuses are unpredictable.
The kind of work you'll get is excellent for your professional growth while still a junior. Senior employees will find the work dull and not challenging enough.

You'll have to work with some incompetent people who will turn a good project that would otherwise be a joy to work on into a hell of bug fixing.

advice: If you want the firm to be agile and successful, able to retain top talent and provide a healthy, happy environment, then seriously look at ways to dismantle the military-like hierarchy. Most of the work in Corporate Services is done by VP level and down (not Exec Directors, not Managing Directors) so find a way to empower VPs, contingents, and associates so they’re not left hanging in the wind. One idea: discourage EDs from presenting at steering committees and other business review sessions and ask that they routinely get their staff to do it instead. And make those sessions less like military interrogations and more like conversation, because right now those meetings are not set up for honesty, ingenuity, or collaboration. Also, MDs need to refrain from calling the shots, or at least realize that they’re never working with the full set of facts because they’re naturally removed from the details and because no one has the guts to imply the MDs need more information or are making less-than-stellar decisions.

If a senior manage (who is removed from day to day) makes any comment on something, even if it is off the cuff or unofficial, years worth of work can be tossed aside or redone. The political climate is difficult. It’s not exactly cutthroat or mean-spirited, but everyone wants to take credit for the very few things that move forward or gain traction, so you have competing interests, lack of cohesion, etc.

advice: To reduce turnover work on to provide steady career advancement for mid-career professionals. Do not employ contractors in long time positions.
pros:
The IT division is a patchwork of teams with different work habits, culture and technology. 

One can usually expect a good work environment, modern(ish) technology, challenging problems, plenty of learning opportunities - especially if joins the right team. Make sure to learn about the specific team you are about to join to.

Great place for fresh graduates to learn technology, boost your resume and master the English language.
cons:
Work in some teams can be stressful, others might use obsolete or firm specific technology with no convertible market value.

Promotions are decided by committees with members from your wider department, therefore advancement is more dependent on visibility and social connections than actual achievements, potential or expertise. 

Think twice before accepting an offer of a contractor role. While treated equally to employees in usual workplace matters, contractors are not entitled to bonuses, more difficult / less likely to get a raise and cannot get promoted. Conversion of contractors to full time employees do happen, but there are no guarantees and chances are different from team to team.

If you are a mid career professional, make sure to join at the compensation and organization level you really want to be. Getting ahead within in the organization will be much more difficult. Do you want to be promoted to a VP or ED from within? Think about embarking on the campaign trail for president.

An interesting pattern however, that some contractors might get converted directly into a VP role if they happen to be the last senior member of a team hit by turnover. This hurts the morale.

Performance reviews are viewed by too many managers as a chore that they have to perform which in many cases makes them virtually worthless.  My last performance review consisted of 5 sentences that were sloppily strung together.  This ties into the general theme of not so great management skills in the middle management group.

advice: You need to revamp the wealth management training program so that you are keeping more of the young blood in the firm. It takes 3 to 5 years to build a viable practice so the firm should lower some of the production goals initially and extend the salary for a bit longer. There should also be better coaching on the team process since ultimately the successful advisors are the ones that are on teams. In this day and age the solo practitioner who can build a business by cold calling is gone. Coach your branch managers on this fact since many of them have been singing the same "back in my day" song for too many years.
pros: The FAA Program is a great place to get your licenses and get the training you need to launch a financial advisory practice. The firm has excellent resources, technology, name recognition. The salary paid during the first part of the training program is important as you try to build your business.
cons: It is very difficult to meet production goals. Invariably, unless you are part of a team you will not make it through the training program. It is clear that the true goal of the program is to bring in new assets and retain those assets. The trainees are merely cogs in the machine and 90 percent of trainees don't make it - whether it is as the end of year 1, year 2, or year 3. Many go on to other firms and do fine so all is not lost, it can just be a little depressing when you figure it all out.
