summary: Great learning experience but with high expectations and very little support
advice: The way the current FAA program is set up, the firm spends a substantial amount of money training individuals to succeed at different firms.  It's rare for younger individuals to have an established affluent network, and building one takes time.  Compound that with a lack of experience in the investment industry and young FAA's start to hit their stride just about the time they get let go.  What's missing is a strong mentorship program.  Young FAAs need successful models from whom they can learn effective habits - it's not effective just to provide info.  Much of the ramp up time is wasted figuring out effective practices.  My suggestion would be to redefine "partnerships" so that established FA's looking to take the next step can take on an FAA as a jr partner without it affecting their compensation and making it an established practice for the majority of new hires.  The military follows the "watch one, do one, teach one" model, I think it would be a far more effective use of capital to have an older FA as a consistent resource to a new advisor.  It would also build in better day-to-day accountability.

advice: Get rid of the multiple layers of management and bring in a select group of leaders who have run a book of business before. If you are going to try and convince advisors to form teams, give them a system that makes forming a team beneficial to all – not just the senior advisors. summary: A Solid Place, If Not Exciting
advice:
Stop the Goldman fetish; it's embarrassing.
Prefer open-source frameworks to proprietary ones, whenever possible and practical. We are not a software company and we should not try to be one. We do not have the patience and the resources to develop generic, polished, supported  and documented frameworks, so we should adopt open source whenever possible, with as few proprietary customizations as possible.
Understand that most time in IT is spent maintaining ancient, poorly written and poorly documented code, and filling in paperwork for each new release. Replace obsolete systems as fast as possible, and streamline the release process.
Understand that adding layers of approvals for code changes does not make the changes safer, because people removed from the code give automatic approvals without being able to verify that the new code is correct.

pros: Morgan Stanley is the epitome of Darwinism.  It is a place where the best will survive.  You are rewarded for doing a good job and generally paid well when you do.  When you are a standout, the rewards are that much better, whether it be responsibility, new project work, promotion or compensation.  Sometimes it takes time for the weaker players to be weeded out.  People like this are usually in positions that require diligence in getting the job done, but leadership skills are not the cornerstone of the role.  It is for these reasons that I have enjoyed my time working for such a great company.
cons: When people talk about work life balance, I think they are being a little harsh to say that Morgan Stanley does not provide it.  It is true that when you do a good job, you are rewarded with more work, and then you have more to do.  It is more a case of you being the victim of your own success.  If you do need time off for a personal reason, I have never seen a case of it being rejected.  Most people at Morgan Stanley are true to the culture that Sr. Management breeds.

Pay is salary based (usually around $40-$60k) plus compensation from brokers. Think of it as a tip of you were a waiter. Except usually as a waiter you make more along with the service you provide. advice: Hire better managment at the branch level.  Unpolished management rewarding employees for unprofessional behavior (because they were part of a recruited team) isn't reason enough.  Local management was top heavy and unproductive with lots of meetings and arriving in the office at 8;00 regularly when the stock market opens at 6:30.  It might look good on the short term, but for the long term qualified employees will leave to go to a more professional environment.
pros: They are an industry leader and as such there are opportunities.  Upper management has good foresight, however depending on your local management, there can be many road blocks.
cons: There is little balance of work/home life, at least at the branch level I worked in.  There was a policy of no overtime, however some employees were rewarded for working extra time regularly on weeknights and weekends.  The rewards came in the form of additional offsite training.  When asked about what the qualifications were for getting this additional training there were no answers given.  There is a difference in workstyle and dedication to work with coming in early and staying late to finish a project occassionally and a continual pattern of working 60 hour weeks of which you were only paid for 40 hours.

advice: Empower your employees!!! Help them to succeed!  Give raises/bonuses to productive/good employees (outside of sales and home office), learn what a perk is...for instance, a holiday party that employees don't have to pay for and organize themselves! cons: There are a lot of very bright people and it becomes quite difficult to differentiate yourself if you're in a large team. Promotions are hard to come by and you need to constantly push your supervisor for consideration.

You get to learn about various technologies and some basics about finance. For new grads, do the training in NYC, come back to Montreal, and find something else.
cons: Once you come back from the TAP to Montreal, the honeymoon phase is over. It's like flipping a coin: you might get in a good coin, or you might get into a bad one. Some of the employees there are dinosaurs that are unwilling and/or incapable of even considering that there is new and better technology out there, and are simply stuck in their old ways. Some other teams are fantastic with very competent people. There seems to be a lot of office politics. Before leaving, I spent nearly 5 months doing very minimal work, waiting for another team to deliver their part of some project, but their funding had been cut.

advice: FAs should have mandatory ETIQUETTE Classes every so often and be reminded of how important Support Staff are.  BSM, Always hear both side of the Story. pros: Great Company #1 in the Industry! You will feel very proud to work for the Best Co. They have the Best system to help you assist your clients. You will work around very Smart People. Many locations to move and relocate if you get lucky!You will get hire by new Co. before you can relocate.
cons: No room for human errors, Always walking on eggshells. Lots of meetings. FAs are very disrespectful and will treat you as Inferior, Not as a Team Member. They Micromanage your day. advice: It is silly to expect recent college graduates to enter this program and have to be in wealth management for the next 5 years. pros: The ability to work in multiple branches gives you exposure to many different teams. The employees in the branches were very kind and very transparent. You are allowed to take as many license exams as you wish and it is encouraged.
cons: The program is unorganized and lacks direction. The communication between the program heads and the branches where the analyst work is very poor. If you aren't proactive you can end up getting lost in the shuffle and not having a role. If you are proactive it may be seen as dissatisfaction. If you have prior finance experience or hands on internships this job is a step back.

summary: MS is a place for bright people that want to work in a collaborative environment offering excellent career development.
advice: Keep up the good work! Let's find more ways to integrate our products to provide creative financial solutions for clients.
pros: At Morgan Stanley, I am surrounded by the brightest minds in the banking industry. There is a tremendous culture focused on first-rate client service, which is achieved by hiring and developing talented people that share an enthusiastic and collaborative vision and drive. Compensation is linked to personal, group, and firm performance, which encourages each person to perform at his or her highest potential. Feedback from colleagues is thoughtful, and often informal. Senior management does a great job of training junior people in the business of investment banking and of sharing strategic information about the issues and opportunities facing the group and bank.
cons: The largest downside of working at any investment bank is the riskiness associated with employment on Wall Street. Like all investment banks, Morgan Stanley has had to lay off some of its bankers to keep costs reasonable in the face of an economic downturn.

summary: Good place to obtain securities licenses
advice: Trainees might do better if they had some guidance from a salaried trainer.  Otherwise, the trainee ends up "pairing" with a senior broker who hopes that he'll snag all of the trainee's accounts when he leaves or is terminated. Morgan Stanley gives you about 30% of that 1%.  So if you have a million dollars in assets under management you'll earn $3,000. Pretty tough.  Life insurance sales are around 4%.  This information is from 2008, so compensation might a bit different

advice:

pros:

cons: They tend to like to give people more responsibility without giving them corresponding salary increases. Since there is no real sense of if and when bonuses will be paid, some people do the bare minimum to keep their job.

summary: Weak Management Layer and run by temporary staff
advice: I wish senior management focused on more valued added decisions instead of actions that have been given little thought and analysis. We tell ourselves everything is great and rather believe it then look at things more closely.

cons: Practically no training offered, management is often unavailable and provides little guidance. You are required to be self manage and self motivate. Manager often have little understanding of what they are supervised and no incentive to develop.

summary: Morgan Stanley - Strong Firm, Good Opportunities
advice: Require functional and business leaders to establish a vision for their areas and develop means to hold them accountable. Human resources needs to better parter with management to help them understand employee terminations and compensation practices promoting a culture of meritocracy.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a reputable firm with a strong management team.  They offer excellent opportunities for career development including tuition reimbursement,  extensive learning programs, job rotation, etc.
cons: Corporate politics and personal agendas sometimes impede projects from moving forward.  Functionalization efforts to increase efficiency have hindered communication resulting in "silos", or departments that tend to work independently of each other. Internal growth is heavily promoted and supported however, individuals "climbing the ladder" often find themselves falling significantly behind market value in terms of overall compensation.

advice: Recognize top performers more often and more publicly (even if they are first or second year analysts.  Positive reinforcement encourages continual top performance.

Vacation time is great compared to some competitors.

pros: Excellent company name, competitive pay, great coworker and easy location for commuting.
cons: One thing that disturbs me about this firm which is the lack of diversity in the front office. I have worked front office at other major investment banks and you can literally count the number on one hand in the NYC office. It certainly is not an issue of not having qualified candidates because I have been part of many interviews with perspective employees. I was actually shocked when certain people would be hired over others based on minor facts around how certain questions were answered vs the candidates proven track record of excellence.

summary: Financial Advisor Associate or Rat Race Telemarketer?
pros:
Generous initial base pay, benefits included personal life insurance, and state-of-art facilities. 

Networking opportunities within firm departments, other banks, insurance companies, mutual fund companies, third-party market researchers, and insitutional asset managers.

Stalemate office environment. Senior management depreciates lower level employees. Highly political. Very little structure led to lots of wasted time, boredom, and late night cold calling. 

The pay grid discourages mid-senior level advisors transfer AUM to new hires because MS pays new hires a higher grid rate.  It's part of the program. In your first year, you get paid a higher rate than your third year.  That's right. You initially make more in base pay + rate of commission, compared to, say fifth year.  It's a downward pay rate slope.  Because it's understood that you should have a larger AUM as time goes on. It's designed to pay upfront in first year, then decreases significantly.  By the end of the third year, you're expected to live off AUM entirely. But the capital raising goals don't stop after you graduate the program. And they will cut your pay grid to about 35% after you hit a certain AUM.

summary: Very hierarchical (focused on job titles) with pockets of excellence (e.g. Technology Investment Banking).

cons: Like other Firms on Wall St., there is still  a "partnership model", with a heavy focus on rank (e.g. Managing Directors are most important). Getting promoted can be very political, and involves having good timing and a strong sponsor, and is less about ability.

advice: No one is truly happy here- take the time to listen for once and diligently work to improve our conditions. Great CEO

advice: Recognize talent
pros: The salaries are competitive, facilities are great, benefits are generous. Some of the managers are extremely bright, talented individuals. cons: It seems that senior management may have a hard time listening to ideas. Maybe the compensation may be fuel to overconfidence--egos are nothing short. There are good times and there are bad times for every company, and for each person there is a different story to tell. Most importantly, working with good people is an important factor to individual satisfaction. For the people who simply do their work everyday, it may not be as exciting. I have had trouble communicating ideas to managers--they may ignore good suggestions based on title. Respect and title means a lot in this firm, so do not expect a meritocracy.

summary: Great company, but really depends on team and area
advice:
People tend to get promoted because they are great producers, not good managers. You need to focus on making sure that people who are leading others care and are well equipped to do it well. 

Pay disparity is pretty crazy and other firms do tend to pay better. You should focus on rewarding loyal employees rather than those who come from another company or come back. Lots of people leave and come back a few years later and end up making significantly more than the person who has been there since the beginning. It breeds resentment and you lose talent.
pros:
Working with nice and smart people, generally speaking. 
Focus on internal mobility, making it easier to take advantage of opportunities to move to different departments or offices across the globe (I worked in NY and Hong Kong)
cons:
Its finance, hours can be tough.
Heavily dependent on the market, layoffs are pretty common
Every team/department/division has its own culture, so people can have vast experiences

advice: Communicate more
pros: First and foremost Morgan Stanley is a great name. It is a good company to have on your resume. Also, the benefits are great and on top of that you get 20 days of vacation. The offices in New York are very nice and for some of the new hires in the Baltimore area they pay for you to train in NY for a few weeks.
cons: At Morgan Stanley you will work long hours and there is no hour lunch, you simply run to get food and then eat at your desk. This often leads to burn out among the employees and moral goes down quickly. There is no overtime and when the technology doesn't work you have to sit there for hours just waiting. There were some days when I was there until 10pm at night for reasons I could not control. Also, the Baltimore office lacks leadership, most of the management there are new and don't have experience within Morgan Stanley.

advice: You conducted an anonymous survey of employees a while back--then trumpeted the results and how changes where going to take place. Nothing changed. The survey was a joke. The level of incompetence evident across all management ranks is breathtaking. Positive change can only come by weeding out the numerous bad managers, and addressing the motivation scheme--as long as it is centered on bonus, decisions will be based on individual's greed, not what's best for the firm or clients.
pros:
It pays reasonably well.
There is good work/life balance, although I think the real reason behind this is that management is too oblivious to care what your doing, hence it is easy to balance non-work obligations with work.
The benefits package is not bad
cons:
Advancement is based on age. If you are near 50, promotion and advancement are highly unlikely. Over 50 there is no advancement except in the most senior ranks.
Management decisions are based on a given manager's bonus calculation--e.g., you will not be rewarded for innovation, intelligence, or even a job well done if it contradicts the politics that impact the manager's bonus calculation.
Innovation, intelligence, good work in and of themselves are not the primary factor in advancement--see last point

advice: Reduce offshoring even if NY salaries have to be frozen/reduced.
pros:
Overall this is a very good company to work for. Some of the highlights are:

 -  Morgan Stanley is full of very talented and smart people
 -  Morgan Stnaley uses a broad technology spectrum and experiments with lots of cutting edge technology
 -  The benefits are generally very good. (e.g. up to 3 months of paid family leave under certain circumstances, such as having a baby)
 -  Most departments operate on very high ethical standards
 -  Good training program
 -  Compensation is generally very good
cons:
Morgan Stanley is a large and some times anonymous corporation. As a result the departments can be very fragmented (eg. if you want to run a database you have to go through the dba group)

My biggest gripe is that Morgan Stanley engages in extensive offshoring, especially to India, which can be a challenge and dampens morale for NY-based employees.

advice: Pay better. Just too much turnover when you a training someone for a good amount of time for them to just leave because of pay.
pros: Work with great people. Lots of really bright colleagues in the Baltimore and New York offices. Mobility after a certain period of you being a full time employee. Looks excellent on a resume for another job. Gives you tons of experience as most groups do a little bit of everything along with their full day to day job. If you are able to make the jump and advance on to NY(main office), it's a company to look at.
cons: Underpaid. Something you'll hear most about working in operations but even more so at Morgan Stanley. They are constantly looking for ways to cut costs and one way is pay people less. Lots of turnover so there are always issues with keeping experience high and knowing the full range of what each group does.

advice:
Value your existing employees so that they won't leave the firm within a year.
Start adopting the latest technologies and eliminate the legacy ones.
pros: Great team, really supportive with each other. Usually, work-life balance is preserved and the current manager is good at maintaining it.
cons:
Lots of legacy tools/applications. For example, deployment is too complex and the process to do is only used within the firm, so it has no use outside the firm/other companies.
Sometimes you have to work on the weekend to deploy the application so that is a poor choice done by the management. 
Even though my manager/team is quite nice in general, the senior management is just awful. They try to keep forcing everyone back to the office as well as finding ways to micromanage more.
The salary is a bit lower than the market due to the recent inflation and the management NOT CARING to adjust the current employees' salaries, so be prepared to get a yearly raise that is lower than the inflation rate.

summary: Stable job, a bit boring though.
advice: Hire the best professionals, pay well, give them interesting problems to solve. Money making may look a bit boring, yet there are lots of interesting analytical problems and ideas floating around to reinvent Wall St.
pros: Since all groups across the firm are different, I'll stick to personal experience. IT infrastructure is one of the best among several financial companies I had a chance working with. Middle management is flexible and encourages innovations and new ideas. Professional training courses available and staff encouraged to regularly enroll. 4 weeks vacation and work/life balance are good benefits hardly matched outside of financial sector.
cons: Again, personal experience only, do not extrapolate. No promotions or salary raises in years. Bonus has been cut lately due to overall economy situation. Problems to solve are not challenging enough which is quite boring. As usual within financial sector there are many limitations to personal 401K fund allocations. Overall job at financial institution is not sexy enough in comparison with hot startups.

summary: Good work life balance, pay below standard.
advice: It's a great company and excellent resume building material, but that only goes so far. You can't compete with Google and Facebook who is offering people with 1-2 years experience what you're paying senior developers.
pros: Good work life balance if you're in a back office IT position. IT infrastructure is first class. Hours are normal 9-6'ish in my team. Good amount of support from peers. If you're at Morgan Stanley, join the "hackers" mail group, it will make the days go by faster.
cons: Turn over is high, the bank is top heavy with lots of VPs and EDs because pay is always below par. They tend to give titles bumps to associates because it's cheaper than giving salary increases. Bonuses are lackluster as well in a back office position... Less than 5% for most of the people i spoke with. A lot of associates and VPs are leaving because of the pay. Lots of H1-B and contractors to suppress the pay scale

advice: Less favoritism, and more professionalism when it comes to keeping teammate's business private.
pros: Company has a good reputation, focus on diversity, good maternity/paternity leave benefits. Depending on the position, the employee gets 2 weeks vacation time, plus another consecutive 2 weeks vacation during the year. That is separate from sick time. Senior leadership individuals visit various offices throughout the year, which I find impressive.  Good culture and values - they place priority on volunteering and giving back to the community.
cons: It is hard to advance within the company from what I have seen, both in position and salary. There seems to be a certain amount of favoritism. Raises each year appear to be below the average percentage, which is discouraging. I find it has been difficult to trust management. Workload isn't divided equally throughout the team, some people work harder than others, but are treated the same as those that do the bare minimum.

summary: I am not gonna leave the company if given an option
pros:
Best company to work for married women, great culture, good pay, work life balance, proper management and what not... 
Its been more than a year I am working here and I must say this is kind of dream company where you get the feel of proper corporate environment, you are getting good money  for your work, able to manage your work life balance, having one of the best leave policy across industry (more than 30sick leaves are allowed). 
Yes u have to be very careful with your work as this company ask for the quality.. error can cost you much. 
 
I am working in Mumbai office.
cons: Job security- as it's an MNC,  I am not sure about job security though it's s depends on accuracy of your work and availability of manpower too.

summary: Great CEO - Delivered on vision to reshape Firm
advice: Replace the forced ranking system - one of the most painful and ineffective annual exercises. Had lead many highly functional teams - everyone contributed and delivered as a team, yet I was forced to rank a percentage of these people a low rating - limiting compensation for these people and potentially clearing a path for security to escort them to the building exit - all for the sake of hitting a cost metric.  Man up and make it known the Firm desires to cut costs and will be cutting staff.
pros: Worked for and with some of the best and brightest in the industry - very collaborative environment - people helping each other to succeed in their careers and deliver mission critical initiatives
cons: Worked for and with some of the worst in the industry - mid to senior level managers using fear as a motivator - creating an environment of distrust and dysfunction.

advice: You have driven out the good talent, you can no longer attract quality talent and you are maintaining mediocre talent.  This is true of knowledge talent as well as leadership.  I wish you the best of luck with your persent management philosophy but it is not a capitalistic, merited based award system.  It has degraded to a "good ole' boy system."
pros: Brand recognition, good benefits package.
cons: Morgan has lost its way.  Focus shifted from Institutional investing (highly respectable and profitable) to servicing retail customers which isn't as profitable when customers can buy a service over the web.  Technology is no longer important or appreciated.  My pay dropped by 30% over 10 years due to market conditions (unavoidable) and a new management philosophy.   I was not alone so it wasn't me.  JP Morgan would be appalled.  "Doing first class business in a first class way" is dead.

summary: Can be a good place to work
advice: Examine carefully the people who are being promoted, and pay attention to the culture within groups, not just in the firm at the highest level.
pros: Opportunities to learn and to push oneself. Some groups can be great, and management makes a genuine effort to make the firm a desirable place to work.
cons: It is a place for young people.  Also, the culture in some groups can be difficult, making it difficult to advance or to move to another group.  The advice in my group when filling out review documents was, "we never put anything negative in writing."  In other words, don't dare say anything unfavorable about one's manager or managing team. That attitude stymies any attempt, including by senior management, to ensure that toxic employees and managers can be identified and that those genuinely seeking to improve will be given needed feedback.

summary: Morgan Stanley Great Place to Work, but Risky and Time Consuming
advice: Make more of an effort to help employees manage their careers.  Have a more thorough year end review process.
pros: At Morgan Stanley, I enjoy a great salary and fantastic benefits.  I also feel great knowing that I work with some of the smartest people in the industry.  My coworkers are all outstanding.  My job is incredibly fast paced, so there's little room for time to get bored.
cons: The downside of working for any large company like Morgan Stanley is that there are lots of politics involved -- it varies significantly by manager, but many managers do not value work-life balance and there are often people who get rewarded for doing very little work.  But you can find that anywhere.  The most significant downside is that the market is very volatile and your job is at the mercy of the market.

summary: Not the same place it used to be
advice: Take a close look at the back office management teams. There are a lot of incompetent managers around. Also, its time to revamp the promotionary process. Its not right that people who you never have had any contact with have a say in promotions..
pros:
- Looks great on your resume
- Salaries are highly competitive
- Great opportunity to relocate to different offices if you choose
cons: I worked for MS for over 12 years. I can honestly say that it is not the place it used to be. Management seems to care less and less about their employees (especially if you are not on the revenue generating side). The promotion process is a bunch of BS. Its all who you brown nose the most and not necessarily about who deserves it the most. Also, the work-life balance has gone down hill. If your a robot, you'll do great!

advice: Read the tea leaves and start paying your FAs/brokers via SALARY and not 100% commission.  The company will save millions and smart/honest/hard-working employees won't be forced out of the business by starvation.  With CEOs earning hundreds of millions of dollars each year, there's no reason why this can't be a financially stable working environment for all.
pros: The only "pro" about working at Morgan Stanley is that you receive lots of education about investments and the market.  But education alone will not pay your mortgage, child care, or gas bills.
cons: For brokers who did not inherit a client book, are without connections, and/or who weren't "born into money"--good luck because you are going to need lots of it.  Or else, you starve.  The company, like other Wall Street firms, pamper senior/upper management but when it comes to its rank/file and/or regular employees, the company could care less about you.  Company has a cut-throat and "churn-and-burn" attitude--not just with its clients but also with its own employees.  You are only as good as what you generate in revenue.  Period.

advice: I wasn't happy with all the decisions managers made (who is), but overall I have no regrets about working there and the only comments would be, keep doing what you are doing because it obviously works.  You understand that people are your greatest asset.
pros: The office culture is great. People respect each other and help when needed.  The senior management are fabulous, and even more so when you consider the tough job of managing a call center operation.  The job was designed so that you were able to treat customers with the respect they deserve and still meet the qualifications of the job.  So many call centers are only interested in numbers and profit.  MSSB is also interested in those but realizes that their employees need to be treated well. The games to increase sales and productivity seemed a bit juvenile.
cons: Call center...  what more do I need to say.

summary: Great company, but tough to make it through FAA program
advice: Actually train your FAAs on the nature of the business and focus more training on financial knowledge, rather than almost entirely of sales practices. When you hit “production”, you are expected to hit the ground running when in all truthfulness inexperienced FAAs have next to no idea what they are actually doing. When reviewing many training videos, I found questionable sales practices being taught to us that would purposely mislead prospects/clients.
pros: Flexibility. Being your own boss almost entirely. Good pay while studying for licensing and building your book initially.
cons: Unrealistic benchmarks, especially for younger advisors who are fresh out of college. They expect you to bring in about $500k/month, which seems extremely difficult to do without luck and/or a prior network full of willing, affluent investors.

summary: Good company with a bad HR team
advice: Clean up your house.
pros:
Good culture 
Stable and consistent profitability
Strong CEO and C-Staff
cons: Extreme partiality within the India HR team. If you are not a part of the 'inner circle' of the HR leadership then you will be pushed aside and find it difficult to grow. To become a part of the inner circle you don't need to be a good performer or have potential, you just need to be from Delhi or your family background must be from the army. Only the inner circle gets paid well and gets opportunities for visibility/frequent promotions/special treatment. If you are not a 'favourite' you will have to go above and beyond to ultimately get an opportunity for advancement. Superficial people on the HR team who "act" like a family and make others feel excluded/less important. Blatantly biased leaders, unfair practices and poor team unity. Worst HR team I have ever worked with.

summary: Morgan Stanley: a rewarding & positive work environment
advice: Keep up the focus on clear communication on the situation of the firm and business direction.  Ensure the best people are retained not just through salary & bonus but also by ensuring they're allocated against key projects that are personally rewarding.
pros: Excellent management support for career growth and advancement.  The environment is very positive and I feel my contributions are valued by both my co-workers and management.  I also feel that the firm is very selective in its hiring to ensure that not only are we hiring the best people we can find, but the best fit for the role they're hired into.  My experience with management and senior management has been direct, clear communication on the issues affecting the firm and on the direction the business is heading.
cons: In return for satisfying projects and decent pay, the culture is long hours, often due to timezone spreads on global calls involving Asia, NY and London.

summary: The Critical Issue is the Absence of Leaders
advice: If you are going to hire at the bottom, please make sure you are either training managers on HOW to manage and communicate with their team or do not allow directors to manage people if they have consistent turnover or weak reputations around the office.  "Managers" thrive off gaslighting, emotional manipulation and micromanaging.  Find out what people are good at and let them do it.
pros: Compensation, benefits, vacation days, unlimited sick, museum passes
cons: There is ZERO leadership training. Upper management is filled with unqualified "managers" who should not be in leaderships roles just because they are more experienced. "Managers" have an absence of any sort of innate leadership qualities. Just because you can play the game, does NOT mean you should be a coach.   They act like you do not understand, belittle your opinions, don't acknowledge your ideas, use your past to avoid their present wrongdoings and inject fear in you to conform to them . Teams consistently suffer from burnout, no one provides direction , people are constantly complaining about how unhappy they are everyday.

advice: Treat your employees like human beings and not stocks to be traded or sold off on a whim.
pros: Some friendly, social people. Opportunity to follow some interesting financial investments.
cons: The clients are all angry, retired pensioners with nothing better to do than call you up 20 times a day asking about their missing $0.50 div check or blame you for the market taking a nose dive. You are GLUED to your office land line because the phones are the primary means of communication in that business so you are not allowed to leave your desk if no one is available to cover your line. Not for lunch, the bathroom, anything. Some coworkers are douchey, money hungry "Wolf of Wall St" types who think they'll all be millionaires in a few weeks time, only to find how easy it is to wash out of that business without a stable book of clients behind them. I've seen so many people quit or get fired in my time there because the pressure to land clients got to them. Bottom line - It's a high pressure sales job, at the end of the day.

advice: Business model is outdated and predatory.  Give new FAA old small accounts to manage so they can float until business closes.
pros:
1) MSSB paid for Series 7 and Series 66
2) Experience life in Corporate Shark Tank
3) Access to MSSB analysis
4) Powerful Name
5) Good benefits
cons:
1) Cut Throat and Back Stabbing Culture
2) Lack of transparency regarding time table; MGMT reneged on time table
3) You are on your own.  Can not trust MGMT or Senior FAs.  Everyman for himself mentality. MGMT says has amnesia about past conversations. Can not trust MGMT
4) Only way to succeed at the FAA role is having having family money or have extensive list of close friends who are millionaires 
5) Business model is to bring in new FAA, use FAA's contacts to close business, give FAA a small % of commission on his leads, then kick FAA out the door when all contacts on his list have been worked
6) MSSB provides no leads or old clients to manage
7) Senior FAs are very predatory and promise the world but will not sign partnering contract before closing FAA's prospects

summary: The Best Company I've worked at
advice: Definitely on the right track! Please keep up the good work and the firm will surely prosper :)
pros:
- Recent additional benefits include birthday leave, well-being days (x4 during summer), compensation leaves x 2 (for vaccine takers), year-end cash rewards and sponsorship to buy work-from-home equipment...
- Existing benefits include well-rounded medical insurance coverage (dental, hospitalization, C-section surgeries, you name it...) , 4-week paternal leave, 20-day annual leaves...
- Extremely smart and friendly people who are always willing to help
- Interesting and challenging work which keeps you learning and growing
- Well-written documentations for internal systems and strong support
- Work/life balance is possible for some teams
cons:
- Base pay and bonus may not be the best in market
- Some teams can be quite political depending on your manager (which applies to every company doesn't it?)
- A lot of time is spent getting the right permissions (which is understandable for big companies like this)
- Climbing up the corporate ladder is much harder than jumping to another company with a promoted title

summary: Laid back employers with positive attitudes.
pros: The brokers that I work for are always kind even under stress and everyone at the firm seems genuinely kind. There are a lot of programs within the company to build your professional career and the firm pays for its employees to receive special licenses. If you want a specific license for your job title, they pay for your study materials, your test, and compensate you when you pass the test and receive the title. They genuinely want to see their employees further their professional career.
cons: The position is not for those that want an 8-4 or 9-5 job everyday. Some days you can count on being in the office for 8 hours but sometimes, especially during the quarter end, expect to not know when you will finish up the work day. The work load is to be expected during the quarter/month end, but during the month you could have a lot to do or not a whole lot to do, it depends on many different factors.

advice: My advice would have been to improve the training program or get rid of it, and John Mack got rid of it, so I guess he did alright!
pros: The firm obviously is one of the few to survive to major market crash and carries a solid reputation.  They have their own research division which pumps out some top notch market research and provides actionable opportunities for their brokers.  The office was well appointed and the computer tools were very nice.
cons: The trainee program was well intended but poorly executed.  The mentorship program was a total joke, and it's a real shame because a good mentor can make a world of difference.  Obviously, this is a sales oriented type position where you are selling yourself, but inter-office competition is very high so brokers were not likely to help each other too much.  The sales manager at the time sorely lacked management capability, though I believe he has since left the company.  Too focused on cold calling and not enough on finding better ways (existing connections) to attract clients.

advice: This is not a real Morgan Stanley any more.   You don't need my advice -- you know what to do.   Next time you hire  -- come to Ivy League schools and get kids from there.  Thank you.
pros: The badge -- you are at Morgan Stanley.  If you like to be around younger people -- this is like high school, age-wise.
cons: The management is addicted to docile Indian laborers.  Management is dis-interested in your strengths or your career development.  Their ideal employee is a robotic creature devoid of any interests,  fast, doesn't have any new ideas, doesn't ask any questions.   Management is not secure or very competent and actively competes with sub-ordinates.    Management is addicted to their personal cult which comes easy with Indian laborers but is weird for the few Americans that are hired.   You didn't go to college for this  -  steer clear.

advice: Provide your new advisors with leads or partner them with successful advisors as part of their team.  Monitor success and be realistic as to the amount of time necessary to build a business.
pros: Morgan Stanley is the biggest investment firm.  They have a very wide variety of products and experts that are available and responsive. They do provide a good amount of time to study for the 7 and 66 exams.
cons:
You will get zero support as a new advisor.  You will complete all new client forms yourself and receive zero leads.  People do not call Morgan Stanley looking for an advisor.  As a new advisor you will be given a cube and phone and basicly wished "good luck" Because you know people does not mean they will change from their current advisor.  The days of making multiple phone calls hoping to find a new client are basicly over with blocks call etc.

It can be done, but the odds are very high against making a go of it with this firm.  Ask what percentage of new advisors stay with the firm.

summary: Slow paced and closed minded management
advice: Efficiency, productivity and team management need to be revised asap. Many managers with years of company are not willing to change and improve anything. They simply do not care if someone or the team is not delivering well. In 2020 they are still struggling to accept agile and co-location (reduce offshore dependency).
pros: Great salary, tons of time to learn and improve yourself. 20 days of vacation standard and you can take all as early as 1st of January. Also usually the life balance is good.
cons: Management is very closed minded and struggles with agile. They will say they are a bank everytime you propose something new or a improvement. Also your experience varies widely depending which manager you have. Some are very strict and against home office. Not so easy to change teams as they say, you can get backslashed. Almost everything is self funded, which contributes to a very poor team building.

advice: You should show a lot more appreciation to the people, make them feel they do valuable work.
pros: It is a good looking experience in your CV, you might work with some of the greatest minds in your area. The compensation is above average.
cons: You have a good chance of being employed by a third-party employer which will lend your work to Morgan Stanley. This causes some very unfortunate discrepancies in entitlements, you will not get a yearly bonus or pay rise even until you are "converted" full-time employee, which I find ridiculous because you go through the same selection process you do the same work, so it is strictly budgeting decision.  The career path is very not clear, the superiors are not supportive. In the 1 year, I spent here I did not get a single performance review.  I think the company is overstaffed due to the high level of fluctuation, I could do my job in 25% of the time. I think this was a good experience for me to not be looking to work in a similar place again.

summary: Waste of Time and Energy working as a Consultant
advice:
Value your employee if they have joined as a Consultant.
Give some recognition for their contribution by giving them certificates or perks. This will motivate contingent employees to give their 100% in terms of work.
Convert your contingent employees into FTE based on their performance as a token of appreciation.
pros:
No work pressure.
Flexible work timings.
Pick and drop transportation facility.
Good co-ordination within the team in terms of projects.
cons:
No value and appreciation for your work provided if you are working as a Consultant. In terms of appreciation, you will get “Kudos" mails thats it. It is not going to benefit you in terms of hike in salary or promotion.
No Team bonding especially if you are joining one team IM (MSIM Reporting Dev)
Conversion process from Consultant to FTE happens sometimes only especially in one team IM (MSIM Reporting Dev) even though if you have done an extraordinary work. Whereas for other teams, it happens frequently only.
Lot of discrimination amongst employees who are working as a FTE and who are working as a  Consultant.
Overall, if you are joining IM (MSIM Reporting Dev) team as a Consultant, please don't join rather than ask them that I would be joining as a FTE. If you are joining as a Consultant, your career growth is going to be stagnant.

summary: Worth working at 5 years ago; MS has ruined it
advice: Remember what made you the company that MS purchased. Don't become MS.
pros: Great people at middle management and lower, which made day-to-day environment great, whether remote or local
cons:
Unless it's in the contract and you saw it signed, you don't get it. Left with 5 weeks of PTO and was told that it's too bad, and that MS would be keeping the $10k+ that I was owed. Yes, it was in my contract; my mistake was assuming that I would have the same contract moving between countries. This mistake cost me over $10k - I'm hoping to saving other people from that.

At one time, this was a fantastic company to work for, to build things at. Now? It's a shell of its former self. Management is promoted based on the ability to adhere to corporate politics and process; caring for your people is downright discouraged and penalized. 

Developers/QA - go to one of the hundreds of other companies that would like to have it. If you can't hack it there, MS has good benefits. Pay will lag the market standard; however, every few years there will a minor adjustment to get closer.

advice: You have brought this company to it's knees by the poor approach to it's workers. Yeah there will always be people that want to work at Morgan Stanley- you can get great experience and there are still some good people working there. I would say the average stay of a person who works at Morgan probably went from 10 plus years to under 5.
pros: Premier investment company. You will get some good experience although the approach is much more segmented. This allows management to plug and play people instead of developing a more broad knowledged individual. This is also why people leave the firm- lack of training and a dead end job.
cons: The company has changed alot over the years- you feel like a number. They don't value effort any more- it's about dollars and sense even if that means putting people in seats that don't know what they are doing to save 20k a head. Sad but that is what the firm has come to. Poor leadership from the top- manage by fear not by what you can accomplish.

advice: For the love of God, work on your technology!
pros: Morgan Stanley has pretty great name recognition so it will look good on your resume for future employers.  The people you work with are usually helpful and the benefits are good.
cons:
1.  For a multinational powerhouse, they have the absolute worst obsolete technology imaginable.  We're talking early 90's at best.  Almost nothing is automated and the functions that are automated don't work half the time.  If your clients want to transfer money online, just tell them to stick with their bank because they probably won't be able to do it here for another 10 years.  

2.  Very little support for new financial advisors.   It's very difficult to get a straight answer on anything.

3.  Very complex fee structure for clients that constantly changes.  

4.  Overly strict company policies make it very difficult to provide the level of service that clients deserve.

advice: N/A
pros: Good pay and fun relationships with coworkers.
cons:
This place is the ultimate meritocracy, and you are going to learn quite a bit about the engine of capitalism.  

If you are new to the business, they will partner you with a senior advisor who has one goal in working with you:  have you help him raise as many assets as possible for him.  These people will sink their teeth into your most personal relationships that  your job is to tee them up with.  Additionally, you will be cold calling all day for years.  This firm provides zero resources in terms of giving you an existing book of assets to manage, or any real leads to call.  Do not expose your relationships to Senior FAs, as these people are polished and master manipulators ... will spin you around and spit you out.  Some of the things you'll see in this environment will be very strange and leave you scratching your head.  

Good place to start your career but ultimately not a good place to build a career.  Might be a good place to end a career.  One year of training with a salary would be perfect for a new advisor.  After that, find a smaller firm.

advice:
Management should really look into boosting the morale and loyalty of the junior members (i.e. associates and analysts). 

MS should also try to follow the lead that other banks like GS, DB and CS have taken in implementing the Saturday-off rule. There is little use in increasing pay when other competitors can guarantee their junior employees at least one day off their schedules.
pros:
The brand name is a big pulse. People recognize the prestige and reputation of Morgan Stanley, and that helps a lot in the investment banking industry. 

The structure is pretty fixed as well, so that means good and clear opportunities to progress through the ranks, at least until VP level.
cons:
Work-life balance is non-existent. It is virtually impossible to arrange for a meal with absolute certainty that it won't get called off. Culture can be pretty passive and it is obvious that top management does not care about the lower ranks.

Expect 100-120 hour weeks, every week.

advice: Those of you that truly support your employees keep it up. We appreciate you. Listen to each employee. Don't forget to check on the ones that seem to be doing well, everyone needs your support.
pros: Great benefits, opportunities to grow within, supportive management in some offices (all offices are a different), they believe in everyone holding integrity, respect for each other in all ways. Management tries to be supportive with financial advisors new to the industry.
cons:
lower pay (if salary employee). Financial Advisor positions are 90% failure rate coming in new to industry. Most won't try to get to know you until you have been their a while. The seasoned advisors are not open to bringing in partners like management wants them to, so new FA's be warned. 
Lots of hours marketing, calling, networking to build your business if new. That never ends as you must always bring in new clients to keep your business growing.

summary: Great place to start, Virtual Advisor
advice: Stop focusing only on new business and focus on taking care of your existing book (which is walking out the door) by providing them with a streamlined service to sales experience that will want them coming back.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a firm with a great reputation and offers individuals just starting out in the financial service industry the opportunity to learn the business. They have a great training program for unlicensed individuals and offer a lot of support. You also have robust access to the firms Global Investment Committee and the research they do allowing you to get as technical as you want. They are competitive and reward you well for high productivity. Time off and other benefits are very good as well.
cons: The MS Virtual Advisor team is a call center and is often run more like a generic call center than an advisor office. Due to most of the advisors being new they try to focus on a limited sub section of Morgan Stanly's managed product offering. High focus on production at the expense of quality. The business model is constantly changing.

summary: Sinking or swimming in the Bering Sea
advice: I think leadership is top notch at the firm. They are obviously competent and strategically forward-thinking
pros: There is a lot of flexibilty in how you build your business.  It's up to you - sink or swim.  If you love talking to people, don't have fear of rejection, and are well connected you can make a lot of money.  Pure capitalism at its "finest."  Brand name provides a marginal benefit when speaking with clients/prospects
cons: Salary is very low versus other careers, and sales pressure is heavy and persistent.  It's nearly impossible to reach the goals that are presented in your job offer because industry fees continue to compress, payouts are slim for newcomers, and clients and potential clients generally consider what you do to be a commodity.  Very few truly prosper.  Don't expect to make a whole lot for at least 4 years unless you have rich family members willing to let you manage their cash.

summary: Great at first-downhill after two years.
advice: Revamp the review process and link it with performance. Stop capping certain divisions due to historical precedent.
pros: Management is pretty open about market changes and the direction of the business. For example, three years ago ahead of the Volker Rule, the former CEO, John Mack, said that he was re-engineering the firm to be less principal activity driven, and more client-focused/flow focused.
cons:
Outside of investment banking and a few algo prop traders still leftover, pay typically is between 25 to 75% less than street standard for anyone VP and below. 

Part of the problem is the review process. For non-officers, there is only one person who reviews you- your boss. You could get rated "Above Expectations" yet get paid the worst quartile in year end bonus. There is no logic to how comp is determined if indeed there is supposed to be a correlation with performance.

The recent rounds of layoffs were all communicated to the media prior to the employees. Classy.

advice:
Listen to the good and even excellent ideas of employees

Reward employees because employee know-how is the company's main asset. This is not a company that manufactures consumer products. The company can only harvest know how about how to manage and invest portfolios on behalf of customers.
pros:
The people and its products are pretty good and fairly well thought out. 

With its retail arms, it reaches quite a lot of people who might like to invest for higher returns

It is a big place with a lot of professionals who can cover the markets properly and connect people with investments
cons: It is a big place with a lot of moving parts. The consolidation of Smith Barney to form Morgan Stanley Smith Barney was not easy but it did get done. The was some dislocation in the combination, but that happens when companies expand quickly.

summary: Technology & Data Division: Good growth, Rewards based on performance, Flexible working hours
advice: More one-one sessions with associates would ensure more opportunities for visibility and feedback.
pros:
Most teams in Technology and Data have flexible working hours and Work From Home policies. There are options for horizontal transfers across business units.
A fresh graduate can aspire to become a Vice President within 5.5 years of joining the firm, at the earliest. The average is around 7 years.
Exposure to a wide range of technologies.
cons:
The firm has a strong grad culture with around 50 engineering graduates being recruited every year. So lateral hires in technology can sometimes find it difficult to fit in. Their growth within the firm follows a slower pace compared to graduate hires.

Visibility is very important. Hard work without the senior management noticing it, often results in little or no increments  or bonus.

summary: Great work place, it can make a difference
advice: I would push for more projects, there are lot of synergies not levereage on. There are lots of silos, where exactly same concepts are developed.
pros:
This work place has a terrific culture. People are given responsibility early, they are listened to and it is really good to work with users directly. It is easy to see the big picture. We can always call our users, colleagues to ask for more information.
It was amazing that the feedbacks I got throughout the years were really precise, and my senior managers advices were really spot on. It is good to work here because I know management has a precise view on my performance.
cons: Sometimes there is too much support and smaller projects are sometimes are complex because the lack of documentation not because they are really complex.

advice: MDs should stop protecting Executive Directors in NYC office who don't know how to manage people.  Listen to Alex Ehrlrich and heed his advice on how to manage and treat your employees.
pros: None in NYC office except proximity to Bryant Park.  Westchester office is a lot better in both the working atmosphere and work/life balance.
cons:
Management in NYC office is horrible.  Avoid working there at all costs.   There is no work/life balance in this office.  Employees are treated like they are kids who don't know how to manage themselves and are micromanaged daily by the Executive Directors.  Management in NYC are threatened by experienced and smart employees.  They want 'yes' men around them and will not tolerate disobedience.  It's an open secret in the office that top management (MDs) are protecting the 'boy's club' NYC managers (Executive Directors) from any scrutiny by the rank and file (VPs and below).

Rank and file guys are genuine, smart and really helpful.  It's a collaborative culture among the peers.

advice: The very high-level executives have high aspiration for their division, but I think we are too top heavy with a lot of senior level executives who try to out perform one another using political tactics.  This causes a ripple effect to the lower-level employees.
pros: There is so much opportunity to learn and grow.  The internal mobility is also great so if you feel like you have exceeded everything there is to know in your current role there are people who will help you move around the company so you can do what you want.
cons: Very political in my team.  It is a toxic work environment and a lot of people are unhappy and don't say anything to senior management because of the politics.

summary: Very Techie, but Management is MIA
advice: Replace current middle and senior managers with outside professional managers that have modern, fresh ideas.  Put in place sincere transformational programs to replace  aging proprietary technologies.   Establish a commercially-minded IT culture which emphasizes better design and strategy.
pros: Staff is incredibly technical and compensation is above average.  Good position for junior people and TAs who like in-the-weeds technical work and coding.
cons: Middle and senior management are mostly long-tenured techies with no 21st century IT management skills.  No strategy, vision, or leadership.  Major technologies are old (10+), proprietary, over-engineered and geeky amateurish.  Out-of-box thinking is discouraged and viewed as a "threat".  Professional hires with more real-world experience should avoid Morgan - they'll be frustrated by the lack of management sophistication and the absence of leadership and direction.

advice: Raise Shanghai's salary, at least we should get the same pay position as Hongkong counterpart. Create more oppotunities for people, especially new people, to visit other region, at least inside Asia. This will help employee feel more existence and exposure, also adding more values.
pros: It's a leading company in the Financial industry. pays people well. As a previous trainee, the training program is great, though we are not going to New York and Tokyo.
cons:
Work Life Balance will not be so great. Hongkong counterpart and collegues get so much more pay than our Shanghai department, although Shanghai guys also work hard. 
Well, there are some lateral hires in Shanghai are not working so hard, always coming late, but I think it's kinda culture in China's IT company.
And the air conditioning in the Bund Center is not so good making people want to sleep

summary: Great people, top talent, turbulent times where some win but many more lose badly
advice: If the Firms "key asset" is it's people, then management needs to take care of its people.  The shift to contingency workforce for short-term cost savings is destroying the culture.  An uncertain comp structure and failure to deliver just compensation will make it very difficult for the Firm to attract top new talent.
pros: Excellent, technical and dedicated employees.  Competent middle management.  Good benefits.  Overall good place to "settle down" with if you don't mind typical corporate politics and the faceless corporate agenda that will always put shareholders before employees.
cons:
Salaries are below market price.  Compensation is based on a "Total Compensation" concept which is Base + Cash Bonus = Total Comp.  In practice this means that your Base is at or below market price with the promise of a cash bonus at year end.  HR plays percentage games because Total Comp has caps for each level.  Typically, Base grows at the expense of Bonus and total comp can stay flat for 3-5 years depending on market and on personal career trajectory.  Although bumps typically happen following a promotion, this is not always the case.  

Odds are that the Firm is re-aligning earning expectations.  The Big Bonus lure is a thing of the past.  Those who can survive the 17-30% total comp loss as a result of this years shift can only hope for a base bump to market price in 2012.  But Total Comp will not recover and you will not get "back on track".  If you're in it, write this and next few years off as a loss.  

Culture at the Firm is still that of late 90s boom.  People are expected to work hard/long hours.  Now that rewards structure is diminished, there is a conflict between cultural expectations and actual rewards.  This will take a few years to stabilize. 

HR will not adjust base salaries mid year unless the exodus of talent is severe enough to cause internal hemorrhaging.  Given churn in the market, odds of a favorable outcome for employees are low.   

More on promotions.  These are typically veiled in secrecy and management delivers an inconsistent message.  Advice for incomers: discuss promotion process and your candidacy openly with your manager.  If your manager will not have the conversation with you openly it means that she is not looking out for your career.  Consider moving on.   Further, promotions are retroactive.  Increase in responsibilities, higher profile projects, management responsibilities typically occur 1 or 2 years before your manager will "put you up". HR defines a quota for promotions.  You manager will compete against other managers for a spot.  Criteria for a successful submission includes a demonstrable successful track record of delivery, mentorship, technical excellence, citizenship, etc.  This is why promotions are typically a 1-3 year process from the moment that you and your manager agree that this is a year for you to be "put up".  So, manage your own career and make sure you have a good manager who is taking care of you.

summary: In A hurry to dump all the Citi People
advice: Too many managers managing the same people causing lots of friction and burnout on subordinates.
pros: Generally a good company to work for if you're in the right place among the right people.
cons:
The team I worked for consisted of a number of women in all the management position. Seems there was a lost in direction and a constant need to prove themselves resulting in worker burnout and a demoralizing staff. Case in point, I reported to 3 managers at one time. They all wanted to shine and had their own ideas on how things should be done. Caused nothing but a quagmire and a dissatisfied group of people.

CAUTION: If you're a former CITI employee that came with the merger, you're lined up to be axed and they will make all the excuses to lay you off.

advice: Management is too focused on short term stockholder and is risking brand equity through squeezing employees and degrading firm culture.
pros: Exposure, ability to assume high levels of responsibility, and have both client and business impacts.
cons: Very poor pay, high levels of key staff turnover and weakening corporate culture are very concerning.  I've worked hard and went from a VP to an ED, as well as from managing 0 staff to 10 experienced staff and an entire business unit, and saw very little increase in total compensation since joining the firm. My pay is currently 30-40% below market according to peers and recruiting firms.  The "do more with less" staff-levels is beginning to impact business, as there are many slip-ups and client complaints are beginning to roll in.  The levels of conflicts of interest are also increasing, as management angles to treat shareholders above client's interests given the currently challenged business environment. What I see regularly is certainly not true to the firm's core values of "doing the right thing" and "focusing on clients first."

summary: Would not recommend - Worked at MS for 4 years
advice: Just be human. Not robots who simply care about their bottom line.
pros:
-Competitive compensation
-Professional Relationship development
-Adds Value to resume
-Great test of financial knowledge; always a learning experience
cons:
-CSAs do not get paid well. You rely on a generous advisor to fairly compensate since the firm puts that on the advisor. If you are on a high producing team, expect to be compensated fairly. If not, then you're stuck with small clients with big issues and an advisor that cannot afford to fairly compensate.

-Company does not care about their clients. Turnover is high for teams/branches that do not produce. They care about their revenue and that's it. If you're not a producer, you mean nothing.

-If you are in the Mountain States complex (they divide by region), then be especially aware of what you're getting into. Again, this company cares about revenue and who has money. People on the coastlines tend to have more liquid money to invest, so that is where company allocates their time and resources. The Mountain States complex, especially from an operations perspective, receives little to no training, attention, or sustainable resources.

summary: Morgan Stanley has a super star culture
advice: Senior management should provide more feedback to junior analysts.  Getting together on a regular basis to discuss skills and career goals should be more focused.
pros: Morgan Stanley is filled with smart people that you can learn from.  They have a super star culture that motivates you to work hard and strive for the very best.  Senior management tries to interact with all levels of employees, giving you more exposure.  At Morgan, there seems to be a decent work/life balance.  People are efficient and productive.
cons: Not everyone is as driven as they should be.  There is less of a team culture at Morgan Stanley, which may hinder some of the overall goals of the firm.  I think there should be more communication across different teams so that the firm can encounter less mistakes.  Having a more consensus driven culture maybe provide goal oriented results.

summary: One of the best internship experiences I have ever had.
advice: I think senior management's compensation should be a little more realistic.
pros: Morgan Stanley is one of the most respected brands in the financial industry. It excels in a number of areas (top 20 places to work at) so having it on your resume is definitely an asset. The compensation package is good, and comparable to those at similar institutions. The corporate culture favors growth without aggressive competition between employees. I had a great time there. Interns have a lot of added activities; they visit the city, get taken to social events etc. Plus the city of New York is a really nice place to be.
cons: You are expected to work a lot. Because much of your compensation is based on bonuses at the discretion of your manager and that everyone else works between 9 and 12 hours a day, you are expected to do the same if you want to succeed.

summary: It's a tough sales gig with significant financial and personal upside.
advice: The do not call list was invented over ten years ago, but somehow the firm still thinks that the phone should be the main marketing vehicle.  After more than half a billion people decided to tell their story on Facebook, has the firm figured out that it might be a good place to let its voice be heard.
pros:
It has the flexibility and independence of owning your own franchise. 
The benefit is that you get a salary, benefits and a good brand to carry around while you get on your feet.  If you get over the 3-5 year bump, you can have a great life balance afterward.
cons:
It's sales in a very skeptical market environment. 
Slow in adapting to technology and consumer behaviors
Stuck in a quagmire of regulations making it ridiculously bureaucratic (that's FINRA + gov't fault more than the firm's).

summary: The hardest job I've ever had - 100% on your own with no direction
advice:
Take an active interest in your trainees, they are your future after all. A theme that I heard over and over from our local senior management was that the FA population was aging and there are few young people coming into this business to replace them.

A fortune (around $75,000 per trainee, maybe more the first year) is spent on trainees but the only support is monetary. You're essentially throwing money at the problem without having a real solution.

1) Be more selective in the hiring. Instead of hiring en mass, hire a few bright people and give those the support they need to learn the job and meet your goals.
2) Place the trainee with a mentor or better yet have them call on existing clients with the goal of gaining a larger share of that client's assets. Even just being able to sit in and observe client meetings would help. The first time I had my own prospect/client meeting was the first time I was seeing it.

The job is complicated and overwhelming to a brand new advisor. I needed someone to show me the ropes.

The once-per week 30 minutes with a FAA coach does not cut it, especially when the trainees are all in different phases or time into production.
3) No leads provided? Really? The cold call training module is corny and unrealistic.

4) I felt the material covered in Warren was solid but 5 days is no where enough time and I came back with a notebook full of notes. Didn't it used to be two weeks and before that a month? In the long long ago?
pros:
Brand name - when you say Morgan Stanley everyone knows what you do.
Generous training salary
All expenses (license, education, training) paid by the firm
Professional education and growth is encouraged. $5000/year for tuition and a $10,000 bonus for completing CFP designation within first 4 years.
Your first 4-5 months are spent solely on studying for the series exams.
Paid salary for 6 months of pre-production training and 24 months once production begins. Salary tapers off by 1/6th per month from months 18 through 24.

Production goals are reasonable (at least they would be if leads were provided).

Fairly easy to get hired considering some of the people I met in Warren.
cons:
Training comes out of a box and you are completely on your own.

This is not something hard work alone can overcome, everyone that I know that made it did some by coming onto a team or being placed directly with a senior FA who mentored them years ago. The business is complicated and can not be learned from reading alone.

Training for the series 7 and 66 is outsourced to a company called STC. They do a good job of preparing you for the test but I recommend buying "Pass the 66" by Robert Walker to supplement your series 66 training. The STC training is lacking on the 66 portion.

You get 1 shot at the 7 and 2 tries at the 66. Failure to pass means termination.

Product training is near non-existent and knowledge primarily comes from the whole sellers.

The only live training comes from a week long crash course held in Warren, NJ where you have 4-5 NDOs (national development officers - trainers) and a class of up to 100 other FAAs. Training is held in a single large room with a ton of information being covered in only 5 days. After this you will never hear from your NDOs again because they're already onto the next giant class.

No leads are provided to trainees, not even a scrubbed cold call list. If you want leads, you have to buy them. No guidance for where to buy the leads from either. The firm's "leads" system does not work, every time I tried it all I got was "0 leads returned".

Upon completing all pre-production requirements (series exams, training modules, Warren) you are given your FA production number and enter into production. A short clock starts ticking. I have never felt so unprepared as I did returning from Warren.

Time given varies from 4 months to 9 months before getting cut for not meeting goals.

Before I was hired I was promised both leads and a mentor. Shortly after I started my manager left and neither the leads or the mentor materialized.

The business model is to hire mass trainees. 15-20% will make it and near 100% of those who make it had a team. The trainee FAs will prospect and bring in some assets and family money. When they are cut the assets are divided among the senior FAs.

On that note, senior/high producing FAs are given anything they want. Trainees are largely ignored. 1 branch manager and a handful of support staff is not enough for 50 plus FAs and multiple offices.

summary: Despite the troubles coming out of the financial crisis, Morgan Stanley remains a premier Investment Bank
advice: Rethink how young advisors are trained and compensated. It would lower turnover. make the hiring process harder but place these young people with potential on a salary/bonus structure so they can learn the right way to acquire and hold on to business.
pros: As a large global firm with a multitude of departments, each area may establish its own culture thus the reader should be aware I am reviewing the Wealth Management part of the firm. MS has undoubtedly been on a roll the last few years as they have revamped themselves and made the firm far more client centric. This has benefitted the clients, both institutional and retail and in turn, the employees.
cons: Large organizations by definition have too much bureaucracy and MS is not an exception. Current CEO James Gorman has been aggressive in hiring/promoting outstanding leaders and the organization has improved in this area.

advice: It may help to train the managers with people management skills (to avoid overwork, to talk more in-depth about career development opportunities, etc). Also, the 3 year (division-bound) analyst program may prevent new graduates from staying in the firm if they become interested in other departments (I can only speak for Operations division in Japan). More flexibility with regards to mobility may help retain the young professionals.
pros: I joined the firm as a new graduate in Japan. The team and the management were very supportive, and I appreciated the regular one-on-one meeting with my manager and other mentorship opportunities outside of my team. Working for this firm definitely gave me the foundational business skills and experience to work with colleagues from other countries across cultural and time differences.
cons: The working hours were very long. It was also difficult to maintain motivation when my team members and managers left the firm frequently.

advice: No idea.  It is a cultural thing. How do you change a company that big?
pros:
Large organization.  Good amentities.  Cafetaria, gym, and so on.  Nice coffee :)

Opportunities arise to advance. Or you can twiddle your thumbs and do nothing.
cons:
Highly political.  Senior Managers seemed to be focussed on protecting their backs.  Knives were out. 

As a results, rather disorganized.  Things can change in an instance. I saw a division closed and people laid off within days.  Atmosphere became toxic.

A lot of people I worked with were also doing something else e.g. writing a book so that were not that into what they were doing.  I was contract. Others who were permanent barely worked at all.  I had to pick up the slack for some very lazy people.  They took boondoggling to new heights.

It was like working for government only the people were better dressed.

advice: Managers could take a more active interest in the business development of their advisors. They tend to be less proactive and more reactive to the majority of their advisors.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a world class firm. The research and platform are top notch.
cons: The most difficult aspect of this position in gathering assets and acquiring new clients.  You are completely on your own in developing your business. The firm is only there to manage you based on an operational, legal, and compliance basis. If you are looking for support in growing your business, you will need to go hunting in their intranet website and call various 800 numbers, hoping to find someone who can give you the answers that you need.  As a sole practitioner, you are isolated and have minimal interactions with other advisors. If you are lack the ability to be highly independent and self motivated, you will most likely not succeed at this firm..

advice: Focus on people development not from sham painting volunteer activities, but from removing face time type of ignorance. Take better care of your data and be proud. Please don't compare yourself to Goldman and declare victory when GS loses.
pros: Promotions are almost guaranteed if you stick long enough. Get in, work for one year, speak with you manager to get on 'track'. one year to get on track and not get promotion and then next year its your 'turn'
cons: Runs like a sweatshop, Face time is more important than actual work, no regard for data quality or intent to fix it long term. Adjustments (scratch data to suit needs) is all over the firm. Every Q4 is bad and when its good, other issues are introduced to not give enough bonus. Raises in base are below market. Senseless job cuts of senior people and then working multiple years to re teach the skills.

advice: Pay more competitive salaries for tenure, quality of work and reward your "star" employees. I never received a review that was lower than the highest rating; however, there were never any raises higher than 4% given to me during my time there. During that same stretch, my spouse worked at a regional bank and received multiple 5-10% raises. I began with a slightly higher salary yet I was way behind when I finally couldn't take anymore and decided to leave.
