My new job increased my base salary by 110% which shows the value MS places on retaining talent.
pros: Job security, great co-workers and very good benefits and perks. Technology was constantly growing while I was there and that is always a positive when you work at a financial institution.
cons: Low salary, constant cost cutting and no clear path for job trajectory. I felt that there wasn't enough of a difference in compensation between the best employees and the worst employees.

pros:
The culture here is great. People help each other. The people I work with and manage are very talented. The company offers very good training opportunities. The projects are also very interesting and provide an opportunity to serve customers at one of the best Wall Street companies.

Management is generally open to comment and usually resolves issues (see also cons below).

Good place for working parents. But the lack of a daycare center at the workplace makes it difficult to return from parenting leave.
cons:
Sometimes it feels the environment is too fast paced to make strategic investments in systems. As with any big firm, it sometimes feels too slow to embrace change.

Work life balance could also be better out here in Asia. Though in theory, everyone gets the flexibility to come in late when they take late calls, but it is rarely a good alternative. Evening time with family can be irreplaceable.

An alternative to neglecting late calls is to lose your career growth options.

summary: Great People, Interesting Work, Slow Advancement
advice: Focus on performance and building high-functioning teams. Empower and enable your teams... they're the ones closest to the work.
pros: I was paid a competitive salary and for the most part I really liked the people with whom I worked with the exception of my managers. With only a couple of exceptions over my 16 year career there, I consistently had poor managers who rarely had my back and seemed to be out for themselves. There was no meaningful feedback, no spirit of collaboration or team. But the company treated me well and I generally looked forward to going to work.
cons: As noted in my Pros, I generally lacked trust in my immediate managers, they largely seemed to be looking out for themselves and not enabling or empowering their teams. It was also hard to advance and get promoted as it required advocacy of your direct manager. Seemed to be more a popularity contest than merit-based.

summary: Good luck, but you probably won't make it.
advice: How about offering the training that was promised and real mentoring from someone who knows what it takes to make it in the business TODAY? Or, tell us at hiring that you NEED to partner with a Senior FA.
pros: Very professional environment. Well-respected, well-known name. It was great to tell people I worked for Morgan Stanley, my credibility went up. Good training salary!
cons: Absolutely no training or support. It wasn't so great that the support staff had pools to bet on which of the new FA's would "make it." It wasn't cool that they promised training and mentoring and is all that was offered were 2 jokers who were trying to make it in the business themselves. The other training of "how to make it" consisted of guys who were close to retirement age and telling stories that were not duplicatable. I think maybe someone tried. And, maybe I wasn't suited to the business. But, I was unimpressed!

summary: A Great Name but Horrible Experience
advice: After 10 years of Do Not Call list legal implementation and the public rejecting cold calls as a sales tactic it's time to move out of the mindset of sales that hasn't worked since bell bottoms, disco, land yachts and 8 track tapes.
pros: The depth of this companies resources are incredible.  Their research abilities are fantastic, their is almost no information you can't have brought to bear about a company, product or individual.
cons:
Their retail experience from an employees perspective is abysmal.  

I witnessed nearly 50 people wash out of their Financial Advisor program within 2 years of initial hire, a 95% failure rate.  Branch management runs the operation like a boiler room operation as opposed to motivating highly intelligent, qualified and capable professionals to be their best.  

Performance metrics are still measured by 1970's and 80's criteria of call volume as opposed to quality of lead, contact or filtered sales prospects.

summary: Good for getting your Series 7, but leave after
advice: Close shop, you're way behind the Merrill Edge or Chase Investment platforms who do it much cheaper and don't screw over clients to get there; long term, your business model will eventually become so unprofitable that you'll close shop.
pros:
Pay you to get your Series 7 and 66 licenses
Nice name to put on your resume
Mutual Fund vendors bring in breakfast and lunch quite often
Get to study in your own office for your licensing
Pays much better than Edward Jones, includes benefits
cons:
Doesn't care about the associate or the clients, only revenue
Churn and burn non-"daddy's book" legacy FA's, essentially throwing young advisors against a wall and hope they stick
The FAs are nothing special, the older ones get the books handed down to them from their daddy or a buddy who's retiring but they don't know anything more than the lower end brokerage advisors
Charge an arm and a leg for crappy investment advice, and MS takes most of the commission from it; they take from their clients and their advisors, as long as they get their pound of flesh they don't care what happens to either previously mentioned party

summary: When they bring you on as a temp, they promise to hire you quickly and increase your pay, but they don't come through.
advice: Management's best move to boost employee morale and attract better talent would be to hire employees directly, rather than going through a temp agency.  Many of the most promising prospective employees have families and cannot go an indefinite period of time without health care benefits.
pros: They may help pay for your Series 7 & Series 63.  If you are fresh out of college and looking to start a career in finance, this can be a good place to consider.  They also have good maternity benefits and tuition reimbursement.
cons: The company is ill prepared for the rapid changes that the recent merger have brought on.  Loyal employees are getting left in the dust as management scrambles to keep up with the changes.

summary: Great Firm, takes care of its people
advice: My immediate supervisor was a friend before I joined, so no problems there. I had little to no contact above his level.
pros: Plenty of Capital to work with. Not just allowed to trade proprietary, but encouraged. Let me clarify. The job is Institutional Equity Block Trader. I have worked for a few firms in this capacity, and depending on ability and desire, you can trade the firms capital to make a profit, not just supply missing block. This can improve your loss ratio, which is a factor in your bonus. Not all firms allow this, and in all cases, the amount varies. Very fair review process. While the atmosphere can be a little formal, it is no where near the level of Goldman Sachs, where I was uncomfortable; though that was many years earlier.
cons: I really can't think of any. Sure, there is a lot of pressure to perform, but that is intrinsic to the business.

summary: Morgan Stanley is no longer a Best Place to work for as an IT professional in Finance.
advice: Focus on retaining existing great talent by restoring good benefits such as pension fund and good medical insurance. Offshoring is hurting the quality of services and is impacting image of Morgan Stanley as an employer.
pros:
Morgan Stanley is still able to attract great talent via its Graduate Training Program, which is arguably the best in the Finance industry. 
The compensation is not bad.
cons:
Employee benefits are declining every year - employees lost pension funds and medical insurance is expensive and requires one employees to pay significant amount out of pocket.
The IT organization has grown significantly of the past 10 year and the quality of IT service has declined. 
Very difficult to hire in core locations such as NY and London, so the options for great talent are limited.

summary: some thoughts from a recently laid off employee
advice: n/a
pros:
on of the top companies in financial industry. lots of good training is offered. access to a lot of resources. mba is paid for.
training program if you can get into it is great.  great experience that is valued in the industry.
cons: Large company so you feel like a cog in a wheel sometimes. A lot of turnover and turmoil. a lot of red tape. SOX compliance can be very painful. a lot of proprietary technology and internal libraries are used which makes and IT person a lot less marketable. Not a lot of freedom in chosing technology. Everything has to go through an architecture committee which means that a lot of good technologies make it to Morgan Stanley a lot later.  Generally hours are long which makes work/life balance impossible. Tough to advance in fixed income IT if you are a woman. In fact most women tend to leave after they start families.

summary: Awesome experience but poorly designed career track
advice:
Need more development of both advisors and staff, as opposed to purely financial equation incentives. People wanna be in a rewarding job. Also there is too much turnover of complex and branch managers. That leads to instability. 

There is too much focus on the short-term (because upper management focuses on quarterly earnings and the value of stock options--not on creating long-term value for shareholders, employees and other stakeholders). 

Despite this it was one of the best eras of my life. There is, however, much improvement that can be had.
pros:
Dynamic
Challenging
Robust investment platform
Rewarding intellectually and financially (the latter potentially)
Respected in the community
Attracts quality people as clients (generally driven and smart)
cons:
Compensation continually changes (every year) so stability is hard to find. 
Treated like a number and not a person at times. 
Very bureaucratic and political. 
Work environment may have tension because colleagues are competitors.

summary: Morgan Stanley is an excellent company to work for in IT
advice:
- Find a better, more fair way to promote employees.
- Encourage more frequent feedback between managers and employees.
- Continue with efforts to improve annual review process.
pros:
- In IT, I found most of the people to be high caliber: i.e. smart, proactive, very good work ethic, respectful.
- IT management is open to ideas from all employees.
- You work hard, sometimes long hours, but there is also emphasis on work-life balance.
- Very good salary and benefits.
- If company has a decent year, and if you did your work well, the bonus is very good.
cons: - The process for getting promoted (e.g. from associate to VP, from VP to ED) is not good.  I know employees who were outstanding for many years and still they were not promoted.

summary: good place to make some money and experience
advice: the management should listen to the low level ppl without having the air of superior because it is proven that they survive because of ppl from the lower position
pros:
- great it teams
- good and great challenges
- some nice developers to work and share the ideas with
- good medical compensation and good , competitive salaries for the new employee
- overall good place
- work from home
cons:
- too much management decision starting from ED level and above. 
- when the time of compensation comes, all the reviews during the year and projects that you work do not reflect the reality on the compensation. 
- if you find some interesting project in the company you would like to work on, you cannot because you are not on certain positions (e.g. VP) so you cannot apply even if you are entitled to work there

advice: Create some positive feedback on a weekly basis for your employees. No scare tactics. They don't work on smart people, and lower productivity for those who are fearful of losing their job.
pros:
4 weeks paid vacation starting your first year at MS. There is a very rich collection of learning materials as part of MS University. Really a fantastic way to learn new products, and skills.

Great benefits.
cons:
Working environment is hit or miss depending on your manager and VP. There were a lot of managers per person when I was there.

Current CEO comes from the retail banking world, and his focus may go there. The retail banking especially MSSB venture is really a problem for the group because they can not cut costs, and the "talent" is costing them over 60% of revenue from the group, compared to investment banking which is costing between 40%-50% of revenue.

advice: Cut some of the bureaucratic red tape to increase efficiencies. Prioritizing retention means paying people market value.
pros: Great perks for FTEs, such as free passes to National Aquarium, Maryland Zoo, etc., plus other perks throughout the year - I got 2 free tickets to the Kennedy Krieger holiday festival. Hours are very team-dependent - I work in trade support and work 9-10 hours per day - but the overtime is nice.
cons: Pay is far lower than equivalent firms, so people with a lot of experience in finance go to other firms and great employees leave quickly to get paid more. People typically have too little experience, so clients and other brokers complain often about MS, which is humiliating if you care about your work. Employee morale is pretty low. There's a LOT of bureaucratic red-tape to work through in getting anything done because of different teams' responsibilities, which slows down our trade processing.

summary: It was not my favorite company, at least in my department.  It's a big name though and looks decent on your resume.
advice: Allow them to be more creative, and listen to them when they say they aren't the one for a particular task.  The very LAST thing you want to do is put your creative talent on a project that is going to destroy their morale and make them feel like dying.  Hopefully it's not like this in all of the departments.
pros:
The name of the company on you resume.
4 weeks paid vacation per year.
cons: Boring projects.  If you have skills, you will lose them in a few years if you don't keep yourself updated on your own.  You really have to like finance to do this job, and I think I don't like finances much unless I'm dealing with my own.

advice: Understand that long term success can be more lucrative and worthwhile than instant profits. Make a concerted effort to reward support staff and treat all employees equally. Recognize that the firm has a very long way to go to achieve gender equality.
pros:
- Nice offices, computers, equipment, stationary and business cards
- Reputation is good, but can get complicated when it comes to the investment banking side
- Several product offerings for clients that help meet solutions
- Philanthropic and charity oriented
cons:
- Culture is still archaic, favoring the "good ol' boys"
- Little to no management support to build a business or take care of clients
- Enforcement of policies can be discretionary, depending on the revenue of the advisors
- Technology/software is glitchy and crashes often
- The firm takes a significant portion of earned revenue
- Advisors are encouraged to sell products, rather than create solutions

advice: My advice is for management to spend more time paying attention to issues that are brought up by interns and operations. Although advisors bring in the clients, interns and operations are the people who take care of the logistics and day-to-day operations that will please the clients.
pros: Although it depends on the branch you work at, in general, Morgan Stanley Smith Barney has a great work environment. Colleagues are very kind, friendly, and helpful. There is a lot of company functions and socials where you can personally get to know the people you work with.
cons: An intern would usually work for a broker or a team of brokers. The experience that you get out of the internship depends on the team that you work for. If your boss is a challenging person to work with, then that will most likely be your experience at the firm.

advice: Need to listen to employees BETTER.  Seriously listen, don't just nod your head as if you're getting anything out of the conversation.  Take peoples live into consideration when you make your decisions that can affect said people and their ability to provide for themselves and or their families.  Need a MUCH BETTER training program for Series 7 licensing.  It is currently very dissorganized and trial by fire. . . do it on your own.
pros: Ability to create your own book of business.  Unlimited earning potential.  Great people to work with.  Nice corporate atmosphere.  Great corporate name and trust in that name.
cons: Distrust of people to the securities industry at the moment.  Your looked at at one of those people, the ones that caused the mess with American money.

summary: Horrible place to be a junior banker
advice: Don't be so judgmental, and don't be terrible to work with if you don't have to be
pros:
Standard investment banking training makes you really good at finance and accounting
Morgan Stanley's name always got the attention of anyone who looked at my resume
Superficial attempts at making the culture better
cons:
Where to begin...

Awful culture. Described on Wallstreetoasis as "dog-eat-dog snake pit" - very accurate description from my experience as well. 
No sense of camaraderie, analysts treated like sweatshop workers (senior bankers recruit by picking those who they think can churn out the most work, no regard for cultural fit)
Extremely judgmental and high pressure / stress-inducing culture from senior bankers
No one cares about your development or exit opportunities, they just want their work done
Split into Corp Finance and M&A group; unfair to Corp Finance analysts who don't get as much technical exposure or any deals on their resumes
Don't expect to be able to recruit outside of California

Four analysts quit within a 6 month period of working there (out of 10 analysts)

summary: Company to settle if you can socialise and do networking
advice: Appraise people on the basis of critical work done rather than  not the basis of networking,
pros:
1) Nice Atmosphere
2)You can communicate with anyone irrespective of hierarchy.
3) Some strategic projects are going and work is really well there, kind off startup
4) You will see most of the team use new technology if had the chance to do.
Work depends mostyl on projects and teams.
cons:
1) Too many unnecessary meeting (Catch-ups with Manager, Manager's Manager, mentor and many more)
2)The actual effective working hour is very less since many people is busy in doing 1 to 1s
3) Indian manager mentality, make me happy ill make you happy rather than awarding on the basis of work done. The networking plays a very important part in promotions and appraisals
4) The hike is very less normally, and they will not take care until you put papers

summary: Great resume builder, great to open doors to new relationships, revolving door
advice: If possible, be intentional in pairing people up regarding Associates and FAs. If you know goals are near impossible, helping of breaking ice or matchmaking good fits could help all parties.
pros:
- Firm has great reputation to building initial relationships and clients, also strengthens your resume
- Get (sparring) access to highly sought after events
- Great intellectual capital
- Diversity
- Great platform
cons:
- Piranha/ shark like atmosphere... people will go after your prospects, and throw dirt on your name to do it (not everyone, but was an experience there). Also there is an eagerness for Senior guys/ ladies to partner with you for business, but not throw any bones to you
- High sales goals if you're a solo practitioner just starting out
- Sometimes the organization is too big... servicing Advisors to getting stuff done, too much information, too many processes, tons of red tape getting the way of business

pros:
1. A growing private bank that is supported by the head office with a lot of new initiatives, headcount additions and challenges
2. Fast paced and resilient to market changes given its flat management and flexible policies and procedures
3. Colleagues are in general smart and friendly that are willing to help and train you
4. Discretionary bonus can be massive if you are a star performer
5. Challenging working environment that helps you grow professionally and remain competitive in the market
cons:
1. Focus on bonus model that could result in increase bonus only without increasing your base salary
2. Insider working environment that you could be easily kicked out if you could not get along with key stakeholders
3. People driven instead of process driven that one person can make all the calls and override all the pre defined rules
4. Poor job security that some employees especially VPs and EDs, are fired prior to bonus announcement every year

summary: The company that once was, can still be by embracing it's history.
advice: Morgan Stanley has continuously succeeded throughout history because it embraced a certain culture, and ways to do business. Changing culture just because times change can have an adverse effect. Strategy is meant to be changed, culture is meant to last forever. You attract people by compensating them well, you keep people by growing their careers and equally compensating them for their efforts. Lack of compensation is one of the quickest ways to lose top talent. Business minded people always weigh the factors of their circumstances, don't give them a reason to leave if they're your top performers.
pros: They are a large company, well recognized in Investment Banking and Securities Industry. They pay well and the Corporate culture is very unique. Respect is given to everyone. Opinions and contributions accepted. Most of the people are very intelligent.
cons: Opportunities for advancement are limited.

summary: Morgan Stanley Advisors say Firm must put Client Interests back on top
advice: Stop screwing the clients (fees, proprietary product, account changes), and stop screwing the brokers.  Your retention will go way up, and your recruiting bonuses could then come way down.  A little more loyalty to your existing clients and brokers, as opposed to tossing all the goodies to recruits, would be a good start.
pros: Excellent reputation.  The company is a "household name", which gives clients a sense of comfort.
cons: Rewards obscene for those at the very top of the management structure.  Incentives for everybody else are minimal, particularly since the stock has been such a poor performer.  Compliance is way out of control...ineffective at stopping the bad guys, and a big obstacle to keeping clients happy.  Also, customer service is poor.  The system is tilted to generate lots of fees from the customers

advice: If you want to keep new brokers in the business you need to help them more in the marketing skills department. Telling them to cold call out of the phone book is not a good strategy.
pros:
Great pedigree
Great analytical market research
Benefits were ok
Some of the sales skill taught were useful but most were a waste of time
cons:
This place was churn city, they would take in new FA's and have them bring in all their friends and families money. Once there they would place unbelievably hard asset goals, knowing that just starting out it is nearly impossible to meet the minimum assets under management and then fire the new hire after 10 months, keeping the accounts and distributing them to te top brokers in the office.

Pay was not adjusted to locality and was almost impossible to live on the salary given while trying to obtain critical mass in assets.

summary: Many Opportunites to Gain Valuable Knowledge
advice: Managers could benefit from training that would help to enhance soft skills which can be just as crucial as the hard skills. Work/life balance is very important and key to retaining the best talent.  It's understood that workloads can very from team to team as well as management but everyone should feel their work time and personal time is valued.
pros:
-Employees have access to a wealth of knowledge and information to enhance skills and aptitude. This is done through optional and mandatory training sessions, open forums, team to team presentations, online courses and others
-Mobility within the firm is highly encouraged
-One-on-One career discussions with management is practiced 
-Baltimore office is very diverse and in a scenic location
-Good benefits
cons:
-Work/life balance needs improvement. Depends on your management
-The firm continues to outsource functions which is designed to save costs but also has the opposite effect when communication is difficult and potentially creates other risks

advice: Vice President has to have Service Desk experience to understand whole processes. First, hire TL to teach them then employ normal agents or give separate training to them. Offer same wages for same positions.
pros: Salary, a bit higher than similar jobs. Useful benefit packages.
cons: First of all, Even VP does not know the answers. From the beginning, they inform that they will not pay extra hours. If you scheduled on the weekend shift you can not take holiday. If you are resolving issues fast this is also a problem. You have to take min 3 chats at the same time. The line is always busy. You have just 2 x 15 mins break and one 30 mins for lunch. TLs got the same training together with agents. You are number and excel tables in front of their eyes. Someone without an IT background can be SME because he/she joined before you. You will learn 1% of job on the training as If you have Service desk experience probably Trainainer knows less than you do. So unprofessional environment. Basically, I do not recommend anyone.

advice: Although you might be managing your career, you have to manage your people with the same respect.
pros: The firm is established and prestigious. The work force is pretty diversed and has a good amount of competent people. The pay is competitive and there's a lot of material to learn new things. You just have to be proactive in researching. People are nice enough to take time to show their day to day. Management escalation is in the right direction for the firm.
cons: Assuming same across all banks but if you can't be vocal then you can't shine or show case your competency. Also the request for transition into new work or groups is hard. This road block can force people to leave the firm. Although if you stay with the group, you can gain a team lead or promotion opportunity, but I personally can't perform the same function for years on out.

advice: Give more consideration to those working to become established.  Make moving on to new areas of the firm a bigger emphasis and one that is more realistic.  Currently, dept have no push to look internally before externally.  Someone with talent in one area of finance, with the right drive, determination and example, should be successful in other areas of finance just as easily.  Also, reinstate the tuition reimbursement program, or at least increase it from the new $10k a yr max (it was 100% reimbursement as early as spring 2008).
pros: Name recognition, great place to begin, networking
cons: Very difficult to advance, especially to another area of the firm.  Too much politicing.  Significant differences from department to department in terms of culture, pay, and opportunities.  Not a good place to develop talent, as it is underappreciated and under-utilized (not to mention the worst error, underpaid!)

advice: Lower the hurdles and give the FAA a chance to actually learn the business (how to service a client, open accounts, build portfolios, etc) before throwing them out to the wolves as soon as they receive their series 7 and series 66 licenses.  Program needs much better structure if the company actually wants the younger FAs to succeed in this industry and at Morgan Stanley
pros: Salary while building your book of business is a major plus
cons: Not a real deal training program that actually sets you up for success.  Very tough to navigate the waters as a sole practicioner.

pros: Brand name is strong and mature
cons: It is amazing the impact of leadership /upper management changes and if the wrong person is chosen to head up a practice, it can ruin ones future and all the years’ of hard work that were put into place to make a practice thrive for so many years. This is apparent when the CCO was put into place where nepotism and favoritism ruled the department and hard work and true talent were out on sidelines to feed the new CCOs own agenda that didn’t align with the values of the firm. This is made evident by the high turnover and attrition within that department. Also, management stood by dismantling a talented team because the head refused to give in the pressure of churning results to appease the business and not be independent and objective to help the firm manage the risks. So if you play the cards right and stand on the wrong side the law, then it’s the place to work.

summary: Not a place for techies in India.Stay away!!!
advice:
Techies attrition would increase day by day ,if you don't want to change or adopt!
Big IT firms are way better for techies than MS.
pros:
1-Salary/Money
2-Multiple events

That's it.it ends here!
cons:
I don't know where to start from..They would brag about MS is this ,MS is that but actually joining MS as a Techie is not worth the effort.

1-No laptop for new joiners,they were like arrange your own laptop or  sit at home.
2-They would tell 5 days a week work but every single prod release will happen at  Saturday only,5 am IST
3-Be ready for a 6 days working
4- Work pressure is expected as a Techie. BUt here in MS they will grind you till te last drop.
5-calls extending till late hours for India people,no work life balance.
6-Tech stack is as old as fossils.No priority on building tech knowledge or moving to newer technologies.
7-Many other pains,which I can't disclose here but you would definitely hate those when you leave a big tech firm for MS.

advice: Pay employees accordingly and treat them with respect. It's not about pizza or lunch. Its about monetarily rewarding employees. Inflation, post pandemic and everything that comes with it. When we had to work from home and change our lives, we did that for two years. Now its time for them to help us transition properly its a turning into a bigger problem than it should be.
pros: Benefits are great. There are a lot of options for families, health and perks
cons: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management has a lot of office politics going on. Employees are exploited to some degree and upper management expect you to show your worth before you get a chance to be promoted. It is very hard to get promoted and it is very easy to get discouraged

summary: Hard work and talent are recognized
advice: Senior management tend to get mired with infighting and turf wars.  One highly politicized group I was in had far too many meetings to try and get everyone on board,  resulting in a syndrome of all talk and little action.
pros:
I worked in IT for 10 years and got promoted twice during that time.  Hard work and talent are definitely 
recognized. Morgan Stanley is fundamentally a meritocracy.  The technology infrastructure is great, and the caliber of one's cohorts is generally very high.
cons: Senior management tend to get mired with infighting and turf wars.  One highly politicized group I was in had far too many meetings to try and get everyone on board,  resulting in a syndrome of all talk and little action.

summary: Overall good investment banking analyst experience, especially relative to other frims
advice: In order to retain the best analysts at the firm you have to create an incentive structure comparable of that being offered at the PE firms / hedge funds.  While you may not be able to match on pay, you can lead in other areas such as work life balance etc.
pros: Great reputation and alumni network means there are significant opportunitiies on the buyside with both Private equity and (to a slightly lesser extent) hedge funds.  Overall work / life balance better than at GS and reputation and opportunities better than at other banks.
cons: still an analyst program so you do get worked very hard etc.  Probably something still to be said about working at GS as well in terms of the incremental opportunitieis..

advice: Keep up the good work - and keep listening to the staff to ensure the awesome culture stays intact.
pros: Fantastic culture, great people. Flexible work schedule and lots of autonomy.  This company epitomizes a work hard play hard mentality and though hours can be long at times, there are always fun things happening and special little appreciation events for teams. For such a large team (over 500 people in the Calgary office) the company does a wonderful job of taking any opportunity to bring the staff together which makes for close knit teams and builds lasting relationships.
cons: Everyone is so busy it can be a challenge getting support sometimes. If you are someone who values handholding in your leadership, this probably isn’t the place for you.

summary: Morgan Stanley is standout firm in the finance industry
advice: I believe that management has done a good job of weathering the current financial storm.
pros: In my personal situation, the best reason to work at Morgan Stanley is the strength that it gives my resume.  Without a doubt, MS is one of the most well respected financial institutions in the U.S.  The career advancements are limited in my position, and I plan to possibly return to school for an MBA.
cons: The technology is a bit archaic.  It would be hard to advance to an Investment Rep position from where I am currently without returning to grad school.  I feel that the prestige of Morgan Stanley has been somewhat diluted by the number of retail brokers working for the company.

summary: good place to grow as a finance guru....if you want that
advice: Talk to your junior people more. Make yourself approachable for honest feedback.
pros: If you really love the job, you can be successful. People who are passionate about it get far, so if you care about finance and the broader theme, you won't mind some of the rough tasks to get you there. Its a place where young people can succeed...and of course, good pay
cons: If you don't think finance is for you long term, you will hate the stuff you do day to day. Analyst are forced to do mundane tasks, often dealing with back office stuff. Only if you truly feel passionate about the job do you put all this aside for the bigger picture. No free food or coffee, not great benefits, pretty sub-prime office

advice: Get rid of the old boy network, start actually caring about your clients and employees, or just retire. You are the reason most people hate wall street firms.
pros: The company does pay for a trainee's licensing education (Series 7, Series 66, Insurance) but that is ALL the training, and it is done by a third party.  Morgan Stanley just pays the bill..
cons:
Despite being told there was a comprehensive training program, where I would meet with the development manager and branch manager at least once a week to develop sales strategies, that did not happen at all.  Those guys were more concerned with playing golf and telling the staff how great they were and how they made so much money in the business.  The world-class training in the New York headquarters was also a joke.

Clients and trainees are just numbers, unless they have million dollar accounts.   What new person is going to land such an account with absolutely no internal support or training.

advice: Less focus on adherence and more focus on allowing employees to hit their metrics organically. Call center atmosphere will drive away employees over time (Let's not turn into Office Space)
pros: Able to garner a strong understanding of wealth management and applicable skills (financial planning/portfolio construction/investment strategies/sales experience). Will allow you to get licensed (Series 7 & 66). Decent compensation coming out of college. Division is expanding rapidly with acquisition of etrade/eaton vance. No long hours. Good internal mobility. Prestigious name to work under.
cons: Disconnect with management at times with rapid expansion/new business initiatives. Politics does play a strong role in terms of promotion eligibility. Very similar to a call center with focus on adherence/calls/inbound time (Lots of employees do get burnt out). There has been a stronger focus on regulating employees with varying policies since working there.

summary: First class business.  Hard work pays (but comes with a price)
advice:
Just because they are well compensated, be cautious of running the employees too thin. Without guidance, resources and vision you risk diminishing returns.  
"Work smarter" and "do more" is only a sustainable model when employees are being well resourced with efficient tech/systems and proper direction from management.  Sans this, employees are chasing directionless noise and unachievable metrics by which even the best will come up short.
pros: Top notch company in the industry. Amazing opportunities. Incredible people. Inclusive company culture. Generous compensation.
cons: High stress and very competitive. Hard to strike work/life harmony. Must be plugged in 24/7 and willing to accept continually expanding (and often-time directionless) job responsibilities. Legacy technology impedes employees efficiencies.

summary: Morgan Stanley - time to go back to the old values
advice: I've a feeling, you are trying to save on technology. There is no understanding that without IT modern financial business is soon dead. That's especially true for Morgan Stanley with it's reputation of an excellent IT place. It is not any more and the best people are trying to leave. Once the market turns around you should expect mass exodus of IT staff.
pros: Big established company with good compensation level and nice potential for carrier advance. It used to be very friendly toward it's IT staff. The place was a technology leader in financial sector. Unfortunately, the respect for IT is deteriorating.
cons: You work 24x7 in highly stressed environment. Corporate politics at any level can be brutal. You either have to go up or be eaten by peers.

advice: Think of ways to keep and develop your high performers, unless the long term plan is to end up with a bigger mediocre majority that talks more than works.
pros: The few high performers that you do come across are truly exceptionally
cons: Meritocracy is not a concept that management is familiar with.  Any employee, regardless of talent or performance, working on "pet" initiatives, is considered to be valuable asset.  Promotion is next to impossible if you're not in the "right" roles.  Internal mobility is a joke because you cannot apply for the next level up - how does that encourage professional growth within a firm?  If you are looking to kill your ambitions, apply now.

advice: Review the promotion process, consider at least giving a title change if a promotion occurs mid-year
pros: Work-life balance, can order free meals after 7:00PM, four weeks of vacation (if you qualify under the Mandatory Vacation Policy), good medical benefits, clear trajectory to move up the ranks especially if you start at entry level.
cons: A lot of bureaucracy makes it hard to actually initiate and see change, the promotion process is flawed because they ask you to take on the work of the next level for a whole year without compensating you with a raise or title until the following year since official promotions only happen one day a year.  Pay is not as good as down the street at Goldman, but work/life balance is definitely better here, so the choice depends on your priorities.

advice: Don't treat this as a 2-3 year program. Invest more into the analysts, increase their quality of life, and groom them to stay with the company.  The model of grinding people out keeps a particular type of person in banking... one that might not
pros: Instant legitimacy when talking to investment funds for the next step in your career. Morgan Stanley and Goldman are widely known as the 2 best firms by a longshot for analysts to start their financial careers
cons: Being an investment banking analyst can feel like a glorified, overpaid personal assistant at times. 50% of your week is spent doing mindless activities that add little value to deals but is a product of the investment banking culture.

summary: Great place to work as an IT engineer
advice: Let smart people choose location more freely in order to retain them. Apply more agile metodologies (scrum).
pros: Suprisingly new technologies (company needs to stay ahead of competition and that means they need such tools before rest of technology world), lot of autonomy, lot to learn. Lot of out-of-work socializing if you want. Very smart people. Don't expect an investement bank to be the same as a traditional bank - it is very different type of company and different type of work.
cons: Mostly backoffice work, very limited exposure to your end users. Almost zero opportunity to relocate to metro offices (New York, London, Honk Kong) from growing engineering offices (Shanghai, Budapest). Lot of tools is in-house developed and that means that many time what you learn hear, cannot be applied easily somewhere else.

advice: Create a training program where new hires have to shadow more senior advisors.  Or don't.  I will never allow a new advisor to manage my money, questionable if I would allow a more senior advisor either.
pros: The best part about working here is the name recognition; people seem to respect Morgan Stanley.
cons: The training program was a complete joke.  They invest little time or effort into the trainees, providing almost nothing that would make a personal successful in this role.  It was sales training (bad sales training), nothing more.  There is no financial education what-so-ever.  They simply through a lot of people into the water and then see what floats (who has family money to invest, who gets lucky with a big account, etc.)  Explains why 95% of my training class of 200 either quit or were fired after 9 months.  I was let go on month 10.

summary: Used to have a very solid reputation...now that is in question
advice: Bringing in lots of "outsiders" doesn't always net the best results.   Senior management needs to step up and make decisions.  The inability to make decisions has been paralyzing for success in many projects. People are afraid to fail for fear of job loss.
pros: Many challenging projects and opportunities.  Exciting work; very skilled and respected colleagues from the best schools.  Collaborative culture among the "working class."
cons: Very political.  Need to be aligned with the group in power to advance.  There is real trouble in the Fixed Income division.  It is causing a huge negative impact on the Firm.  Rumors of more planned lay offs in early 2016.  People work in fear for being in the next wave of reductions. The current CEO(Gorman) is set for a few more years here and that forced the former president (Fleming) to resign.  Both actions are of concern.

summary: Fine stepping stone - don't stay too long
pros:
My original review is much longer than this, but Glassdoor lost my review when I submitted it. So here it is again, in a much shorter form.

* Smart colleagues
* Very good technical infrastructure
cons:
* Lower pay than the market
* No work-life balance
* Prefers to let go good people rather than paying market rate, adding the burden to the team to interview the cheaper replacement. Rinse and repeat with about 20% of the team on a yearly basis
* "We offer something else other than money" means you're getting paid lower. Which is fine at first, but as you stay longer you realize those nice things don't get any nicer, whereas your pay becomes lower and lower compared to the market.

advice: Focus on Client experience and service, listen to the employees that service the clients.  Stop building multiple large groups that do the same thing and then communicate different messages to the financial consultants.   Increase investments to focus on decentralized community philantropic endevours
pros: Well recognized brand, strong investment platforms that allow you to utilize outside money managers, mutual funds and ETF's that are priced at competitive level. Strong Institutional devision with Graystone Consulting, that allows financial advisors the ability to select Graystone Consultants that are knowledgable in the $20-$500 institutional space.
cons: Company is not run by people that came from the wealth management.  Client experience is not as important to Morgan Stanley as it was in the Smith Barney environment.  Managers decision making capabilities in centralized and they branch managers have to manage up.  The firm has decided to build its own CRM and performance report which has been very challenging and costly.

summary: Great Culture, Great People, Slow Salary Growth
advice: Stagnant salary growth can be very discouraging. Even if someone doesn’t want to go into management, their knowledge, skills, and contributions only grow the longer they stay, and pay should reflect that. We are not ignorant of the fact that newcomers frequently start at a higher rate than veterans. For the veterans, pay isn’t keeping up with the market and I’ve seen many of my colleagues leave in pursuit of better pay.
pros: Morgan Stanley has a great culture. There’s a drive to do our best and find smarter ways of working, but at the same time it’s a fun environment and there’s great work-life balance.
cons: Salary growth is basically nill unless you get promoted. Bonuses are rare and except for the highest performers.

summary: Your Advancement Is Up to You
advice: Open communication and a sense of ownership are key to boosting morale and maintaining loyalty among the workforce.
pros: The firm is truly world-class and comprises the best and brightest talent in the industry.  There are many skilled professionals who are ready, willing, and able to assist you in your career advancement goals.  If you are aggressive, outgoing, and optimistic, you can get to know people and get yourself involved in noteworthy projects and initiatives.  The benefits are also top notch - medical, dental, vision, 401(K), pension, etc...
cons: The firm is very large so you can easily get lost in the rank and file.  In addition to focusing on your work, you must make an effort to network internally and get to know people in senior management.  Also, the firm is prone to volatile ups and downs due to being in the financial services industry.  Therefore, the chances of being laid off are ever present.

summary: Morgan Stanley Smith Barney is a world class company going through a lot of changes; some good, some bad.
advice: Flatten the hierarchy of command. Even the most mundane decisions or ideas can take considerable time to filter up and down the chain which can hinder those on the front lines from doing the best job possible for their clients.
pros: Reputation of firm, name recognition, global presence, research capabilities, expansive investment platforms, diversity of investment options, personal practice autonomy, opportunity for teamwork, good associate training program
cons: Lack of corporate culture (product of merger), inefficient management/decision making structure, loss of true client service responsibility over sales (this is a con of the industry as a whole, not just MSSB), limited opportunity for advancement, while there is opportunity for teamwork I for one do not feel like it is encouraged enough.

summary: Good Work. Bad Culture. Favoritism on Top - for Bangalore location based on my experience.
advice: No use of any advice to management, They are beyond advice. They are happy bosses, keep your advice with yourself.
pros:
Work is good, but people are involved more in politics then delivering the good software. Work complexity is not difficult but Managers are too outdated, for them its a rocket science. For a developer, who love challenging work, work side is a huge disappointment. There are very few people who are really working, rest of them are eating on their work. But every one looks like they are working 24*7, 

If you can do "Yes Boss", and if you are good at show businesses, self praising, you can easily survive. You can earn credits and wonderful salary hikes. You should be available for 24/7.  If you know the  so called "Socialization" You can easily eat with out doing anything substantial. You can easily postpone your time lines, after a while, the task will be termed invalid.  If you have developed a small working software , which would take your 2 month, you can easily eat for building that software for years. 

BUT 

if you love developing wonderful software, If you find difficulty in saying "Yes Boss"  to each and every thing,  If you lack that so called socialization skill, If you believe that your work and performance would bring you success in this company, Then No. .. If you dont keep your bosses happy, then  your work will be completely ignored as if it is not developed at all. If you check in the code, it will be returned back saying that its not complete.  Inside the company, every thing personnel. If you dont keep them happy, they would not let your code out.  if the functionality is critical, your code will be out by another person's name. If you dont agree for it, your manager would postpone that requirement to another release, another person write a small code may it be buggy or copy of your code or  what ever that code be released and  You would be blamed and questioned.  

You have two managers, One in India and one in US. Key to success are only the 2 managers, for whom you would be working. Keep them happy and you would be happy.  Keep them happy on ANY COST, may it be extending your business trip over weekend to roam around in Mumbai with your boss,  No matter if you are a woman,Your boss can still expect this from you. Or if you can not do this, then Be ready to write a wonderful code and copy paste it in your manager's computer so that he can commit the code by his name. Dont stay late, But go home and work from home through out the night.  Your boss can question you 7 AM in morning, for the task which the US Boss has given you 3:30 AM of India Time. when you would be sleeping, You are expected to complete the task ,  3:30 to 7 AM have 3.5 hours, which have been given to you to complete the task. By the time you wake up, your task deadline are over and you missed your deadline. so now you have to handle this situation with your boss 7 Am in morning. You have to keep both of the managers happy. 

All such things are open.  They have clear principle - "Work : you are doing for company, What you are doing for us?"  If you cant do even this to you managers Then be ready Pack your begs, You may survive for one year or one month.  depends upon your own luck. .. 

You can be fired by any of the managers, If indian managers nominate you for promotion but if that bring complexity to the US manager, that can also ensure your last day at the company. Means you don't know from where who can bite you, Don't do so good, Don't expect fast growth, just stay where ever you are. and relax.  

Lastly if you make them angry, chances are that they will not give you proper documents after your resignation. So you cant prove that you resigned. They some how want to destroy your career and wanna communicate this to your next employer that they kind of fired you.  There are many internal systems to complain but Everyone is naked in the bath..  

Keep your boss Happy, Live Happy, Work or Dont work, Just keep a statement ready  and you can survive.  .. 

One more thing - if you are not afraid of your boss, that is still fine, but if you are not afraid of your contractors or the service providers  , then you are in hell. They are clear - Employees can be sacrificed for the contractors , So actually no matter you are their client, but you better keep them happy, else you dont see any future here.
cons: Cons written above, They will pay you high, but then job stability can be a serious problem.  so make your mind before you take a decision on joining.  If you have any other offer in hand, Go for another offer.

advice:
Continue the management changes that are taking place currently. 
You say the industry is changing, and you want to be on the forefront, yet nothing is done to pioneer a new way for people to enter the business. Champion a new precedent for success from the beginning of a finance career.
pros:
One of the best wealth management companies in the business. Great investment options. Supporting management. 
Partnering encouraged. Ability to work as you see fit, or with all the help you could ask for. 
At the core they want you to be successful.
cons:
Beginning numbers are more difficult to hit than most wm companies. 
Managed money is the only option to see success. 
Not the best place for someone starting in the finance industry.

summary: Work Life Balance varies on position, mgr and projects.
advice: Don't take credit for your employees work. Give them exposure. Have managers actually work. The baloney of "working from home" is great....provided you actually stay on the calls and participate in discussion.
pros:
Great benefits.
Tons of vacation.
Looks good on your resume.
Ability to work from home.
cons:
When you support investment bankers you work banker hours. So that would be ALL the time. Weekends? Evenings? If you are building software expect to be on high alert if you're not working. 

Ridiculous amounts of meetings. Layers and layers of approvals to move at the speed of molasses.

Also, an eye boggling number of employees exist (and are promoted) due to how they speak of their work. Meaning, they're not actually doing the work. If you end up working here remember to nod and smile. (You'll be shocked at how behind some of the technology is. Also going along with the program is important. It will impact your compensation if you're deemed too )

summary: Good experience, but dont expect much...
advice: Don't go full retarded. Do not make decisions in a field you have no experince with. Good luck with paying the penality from the Regulators.
pros: Not too difficult job,  not much responsibility. Work life balance is ok, you do not have to do overtime, but it really depends on the division you are associated with.
cons: No flexibility. No recognition. No loyalty from the company, your are only just a number on a statistic.  They keep you motivated with promises to receive promotion and bonues which you will never get. Your knowledge and experience is not appreciated, they can replace you anytime with an employee in a third world's country, who can't even read.  It's a big name in the industry, but it is all about reputation, in fact it is absolutely not serious....

advice: Managers should probably have actual management training before they are put in roles with 25+ people underneath them. And if they are being trained, they need to be vetted much more thoroughly.
pros: Your team completely defines your job satisfaction. If you are on a good team, you'll be happy. If your team is mismanaged, it's not going to be fun. It's hard to rate a company this large because individual experiences may vary greatly. Compensation is decent, work-life has been decent, not many complaints regarding my day-to-day work.
cons: Middle management is atrocious. There's a lot of politics and favoritism to the point where if you aren't one of their stars, you will likely not even get a call back when you need something. It leaves many feeling completely undervalued and breeds disloyalty. I have been on both sides, as managers seem to come and go every other month.

summary: Highly political, employees are seen in dollar not human terms
advice: Clean out the reigning middle management who put the company in its current rut.  They got to the top in a time when the market was moving so fast that short term focus and cut throat politics were most important.  Now the operating environment is different and we need to think more long term and creatively.  Management continues pulling up politicians like themselves into leadership roles and stifling innovation while ruining the MS culture.
pros: Still employs highly intelligent and motivated people.  The highly complex, global environment and fast pace offer challenges and learning experiences unavailable in smaller domestic companies.
cons: Simply put, you're asked to give more than you get.  You'll need to work long hours and weekends.  Your personal life and academic interests will have to take a subordinate position to the firm's current agenda.  Politics rather than results are rewarded.  Innovation, dedication, and results are not valued beyond rhetoric.

advice:
Clear big picture plans are not enough if nobody translates them to medium/junior level tasks.
Also retention is becoming an issue and many people are only leaving for better money. Should try to keep them.
pros:
Challenging and creative tasks, great career opportunities and trainings.
Great CRO with relatively clear visions, who's also able re-calibrate his thoughts.
Many great people who are also socially active.
cons: The Risk department of Morgan Stanley was relatively small but grew a lot during the last few years. This growth made middle-to lower management lost in changes. Of curse new joiners have no clear idea what to do - the problem is 30% of people are always new. Also, the need to urgently hire so many people lowered standards.

summary: It is a wonderful Culture to be apart of.
advice: Keep up the good work. Make sure to stay compliant and continue improving the transparency. Continue to improve employee job satisfaction.
pros: MS believes in working as a team. They don't want star employees but rather star teams. Therefore, they will put in the time and training to help you achieve success so you can learn "the business". They also have a wonderful open door policy for the managers and upper management. Everyone is willing to listen to an idea or worry that you might have.
cons: There are so many departments at MS so you may find it hard to understand what everyone does. Also, depending on the position, if you are not an admin then changes are you will be working an average of 10 hours or more a day.

summary: At Goldman Sachs when someone says something you do it, at Morgan Stanley you begin negotiations.
advice:
Take more responsibility for the risks and actions that the subordinates underneath you take.
Have more vigilance and deeper understanding of the business needs and environment we currently work in.
pros:
One of the best known investment banks in the world.
Incredibly smart people at all levels of the organization.
Good quality of life benefits compared with other investment banks.
Compensation on par with other banks.
Great opportunities for training and learning.
Big brand name which stands out on the resume for follow on work with other financial institutions.
cons:
Long hours.
A very large hierarchical organization with little room for "the grunts" to provide feedback and show thought leadership for senior management.
Will always be one step behind Goldman.
Sometimes if you do not have the right pedigree you will not fit in.
Very political.

summary: A fairly uninspiring place to work as a technologist.
advice: Set budget targets and then do whatever is in your power to hold them relatively constant.  This will allow the departments to plan their workforce strategy and reduce the loss of intellectual capital from forced consultant roll-offs and regrettable attrition due to overworked high performers.
pros:
They have competitive salary and benefits
There is free coffee to keep you fully charged
Good communication tools for collaborating with teams around the world
cons:
The firm commands a healthy market share and profit margin which was built over 40 years of technology investment, yet the firm's management continues to stifle innovation with an overly-aggressive cost cutting plan across all areas of technology & data.

Within the technology divisions,  the firm has lost its positive culture and the loyalty of its employees resulting in high turnover and low morale.

advice: Do as you say and consider interfacing with the "little guys".  You might actually get some advice from the people you see what goes on behind the scenes.
pros: Salary is very competitive, Technology is up-to-date and people are generally nice (depending on the team you fall in with).  Able to work remotely in urgent situations or if sick.  A lot of room for advancement and very supportive of continuing education and tuition reimbursement.  My manager was very understanding if I had to leave for a class or training session.
cons: Typical banking-egos.  A lot of implied sexism.  Still very much a "boys club". It's a dog-eat-dog industry, so that's to be expected.  Some fairly unethical behavior that subordinates are expected to ignore.  Too much money spent on lavish dinners and events and not enough on employees.  Work-life-balance is encouraged but in reality, you are expected to be attached to your blackberry and laptop 24/7

advice: So much upper management being restructured all the time, causes a lack of continuity in institutional knowledge and could be resolved if they are willing to make significant change.
pros: good pay, fair hours,
cons: Behemoth size makes if difficult to get job done.  There is such an abundance of resources but so many no one knows how to navigate any issue in simple fashion.  Basically, one division does not know what the other is doing and there is tons of overlap that creates confusion not to mention the ridiculous waist of money since multiple teams are doing the same thing or working on projects that would naturally need to be aligned with other projects but everything is getting done in silos.

pros:
- Didn't have to work overtime
- Work was easy to do
- Good team (I got lucky)
- Pay on time
- Semi-decent starting salary
cons:
- No carreer advancement unless you go way over the top and make yourself highly visible (preferably be on the phone all day with some managers)
- The bonus you get after your first year is really the last bonus you get. Meaning that the next year your cash bonus will be exactly the same amount less as your salary got more. So every raise you get will come out of your bonus, making your total reward flat. (This was the case for me and my teammates as well)
- Boring, outdated technologies
- You need to familiarize yourself with uninteresting financial term and rules otherwise you'll be just a codemonkey. (I was a codemonkey pretty much myself, couldn't get myself interested in the whole business)
- Lots and lots of redtape

summary: Exciting place to work if your heart can take it
advice: Put some teeth in a 360 process that is truly year round.  Hold managers accountable for managing and employees for meeting goals.
pros:
-- Prestigious, top-tier financial services firm
-- Excellent benefits
-- Plenty of smart, committed, and competent people to collaborate with; lots of super stars to learn from
-- Strong senior leadership; leadership communicates openly and frequently with employees  
-- Very ethical and professional corporate culture
-- Plenty of opportunity and room to take initiative
cons:
--Too many EDs and MDs with god complexes
-- Less than transparent promotion practices
-- Too many reporting lines; 
-- Too many managers with poor leadership skills who tend to be more interested in deliverables and less inclined to develop reports
-- While training opportunities are offered, training is not part of the corporate culture

advice: If you value your employees, treat them well and the firm will excel further.
pros: Good company brand. Not sure why most of the employees are based in NYC except the ones in Purchase. Those Purchase employees are considered a tax write off casualties because many of them commute. It's a horrible commute if you encounter traffic from CT, NYC or NJ. Good people who work for the company and want to see the firm thrive.
cons: Morgan Stanley loves to give praises but not raises. If you get promoted, don't expect an increase. A lot of good talent has left the company because outside firms actually pay. The way the company makes money off of their margins, the company will lose a lot of good people and have to retrain other ones in a short span if at all. Many people resign as well because senior management has wanted to relocate certain locations. Why don't we uproot senior management and see if they like it?

summary: Sr Developer@WM Tech  for the past 1.5 Year
advice: Provide adequate resources to the project else you will see more attrition.
pros:
1. You really get awesome package if you negotiate well.
2.Top level management is really accessible and they listen to you.
3.You get an opportunity to work with some good talent.
4.I don't see management shows any partiality between consultant and FTE(I worked as consultant for 1 Year later on became FTE).
5.You will enough Paid leaves -23 per year and unlimited Sick leaves.
6.You can take WFH by informing manager even during non pandemic time also.
cons:
1. Some times it is really difficult to manage work life.
2.the projects are poorly resourced and management must hire resources to fill gap.
3.Management should focus on giving both Technical and Domain training.

advice: Trade off for pay for job security will prove to be a better business model and better training and advice. Builds the brand and retains your talent. You don't need to pay someone $1MM a year to be a talented advisor, but you will succeed at creating lazy privileged advisors that hold their managers hostage
pros: Paid to study, pick up business best practices, understand the business, good resources and tools, mentor ship opportunities
cons: Similar failure rate against the industry 90% attrition, scratch business is a recipe for disaster, stress, lag time , lack of support, must produce 150k annual gross production revenue before getting back end support, company is not oriented toward your success but your failure and pass along what business you obtained to pass along to senior agents in your office for retention purposes.

advice: Make promises that you intend to keep.  People deserve a quality of life.  No one deserves to have to stay 24 X 7 just to keep the company afloat.  The people who work for you have families, and are entitled to be able to spend time with them.  Keep the people who work for you happy, then you would get better productivity.
pros: The company name garnishes respect from others.
cons: You are sucked dry until you have nothing of yourself left.  They take the best years of a person and then throw them away for someone who is younger and fresh.  It is not what you know, it is how well you kiss up.  It is a peyton place, a company that has no soul.  They expect you to be married to the company.  Management will promise something and not follow through.

summary: Great people, Tough culture to integrate into
advice: If you selected point people at each of your global offices to be communications and culture carriers instead of centralizing everything in NY it would solve a lot of the issues I see in these areas.
pros: There are many extremely talented people to work with, and there is lots of opportunity for growth and career advancement in such a large company.
cons:
Going from a tech startup environment and culture to a massive bank that is highly regulated is hard. The culture has suffered and the amount of bureaucracy and red tape to get anything done is astounding.

Everything - and I mean everything is centralized to teams in their NYC headquarters and their very US centric viewpoint leaves other regional offices feeling like they’re a second thought at best - very poor communication from a timeliness perspective and very little interest in ensuring successes are celebrated .

advice: Be more open to feedback and communication from the rank and file.  Also, there is still a lot of work to be done in breaking down silos and facilitating communication and sharing across the different businesses and channels.
pros: Morgan Stanley has a great infrastructure, abundant resources, and the tools to help someone flourish and thrive in their career.  The people are also professional, knowledgeable, and open to helping you succeed.  The culture rewards hard work and collaboration.  You will definitely get back what you put into your work.
cons: There are people who can be abrasive, rude, and overbearing.  Also, senior management can be too quiet about upcoming firm changes or reorganizations.  During times of market turmoil, the middle managers were conspicuously silent and did not emerge from their offices or cubes.

advice:
Provide more training programs to CSAs
Have consistent management styles across branches
Oversee how much work FAs are assigning CSAs to be able to have a consistent work level across most CSAs, so that some are not more overworked than others.
pros:
Great benefits
Great work schedule
Good resources
cons:
Lack of training opportunities
One branch could be awesome and have a lot of support resources while another branch could have a less supportive management style. So you know which type of branch you are at until working there.  Worked at 3 branches, and the variance in the branch management styles is very apparent.  Also work depends on the FA, so FAs could be amazing to work for, others could be cheap and over work you. Hopefully you get a good balance, but you never know who management will assign you to.

advice:
They should separate Tech from Finance completely and sell the tech as actual Products than as a Service.
Tech doesn't get  the respect that a Finance guy would get here.
pros:
Mostly good people around.
Good if you are joining as a Grad. You will be pampered.
Brand name. One of the best in Finance/Investment Banking.
Tech is good if you are lucky in getting into a good team.
Good for people who would like to know/work more in Finance than tech.
cons:
Work life balance may.
Not good if you are not interested in Finance but in Tech.
Java developers command respect compared to others tech stack (.NET, UI, etc)
Not so good for Consultants. They are regularly removed compared to FTEs.
There's a Grad culture here that prefers them over laterals. Specially in promotions.
Advice: If you have 5+ experience don't join below Senior Manager, if you have 7+ experience don't join below VP.

pros:
Learning about different equity plans and stock options of companies. 

Able to work from home during Covid-19 is a huge plus. 

Team meetings are helpful to build Team cohesion and newest updates about any changes that may arise. 

Great team that will support you if you are in need of assistance, the people you work with are super friendly and willing to assist you. Especially when you first start out and are unsure about how to approach issues when they arise.
cons: The PSG is a customer service focused call center role. Most people you deal with are amazing but sometimes participants are not happy due to things outside of your control. Market fluctuations, Stock plan restrictions etc. Customer service skills is a must. However, the PSG team does offer great support when issues do arise.

advice: Hire a consulting firm to go into your wealth management area under cover for long enough to know what is really going on in your company. Have them go in as a new Financial Advisor with no tie to upper management.  Then, have them try to preform tasks.  The tools look robust and the support looks available but try using it.  The infra structure doesn't work.  Even employees with long histories of success in this field can not function.   Quality control on the information lines is not adequate.  You low chance of getting correct information.  Currently upper level management scurried off to lunch or golf with lower level managers, who know that it is not in their best interest to know what is really going on.  Integrity and quality builds market share and the absence of both destroys it.   The urgency is great.
pros: former reputation and investment banking, not investment management
cons: Don't go there.    Check out the significant employment law suits they have lost .

summary: Henry and Harold walk down the block.
advice: John Mack should not retire.
pros: Great Company, High Prestige, Great Compensation if sucessful.  Benefits are great, flexible schedule and high degree of freedom.  Senior advisors are able to mentor junior advisors to help them be sucessful.  Great technology platforms, and you can do your work in whatever way you see fit.  Large amount of autonomy can lead to sucessful practices.
cons: Long hours, highly competitive, sometimes everyone is too busy to seek help.  Large degree of autonomy can also lead you to large degree of failure.  Goals are hard to reach.  Large amount of trainees fail to complete the training program for one reason or another.  Second chances are given only in extreme circumstances.

summary: Terrible experience, if I could rate zero stars I would do so.
advice: My statement above says it all.  Office morale is abysmal, it's obvious they don't care about the support staff versus their all-important Account Executives (brokers). The way I was treated then thrown away is just one example.
pros: Cannot honestly think of anything positive to say about this company, sorry
cons: I had worked out my problems with local management but HQ decided I had to be discharged even though I still received my full unemployment from the state which means they agreed with me that there was no final offense. MS also unnecessarily reported my minor infraction to FINRA who then had to issue me a Cautionary Letter which is like a slap on the wrist does not need to be listed on my U4 as it's not a client complaint or anything illegal but in this politically correct environment no one will hire me now. I'm having to change industries which at my age makes an already difficult situation even harder. I thank this company every day for ruining a perfect work record & making my job search a living hell.

advice: Sell the retail business.
pros: Positive brand name to have on resume.  In the right position you can learn a great deal about the investment business with opportunities for advancement or overseas work.  Comp is competetive although it can be confusing as to how they came up with your figure.
cons: Retail (the former Dean Witter) and Institutional (the white-shoe firm you know of) are at odds with one another.  The retail side is in dissaray with old cultural barriers preventing positive change.  Many employees seem beated down, unappreciated and unknown.   Promotion policy is restrictive to # of years with firm and is challenging for high performers to be offered promotion prior to the HR approved length of service requirement.

summary: Cares too much about the bottom line to be a competitive employer.
advice: Realize the value of keeping existing employees, invest in those who are already dedicating their time to the firm.
pros: Employer annual match contributions to your 401k are excellent, which should be expected of a brokerage firm. Growth in my retirement savings has been more aggressive than with other employers in the past.
cons: The average employee never sees anything of an annual bonus, not even around the holidays. Operations is seen as gruntwork and viewed as a liability more than as an asset. Despite what lip service management may give, the lack of competitive salaries does the talking. In a firm whose business is money, operations cost centers are the red-headed stepchild. Hard-working employees are recognized with printed certificates or mylar balloons instead of any real compensation or bonuses. Employee engagement activities are frivolous and only serve as a distraction to how unhappy most in the call center actually are.

advice: Provide better growth potential and enable assistants to play larger roles with financial advisors.
pros: Morgan Stanley offers job security, nice 401(k) match, and decent salary if properly negotiated and if hired already having your series 7,66 or 63 &65.
cons: No growth potential for an assistant unless you want be an FA or a manager of some sort. FA training program difficult unless you join a large team (very rare). Managers are generally too focused on auditors and not on the people. Company culture is old and boring. Salary increases beyond a cost of living  are few and far between. Company expects Financial Advisors to pay for assistants bonuses to make up for the lack of competitive salary most FAs either don't make enough or don't think assistants deserve additional compensation. Some Advisors are great and compensate their assistant VERY well but they are hard to find.

advice: The firm needs a dramatic overhaul of its technology. With the appreciation this will increase expenses at a time of record-low ROE, the current firm is simply not sustainable. What management often overlooks are the unreported or less easily documented costs from dated technologies, including dampened productivity, lower morale, and ultimately an impairment on the firm's competitive advantage in attracting clients and top talent.
pros: Collaborative culture where employees from different groups are eager to help one another. It is not an "eat what you kill" place but rather more team-oriented.
cons: Management aims to run a process-oriented firm while the infrastructure is dated and technology lagging peers like Goldman. They are focusing on cutting expenses (i.e. compensation) but they don't have the infrastructure in place to not have to rely on attracting top talent.

summary: Top-Heavy with management that does little but resource allocation.
advice: Chop off a lot of the senior management that add little to the bottom line.  When most of them are gone during the holiday season, the company runs fine without them.
pros: Good and robust technology infrastructure
cons:
Company has an upper level management that manages technology with little understanding of what they are managing.  Most managing directors have not done anything hands-on in years.  

There's any army of PMO people who are highly paid to ensure that allocation are done properly.   The focus is on how to save money by outsourcing to India and reducing headcount.  One of the highest level Managing Directors in technology was a lawyer who barricades himself in his corner office. Much of the IT talent has fled.  Very hierarchical, almost with military rigidity.    

The place has become so cheap that they cut out bagel Fridays, even though most of the cost was covered by employees anyway.

summary: Lead Business Analyst for Middle Office Role
advice: Take risks on rising stars by rewarding them accordingly. Become more open-minded to change and technological innovations.
pros:
* There are lots of ongoing projects and usually a scarce bandwidth, so this can allow for significant exposure of skills if you put yourself out there.
* There are quite a few people who have 10+ year tenures with the firm, so it is assuring to know your chances for longevity.
