* Firm with a good degree of prestige when networking or job hunting (depending on the industry you are targeting).
cons:
* Terrible process of converting from a contract resource to a full-time employee. Too much focus on years of experience/out of school as opposed to the roles/responsibilities of the job and the skills of the candidate.
* Difficult to influence change for such a large organization.

advice: Realign goals as much as you can with your teams. They are diametrically opposed and because of this, the good advisors and teams are not reaching their full potential and you are losing people who lose patience with you.
pros: There is stability that comes with a large company such as Morgan Stanly. It is a solid name and an amazing brand which makes it easier to sell clients despite weakness in management. If you truly have your clients best interests at heart and can get around the bureaucracy you can survive and use the brand to your advantage. If you are entrepreneurial and create a good business plan, once you learn to bypass the corporate debacle you can really thrive, but this is a very large barrier.
cons: You are essentially running your own business, but management is of such a different mind set it is  debilitating and counter effective to the goals you are meant to be achieving. Management is the biggest con here. It is a huge barrier on the success of the wealth management side of the bank.

advice: I'd delegate the dress code related rights to the local management - they can decide which level of formality is needed in which department and when. Keep TAP graduates - give them interesting tasks and at least industry average salary and they won't leave the firm.
pros: After university courses the Technology Analyst Programme ads an extra boost to your knowledge and you can easily start solving any IT problem that might come up during your job. The corporate culture is strong.
cons: Slow adopting to the changes of the outside world. The dress code in a backoffice (where you never meet any customers) is an unnecessary pain in the neck. Starting salary is not bad especially after university but you can forget about raises afterwards.

advice: Raise salary, promote the hard-working people not the most visible ones who are great networkers.
pros:
Superb infrastructure (monitors, chairs)
Nice office location and design
Relaxed dress code
International environment
Good benefits (cafeteria, gym subsidy, language learning opportunities) but not salary
Good reputation
Budapest office is expanding
Lots of committees, social life
Mentorship
Some very bright and friendly colleagues
cons:
Not competitive salary
The best colleagues left after a couple of years, the mediocre ones stayed in my department
Monotone, droid type of work
Legacy systems and workflow
Lots of unnecessary meetings, constant repetition of firm “values”
Incompetent mangers above officer levels (VP and higher) who always speak endlessly without any content
Performance does not count when it comes to promotion, networking and visibility are everything, cut-throat, backstabbing and fake friendly culture
Diversity initiatives are exaggerated
High workload, unpaid overtime
Very hectic hiring and firing, frequent reorgs, cost-cutting culture
Open office
Glass door above a certain level in your career compared to financial hubs (VP is realistic, above that is not really)

advice: Diversity and Inclusion is just an empty phrase until long-time employees can bully on new comers. Utilize on new hires' experience and embrace their background and expertise. This is the way forward.
pros:
Relatively good pay, compared to the market. Good for young talents to start on a Financial career.
Good office locations and benefits, including WFH equipment during the pandemic.
Regular sports activities and community events in various topics.
High-quality professional trainings are available.
cons:
The work culture is just toxic.
Overtime is not necessary for the tasks, yet it is a sport and people compete in it voluntarily.
Junior colleauges think it is all right to organize their calendars full with meetings and then complain about it, because they see that senior management does this.
Work-life-balance is preached but not exercised.
Managers who are here for a long time can create a cut-throat enviorment and there is hardly a way out of it.

summary: Best investment banking employer on Wall Street
advice: Focus on ensuring worklife balance for investment banking employees
pros:
In short, great pay, great colleagues, great internal and external opportunities, great name brand recognition, relatively few strong and difficult personalities (relative to other banks on Wall Street).

Morgan Stanley has demonstrated time and time again a truly differentiated culture that empowers employees to succeed and to get paid well for their efforts. As an analyst, there is no better investment bank to work for than Morgan Stanley.
cons:
Unpredictable hours, long hours, sometimes subordinates are forgotten (when credit is given)

The standard issues with being an analyst at a bulge-bracket bank - working into the early morning on transactions, needing to break previously scheduled appointments, or generally having a difficult time balancing work and life

advice: Get more operational controls in place; stop the bleeding over bad trades.
pros: Lots of very bright and enthusiastic people.  Productivity is high, and people listen to good ideas.  Benefits are good, and there is the opportunity to travel to Europe and the Far East.  This is a place where the smartest can succeed, without necessarily being the loudest.
cons: Can be a sweat shop at times.  Frustrating dealing with so many outsourced departments.  Getting information on likely salary progression is impossible.  Despite work-life balance seminars, there is little sympathy for family events/sickness, and you are expected to check your Blackberry on weekends and during the evening. Can be a lot of pressure -- the work will be piled on until you shout No!

advice: Open your eyes and speak out for your employees. You are losing talented people every day when you are not on their side.
pros: Mature International Organization, Well-structured. A good place for new grads for learning technology/business/communication
cons:
MS is doing worse every year since 08. The reward was not quite correlated to the contribution you made. I was doing better in the projects each year yet getting fewer bonus. 

The firm was going downhill. Gorman was trying to get MS out of risky business then the return can't be too high obviously. Plus, Gorman was putting share holders' dividend more seriously than its employees. What can you expect you can get in the end?

advice: Employee advancement should be based on work performance rather than politics.  Happy employees can more productive.
pros: Great opportunities for advancement.  Flexible working hours. The company promotes diversity.  Exposure to institutional clients globally. Excellent employee benefits. Overall it is a good company to work for. But cultures may vary from department to department. Over the past few years, the trend is changing to a less pleasant path.
cons: Long hours. Internal politics can hinder promotion. Management is inconsistent in philosophy and unsupportive in taking the side on what is morally right.  The training is inefficient for tenured employees, and you receive more negative feedback opposed to positive. I am not sure that this strategy motivates workers but it does deter them from receiving raises.

summary: Good company to work for, still finding its way in the client advisory center
advice: Consider more interaction with employees, make sure incentives are aligned with what you want from financial advisors. More detail on future opportunities would be good as well.
pros: Good work life balance. If you produce, you can ultimately come and go as you please. Company does try to do the right thing for the client for the most part. Good place to start a career
cons: Top down orientation, a few bad apples will also ruin privileges for those who consistently produce. You really only start to see the compensation increase after a few years of being there, so it is tough as an entry level job, if you know from the start this is not your future.

summary: Soon to be a referral consultant
pros:
Become a referral machine or an asset gatherer and make a very good wage. 

Very little use of licenses required because compensation structure is focused / aligned toward previous point. 

Focus on E*TRADE's goals and you'll do well financially. 

Morgan Stanley has great benefits.
cons:
Morgan Stanley has placed a lot of focus on Morgan Stanley financial advisors to current E*TRADE clients. All marketing campaigns advertise MS FAs to E*TRADE clients, however E*TRADE FCs were never advertised to clients before or after the acquisition. 

E*TRADE FCs are now compensated to be referral machines. 

The writing is on the wall when the generous NNA comp grid is reduced. The writing is really on the wall when the segmentation starts. It has started in a hybrid manner... 

No path forward for FCs has ever been announced.

summary: Great firm with really talented colleagues
advice: I feel we are no longer elite and compromising on quality globally and not able to retain talented folks. We have stopped going to top colleges because of compensation challenges which is a shame.
pros:
1) Great team mates and a very collaborative environment
2) Individuals can play various roles even being the IT development roles. The firm encourages folks to take ownership & lead from the front by providing enough opportunities
3) Good IT- Business partnership and transparency for projects
cons:
1) Work life balance goes for a toss if you work from India and need NA overlap. Many overseas colleagues are conscious but there is always "someone" who isnt.
2) Retention of good talent is challenging and no longer great compensation
3) No benefits like food, cab drops(only after 8:30 pm)

advice: Should have a review of the seniors in the organisation some are old that they don't even understand systems, evaluate their performance, take action against the ones against whom complaints are raised in the exit interviews, look at the team attrition rate diggin deep down. Losing some good employees because of these seniors will devalue the organisation and ultimately lead to death.
pros: Good payers, good culture and comprehensive trainings.
cons:
Careless attitude of Senior Management towards the grassroot employees
They lay off people without even notice or enquiring about the person, just by word of mouth from seniors.
Total politics, performance of a person is not at all considered.
No work life balance.
I see this organisation not long lasting
Layoffs is a common thing here

advice: Stop throwing away your intellectual assets.  bring the SB people over and fill their jobs (which are going away soon anyway) with consultants, so that you do not lose the intellectual assets when you sunset large pieces of the overall platform space.
pros: Exposure to technology, opportunities for growth for people that are ambitious, prestegious firm reputation.
cons: VERY VERY consultant heavy.  With the merger in the IT space underway, senior management has literally outsourced the whole IT shop, instead of tapping inot the deep talent pool from the legacy SB side of the firm.  Senior managers at this firm more than any other would rather go crying to HR than actual do their jobs in too many cases.  A very political environment that rewards networking rather than achievement and track record for delivery.

advice:
It is the first company I have seen where Managers have, literally, no responsibilities towards developing their team members' career path.
There is no skip level meetings.
HRs are merely recruiters. 
If an employee has a problem and his/her Manager is not good, there is literally nothing they can do (of course, on paper they can but I am talking about practical life.)
pros:
- Hire at good package.
- Office is nice
- Global exposure
cons:
- Technically very good in certain teams while equally bad in others. So, it is very team dependent thing.
- Culture is again team dependent. For some it is average while for some they have "Yes Sir" culture.
- Implementing any new idea is difficult(not impossible though).

summary: Once top employer now going downhill
advice: If you don't listen to people who have something to say then you'll eventually end up surrounded with people who have nothing to say.
pros:
1. Tight knit and shared responsibility across multiple tech offices across globe
2. You don't really work in silos but NY used to drive almost all juicy projects
3. Review are well organised
cons:
1. If you are techie and you join MS, you have to aspire to become manager which results into you becoming bad manager and incompetent techie
2. Some managers are jerks. Specially a few sitting in London office. Bunch of them have formed group of old timers and play "you scratch my back and I will yours" with new hires who question their management style.

summary: Good place to run with your ideas
advice: Keep encouraging your employees at all level to bring in fresh ideas and allow them the freedom to pursue those ideas to the end. However, to keep the best employees around, you need to more aggressively reward/compensate them.
pros: You get to work with some incredibly smart and dedicated people. Management genuinely wants to hear your inputs and ideas for process improvement. If you have a good idea and come up with a some-what convincing business proposal, there is a chance that management will green light your proposal and even let you take lead on the project (even if your role is really junior).
cons: The hours can be long, and the work can be grueling during the busy season (usually around quarter-end) and holiday season. There are a lot of inefficiencies/wasted resource, but that's getting addressed with certain business implementations.

summary: Not a good place for career growth
advice: Restructure the career development and promotion process, and look into why some people are not promoted for years. Assist them to go up in their career development paths. Most improprantly, create a promotion path for associates (as you have for EDs/MSs --- distinguish engineer). It is discriminative that associates/VPs do not have a path to get technical titles (as distinguish engineer)
pros: good culture, multinational company, lot of support
cons: career growth is not satisfactory (takes years to promote, rt no promotion until quit). The pomotion process is highly bureaucratic . Also the promotion process is more targeted towards the management track (e.g., vice-president, executive directory), and no technical promotion path for associates. Salary increments/ bonuses are very low (not even keeps up with the inflation)

summary: Great analyst community and exit opportunities - not a place to build your career
pros: Great exit opportunities and amazing camaraderie among the analyst classes. The tech banking group will open doors for you that no one else will have access to.
cons: Layers at any place lead to inefficiencies. Some people in the middle are genuinely good-hearted and awesome to work with. You'll never have 100% exposure to them because of the diversified (and sometimes random) staffing procedures. Every single analyst who has stepped through these doors has had some awful unnecessary all-nighters or misdirected work. This comes from bad, insecure managers who don't understand what the actual requirements are for the client, and instead see you as a resource they can use to make themselves look better as they try to climb the ladder internally.

advice: clean up; review; develop not only a new strategy, but the whole approach to creating a truly efficient work environment where it would be impossible for a manager to 'hide' a talent, and everybody's pe3rformance/results would be visible and objectively rated. good luck!
pros: One of the most prestigious investments banks in IT area to work for; relatively high end software development; higher management willingness to invest in technology; relatively good peer-peer relationship (of course that varies from team to team, dept to dept)
cons: Still lacks organization and structure of the leader in the industry/field; real team work/efforts is not stimulated (read: enforced) enough to provide for the environment where the above will be inevitable; politics takes over competence more often than is unavoidable

summary: For an application developer it's a continuous learning
advice: It would be beneficial for officers in a project manager position to get training on how to manage a project and how to regularly communicate changes to the project plan to the developers.
pros: The IT infrastructure is give out of the box, you as a software engineer can focus on doing your job without needing to download, install and hack everything yourself. You can always ask your colleagues if you're stuck with something. There are many smart people with various backgrounds whose opinion you can ask for.
cons: Time pressure sometimes eliminates the time to create sophisticated solutions, but this is general with banks - the time to market is key. The time pressure sometimes also becomes visible on project planning - project plans are not updated in a timely manner, meaning confusion with deadlines and available workforce.

advice: Instill a constant culture of innovation and prove to your employees that Morgan is willing to be on the bleeding edge so their skills will always stay relevant.
pros: Morgan is a great place to work for technology enthusiasts. The culture is extremely collaborative. They have centers of excellence where different groups manage different technologies which allows you to go very deep and gain brilliant expertise working with highly talented individuals.
cons: Technology in banks works differently. It beats the industry on some efforts which actually make the firm money like algo trading while it could seemingly lag behind the industry on other topics due to a general culture of caution. So make sure you choose a team that deals with technology you love as you won't be moving away from it into something more recent anytime soon.

summary: FAA Program is strictly sales nothing more
advice: Use teaming with young FAA to senior FAs with a a clear written contract.
pros: Potential to earn a significant amount of money.
cons:
Solely Sales. Cold calling, Seminars, Social Networking solely for the intent of new business. 

Constantly prospecting no time to learn anything else. 

Teaming with senior FAs does not mean you will make it either.

No support from anyone. You must make it on your own. This is a fast paced cut throat environment. You must source your own leads to high networth individuals. Even if you make it through the 3 year program this is not a guarantee that you will be a financial advisor with Morgan Stanley. 

Training last about 3 months is this time period you must also pass your series 7 and 66. 

You have 6 months to stay within your sales metrics. if you fall out and stay out of tier for too long you will be let go.

Base salary decreases after one year.

advice: Implement a formal training program for support staff.  On-the-job training seems a bit haphazard for such a large, well respected financial services company.  Make some of the support staff either exempt, or at least approve overtime or provide remote access.  It's hard to be an enthusiastic, driven employee when one is treated like a high school student:  (Bell rings, go home.)  Registered assistants are the foundation and infrastructure to any successful practice.  Some want to work just as hard and as long as their financial advisors.  Let them.
pros: Sincerely nice people.  Employees have lots of opportunities for advancement.  Very accepting of diversity.  Very good research.  Outstanding alternative investments platform.
cons: No classroom, hands-on training for support staff--just conference calls with slides.  Client contact and operations software a bit lacking, but it's improving.

summary: Has lost some of its luster, poor strategic business decisions leave me wondering where this ship is headed
advice: Get it together with the overall strategy...acquisitions and divestitures over past 5 years have been a complete disaster.  Decision to grow a retail business which was unprofitable / barely profitable during good times, in a market flooded by low cost retail brokerage offerings is just mind boggling
pros:
-- all employees given a chance to contribute and succeed regardless of level
-- excellent opportunity for promotions
-- good work life balance and ability to periodically work from home (highly dependent on which group you work in)
cons:
-- terrible erosion in benefits package over past few years
-- some hefty bureaucracy in some areas
-- performance evaluation process not very well linked to compensation

advice: Capital markets education is needed and is received, but the sales part of the business is more important to a new advisor. Help with leads, lead sources.
pros: Education, training, friendly competent colleagues, allows a runway to build a book of business while supporting with a salary  initially. Other FA's helpful if I had questions on systems, investing questions and other.
cons: In my case and a my branch level, there was very little to no help with my prospecting efforts. Never called in by  my manager to see how things were going, no interest taken to my success. If you don't have a large network of prospects going in the ability to build a book in a years time and being aggressive in bringing business over, you won't be around very long.

jobTitle: Analyst - Fraud Operations, Technology and Operations Risk
summary: Horrible Management and no possible job growth
advice: Clean house and redesign the job; or lay everyone off and outsource to India. Team is rotten to the core
pros: Once you realize you can game the system, then you can basically do nothing all day
cons: Hourly. Management is horrible, cannot stop the attrition that has been happening, has no idea why people hate the job and frankly do not care. I have voiced concerns and been laughed at. Extremely condescending management and team leads. Started earlier this year and over 15 people have come and gone including people hired after me. Can easily master the job in two months. Absolutely no growth opportunities and that's why so many people have left. Management blames the Morgan Stanley integration but I have spoken to all the people who have left and that is not the case; job has not changed one bit since integration. I am going to be leaving soon with or without another job. Would steer clear of this position!

advice: Pay better- and staff appropriately you can’t experience over 50% increase in business and expect the same amount of people to do the work
pros: Networking, great exposure to industry leaders
cons:
Triple the work with the same staff and below par technology. Not a place conducive to young professionals with families. The only way to meet all the demands is to stick around until 9-10pm every night- forget about work life balance 
Below market compensation- my subordinates were making more money than me because they were entitled to overtime and I wasn’t as a manager- honestly should have stayed as an associate vs. getting promoted - the raise accompanying the promotion was pocket change compared to what I was making as an associate working overtime 

Long hours, unfair compensation, and an environment where everyone cares more about themselves than the team- no real sense of teamwork. Recognition comes to the employees that slave away - those that accomplish their work within a reasonable amount of time are seen as not doing enough

summary: [Investment Management] An OK place to start your career
advice: Your organization has grown out of its proper size a long time ago. Your competitor I've moved to a fraction of your size and still maintains a similar market cap. That says a lot about how much value each employee adds. Without a major reorganization and cutting out the BS, I don't see your company growing.
pros:
Brand recognition helps with recruiting afterwards.

Very good work-life balance, as there isn't much to do. For at least 6 months towards the end of my tenure here, I worked out 3 times a day and was still able to handle everything at ease.
cons: Some of the people I worked with were total garbage. Few people actually do the work, and most others are free riders. Even my MD was a free rider. I still don't know what he does day to day.

summary: Review of life as a private wealth management associate
advice: If you bring on new associates into the program, make sure they have the tools to succeed and help integrate them onto teams who are committed to supporting them.
pros: Great brand and reputation, many opportunities for growth, excellent training in New York, top notch benefits, exposure to senior management, and open architecture platform that allows the investment rep to keep a high commission.
cons: The PWM program for Associates is a mixed bag and has had a very low rate of success of Associates going on to make it as Investment Representatives. If you're not paired with a team, you're basically going it on your own, and it can be really hard to succeed that way.

advice: With how much money Morgan Stanley makes, start taking better care of your employee's health. This doesn't mean providing more discounted or free programs, it means lowering the premium for medical benefits. Also get rid of the stupid 18 month rule before you can transfer to a new role.
pros: Benefits like headspace and lyra are offered for highly discounted or free, as well as gympass.
cons: I was originally hired at E*Trade, but morgan stanley took over. Benefits that E trade were considerably better. My monthly premium tripled after the merger. There are additional benefits Morgan Stanley offers which are nice, but having a lower medical premium would be a lot nicer. Everything goes really slow here. HR feels almost useless. If you reach out to HR with a question they direct you to your manager and then your manager directs you back to HR.

summary: The merger with MS is a win-win
advice: - focus on transitioning our advertising to be Consultant focused. In our branch, the average industry tenure is 15 years. Fee based clients/planning clients are much more profitable than self-directed investors. Changing the perception of existing and new account holders of the full scope of what ETrade and MS can bring to the table would go a long way. I believe we will get there over time. I am happy a few years ago I turned down multiple offers to come here.
pros:
- very competitive compensation plan
- good benefit package
- ample vacation/sick time off
- good work environment
- The ability to leverage Morgan Stanley has been a big plus
cons:
- the client base is much different than at Fido, Schwab
 - It is a sales job. You have to roll with the punches sometimes

summary: Throw back to stock jockey years
advice: Read above!  Go back to treating employees as people and not something for you to keep your own job. Get back to core training for new reps and give them more time and attention.....not like 3 year olds.
pros: Name recognition is always a plus ... Very deep in proprietary products. Decent advisory platforms to work with your clients and in meeting their needs.
cons: HUge turnover!   Mgmt looks at new reps as dispensable items. Had three managers since being hired. Goals not realistic. Training is a joke.... Again, old school stock broker mentality... Pass your series 7, here's your desk..there's the phone... Now cold call!  Beware .. The merger with smith Barney has been anything but smooth. The technology  integration has been a nightmare.

summary: Might one day day be good again - Not now!
advice: Give your emplyoees the tools necessary to do the job.  Improve your long and mid term planning.  Be upfront and forthright with employees.
pros: Generally has a good reputation in the industry.  Compensation levels are comparable to other companies.
cons:
Poor leadership and higly stratified environment.  A great deal of emphasis placed on title and level.  Big differences in what you will experience depending on who your management team is.  Very insular and clicky - reminded me of high school.  
You will go through a very long hiring process.  Approximately 5 to 10 rounds of interviews depending on group and level.  Very hard to get hired from outside above the vice president level.  

There are many different of work life balance programs available, however, they are more likely to be supportive of women wanting modified work arrangements then men.  

In genereal you MUST be very good at navigating internal politics to survive and especially advance.

advice:
listen to your employees, especially when they complain about working conditions.
or just read 'peopleware' book carefully.
pros: good company culture - they try to care about you. number of of ways to learn: online traings, safari ebooks.
cons:
if you're not on business side and/or in NY/LN you're chances to grow or to get promoted are ±0.
the working environment is also from a previous paradigm:
 - open office
 - cheapest desktop: might be cheap on paper, but unflexible compared to a laptop, creates a number of problems ( the need of videoconf rooms, hard to retreat to some silent corner to work )
 - ms windows + office + skype in a one size fits all manner - even they're rather in the way of making meaningful work.

advice: Yes, advisors are your cash cows but it’s shameful how underpaid the “staff” are.
pros: Company name and reputation on the street is good. Benefits are okay but average across the industry. Website is above par
cons:
Constant meetings, new learning and “updates” to deal with. Management will
always side with advisors so no one has your back. Management assigns you advisors to work with and it makes all the difference in bonus potential not to mention the different egos you’ll have to deal with. Long career with firm (Smith Barney alum) seeing maybe 3% raise per year doesn’t get you much. New hires coming in making more in salary than long timers. Loyalty certainly not rewarded here. Local management makes or breaks your experience. Only avenue for advancement (locally) is to step into a vacated manager role (with the right licenses) or become an advisor.

advice: -As part of the commitment to mobility, improve HR capability to facilitate internal mobility across divisions, not just intradivision. Improve compensation to retain the best managers/maintain employee morale.
pros:
-Culture, coworkers. Can expect a fruitful experience work with a professional/results minded individual in most interactions
-Continuing education/ opportunities to learn about the markets and finance
-Management that cares, open door to discuss issues
-Professional colleagues, open-minded thinking to problem solving/project work
-Good work/life balance, flexibility on working from home where needed
-Great brand name
cons:
-Compensation is not at the level seen in other firms (consistent cost of living increases)
-Limited opportunities for movement across divisions
-Promotion process uneven (Perception weighs heavily vs. actual production, value of work done)
-Performance review process can weigh employees who put in a lot of extra work and are dedicated at the same level as those minimally invested in their job
-Bureaucracy, redundancies, excessive signoffs needed for inconsequential processes

advice: Senior Management should focus on work life balance and treating employees fairly.
pros: There are generally very smart people who work at MSCI Barra.    The kitchen is also stocked with lots of free food.  The computers are resources are very good.  The benefits are also top notch but you do not go to a firm like this because of the benefits.
cons: The management is poor and the managers drive out the young, hardworking people who do all of the legwork.  The firm as a whole has poured a lot of resources into risky proprietary activities that have hurt the rest of the firm.  Morale is low but better than other places.  Hours are very long given the low pay which leads to low morale.

advice: In the last 8 year, a lot of agility was lost on the IT side due to politics and red tape causing the firm to be a lot less able to quicly react and adapt itself to market change. In addition, there is a lack of interest in the upper management to pay off the tecnical debt causing a lot of hurdle to be in the way of new project. Cleaning up in depth the technical debt would allow us to have a much simpler ecosystem driving implementation time down.
pros: Colleague are great technologist. Get to see some very interesting technology.
cons:
A lot of red tape and politic (budget, managemet change, cross-divisional priority) cause a lot of project to crawl.
Often have to carry a large technical depth

summary: Best equities house on Wall Street by far
advice: Keep promoting people with character and integrity--it shows.
pros: This review is strictly for the equities floor; the bank is a big place and I am not familiar with other divisions. Equities, however, is a powerhouse, and more importantly, it is a powerhouse full of (for the most part) good, honest people who do the right thing. I started my career at Morgan Stanley, and it took me moving elsewhere on Wall Street to realize fully what a truly unique place Morgan Stanley equities is.
cons: It's a trading floor, so sometimes can be rough around the edges. And as with any big company, there can be bureaucracy and politics. Days can be long, but that's pretty much expected at a top-tier bank.

summary: Great technology shop, people management & development needs improvement
advice: I would focus more on people management and development and less on the illusion of MS being a meritocracy.  IT Engineering staff treated better than IT Service or IT Operations teams.
pros: Pay & Benefits package is very good for Financial Services industry. Working with really smart IT people provides a challenging environment from which you can learn a great deal. Global footprint makes for a 21st century multi-cultural work environment. Emphasis on excellence and achievement causes one to reach for higher goals and achieve them.
cons: Too many hours expected; the norm was 50-60 hrs a week. Senior Management had conflicting priorities i.e, everything is top priority. Management's time horizon was too short-term. For example, tasks that were know well in advance we only delegated at the last minute, due to poor planning and time management.

advice: Change the negative atmosphere. Stop talking about everyone, and I mean everyone, negatively. Toxic atmosphere. Lead as a team, lead enthusiacutallu. Actually give praise (recognize long hours/huge solved problems) where it is due. Grow up.
pros: Compensation, young people to work with, exciting day to day challenges, over time pay, pleasure to work with clients, beautiful environment, great perks
cons: Stressful is an understatement. 11 hours a day nonstop. Not sustainable. Judge mental management. Mind games. No positive feedback. Constant negative one on one “meetings.” Asked to give “peer reviews” of coworkers which are always fished for “things to improve on” aka weaknesses to have a reason for one on one meetings. summary: Morgan Stanley - good place to work when it's not in crisis.
advice: John Mack - great job. IT - stop the constant churn and adopt a consistent vision.

MS does its best to treat employees well, attempting annual performance evaluations, promotions, etc. Bonuses are typically good, when the fiscal year and business is good. They offer a solid benefits package, with emphasis on work life balance to compensate for certain things they can't provide being based in New York City (e.g., on-site childcare, health center for all employees, etc.). The people there are by and large very smart, accountable, and respectful.

pros: The benefits the company offers is well worth it! And I do love the company, they seem to value their employees at a high level. I’ve got good coworkers who I enjoy seeing everyday.
cons: The management at each branch will make it or break it. When faced with a team of advisors who rotate through assistants like daily coffee, some management finds error in the assistants without really seeing the actual issue is the advisor. There is so much politics in the backoffice groups and all groups for that matter.

cons:
People don't like to see ambitious people succeed and you have to wait atleast 2 years to move internally. 

Seek out training the street internally and use the 10k for tuition reimbursment! Make sure to use ALL company resources.

advice: take greater disciplinary action against people who make the workplace an unpleasant place to work in and maintain the cultural values espoused by not only focusing on diversity but the way people treat each other as fair and just.
pros: wealth management business is growing, excellent access to market research and insights, on-going Tech training, opportunity to learn about all facets of the business, treat clients as top priority, great service to customers
cons: management is not actively involved in making sure it is a workplace of respect and integrity. the firm always does the right thing for the client but not always for its own employees. certain advisers are very disrespectful and management does nothing to change it because the advisers are tied to revenue

pros: Some great people to work with. Non-health benefits are great once you figure out how to navigate them.

summary: A retail brokerage, not an investment bank anymore
advice: Stop focusing on reducing cost as the only route to profit. Every study ever shows that long-term growth comes from investing in your employees, paying them well, making them happy and productive.

cons: Compensation has been on a pretty steady trend downwards - double-digit percent cuts are not made up by the occasional "better" year that goes up maybe 2%. Opportunities for career growth have always been limited by a highly competitive environment that has gotten more competitive as management has chosen to flatten the org by letting go of people with more senior titles.

advice: My advise to management is to actually hire real effective leaders and managers who can stand their ground. Also make sure you compensate the CSAs well! Anything under 100k is not cutting for everything a CSA puts up with.

FAs treat the CSAs poorly. I had many incidents that I should have reported to HR. When you discuss those incidents with the manager they are very dismissive. Managers there are puppets basically and do everything the FA asks even if its unethical.

Morgan Stanley is not very diverse. They lack woman and woman of color in the industry.

summary: MS in a nutshell from an IT perspective
advice:
Enforce technology standards rigorously. Don't let people bring in 3rd party crap that hasn't been vetted by a tech team. Make build/release/test architectures standardized. It wouldn't be a bad idea to force everyone to use a single programming/scripting language either.

Create a point system so you can track your improvement. Yearly reviews don't do much other than ask you to give comments that won't be read and choose 1-5 on a question that doesn't make sense.

Make QA better. Hire better people. Make a better plan. I don't really know, but just make them better.
pros:
Lots of smart people who are very hardworking. They come from a variety of backgrounds and always give their best efforts.

Employees and consultants are treated pretty much the same. If you're doing any kind of IT work, everyone is pretty much standardized and work is delegated based on technology and business experience. If you want to get the "best" work, you have to know everything about it beforehand.

Compensation is good and also guaranteed. I used to work in an IB that didn't give me bonuses due to the small size of my team and my rank. MS gives you a cut end of story, but that doesn't mean it's good. Benefits are also good. You get decent coverage from the basic medical plans offered.

Depending on your team and nature of your project, the work from home policy is pretty lax. A lot of co-workers have families and commute into the city so sometimes they need to be home.
cons:
Work can get repetitive. Many times I find myself doing a glorified refactoring of poorly written or poorly planned code. You'd think there would be an extensive process in check to prevent poor code from going into production, but that's not the case. Teams need to enforce their own code review and audit policies and sometimes that's difficult when you are trying to hit big deadlines.

IT support staff could use some work. There are no doubt talented individuals who keep good notes and are very good at drilling down issue solutions, but that doesn't save QA overall from being a giant sink. I think the QA teams need to be closely situated with the developers and create their test-cases co-dependently so they can actually understand the software; otherwise, developers may as well be the first point of contact.

Ranking and compensation improvement is slow. There's a big bureaucracy in place for promotions and it can be very frustrating to work year after year without seeing any improvement. Getting ahead requires you to be very social which is not always the easiest thing to do.

summary: Gradually degrading workplace, mix of average to amazing talent
advice: Please Allocate travel budgets across teams fairly. It is demoralising to see your colleagues in some other teams getting a travel oportunity so often while some other teams hardly have any travel policy
pros:
- Some coworkers around you are awesome and talanted. World class!
- Technology is state of the art. What you take forgranted at Morgan Stanley is not even visualised in many organisations outside MS.
- Really global workforce. You get to work with people from all over the planet.
- Very good vacation policies. Comparable to the best in market.
cons:
- Lots of cost cutting
- Degrading quality of work in India.

- lack of many ameneties like a sufficiently large cafeteria, gym, breakout areas, etc

summary: Firm tends to get rid of employees of a certain age and/or salary in order to control costs.
advice: The wealth management industry in general is declining as clients move towards RIAs or even discount brokers.  Wealth management firms need better ways to differentiate themselves - and cost cutting alone is not the answer.
pros: Most employees are nice people. Decent work / life balance for the most part. Good benefits. People seem to genuinely care about the client.
cons: Entire divisions are eliminated and replaced by employees 20 years younger (or consultants). Salaries are below what are paid in other firms. The term 'Morgan Stanley Poor' is a common phrase. Many senior executives don't have advanced degrees & it shows.

summary: Great place to work, good technical work and plenty of opportunities around!
pros: Usually the experience will depend from team to team. But in general, the work culture is very good. People are mostly approachable be it at any level and there is a good amount of communication between employees and senior management. Promotions are mostly based on good performance of you and your team overall. Compensation is again related to performance. Lots of opportunities to switch teams and learn new stuff.
cons: The work hours may get long at times as the product is near its release. Sometimes the software deployment will take place over weekend requiring you  to work.  Work timings are dictated by region you team is working for - say US based team will have calls till late evening etc.

advice: I would say that if someone has a medical issue that you need to be more understanding to that person, especially if that medical issue was a temporary issue that included proof of medical condition with a return to work diagnosis that states person will return 100%, but know you need to make some special considerations.
pros: MS was a good place to work, as I had a boss that was out of state, and was pretty hands off.  The salary and benefits were nice.  Great people, diverse workforce.
cons: Salary, when compared to hours work per week would have been about $5 per hour.  Included weekends, and there was little recognition at the end of the year for those hours spent.

advice: Listen to your employees.  If they express a desire to do something else in the company, work with them to fulfill their goals.
pros: Decent benefits and and pay (if you work with a high producer).  Company name looks good on resume.  Great co-workers.
cons: Easy to get pigeon holed in this position. Especially if you are knowledgeable and efficient.  No opportunities for upward mobility at the branch level unless you want to become a FAA.  I told my manager that I was interested in a tech training position and his response was, "Don't you like being a CSA you are so good at it!"  After doing this for 15 years I find the work very boring.  Risk of limiting your skill set.

pros: The company is extremely employee centric. The individuals at MS are focus and driven. My partners work together to deliver the best possible solution for our WM clients and the Financial Advisors. The firm is very support of worklife balance which makes MS an employee of choice. The value of the company are strong and consistent across Operations. The Ops management team is strong and has deep understanding of the business drivers within Operations.
cons: The WM Operations systems are quite dated and require an overhaul. As such many functions are being considered for outsourcing (...which has been a similar trend across Wall Street). Management is aware that the salaries in Utah are rather under market and is working to address this historical trend.

summary: Bad comp for wealth management home office
advice: Back off, let midlevel managers run their LOBs and teams. Invest more in being best in class in technology and let technologists have more say in what that means.
pros: Lots of capital to spend on the business.
cons:
Prepare to carry out the bidding of the highest level executives. They will micromanage to incredible levels. 
One promotion cycle per year so if coming from a tech co or anything other than traditional finance, be prepared for a lot of politics and less results to influence promos. In wealth management, comp is terrible for home office employees. In general politics are a massive influence on the way the business is run with big FAs having a huge say in the way home office solves problems. Culture is nonexistent. People don’t matter.

summary: Morgan Stanley, a good place to work - if you can handle working for a large sized company.
advice: Not applicable
pros: Salary and benefits are excellent.  Company follows through on their committment to balancing work / life issues with real incentives and suggestions.   They also support additional training or education efforts with their wallet - not just lip service.
cons: Everything you might want to do - no matter how large or small - requires you know the policy, and follow it.  Need a new PC?  New PC arrived with 2 business days.  The staff to set it up (must be union person) - 5 weeks.    On the plus side - it's usually pretty easy to find the policy - very good search features on intranet.

summary: Felt like a sinking ship. Glad to move on.
pros: I was given tremendous flexibility and autonomy with my work - self directed and self guided.  Over the course of my 10+ years I had several managers who simply checked once or twice a year on the value I was providing.  All they cared was that they received positive reports on my work efforts.  Compensation prior to 2008 was good.
cons: Low morale.  Hard work and valuable contribution not rewarded.  There is a revolving door with workforce.  There have been years of large waves of layoffs in NYC.  I had 4 managers in my last 11 months; two were part of RIFs and the other two did not have an understanding of the products and processes I supported.

summary: Overall good company to get exposure
advice: Need to increase compensation to compensate for the lack of work life balance.
pros: The exposure and learning opportunities you receive at Morgan Stanley are great. I worked there for three years and learned a tremendous amount that will help me through my career. The people are intelligent, passionate, and collaborative.
cons: Very corporate and people are “forced friendly” if that makes sense.  Although collaborative it at times feels forced/fake so that one receives good 360 reviews. Compensation well below market compared to other banks and even other industries.  Difficult  to receive increases unless promoted.  It’s good to get the exposure and MS brand name on your resume and go elsewhere.  Long work hours. Very political. Lots of favoritism.

summary: Interning at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney
advice: Morgan Stanley Smith Barney is a great company to work for and compared to other wealth management firms can fare on its own. If there were any problems with the company, it would be that the name recognition of the company with the public isn't too strong as with other companies.
pros: Morgan Stanley Smith Barney had great managers who took the time to teach interns, interested in the field of wealth management, anything they inquired about. Whenever had questions or wanted to learn something new, there was always someone there to mentor me.
cons: In the office I worked at, the office culture was definitely more "old-guard" and very mundane. The average age of all the individuals working there was probably around 40 with only one or two young minds to bring fresh perspective.

summary: Baltimore office specifically - ok place to start a career, but not worth more than 3 years of crawling up the ladder
advice: Invest more in fresh talent to increase morale.
pros:
- Well-recognized name
- Huge resource pool seeing as it's a 50,000+ employee firm
- Potential for working internationally
cons:
- Extremely top-heavy
- Competitive, cut-throat environment on management level
- Growth opportunities come on an as-needed basis rather than as-deserved basis as would expect to exist in a large firm
-  It felt like there was a rift between the Baltimore office and the New York trading desks we were supporting.  It was pretty clear that the company moved those hundreds of positions to Baltimore to cut costs, and the relationships with the NY office reflected those undertones.
-  Entire department was underpaid and overworked to keep costs down.  Worked disproportionately long hours.

advice: Make the TAP program more focussed on giving technology training on various languages rather than evaluative on each of them after every week, since every one  can't be decent at every thing
pros: I attended the Technology analyst training program for campus hires. The instructors are pretty good,  and you get to learn and/or revise a lot of things. Also different company employees gave sessions on proprietary technologies  during the training
cons:
The instrcutors try to teach a lot of languages within 2.5 months training  as part of the TAP program and have weekly tests with passing criteria of 65%, which is harsh for anyone. 
The company is very strict w.r.t  company policies like making company data public and sending emails to outside domains, which is generally the case for any financial service company.

advice: Learn how to do your job and stop passing the buck.  I can’t tell you how many times I heard managers say that’s not my job. It’s shameful.
pros: There is nothing positive about this place.
cons: Too many chiefs. No accountability and they fee their clients to death.  No one wants to take ownership of anything and management doesn’t have a clue what is going on. The systems are old and getting things done at this firm is like watching paint dry. Every single thing at this firm needs to be approved by legal which totally negates the purpose of compliance.  Managers couldn’t careless about your career progression. It was one of the most depressing places to work.  Current employees are jumping ship at a rapid rate because this firm is poorly run.  I wouldn’t recommend this firm to my worst enemy and I would tell clients to seek other financial firms to save themselves money and time.

advice: Recognize people for their hard work, take leadership classes, and if things are socially unacceptable elsewhere including in your own home, then they are not acceptable at work and this should be addressed.
pros: Location.  Worked in other companies their systems of accessing docs and opening new accounts requiring approval of various departments are one of the best.
cons: Depends what group or area is worked for.  I understand other groups where as widely publicized that you can work from home and be able to raise a family my area was all about show, everyone stayed as late as the boss and when the boss was away of business trip they left at decent hours.  I was sick one day and was still asked to come in even though I had worked from home all night and was still able to be logged in.  Their computerized systems shows when your computer goes to sleep to whomever has you listed in the internal IM system, so they know that you are logged in working even from home, but that was not enough.

summary: It's a nice place to work if it wasn't for the yearly layoffs.
advice: Have some thought to reassigning people instead of laying them off because their department doesn't have budget.
pros: Professional, lots of smart people, good technology.
cons: I would say you have a roughly 10% chance of being laid off every year. So, the longer you work there the more likely it is to happen and it can be for no reason at all other than pencil pushing in New York. I have known people to get promoted one year, then laid off the next. There is no thought as to the knowledge that person holds because they know they can get younger people on a much lower salary. You will notice very few people over 40-50 in Montreal and even MDs can get fired.

summary: Mixed bag working for IT at MS
advice: Compensate your talented people.
pros: There are some very talented and brilliant people at Morgan Stanley...  it is a great place to learn and grow.  Like any large corporation, it can be a great place to work, if you work for/with great people.  They do foster an environment where mobility is encouraged; I know of several people who have been there for 15+ years in various roles over time.
cons: Their HR pamphlet speaks of a "work/life balance" that the company supposedly promotes.  In reality, in IT I have not seen that balance, particularly among infrastructure teams.  I have seen people work 20+ hour weekend shifts with no sleep breaks.  Also, it is very common in IT (more often than not) that people get promoted but do not get the salary bump to match it.   Also, year-end bonuses in IT have been few and far between, and not very generous.  I have seen many talented people leave for greener pastures at other companies.

advice: Right now management is hiring FAAs with no real background or drive in the business. Morgan Stanley's approach is to throw spaghetti on the wall and see what sticks when it comes to new FAA's. Tenured FA's feel sorry for the disillusionment these new hires will face. Morgan Stanley gives a very short runway to take off. You have to hit the numbers or your out, no matter your pipeline, your progress, or your business focus.
pros:
Build your own business how you would like
Open architecture in investment strategies
Well known brand
cons:
No guidance or support in building business
Very competitive within your own branch 
You have to build from the ground up but the firm is moving from smaller accounts

summary: Starting to feel like a 2nd class firm

I'm not going to do more than hint about this, as the MS way lately seems to be to require more out of employees without compensating them for it.  Shortsighted at best.
pros: Flexible hours and work from home arrangments
cons: Compenstock purssation and benefits have declined over several years.  The firm switched to a health insurance provider that doctors are reluctant to accept due to low payout ratios, and premiums and deductibles have increased substantially.  MEanwhile, pension plan has been erradicated, as well as employee stock purchase plan.

advice: Salary is pretty much what you would expect at the start but it would be easier to give raise and retain more people.

-My immediate manager are great and always fighting for their colleague

cons:
-Even though my team use recent technology and that my direct managers are really great technologist, it is obvious that most other team spend most of their time supporting old software on old stack.

1. Please stop politics 
2. Appreciate people verbally and on emails as well
3. Look at work performance  and skills for appraisals and not at input of unrelated seseniors.
pros:

1. Good Pay
2. Nice company policy 
3. Flexible working environment

cons:
Following are some of the changes  one may face at Morgan Stanley :

advice: Promote and hire internally for management level positions. Why hire externally and pay more when you can hire internally and not waste your analysts' and associates' time training new managers.

Excellent place to position yourself to move further into trading. Additionally, with good management, you can put yourself on multiple projects and expand your scope considerably.
cons: A lot of management is not good. Pay is pretty poor, and promotion works slowly if at all. You need to leave and come back to this company to increase your salary. Lastly, they hire externally too often for management.

Tons of unpaid  overtime and weekend hours is illegal if brought to light and more worker discontent continues. The 360 annual reviews is too overly picky and unjustifiable. Recently more focus on agile means more frequent layoffs for all workers who cannot match extremely high and painful pressure, sending workers to earlier death (See Karoshi and also Chinese 996 work hours culture news).
