 Be prepared for more revolving door and higher staff turnover rate should this continue , mark my words: your own excessively demanding and  incompetent IT managers shall seal the doom of your own company.
pros: Slightly higher than average annual fixed salary, and good health insurance benefit
cons: Stingy and abusive demanding managers,  frequent inter-team conflicts. long working hours with unpaid overtime and unpaid weekend hours,  cut in yearly bonuses,  stagnant salaries,  lack of clear company directions, outdated technology,  majority cheap offshoring &  AI replacement worker abuses.

summary: Dream company for the right motivated individual
advice: Hire more women and minorities.  The binghamton branch had literally none of these hired as financial rep trainees!
pros: If you are good at your job you will move up in the company and enjoy many perks.  It is all about how many clients you can bring in and the quality of clients (i.e. amount of money they bring with them).  You build up your own client list
cons: It's not for everyone.  You have to be a go-getting type of person with an entrepreneurial spirit who doesn't mind cold calling to acquire clients and build a book.  How well you do here literally depends upon you.  The salary is nice but most of your pay will come at the end of the year in the form of a lump sum bonus.  If you don't get a bonus, well then, don't expect to be with the company much longer unless you make some serious changes for the better.

advice: Treat employees with kindness and respect. Nobody likes to stick around in a job where they are demeaned everyday by bullies in powerful positions. Modernize and adapt to the changing needs. Do not tolerate brilliant jerks. Be grateful and care for your employees.
pros: Big brand and reputed, decent pay, financial stability and job security (unless you're a poor performer). Generous PTO. Flexible WFH policies and international presence.
cons: Employees are not treated with respect and dignity. Poor work life balance with deployments on several Friday late nights and weekends without extra pay or vacation. Ungrateful colleagues who are unappreciative and will jump to attack at any chance they get. Shouting and raising voices at coworkers was tolerated without recourse or consequences. Rigid HR and immigration policies, pretty useless. High attrition rate. The loudest voice in the room wins the battle.

pros: You can build a huge network. Practice English. Get to know  company philosophy and financial markets. Free lunches at expensive restaurants. Stable workplace. Salary paid before the end of month. Water fountains. Ice cream vending machines. A lot of smart people. Relatively good salary. Lectures organised time by time. Massage was possible at workplace. Sometimes friendly people. Free bank account at Citibank.
cons: Bosses have full control.  They may pretend to be friendly. You may judged superficially. Pseudo- democracy. Survival of fittest. Poor quality sausages. Long working hours. Low integrity (supposed to be a value in the company). Some people are afraid, distrust. Many people are smart but can have low morality and low empathy. Not always reasonable.  Unreasonable demands.  Not enough testing environment.  Could not work because of that .Some people can get offended too easily.  The boss threatened/bullied/ false accusations. (Not all bosses did that) Broken words, disinformation? (Not all bosses did that)  Office was too hot in summer. (That is not a general problem). Boss with extreme temper.

advice: Fire the entire mid level management in IT. They have nothing to deliver. Learn quickly and move fast before things become unsalvageable.
pros:
CEO is visionary.
Business is well connected with Policy makers so can survive any recession.
Business can pretty much manage without IT. 
Very good in managing PR and branding.
Excellent place to learn corporate politics.
cons: There are 2 organization inside Morgan & Stanley both terrible however one is worse than other. Your experience depends on which part you belong. IT is more like a toilet in a mansion. There is profiling everywhere & no place to dissent.  Management culture like my way or highway no discussion on critical issues. High velocity ZERO displacement workplace. Open culture is hollow & only exists on paper. Titles are just eyewash don't count on it it means NOTHING of course it comes for free from management point of view. Thousands and thousands of Executive/Managing Directors are there to just say YES BOSS with no voice of their own. Internal culture is SICK. Your have been warned join at your own risk.

advice: Hire from India, NOT from Cornell, MIT, Columbia and NYU, only to suck their productivity and lay them off. You have made this company cheap!
pros:
- Good Training Programs
- Flexible work schedule
- Ability to work from home
- Good Pay
cons:
"You will loose your skills, dignity and job over a period of time"

Career prospects in IT are bad. Morgan Stanley is an outsourcing factory. They hire people in India, transfer knowledge to them then lay you off. Most people in IT feel they are the next lamb of slaughter. This is how it works. They will introduce you to a few consultants, then they will ask questions about application and you will help them set up.. They will then be assigned new tasks and you will help them cross train. Slowly they will do the work and you will be on sidelined. After 6-12 months when management feels consultants know most of the application, you will be marked for layoff. Consultants then will be hired as full time employees at Morgan Stanley in India. My colleagues who have been with firm for 15-20 years are now training their replacements.

It is a terrifying situation for technology professionals. 

If you are an IT professional, go somewhere else.

pros: Some smart people there, especially within their field
cons:
WARNING TO WOMEN: I had a boss that harassed me on a daily occurrence for over 4 months, the details of which are definitely 'crossing the line'. I refused to do something that was against the code of conduct and borderline illegal and that was the repercussion.
I went through the appropriate channels, HR, asking to be directed to someone else in the Firm, etc. He wanted me under his control, and fought me and another Director when I asked to be transferred to another Director within my small 10 person team. He would often threaten that "he knew how to manipulate senior management".
4 months later I was laid off, and during the separation talk the MD on the team didn't understand why I was being laid off but signed off on it since my former boss suggest my name (if you didn't know that's how the lay offs work at Morgan, now you do...someone suggests your name).

advice: Often I hear Management (business development management) complain about loyalty when a multimillion dollar producer or team leaves to go else where. Funny, there is no loyalty from management, but somehow its logical to complain these titans have no loyalty. Why would they have any if your provided nothing more than an office and phone, which every other company is running over each other to offer the same (with a bonus upfront and contract)?
pros: Salary, plus partial commissions (25% of revenue) as long as you meet performance goals; which are impossible unless you have a book or are hired onto a team who will insure you meet your performance goals. Will pay you a salary while your studding for your licenses. If you fail you series 7, the first time you take it, your fired. So do take it seriously.
cons: No support of any kind. The interview is purely a sales pitch. Its your business. Do not look for any direction or support on how to succeed. The training is of no value unless you've never been a salesman; the training is exclusively sales training with no training on "how to" open accounts, build a portfolio, or basic investing (you will be left to learn that on your own). Corporate culture. Either you're in or not; if so, you must drink the punch. Very difficult to succeed. They will not hesitate in canning you; I saw four guys get the axe with no notice, just "today is your last day". When they cut you, that same day clients who believed in you enough to hire YOU and open an account with you, will be reassigned to senior guys. They will start calling every client the next day to inform them you are no longer with them. This is the made greed dash to take whatever clients you build while there. Every client I had refused to even talk to these guys out for a easy buck.

advice: Management keeps saying people are its most valuable asset but doesn't develop or reward appropriately.
pros: Great people - truly, they attract smart and pleasant people for the most part. The work is challenging, and it's easy to build marketable skills. If you can find a sponsor you will be promoted quickly.
cons: Managers aren't trained or coached, and don't know how to retain and motivate good people. Favoritism is apparent at comp time. For the money and hours, it ends up being the smart move to do a few years and rotate out of the company instead of building a career there. The company recently came off the friendly to working moms list.

advice: There is a disconnect between the type of people that Morgan Stanley hires and the type of people that will want to stay in the investment banking world post Dodd-Frank.
pros: Extremely profession firm that has embraced the correct strategy for the new financial regime post the financial crisis.  Morgan Stanley has exceptional people who work very hard. The firm's culture is strong and healthy for young executives and entry level employees.
cons: The regulatory burden has changed this industry significantly. While the risk taking attitude of the banks has been removed, the dynamism and entrepreneurial spirit of the industry has also been removed along with it.  Morgan Stanley remains best in class under the new rules.

advice: Fire the jokers that run groups for no reason besides they got grandfathered in.  No one cares about analysts and its becoming more and more laughably obvious.
pros: Good pay and lots of different roles in the division
cons: Literally all talk and no action.  FID leadership changed while I was there with no change in company loyalty or performance.  Completely political atmosphere that swallows young people if your family or college lax team isn't well-connected enough.  HR is a complete joke with no support network.  I would highly recommend taking ANY other bulge bracket or even middle market FID offer if you want to feel like you are doing anything or are valued.

advice: If you’re going to boast about company culture and “teams” then make sure you’re actually aware of what is going on within the teams....
pros: Opened a lot of doors for me down the road. Learned how to be proficient with time.
cons: Really no training program for new hires. I went from intern to CSA after about a year but was never any on-boarding for my role which led to conflicts down the road. Pay was bad, didn’t change from intern role. Team culture was every man for themselves and those in the FAA program would often times try to go around their superiors and hand their work off to people on the team who really did not have the time.

advice:
Think hard and ensure competent people are made managers /VP.
Please ensure , what vision  you set in town halls meetings , are understood and carried out by  Team managers . They are indecisive and lack skills to make decisions
pros: Excellent suite of technology stack . Employees seem very dedicated in general . You will find plenty of time to  learn and “survive “  even if you are raw on some skills . Upper management has  vision
cons: Very poor , selfish middle managers .all over  the floors .Incompetent to lead teams , and carry the vision set by upper management . No career path for tech-oriented folks

summary: Dont get fooled by the Morgan Stanley brand. Most people are not happy and only stay because of pay and the name
advice: focus on your employees and try to get away from all these customized internal tools and dont morganize everything.  care about people and dont hire fire all them time
pros: I've learned a lot of skills
cons:
*extremely stressed environment
*no proper direction for firm objectives and technologies to use 
*mostly internal tools used which makes learning and investigation really hard 
*very bad social vibe and people are always under pressure 
*layoffs can happen and cut you any day and it can be all because of the stock market
*a lot of meetings with over sea staff and sometimes you need to work outside business hours 
*not able to negotiate your salary after couple of years
*dont value their employees and senior staff and only consider them as resources

advice: I think top management has navigated the waters of this rocky financial environment very well and has done a good job of communicating their efforts for the most part.  However, there is a lot of confusion and dissatisfaction in the field, and the result is hard feelings.  Middle management is too layered and branch management is either micro-managed or ineffective as a result.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a strong and good company.  Opportunities are there, but because it is so large it is difficult to be small starting out, and you are often lost in the mix.  Be very concerned with your branch and its management, because it has a huge impact on whether you will get the resources you need to succeed or not.
cons: You really need mentorship early on, and if you are not in a well organized branch, or if you are in a branch where the branch manager is also in production (i.e., worried about his/her own book of business) you will not get much coaching or supervision.

summary: Morgan Stanley is a great place to work if only for the name on your resume
advice: Take less risk
pros: The best reasons to work for Morgan Stanley are the prestige and weight that the name carries with it.  Even as an Operations Associate, a middle office role, I found that the name, Morgan Stanley, at the top of my resume opened doors for me and gained me respect.  This was invaluable when looking to expand my career and take steps towards a more fulfilling career.  Morgan Stanley's management is also a plus as they are highly intelligent people who will do whatever it takes to ensure the best interests of the firm.
cons: Risky business model and somewhat arrogant attitude

summary: Industry Powerhouse who lacks negative publicity
advice: Focus more on the younger generations for they will be the most important piece for the survival of this firm.
pros: MS offers it all, a full immersion into the world of finance and all the great things to offer. I find my colleagues to be like minded, dedicated, and honest. I do not feel that anyone is trying to outdo anyone else and that there is more of a team environment then I would have ever expected. I highly recommend MS to anyone interested in great career growth and empowerment. A lot can be achieved with such a great experience.
cons: There is quite a bit of disparity in age. Having this can make it often times difficult to be on the same page with seniors who are unaware of changing environments and matters faced by the younger generations. You can find that unless you really push, you are often pigeon holed in your current role making it difficult to rise up.

summary: Traditional Investment Banking culture with exposure to many different areas of investing
advice: Pride of association has suffered in recent years due to overall performance relative to industry peers, so it's important for employees to see evidence that Morgan Stanley is still in the fight.
pros: Exposure to myriad aspects of investing, good training, supportive culture, good work/life balance.  Town Hall meetings allowed employees to feel updated, and the MS Today home page helped to "shrink" the size of the organization and make it feel more local.
cons: Challenges typical to very large organizations -- efficiency can suffer b/c of many layers.  Comp not always competitive relative to smaller firms focused on just one area of investing (PE, hedge funds, asset management).

summary: It's still the dog-eat dog, client-last, boiler room culture of the 1980s
advice: Ethics is not just a buzz word which should occasionally find its way into company verbatim.  Client first, always!!!
pros: If you are the family member of a senior employee, you will be set for life,  Compensation structure, even after the restructuring for FA comp, is still very generous
cons:
To succeed, at least at first, you need to put your own ethics on the back burner and be comfortable with hurting your clients.  That is, if you don't, you won't make enough revenue to keep your job.  

Now if you are inheriting someone's book of business or joining a team, it's a much different story.

Old style marketing expectations.  Dialing through the telephone book in the days of "Do Not Call Lists" does not work.

Other advisors, at least in my office, will stab you in the back if it means stealing an account from you.  Unfortunately, there is nothing you can do about it since they are senior and have certain privileges.

summary: I love you, like I hate you.
advice: India and China are the places to be, and if you are not invested here, you will lose out. Same goes for attracting talent at high compensation packages from these regions.
pros: The place offers you brillant exposure and experience. I loved my job and was happy going to work each day. The work environment is very good but varies from teams to teams.
cons: It's a huge firm and you need to work really hard and long to work your way up. Due to lack of workforce, you may find yourself working really long hours and taking more responsibilities than what you get recognized for (unimportant side-work e.g. in technology projects).

summary: For a huge company, Morgan Stanley is pretty good
advice: Salary should be more performance-based. Whether you are awful at your job, or excellent at your job is less relevant than the amount of time you have been at the company.
pros: Environment is encouraging and open, management is easy to access/talk to. Easy to foster relationships in various back-office specialties, even across the country, which makes solving problems and getting questions answered more efficient. Benefits are excellent.
cons: It is almost impossible to get a meaningful raise here if you are support staff. They will promise you one, then end up freezing payroll, then give you a couple thousand bucks the next year. Not a ton of opportunities to move up to other positions. They seem to transfer in Morgan Stanley people in the same position from other offices when something opens, and employees don't find out that the position was open in the first place until it is filled. Management often does not seem to have the power to fix things or get something done.

advice: None at the moment.  Keep up the good work!
pros: Decent benefits - 401k match (4%), medical/dental, great vision plan, 9 sick days, 3 weeks vacation after 3 years, 16 weeks maternity leave, supportive of working mothers (at least in my branch), backup daycare for working parents (I love this benefit!). The wealth management side of the business is in a much better place now than than it was 10 years ago.  Technology is always improving (mobile app, docuSign for new account/money movement forms, eAuthorization for wire transfers , etc.) and the firm has the resources to develop more efficient processes.  I’m very proud to work here and have no desire to work at another financial services firm.
cons:
-Can feel very bureaucratic due to the size of the firm and sometimes you feel like there are so many obstacles in the way of achieving your goal.  
-CSA comp depends on the generosity of your FA/team.  Some make base salary and others make well over 6 figures.

summary: Great company with a few glaring issues
advice:
1. We need to allocate more money towards yearly raises; the situation now is embarrassing and all of the attrition in my segment of the company is easily explained by compensation. How many people in my group need to leave and get a 50% raise externally before senior management sees the problem? The kicker is, when we backfill those positions, we have to pay the higher rate anyway otherwise we wouldn't find an external hire to do the job!
2. Messaging around return to workplace has been a complete disaster. Senior management (meaning CEO and a few levels downwards) appear to be completely ignoring middle management on this issue and we are being forced to execute edict after edict with which none of us agree.
pros:
Great culture, people, and prestige
Middle management tends to be excellent
Attracts the best and brightest
Exciting work and lots of opportunity for upward/lateral mobility
cons:
Compensation and raise structure harms homegrown talent
Top management has botched the return to work (after COVID) situation

summary: Luck will shape your experience here
advice: Pay your top talents at the very least what they are worth in the market. At some point, we all get tired of getting less money and we will eventually move on.
pros:
If you happen to pick the right group to join, then your experience can be awesome...at a discounted salary compared to other banks.

There are a lot of fun projects to migrate archaic platforms to a new technology stack.

If you're interested in learning something new or stretching your knowledge, make sure to pick the right group and right boss. You'll know it's the right group when people in that group are smiling and happy even when they are crazy busy.
cons:
Salary is relatively low compared to other banks. However, if you're in the right group, you have the flexibility to learn and do new things that you wouldn't be able to do in other banks.

There's a big chasm between employees who are working on legacy applications versus the employees building the new applications. It's sad because I like the people here.

advice: Please be kind and considerate regarding rto if the seat availability is not 100%, teams are outside located what’s the point of rto.
pros:
Good culture.
Considerate team.
Flexible leave policies.
cons:
From where do I start, forced RTO is apathetic.
1) Old tech stack, it takes ages to get things done. The Citrix workspace is somewhat slow.
2) No open source, not open to change or update techs.
3) Takes a hell lot of time for new hires to understand internal tooling, less scope for showcasing problem solving skills without open source systems.
4) Geographically diverse teams, one ends up with out of normal hours work trying to get hold of HK, LN, NY folks.
5) Slow promotion processes, no scope for mid year pay adjustments.
6) Internal documentation is crappy, it’s hard to understand or find things at one place.
7) Many apps to chat, many apps for meetings, this all feels overwhelming for noobs, but none wants to streamline the internal communication process.

These overall cons make day to day life and work frustrating and one tries to get out of here asap.

advice: Open your eyes,.. morale is low,.. all fake faces in the office. Reconsider your position as you might only know the business but lack people management. Your subordinate only have their own interest at heart.
pros: You do get to experience & learn your role thoroughly. Great systems & processes.
cons: Full of office politics where also once you're in Operations the feel is they don't want you to move elsewhere but Operations. Same Learning Development program running over & over again with no encouragement from management to take on any other course BUT operations related. All and everything seems to be about budgets this & budget that. Seems like the only people left over are the one that does not mind being a Robot or need job security to get ready to start family. Plus we're located in the middle of nowhere! Outside the financial HUB where back-office belongs... No chance to inter-mingle with other banks. Very anti-Social this location is. I believe other location is better than Shanghai/ China.

summary: It was fine - good place to start
advice: Some of the sales assistants are pretty talented but end up leaving because there is no real chance to advance. Not all want to be brokers but rather find other divisions to be apart of but they are not often considered.
pros: You see exactly what the brokerage business is all about and if you want to do it you know what you are getting into.  You can learn a lot based on who you work for.
cons: Advancement is tough when you start on the low end of the ladder. Hard to make it to another level unless a broker likes you. Even then still tough. Also if there is ever a problem and depending on who you work for I have seen SA be blamed for things they had no hand in. Easier for the low moral broker to blame someone else than eat their mistake. If something looks bad take notes and protect yourself - just in case you get pushed under the bus.

advice: I speak from a perspective limited by my experience. Although I did not have experience in the financial services industry before the recession, it is reasonable to assume that it impacted corporate climate; market volatility causes anxiety, regarding job security.  Allaying anxiety compels groupthink, limiting innovation inspired by coupling fresh perspective and collaboration. Management would benefit from more clearly defining principles, which prioritize openness/inclusion and factor both into situation assessments.
pros:
1.  Compensation fair; ranking in industry's 50th percentile.
2.  Bright/driven colleagues, who challenge you.
3.  With initiative, plenty of opportunities to hone financial services expertise.
cons:
1.  Disengaged management that prioritize rapport over sound judgment; favortism.
2.  Some colleagues engaged in cronyism, gossiping and overt smearing tactics.
3.  Some saw Information sharing as threatening.

advice:
Protect your existing employees rather than laying them off and then hiring new ones almost immediately.

Spending money on their severence pay and then even more to get the new people up to speed is not exactly the wisest strategy.
pros: Morgan Stanley is one of the top Investment Banks in the world.  The brand name associated with this company can take you places.
cons:
The revenues have never seen an upside since the bubble burst in 2007.  Although they offer competitive starting salaries, they don't increase like they used to. The performance bonuses are non-existent as well.

They have been laying people off in big numbers since the last 3 years which creates an environment of animosity amongst everyone working.

summary: Good Training, But overall you are on your own
advice: Don't protect big producers, everyone should be accountable and ethical.
pros: Vast resources available to you on their intranet.  Best of the best co-workers-all are highly educated and smart.  Management laser focus on revenue. You are treated like a professional and expected to deliver.
cons: Vase intranet resources hard to navigate to find what you need.  Some old Smith Barney training still on intranet. Compliance staff out of touch with the reality of doing business.  As a newbie advisor, little help from manager.  Advisor "Coach" only interested in the $ he made from being my coach. Many senior advisors are only $ driven and rip-off their clients. It's all about revenue, revenue, revenue.

advice: Keep doing what you're doing, keep making people happy, keep helping people grow, and keep driving toward automation.
pros:
Ops Management - Stellar management 
Autonomy - Freedom to run with your ideas (if they are good ideas)
Growth - Utah is a fast growing business state and it's looking like much of their growth will be directed to Utah
cons:
While my job specifically is not this way, I've heard much of the ops work can be monotonous. They are trying to automate much of that monotony out, but a lot of the work is still monotonous.
18 Month Lock In - One you accept a position, you are supposed to remain there for 18 months before moving laterally or vertically

summary: Great Culture and I was Lucky enough to work with a professional and great crew.
advice: Try to take in less numbers of FA's and train the ones that do come in on a team so they can start learning the business right away. Without a client base it can be a "catch 22" if you have zero investment experience.
pros: Very supportive on training . Alway's ways to learn the business. Wonderful culture within the organization. Really loved the people I was working with.
cons: High Goals to reach in FA program. But they do all they can to prepare you. Most is up to you . Getting all the exams passed can be challenging if your not used to doing this.

summary: The FAA program needs an update!
advice: Review the FAA program! Put some "spies" in the "coach meetings" so you can see if they are doing a good job with the rookies..
pros: Good name in the Street, good equity research. It's still a prestigious firm to get your licenses, spend a year there and get out!
cons:
They keep changing the managers!
My coach didn't believe in the program, in the lending firm capabilities, in the new rules in the industry....I don't know why they kept him as a coach!!
Also, cold call is such a waste of time!! We're not in 1985 anymore!! You will compete with hated robo-callers, nasty sellers...(who likes to receive a pushy cold call??!!)

advice: Bring some maturity into leadership. Grow up from the mentality of hire-and-fire.
pros:
Some folks joining from Indian IT majors like Infy, TCS, wipro may find salary lucrative.  
If you are laid-off, you may get few months of salary as severance pay.
cons:
Wealth Management Technology division seems to be too confused.  They hired an MD few years back and made him leave within 2.5 years because he was trying to bring power to Mumbai office and trying to create true leaders. On the US side, another MD was hired who was also made to leave within 2 years. Then, another MD was brought in his place who resigned within 1 year and then took his resignation back within a month. But resigned again after 1 year.

The folks at Executive Director level (which is equivalent to a Manager role in other IT companies) seriously lack team leading skills. But  they are not to be blamed because they just adapted themselves to overall company culture. 
Strangely, Management's ideology is to maintain an insecure environment because they feel that is the only way people will perform to their potential.  Do not ever raise concerns unless you have another job offer because you will be next in line in the firing range.
Layoffs are very common irrespective of company's performance.  Mumbai office management is still struggling to create a positive culture even after so many years. Senior management recently did a brainstorming and came to the conclusion that reason for bad company culture is the employees hired from Indian IT services companies and they feel folks from other Investment banks are better fit for their culture as they already have the habit of being a slave. So, they have now started to target those employees for layoffs. Very intelligent management, I must say.

advice: The firm is terribly unprepared for millennial at the work place - culture, managers, empathy, perks, empowerment, etc. Middle and lower management are in the weeds and management directives are either ignored or implemented half heartedly. Time to take a breath and ponder.
pros: Very smart people and can learn from each other. Well oiled machine with very mature processes and procedure. Culture of consensus, teamwork and respect.
cons: Parts of the firm are under staffed leading to a stressful environment. Career and pay is based more on politics and less on performance. Out of touch with the external world especially in the technology divisions.

summary: Nice run, but now is the time to run
advice: Open your eyes and ears.  Ask for feedback not just from your cronies, but from everyone.  Make feedback truely anonymous.
pros: Over the 12+ years I worked at MS, the best were in the first 5 yrs when it was truely a diamond in the rough.  Great place to work, great comraderie, everyone worked together toward a common goal.  No egos got in the way.  Now, egos rule the roost and only those who stroke them get ahead.
cons: Be prepared to work harder than you ever have without being fairly compensated.  The only way to get paid what you're worth at MS is to get a job elsewhere and quit.

advice:
- Be honest to potential hires: the tasks promised (fintech tool development) were nowhere close to the actual tasks (basic database manipulations that should have been automated eons ago)
- Having any longer term vision than the next end of month or quarter would improve processes immensely
pros:
- Competitive salary
- Great people
- Interesting projects to work on
cons:
- Crippling bureaucracy
- Office politics
- Upper management with short term vision only
- Completely wasted talents on time consuming but ultimately trivial projects, having PhDs do left joins for client-facing salespeople instead of giving them the time to develop powerful, useful tools that use cutting edge models and technology

summary: Great People leave their leader & culture
advice:
Improve the Management in terms of Technical & Behaviour.
Be Impartial & Transparent
pros: Leave Policy is good.But depends on your manager.Its very difficult to get approve at times as one is always over utilised.
cons: Just because its a brand Please do not join.Still Old Technology is used.All old methods & Practices.People with mediocre knowledge gets promotion while a genuine talents are crushed. New hires are over burdened with work. One ends up staying in office for long hours.Managers is never concerned about the employee staying late hours.Managers expects to work stretched hours ,Micro manage things. If you are away for 10-15 min Manager will ping you checking the ticket status.Lot of Mental pressure to close the tasksEven if there is no pressure from the client.There is no proper support & guidance from Manager.Technically weak & One will burnt out working here.Over Utilization of resources by managers.I was never peacefull even for a day.

summary: Nice work environment, friendly co-workers, but experienced frustration with lack of career path.
advice: Promote transfers between groups.  Foster an environment that retains quality employees by being willing to offer new opportunities for them.  Be more open to employees about how the company is really doing.
pros: Knowledgeable collegues, upper management made efforts to keep employees aware of what was going on in the company, some opportunities for employees with initiative, overall a good learning experience.
cons: What upper management would say didn't always match what was reported in the news and created some suspicion about what they were saying.  Integrations for past mergers and joint ventures took a long time and created operational inefficiencies.  Compared to other work environments, didn't feel movement between groups was promoted.

advice: Protect the franchise.
pros:
The typical employee is smart and hard working.  There is a good opportunity to learn from others.
Compensation and benefit package is good.
Good place to establish a strong professional network.
Despite recent events Morgan Stanley is still well perceived when compared to other companies.
cons:
The recent market turmoil is keeping many people on edge.  This isn't good for productivity or morale.  This tough times will pass, but it is unlikely that the financial rewards will ever match previous ones.  Despite that it can still be a rewarding place to work.
Work hours are long.  Promotions are difficult to achieve as it is a very competitive environment.

advice:
Improve the systems.
Organize less meetings.
Make sure that flexible hours are flexible.
pros:
Ability to work home-office 5 days a week
Salary is great compared to other local jobs
Overtime is not significant
cons:
No laptop granted, they send a mini pc+accessories, until than you have to use your own.
No company phone, you have to use your personal phone in meetings redirected, and everybody sees your phone number.
Really slow and old systems. Takes a lot of time of them to load and the system itself is very slow.
They develop their own systems and programs which you learn to use and cannot use anywhere else.
The working hours are strict, while they say everywhere that it's flexible. Its not. You have to work 9-18 and month end closing there are a few overtimes.

advice: Promote a model of skipping tiers in management one-on-ones with employees less than Directors.  If you really want to know what your management is up to, you should start asking questions to those that are not in leadership roles.  Give actual feedback from upper management to staff.
pros: The flexible work schedule and my salary compared to other companies is better than any where else in my area.
cons: I have noticed management does not even know their own department's day to day work.  Management cannot even perform any of the day to day work on their own.  I am one that believes in leading by example and this seems to be something MS leadership is seriously lacking on.

advice: Restructure sales and trading businesses (ie new mgmt, new structure)
pros: Brand name, global reach, innovation, solid research

advice: I would advise that meaningful on going training for its advisors would benefit the firm.

summary: Smart and Nice People, Need to care about Finance

business has a general appreciation for IT
pay

good resume builder
good community perks
the experience will still help you get your foot in the door elsewhere

summary: Financial Advisor Associate - Zero experience prior to this role

cons: Don't expect much help as a solo advisor.  The training program is watered down and much attention is payed to the top performers while the people in the middle are often ignored.

summary: Satisfied only for a short time

summary: Wonderful experience, but needs just a tad bit more....

cons: The visibility from Senior management at the analyst level is as expected. As an analyst you are there to learn, so not much action (respect if you will) is taken to ensure the develpment and growth of the analyst, deppending on the program. Dog eat Dog atmoshere off and on.

advice: Help your new employees to learn and understand the products offered, instead of just focusing on mock meetings with clients.
pros: Flexible schedule.  Most of the senior advisers are helpful if you go to them.
cons: The "training" was 95% about selling yourself and selling the company.  I was in disbelief as to how little had anything to do with financial markets, or the actual products offered.  The "training" in New Jersey was useless and basically just a time to party.  I would NEVER refer any of my friends or family to and adviser here now that I know just how limited their actual knowledge is.

advice: Spread the wealth - it's well known that the large bonus pools are only in the front office. Develop a more fair year-end evaluation...seems like managers have too much say in controlling people's careers (for better but usually worse).

summary: Go there - Learn stuffs - Leave after a year

Trust is missing from the culture.

advice: Treat people with respect and make sure FAs do too, provide real training and possibility for overtime. Dont just expect people to get everything done.

advice: Give your Sr Risk Managers an assistant. Easy way to potentially avoid the massive turnover in the role. Listen to the managers, they've been telling you this for years!

You either are single, divorced, near divorce or you have enough money to hire a nanny (if you had time to conceive a child) and to buy your spouse's happiness (assuming you got married before you took the job).

advice: This is a great firm, however, management needs to stop worrying about next quarter and worry about what the brokerage operation is going to look like in 10 years.  It's time to get back to the fundamentals.

cons: Financial Advisors are lately talking to their clients about the fact that the market as a whole has been focused on the macro issues and largely ignoring fundamentals, thus missing huge opportunities. MSSB is having the same problems.  The senior leadership at the firm is quite frankly outstanding, however, they have not addressed the disparity between the MS and SB offices whatsoever.  While spending their time worrying about the "big issues" branch support has fallen drastically, the average age of advisors continues to climb and their training program remains a largely ineffectual avenue for promoting "organic growth" .

summary: Great experience, lifetime colleagues, excellent brand recognition
advice: Encourage more hiring from within, lateral moves and mobility so that employees don't need to look elsewhere.  Try to encourage and reward fewer, more focused meetings and more execution.
pros: Excellent brand recognition, great way to start a career or move a career forward.  There are a lot of very smart people in the organization to learn from.  Good compensation package, benefits, vacation days.
cons: Morgan Stanley like any investment bank is not for someone looking for a 9-5 job.  You need to be able to dedicate substantial hours to company, but possibly somewhat fewer hours than Goldman Sachs or Citigroup.  The company size may be a negative for some people, because like other large companies Morgan Stanley has a "meeting culture" - there are a lot of meetings and it takes a while to get anything executed.  Getting promoted to higher levels is a bit political and requires you to have a strong network and strong champions/references.

Upon joining MS, I was quickly told that information was untrue, but was tempted with that carrot again when I gave my notice.  Everyone is out for themselves, don't trust anyone at Morgan.

advice: understand that your people are your most important asset. and focusing solely on the bottom line in an affront  to the hard working staff is not a way to run a company.

cons: Morgan's culture can only be described as the gladiators arena, where you are expected to justify your existence constantly to ancillary managers and vps who have no clue about how a team functions or what is required of the job. technology is poor. don't even bother discussing your career track. there is no loyalty to managers or staff by higher ups. Majority of NE staff have been downsized and replaced by consultants from India or off shored in some other way. no bonuses, paper tiles and promotion. pay became very non competitive while you were always expected to twice as much with half the resources.

advice:
Don't skimp on compensation for IT! You will have higher staff turnover and lose talent.

Spend more effort on making the office a fun place to be. A lot of the time, it's the new grads who show any social initiative. It would be nice to have senior mgrs do the same.

Make business training more available for IT and encourage more cross-functional training.
pros: From the moment you start working at Morgan Stanley you will be impressed by the number of top talent they have at the firm. For a large multinational bank, their technical systems are impressively agile and up-to-date. The employees clearly like working there and hardly suffer from a stagnation in skill-building. I was constantly challenged to push myself harder every day. So unless you're a cruiser, you might want to seriously consider Morgan Stanley Montreal as a very viable tech shop to work in.
cons:
Since the Montreal office is purely a tech shop, you will be separated from the business units. If you're looking to work closer with the business you will find it an uphill battle here, but not impossible. You'll probably still be on the phone with them (often way longer than you'd ever want to), and eventually if you build a strong enough case for it, you may be sent to business offices around the world (perhaps even relocated permanently), but it can take a while for any of this to materialize.

MS has become noticeably stingy since the financial meltdown (even compared to much smaller firms), so expect some budgetary politics to play in, including, infamously, the painfully noticeable drop in annual compensation.

If you're a pure techie, you may also find yourself doing so many things that are not part of your core interest, e.g. filling in lengthy documentation meant to gain senior mgr approval on any changes. Sometimes you may be wearing far too many hats, as well.

advice: Improve the messaging and transparency around the business environment and restructuring decisions internally rather than leaving it to messaging on CNBC - the current behavior and (lack of) messaging is driving down morale and creating a broad feeling of unease, uncertainty, and fear

summary: Great Company, poor program structure and benefits
advice: Construct a program that's actually designed to retain advisors.  Your attrition rate is ~ 80%.  You're one of the biggest, best run banks in the whole world.  You don't get 80% attrition from bad hiring policies, or simply because people are "bad at sales".  It's because you aren't willing to take the risk to actually invest in your associates, ie, fronting some REAL money their way so they can get off the ground. This is a relationship business, and relationships need time to build; so you need to make sure your advisors are given enough time and money so that they can build these relationships.  And don't give me the old "You need to bring your pre-existing relationships in when you start the job".  Last year, the average hiring age of advisors at your company was 25.  Guess what?  25 year olds don't have pre-existing relationships, at least certainly not enough to meet your standards.  They're pretty much starting from ground zero, with student loans, and minimal capital to spend.  Construct a program that's ACTUALLY designed to retain them.

Great, smart people regularly available
Abundance of resources available
Very flexible work hours (but as a financial advisor program that is to be expected)
cons:
Slow processes for some very simple tasks (aka bureaucratic), but that's to be expected at any big firm really

Compensation is unacceptable.  Inadequate starting salary for surrounding cost of living, and it begins to go away after 1 year.  There's virtually no aid in getting your business off the ground (they give you $260.00 a year in expense reimbursement, which is an insult coming from a Top 5 bank). They also take 60 - 80% of your sales, depending on your performance.  So they take the lion's share of your money, then expect you to then spend even MORE money to build your book.
