advice: You should focus on keeping good talent, the current strategy is not going to work.
pros:
Even though the firm is based in New York, we do really important and visible work in the Shanghai office. It's great to know that what we do actually matters.
The firm culture is great, working hours are long but flexible.
I'm very happy with my management line, I got strong support from them and good feedback regarding my work. My colleagues are smart, and the firm organizes special events reasonable frequently.
cons:
Being so far away from the headquarters is not easy, we have to focus a lot on visibility, to get the same recognition.
Salaries after a first few years are not so great, and even though firm management is aware of this, they don't seem to take actions to fix this.
Hours can be long, especially if you have to work with New York or Montreal.

summary: Good company, outsoucing is killing it
advice: Focus on cost cutting and oursoucing has reach extreme level, hurting moral of NY emplyees, this must stop and reverse.   NY employees felt they were not engaged, not being considered for strategic projects.  Management should not just paid lip service to NY employees, and focus on their growth.
pros: Compnay generally has talented employees, very good enterprise infrastructure and resource, which is very helpful for IT team.  Cutting edge technology, many in house trainning available, both online and in person.
cons: Management push to offshore outsourcing has greatly reduce quality of support to zip for both IT and business.  New York employee felt marginalized, and moral is low.

advice: This wasn't a traditional internship via the college recruitment process, so there wasn't a formal program or organized work process. My only thought would be to develop more of a clear responsibility for this kind of internship so there are no excess capacity issues in the future.
pros: Great exposure to the work environment of a large office. Great learning experience. Really helped me get a better idea of the role of a financial advisor.
cons: Had a lot of excess capacity that my supervisor filled with busy work... Nothing against busy work--I completely understand that part of being an intern is paying your dues and doing the tedious work that others don't want to do--but it felt like this particular busy work wasn't even work that needed to be done. i.e. my supervisor asked me to spend a day reorganizing our client management system despite the fact that they were planning on changing over to a completely new enterprise software system later that month.

pros: More highly technical colleagues than in the other 5 large IBs I have worked over. Turn over among mid level and senior manager is at a healthy enough level to maintain the culture the bank values so much: "doing the right thing". Heavy investment on technology at all levels: hardware, software and people. Critical to join a group where you get to prove yourself woking for a fair and technical manager that has a solid relationship with the business; it is the best way to achieve a sense of stability and fulfillment, and every extra mile you give will get recognized and valued.
cons:
Firm and organization wise, none. It really boils down to granularity, i.e. to the group you get to be part of and your direct manager(s). In my case, I'm very pleased.
Total compensation can be in average 25% higher in a top hedge fund, but base on my experience, the culture and commitment to technology investment at MS are very hard to match.

advice: Certain investment platforms are only accessible to larger accounts with minimum account values. If some of these platforms tiers were lowered it would allow clients more investment options.
pros: Morgan Stanley will start FAAs with a good salary and you have a great platform of investment options to choose from. The program provides some great training and puts you in touch with senior FAs and great trainers.
cons: When prospecting for new clients you are pretty much on your own. It would be nice if the firm could provide cold calling lists or other means to help generate leads. But speaking with other advisors or FAAs who have been through the programs they can recommend what worked best for them.

summary: Lots of Money (Maybe), but with Trade-offs
advice: Reward collaboration and give employees incentives to move around within the organization.
pros: Historically, employees at Morgan Stanley have been paid very well.
cons: However, there is no guarantee that things will get better for the financial services industry and many of the legacy business models will not work in the future. Unfortunately, management has not given any indication that the firm is planning on adapting. There is high employee turnover, and as employees gain seniority they are at increasing risk of being laid off. There is terrible work-life balance, especially at the junior level, when employees are expected to be available 2/47. There is a lack of information sharing across the firm, and it is very difficult to change roles within the organization.

summary: Morgan Stanley: Great pay, spotty training
advice:
When an employee is in training, she should be immune to problem calls; these calls sacrifice the  full benefit of the [expensive] training.
Allow employee to report a problem without fear of getting piled on with another task in an already overflowing in-box.
pros:
Pay was better than most wall street firms, not even counting bonus.
They really do make an effort to train their tech staff in new skills.
Easy to telecommute.
Managers are there in the trenches with you.
cons:
Always on call.  You will be called to handle problems when you are on vacation and in training classes.
Corporate culture discourages genuine friendliness between rank-and-file and management. Claims to encourage "due diligence" but the person who reports a problem gets saddled with the responsibility of fixing it.

summary: Good environment, but limited room for growth.
advice: Try to make the interns feel like they're actually needed and accomplishing something. I realize the PMs are busy a lot, but some insight into the industry or personal history would be nice.
pros:
Great resources, as far as information on equities go. I had access to a ton of research and was able to learn a lot through that.
Great building/office
Occasional Free food
Really nice people. Given the industry, this was a pleasant surprise.
cons:
Lack of performance review/feedback from supervisor.
A lot of my duties, like compiling and summarizing the weekly reports from various sources, I'm pretty sure were never even looked at by my employer.
Interning there is kind of a dead-end position. To actually get hired as a FA there you need sales experience.

summary: Good for new grads, but limited growth for seasoned ppl
advice: please create more opportunity to employees in shanghai IT office, if impossible, please raise more salary to skilled people,  otherwise people will leave
pros:
1, Pure english environment, good for english practice if you would like to
2, Training program is OK
3, Salary for new grads is attractive, but will become less competitive gradually after staying here above 3 years
cons:
1, tedious work
2, old fashion technology
3, no innovation
4, limited growth in career development
as a  IT guys, you don't have too much value added for the firm so that cannot get too much promotion opportunities here. shanghai office acts as a offshore development center and ppl here don't have too much exposure and chance to step up to front office

summary: This company was formed as a merger of two firms both crippled by the financial crisis of 2007-2009.
advice: Be human.
pros: It is still a good industry with solid upside earnings potential for the right person who will work hard.
cons: Poor integration of 2 companies' systems that Financial Advisors must rely upon all day long. Compensation changes for Advisors and new fees charged against client accounts for inactivity.  Lack of respect for Advisors doing what should be respectable levels of business and no understanding or  help Advisors who were impacted harshly by the financial crisis. A quote from a 30-year veteran producing $400,000/yr gross commissions and fees who has been with Smith Barney (now MSSB or MS) that entire time:  "I feel disrespected every day when I walk into the office".

summary: Decent, but too much required overtime
advice: Pay people more, don't expect as much overtime, hire more full time employees instead of contract employees.
pros: I get to work with great people (I love my team), there is a variety of work, lots of opportunities to work overtime, good benefits (I get 20 days PTO, 7 sick days, and 9 holidays).
cons: There is very little work/life balance. I know some people who worked over 300 hours of overtime, and it's pretty much expected that you'll get at least 200 hours of overtime. 10+ hours of overtime are expected for months at a time. Too many people are hired as contract workers, but are never converted to full time so a lot of effort and resources are wasted training people who don't stick around.

summary: Great coworkers but very micro-managed and dishonest workplace.
advice:
The salary of call center agents should be reviewed as we do a lot of work and take a lot of heat from customers who are angry, which is no fault of our own. They believe hiring more agents is the key, but upgrading the platform should be done to limit frustrated customers.

Limit micro managing to achieve better results from agents and provide growth opportunities.
pros: - You learn about equity plans and stock options, and an okay training system as they take two weeks to train you into your role.
cons:
-This is a customer service call center role, so it may not be for everyone.
-Managers are constantly on you for breaks and service levels.
-No growth opportunities.
-Always busy and displeased customers all the time.

The call center is micro managed by managers and so favoritism is very high and that's how you are evaluated at times. Unfavored agents are always criticized and micro-managed way more.

advice: Listen to what the developers say and give them breathing room to make the right decisions and fix existing, outstanding issues. Put more focus on the tech side of the company; it's the part that's holding the company together.
pros: Good place to start your career after college if you get placed on a good team. It's a global company so you get to work with people all over the world.
cons: There are a few SMEs who know everything regarding the legacy systems and business logic, but many are starting to leave. Devs are worked to the bone without praise. Working a global company means working ridiculous hours to attend calls in other time zones. Not much room for tech career growth, unless you want to become a people's manager.

advice: No incentive is there to work at Morgan Stanley except for good pay, if anyone wants to grow in their field, then this is definitely not the company anyone should go for, if the pay is essential for you, then you can go for it.
pros: Morgan Stanley, Nirlon Knowledge Park, Goregaon is famous for its back-office and people who are working at this location don't even have basic manners of how to talk with their colleagues. There are a lot of office politics to even managers do support. Very hostile surroundings and no one has any goals, they just want to come to the office every day and do that copy paste work.
cons: Morgan Stanley, Nirlon Knowledge Park, Goregaon's back-office hub, is one of the worst workplaces.

summary: Decent company whether you are on the sales, operations or other department.
advice: Consider paying the quality people well and not just give the typical 0-3% raises. I don't even think that's cost of living adjustment.
pros: The training if amazing as far as the technology goes. We have trainers that come by regularly and train us. The system was built by us for us. Our feedback on the systems goes up the chains and implements things to make us more efficient.
cons: Salary, turnover (FAAs) and paying good quality people a good amount to keep them. Every branch is different. You just have to ask around which branches are a fun and positive environment, while some are not.

summary: Keeping a job through the recession. Many people in finance don't like their jobs.
advice: There needs to be a better compensation strategy to attract and maintain talent. No one wants Morgan Stanley stock as party of their package.
pros:
High caliber employees with strong intellects, work ethics, and standards. Global reach and depth of firm is great advantage.
Human resources does a good job of partnering with companies and organizations for community benefits.
cons:
Morale changed after Mack stepped down and Gorman took over. Institutional side does not like the new emphasis on wealth management.
Like any bulge bracket, the company has an up and out culture that grinds many people down. Employees are continually being asked to do more for less in the industry.

summary: VP- IT in algo trading. Sweatshop... All stick, no carrot.
advice: Treat your people like you actually value them. If you aren't going to pay them, let them work 9-5.
pros:
You work with smart people- there is a comraderie in being underpaid and overworked. The work was often fairly interesting, and what you did mattered- you learn that all too well the first time you make a mistake. 

Its easy to get promoted. If you are reasonably competent, you are pretty much guaranteed to be a VP in 5 years!
cons:
Stress is off the walls. In the algo trading group, you have billions of dollars pushing through your systems every day. Thousands of boxes, dozens of strategies, tons of connections. So much can go wrong. Yet the pay is mediocre- most guys on my team did not get a bonus or got a token bonus (under $3000) in the previous 3-5 years. 

The IT division is 70% consultants. The consultants get paid on a day basis, so that means the remaining full timers get stuck with all the weekend work because they don't want to pay consultants. So if there is some kind of release, server upgrade, network change that needs to be verified, its all on the remaining guys- and that 30% that is left also includes managers, who won't be joining you on those calls. 

The red tape is torturous. On one side you have your managers and business counterparts who are all over you to get a change out, and on the other side you have this vast machine who  is pushing hard against you to force you to fight to get it out. 

Every year there is a new excuse as to why the bonuses were non-existent. ROE is too low, Earnings are up, but revenue isn't... its all a bunch of BS, IT is a cost center, and they aren't getting paid, regardless of whether you are some kind of server monkey or in the front office writing strategies.

summary: The pros and cons of being huge
advice: Morgan Stanley is competing with major tech firms like Microsoft, Google, Facebook, etc, as well as tech start-ups, for the best tech talent. The firm needs to educate potential employees about their world-class software infrastructure.
pros: Morgan Stanley has a superb technical infrastructure which allows software engineers to develop, deploy and maintain software around the world with ease.
cons: Morgan Stanley is a huge, regulated company (more the 50,000 employees) and with that comes all of the problems of trying to manage such a huge organization. For example, large amounts of time every year are spent dealing the review process. Another issue is the extreme control the firm must, by regulation, apply to their technology infrastructure.

advice: Life for analysts across the company needs to be improved to try to keep them from leaving for other opportunities (or going to business school).  How analysts and associates rate VP's and above should be given a substantial weightings during promotion discussions to ensure that analysts and associates want to stay at the company.
pros: Working at Morgan Stanley provides a great opportunity to learn from smart people, work on interesting projects, and take on substantial responsibilities
cons: Respect for personal time is pretty low for analysts and associates.   Groups across the company are understaffed and because no one expects analysts and associates to stick around for very long (on average), they are overworked while they are there.

advice: Get people who actually understand what marketing means in 2018 in positions of management, and cull the dead weight currently leading these efforts.
pros: The actual tasks you're required to do are simple (if not simplistic). You often work regular 9-5 hours. Most people are satisfied by strings of buzzwords in meetings.
cons:
The entire marketing organization has little to no cohesion. Groups are siloed to the point where people on the same floor—or in some cases, the same team—don't know the same details for both small and major projects. That, and the department heads have zero marketing background, and therefore are not in a position to actually create dynamic strategies.

If you want to build a portfolio-worthy career in marketing, digital content, or content strategy, look elsewhere. 

There's a reason many people stay at Morgan Stanley for 10-15 years: they simply don't have the requisite skills to go somewhere else.

summary: One of the best financial firms to work with
advice: We understand that we all have to protect the firm, but sometimes we have to think outside the box to put our clients first.
pros: There is not a financial product or service that the firm cannot offer. The technology is second to none. At the end of the day if you want to build a successful business, there are not too many other firms that offer what MS has.
cons: Because the firm is so big, it is basically run by lawyers with many managers operating from the standpoint of not losing their job. I miss the days when it was smaller and local managers could make things happen. No longer unfortunately.

summary: I enjoy working here but feel powerless on the big issues
advice:
Lack of stability about their livelihood spooks people like few other things. There are still some people worried about being laid off or replaced by Morgan Stanley.

Consider doing biannual performance reviews to maintain competitive salaries throughout the year.
pros:
Many passionate software devs who really want to make a difference.

Good social scene in Calgary with many employee-organized clubs like board game nights, chess club, fantasy hockey, playing soccer in at the park, etc.

Free beer on Friday.

Calgary office had a great location near Prince's Island Park and Kensington. Is attached to the +15 network for those days with really bad weather.

Teams are self-organizing and you can affect a lot of change there.
cons:
Some developers have grown complacent and do not want to improve, making working with them frustrating.

Managers are overloaded. Too many meetings and too many reports to effectively manage them all. Some developers have 1-on-1s with their manager much less often than others.

Senior to intermediate to junior developer ratio feels skewed. Difficult to find mentorship. Not enough oversight on implementation and code reviews for teams composed of juniors and newer intermediates.

Three years of focus on new features coupled with the above have led to insane amounts of tech debt. No communicated plan to pay off this tech debt.

Executives do a poor job living the company's espoused values. E.g. despite Transparency being a 'core value' a big change like the QA department being abolished was never communicated beforehand, leading to a great deal of stress and uncertainty and some high-performing QA analysts leaving the company.

Being acquired by Morgan Stanley, a company deeply involved in the subprime mortgage crisis, does not feel good. I liked working for a Canadian company and feeling proud of my employer.

Vision benefit is getting better in 2020, but paramedical practitioner benefit is becoming much, much worse if you visit two or more types (e.g. massage, physiotherapy)

Quality of your experience varies greatly depending on your manager and product owner. Good ones are able to help manage client expectations and your workload, while inexperienced ones lead to you feeling overworked and underwater.

advice: More operations training for FAAs instead of only sales training, hold senior advisors accountable for lying to FAAs, lobby for slightly more marketing freedom online, if you are going to restrict marketing efforts please hold those who break the rules accountable
pros: Morgan Stanley name, Base salary, learning all parts of the sales funnel, independence
cons: Absolutely ZERO training, thrown to the dogs on day 1, industry ethics are questionable, compliance is unbelievable restrictive (more FINRA than MS itself), people who break rules get reward while people who follow the rules get punished, management will always take a senior advisor's side in a dispute no matter how bad a senior advisor screws you

summary: A culture of high performers that recognizes & rewards the best.
advice: Remember what you have under you -- a strong company of exceptionally dedicated people, a culture that will long outlast you -- do what it takes to reinforce that culture, and we will get through even the most difficult conditions.
pros: It has a strong culture of excellence, smart people, and is a meritocracy; there is very little hard politics in the organization. The pace is fast and the work very challenging, and the people around you are most focused on getting things done, and done well.
cons: Can be high pressure some days. It's not bureaucratic but sometimes the drive for consensus and input can slow things down.

summary: Company is great, but the advisors are not always great
pros: The company as a whole is EXCELLENT with different programs to advance your credentials. The processing systems are very advance, which makes actual operation work seamless, accurate and transparent. Management for the support staff are always dependable,
cons: Some of the Financial Advisors have a huge egos, super type A personality, can be very cold, and think the world revolves around them. As long as someone can handle those kinds of personalities, you will be ok working here. Not all advisors are like that, but you cannot pick and choose who you work with. If an advisor or team has a high turn around rate with assistants, run for the hills!

advice: Focus more on the latest technology & make technology implementation quick & easier.  Too much scrutinizing behind every tech decision. (understandably as its an investment firm)
pros:
Open door policy. No bureaucracy or Autocracy, upper management works with you for all the policies & announcements. Your opinions are heard and respected. Despite working virtually, haven't found any issues in terms of connecting with management & peers. Senior Management tried its best to keep everyone in check & they surely prioritize the health of employees above everything else.

PS: I am just 18 months old in the system.
cons: Haven't found any yet but I know every pro has Cons, will update if I see any concrete issues.

summary: Stay away from the RFE Program unless you are a sales superstar.
advice: Make it more possible for someone to succeed as a financial advisor other than 3 months.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a very large company with alot of advancement opportunities.
cons: I chose to be a financial advisor trainee and the turnover rate for this position is nearly 80% and are basically given 3 months in production to make or brake an almost impossible sales goal. If you know alot of people with money you should have no problem. Managers also treat you as the statistic just to meet hiring goals. Great opportunity for the right person but just don't get to comfortable unless you are a sales superstar.

advice: Better organization and group leaders necessary, especially to incentivize people to continue to part 2. Start earlier in the quarter to fit the information in less rushed.
pros: This was a 10 week internship very popular among UC Davis students that I thought was a great learning experience. It combines the information from multiple classes into one fast-paced internship. Great name and knowledge on your resume and helpful in deciding if investing and finance is a direction interested in.
cons: The quarter I participated was very unorganized and demanded too much of full time students in such a condensed time. Culture and people was a strange mix and not the friendliest.

summary: A large merged company that is still separated after all these years...
advice: Be more honest with the staff and follow through on your promises.
pros: Big company with the ability to advance.  Located in many locations such as NYC, Westchester, and Jersey City, NJ.  Good benefits and a great stock purchase plan.  Many of the manager that I worked with had been with the company for many years working there up through the ranks.
cons: Even after all these year of the merger between Dean Witter and Morgan Stanley, there is still a big difference as to which side of the company that you work for.  The current title structure is very flat, there is no Assistant Vice President (AVP), so Vice President is the first title position.

advice: Don't let them take us down.
pros: Prestige, opportunity, excellence ... MS is a fantastic place to work, I enjoy what I do.  Everyone goes into work liking the people around them, and you are part of a team of performers.  There is a great deal of trust in what you get done, you can get more chances to do more important work if you show what you can get done.
cons:
It's the street, and life can be tough.  Obviously, you have to have the stomach for the hours, the brain to do figures, and character to thrive under adversity.

It'd be a lie to say that people aren't worried, but we'll pull through.

summary: Great name on your resume,great work experience
advice: Let CSA's study for Series 7 and 66 while they are at work just as the Broker trainees get to do. It will create an opportunity for all employees to be registered regardless if they are a broker trainee or not.
pros: The job is interesting and a great introduction to the world of investing. You will learn a lot from the brokers, the work you do and the processes that take place in Wealth Management.
cons: It's kind of a dead end job but there are a few opportunities to climb up or apply elsewhere. You're looked at pretty highly at commercial banks so you may be able to leverage that.

advice: As far as the face of Morgan Stanley is concerned, place more likable people in the sales roles.
pros: Morgan Stanley is a great company with an outstanding reputation.  The money is good & everyday at work is interesting in different ways.  An employee can really learn how the financial world is affected by working here.
cons: It is very hard to get promoted if you do not have several upper level contacts in New York.  Morgan Stanley only likes to recruit at "top schools" and often times the people that we get at the undergrad level start out making large amounts of money when there are superior people that already work here that could be promoted and given an opportunity for more responsibility.

advice: Provide Private Wealth Management teams with more structure on how to manage their book and keep up with regular client reviews.
pros: My group at Smith Barney proved a great place to get my feet wet in the financial industry and learn all about different types of investments and aspects of building a portfolio. My team was fantastic at giving me on-the-job training and giving me more and more responsibility as I proved myself in each assignment.
cons: The FA compensation is structured such that, at least for my team, it is in their best interest to provide their wealthier clients with the best service while mostly overlooking their smaller clients.

summary: Great FICC capital markets starting ground for first 3-5 yrs. Freedom to advance in sales or trading.
advice:
Be more transparent with employees
Better pay based on merit
Don't roll over into an agency desk
pros:
Opportunity to take your career in any direction you want within capital markets. There's a seat for every product with real front office responsibility and experience.
Great launching pad to land a more specialized role with higher pay once you figure out your career goals.
Work life balance and great people to work with
Take care of their people with comp and benefits
cons:
Retail focus... second in line to institutional business
Paid 20% below street (but still paid well)
Management turning desk into agency business and a lot of red tape

advice: Be open to fresh ideas; acknowledge the world is changing; suppress nepotism and instead emphasize merit.  This will add more value to the firm.
pros: Some very high-caliber talent at all levels.  Overall tone is supportive.  High standards, which is good for the career.  Not mean-spirited.  Not a sweatshop. Reasonably good benefits. Convenient midtown NYC location.
cons: Nepotisim and hiring of old cronies is more rampant here than at other Wall Street firms; this limits the potential of others who are not in the "in crowd.".  Only a very few women at the top.  Those who made it have either been around for decades or have met extraordinarily high hurdles.

summary: Only work here if you have an established book, otherwise prepare to fail.
advice: Give better training on what to expect from people not from the industry.  The training program was awful, not very good at explaining anything.  Asked for help multiple times, yet wasn't really shown anything.
pros:
Big well known name, lots of knowledge of stocks, bonds, etc.  
John Mack seemed very positive and cared for the company.
cons: Company felt too big, no one cared to mentor new trainees.  It is a very cutthroat company to work at, unless you know someone already, don't expect to succeed.  Be prepared to bring your OWN book to work from.

summary: Morgan Stanley - an organisation with talented individuals, mature processes, severe cost cuts
pros:
You will work with talented people, with efficient processes and have internal mobility options. 
It's a great place to start your career as you will learn a lot and it also looks good on your CV.
Good benefits and volunteering opportunities.
cons:
There is an aggressive policy to cut costs, with a lot of outsourcing projects. I have seen two salary freezes in 4 years.
Knowing the right people is key to your career development.
The atmosphere is quite competitive and expect to regularly eat your lunch at your desk (and get bad looks if you are away for more than 30 mins from your desk during lunch time.)

advice: If an employee comes to you to discuss career growth be a manager and lead the employee to the path of advancement. Provide evaluations and do it in a timely fashion. Provide guidance and highlight contributions and areas of development. It is critical to an employers performance. Employees should never be in the dark in their performance and contributions.
pros: Work-life superior, Military Supportive, Pay and benefits excellent.  Many opportunities for growth and moving around business units. Ability to work independently as well as within teams.
cons: High stress, evaluations not often delivered, lack of communication regarding career advancement opportunities.

summary: Very smart people, good organization, but room to improve
advice: Retain your talent through compensation.  Find the up and coming talent in the organization and groom them for future opportunities.
pros: Very smart people.  High performing environment.  You are challenged in your work.  Relatively good balance with personal life if needed, especially for family issues or emergencies.  Opportunities for creativity and innovation are rewarded.
cons: Very difficult to take the next step in your career.  Organization remains very siloed so hard to move to different areas and find new opportunities.  Easy to stall out.  Pay is nowhere near as good as competitors at this time.  Easily 20-40% under market.

advice: Compensation in IT is not inline with the street
pros: As a company I have found that they excel at creating strong bonds between employees and have definitely succeeded in creating an environment where success of the team is more important than individual success. The net effect is that the working environment is excellent and that cross department & rank discussions are frequent and frank.
cons: The company is often more risk averse than its peers so this can make innovation more challenging. Their compensation structure means that long tenured employees lose out and the only effective way to be baselined to the market is to leave (and possibly rejoin).

advice: Pay your employees what they are worth or there will continue to be serious job turnover
pros: Morgan Stanley has a great name that is recognized world wide. People are impressed with the name and since you work for such a well know financial firm it is easier to get interviews with other big name companies.
cons: Expectations are high and compensation is low. This firm does not look at you as individual human beings, they look at you as replaceable. They are also not concerned with customer service at all. They claim that this is of most importance, but actions speak louder than words. They do not reward for high levels of skill and customer service.

summary: Great place to start a career
pros: I came through the graduate training program, which for me was a big selling point. I received three months of solid training and it nicely prepared me for the kind of work I am doing now. Over the last few years I've found lots of opportunities to take on new responsibilities and become more involved in the business of a large IT division at a bank. The senior managers that I have interacted with have been of very high quality and they operate on an open-door policy.
cons: Pay has gone down over the last few years but expectations have not. Working with global teams over long periods of time can be challenging.

summary: Not at all what I was sold on!
advice: you pay us trainees pretty darn well, maximize the expense, don't just count on the natural attrition of 85% by year 3.  Brainwash new employees with why MSSB is so great and all that it has to offer.
pros: Paid Studying, potentially good name on your resume, pretty flexible time wise depending on your location, good benefits, Potential to learn a lot
cons: Mgmt has no follow through, a lot of empty promises.  if you aren't a self starter and can't bring money in immediately don't start at MSSB.  The training program is a joke, you will be lucky to sit down with your manager at all during training, very unorganized, sink or swim mentality.  Office dynamics can be very uncohesive, don't expect to hang out with people from work. don't expect any product training, and be okay with finding clients and then learning the job.

advice: I had one manager telling me to go out and look for new business but then I had another manager asking why we were not in the office. There seemed to be no communication between the two at a large office where they saw each other daily.
pros: It was a good entry-level job for resume building and the program taught you how to give good meetings. It was a sink or swim style that kept you on your toes.
cons: There were 0 vacation days, 0 days off, extremely high quotas you would need to reach so your commission kicks in.

summary: Senior management is great at patting themselves on the back.
advice: Pay your employees fairly. Cost of living has gone up, but pay has been stagnant for years. If you are raking in millions in bonuses, there needs to be some level of fair incremental raise for the rank and file employees as well.
pros: Free coffee. Motivational posters in the elevators speaking about how great the company is doing.
cons:
No raises or bonuses in the three years I have been there, despite having the highest possible performance reviews.

The CEO is an arrogant man full of himself. The level of disregard he shows to the employees is astounding but is rewarded by the board.

Any kind of promotion within the firm is by title only. HR refuses to bump up salaries equal to the new title.

Only way to get head from a salary stand point is to leave for another role.

summary: Low morale in some sales and trading divisions is hurting business
pros: Decent pay, good hours if in sales and trading, smart people, relatively stimulating work
cons: Plenty of office politics and unpleasant work environment, especially given recent uncertainty regarding the future of certain divisions. Excessive regulation makes it tough to do business, so volumes/pay much lower than five years ago. Low internal mobility unless one has a powerful mentor. Double standards abound, i.e. firm sponsorship of MBA programs no longer exists officially, yet some individuals receive sponsorship nevertheless. While this is not true of all divisions, the old Wall Street boys' club mentality is alive and well in some areas, which makes it tough to thrive, or even last, as a woman.

summary: Decent Company with great employee perks
advice: There should be more opportunities to get better transparency on management from employees in teams
pros:
- one of the top financial companies that are doing well recently, which means increase in bonuses each year
- maternity leave of 4 months 
- employee perks such as free access to prime museums and discounts in shows and movies
- great cafeteria with affordable prices
- sophisticated gym in the headquarters with discounted membership fees
- free flu shots available during winter
cons:
- depending on department and team, it can get very political
- getting promoted means getting people outside of your team to like you and consider you important

summary: Great firm to start your career at
advice: Brainstorm policies that give junior employees advancement opportunities beyond the standard 2-3 year analyst program.
pros: It's very gratifying to work with smart colleagues on significant and interesting deals. In many front office roles, Morgan Stanley attempts to differentiate itself from competition by providing complex and tailored product offerings  – it's more interesting work. The firm has a strong reputation and employees learn transferrable skills Mobility within the firm is also excellent.
cons: For many junior employees (tends to be true across finance), there is a dearth of advancement opportunities within the firm. Motivated individuals often need to find a next job outside of MS within 1-3 years of initially joining, which can be tricky if working long hours.

advice: Outsourcing or offshoring is fine if there are costs that needs to be cut - but don't expect the similar quality.
pros:
MS is probably the more envied employer (compared with other banks) in terms of culture. People/teams are less defensive & inhibited in working with each other, which really paves the way for working towards a given objective. Also of note, the staff spends more effort in fixing/preventing problems as opposed fault-finding and passing the blame.

Also helps that tech is good. And of course, the widely recognised/respected brand name.
cons:
Management: A slightly more hands-on upper management and better-trained middle management - less BS and/or being more straightforward would be good too.

Tech: not every tool/system actually solves a problem, but in fact causes more.

pros:
-People are very intelligent and competent
-Opportunities for a lot of mobility to/from different departments
-Given a lot of responsibility
-Very open/welcoming culture for new hires, even in a virtual work environment
-Respected brand name
-Good benefits for a first job
-Puts a lot of emphasis on diversity and inclusion (with a lot of opportunities to meet others through clubs, scholarships, leadership opportunities, etc.)
cons:
-Pay is below market (not that important if you are just starting out but keep in mind)
-Mobility is great, but have heard from some it is easier to leave MS and come back to a different department if you really want to change due to bureaucracy
-Some positions are only available in NY at headquarters

summary: If you are looking for work-life balance this is the place.
advice: Needs better ways to move up the ladder.
pros: The best thing about Morgan Stanley is the work-life balance and there's no micromanagement.  The manager is very lenient about the times you come in as a Technology associate as long as you get the work done.  You also get a company blackberry which has its own pros and cons.
cons: Quite a lot of politics so you really have to kiss ass if you want to move up faster.  Generally the people are smart but to really get things done you need connections or people will move at a snail's pace.

summary: Great Company, just a few but's
advice: Cut down waste. Be result oriented in the staff support department. If a expensive project did not bear fruit, that has to be reflected on that project sponsor's record.
pros: Great team culture. Learn a lot of different aspect of equity market. The company is so deep in many areas. Say you need IT support in a python package or you need to setup approval system for some resources, you can expert help after writing a few emails.
cons: As you climb the ladder, there are a lot of politics. I feel higher up sometime value loyalty way over abilities. Another thing is that there is waste in the company, sometime i see consultants are hire for not very good reason.

summary: I worked as a financial advisor associate. Base is $55k that goes down towards end of 3 year program.  Lots of upside.
advice: Encourage teaming of younger advisors with senior advisors who are actually willing to help. Improve firms technological capabilities.
pros: Plenty of opportunities to increase compensation. You have the freedom to work whichever, wherever and wherever you want. Lots of resources at the firm to assist in meeting goals.
cons: Challenging career path nowadays. Price compression and increased regulatory oversight allows for less compensation in some regards. Competition is Fierce.

summary: Look through the curtains and change your mind...its ok.
advice: Encourage work life balance especially since the big money years are over. We as employees need to be compensated with something.
pros: The only reason to work at firm like this is to know that you have a job in these trying times. The benefits are great but you need them because with hours you work getting sick will become the norm.
cons: You will sacrifice you personal life, family time, outside interests, and possibly your health working long stressful hours in this environment. This may not seem like much but if once in you realize that you are not a "culture" fit you may really hate it.

advice: Evangelize technology skills, and software craftsmanship. Try to improve CI, DevOps, CD where it makes sense. Promote people who make the right decisions and who are competent all around, rather than those who yell the loudest.
pros: Lots of room to grow up. It is a huge organization, lateral moves to different teams and projects are always possible. Suite of developer productivity tools means less time solving IT issues, and more time solving business problems
cons: Very clearly a bank in culture. Technology adoption moves slowly, although they have been trying to improve this. You'll encounter lots managers who have little-to-no tech skills. Once past VP, keeping abreast of technology trends seems to be looked down upon

advice: Raise salary or stop expecting the best talented people.  Provide clear growth paths to your personnel - it's not at all obvious what needs to be done to gain promotions.  And coffee with some MD for 15 minutes with 20 people doesn't help.
pros: Come in, do your job, go home.  Hours are reasonable (8:30-6), so this place is good for people with children who want to go home to their wife.
cons: Slow promotions, tiny bonuses, little opportunity for advancement.  But I was working in commodities, which is nearly closed (whole sub-departments are sold off or shut down).

summary: As an FAA, you are required to take and pass all exams, and bring in and manage 3-5 MM annually to keep your seat.
pros: They provide you with plenty of access, and equipment to get the job done, they don't care whether you come or go, as long as you produce
cons: Don't dare asking them for help, as you won't get it. Because they only care about the money you bring in, they don't really care too much on how you're doing day to day

advice: Sr. Management needs to enable a change to this common self-promoting agenda and promote those that are consistently running lean teams that return on investment rather than promoting those that are an obvious cost impediment to the Business.  Promote those that consider low cost high ROI as opposed to those running empires that don't add value.  Automate using current technologies - taking advantage of what is available today.  This will meet your "Innovation" goals.
pros: Good hard working employees that put their trust in their performance.
cons: Extensive hires to meet Exec. Dir.'s agenda of having large team of reports enabling their advancement.  This is followed by reduction in staff, thus presenting to Sr. Leadership cost savings to further support personal advancement agendas.  No automation in mind because it would defeat building a large team.  Too many unnecessary manual processes.

summary: Fair starting place for a quant
pros: Good opportonuties as a starting quant, multicultural environment with a lot of good industry examples and practices if someone walks with eyes open. There are a lot of different courses (IT, finance, foreign language, soft skill, management). Good working from home possibilities and infrastructure. Good company culture and quality of life with people working around.
cons: Work is sometimes really stressful. Management, especially on the London side is awful, several ppl there do not know their job and the direction they want to lead their team and department. The salary is now the absolute lowest compared to the other similar companies and positions in Budapest, so attrition is extremely high in almost every department I can see.

advice: Compensate more towards the lower end, they are a vital part to the company.  Higher management does not seem to take care of them.
pros: Working for a top name company has a lot of perks and recognition.  It is also a good stepping stone in case switching companies and having Morgan Stanley on the resume.
cons: Salary is not great, seems pretty low in the start.  Compensation is laughable at the start of your career, but comparing with others who has been there a while and what they make would give a motivation to stay.  Yearly-review bonuses are also a joke, comparing to others in companies in the same industry.

advice: Re-evaluate the pay and benefits of everyone, including officer-level and those below, and including all departments regardless of whether it's sales & trading, operations, legal, or finance.  We need to make this at least close to our competitors if we want to retain top talent.across all our areas.
pros: Opportunities to advance internally are definitely available to those who work hard and take ownership of their own professional development.  Knowledge sharing is also definitely a plus as everyone is willing to coach and train.
cons: The salary and benefits are below market rate.  Work life balance is also deteriorating as everyone takes on additional responsibilities with less pay.  Morale is decreasing among the teams due to these downsides.

summary: One of the better wire houses to start career
advice: Engineer the business model to provide new advisors (especially those coming from other industries) with a starter book and help them grow that book.
pros: For second acts and self-starters this is possibly the best of the big wire houses. They do not lead you by the hand so have a well developed sense of how you will build your business from day one. They are fair in compensation and benefits.
cons: Its a tough business without great credentials and its still tough.  Smith Barney does not had you any business or a starter book of clients. Its all up to you. Other firms do seed new advisors.

summary: Rookie advisor received great training, long lasting relationships.
pros: As a rookie, great training and access to top planning software and other technology. The breadth of product and platform offerings is staggering.   My office housed experienced top advisors and were accessible nearly to no end, without them I would have had nothing.  Overall a great position assuming you join the right branch.
cons: The back office without question, my particular office flipped the standard for serving the advisors. They believed the advisors existed to serve them. Morgan Stanley, at the time was transitioning to cutting low producing advisors and dealing with advisors leaving in mass with the purchase of Smith Barney, and maybe my experience was a timing thing.

summary: I obtained excellent Back Office financial skills at Morgan Stanley that enhance my Administrative background greatly.
advice: I went out on a few "volunteer" outings with co-workers and managers.  This is really enjoyable as I got to know my managers especially as "real" people and I really learned a lot.
pros: You can obtain great skills at Morgan Stanley working as a Service Associate.  There are many opportunities to advance and they have great benefits.
cons: If you are coming into Morgan Stanley from a background that is not "brokerage firm" oriented, the culture shock can be a bit much.  But it is like learning anything new, you just have to keep trying and then it becomes second nature.

advice:

cons:
Average food in canteen(not free)

Hike's less.

summary: Breakdown of the structure at the MSVA(Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisory Center)
advice: Help your employees grow and succeed, you only license them because you have to. once licensing is done there’s essentially no more opportunities to continue to educate yourself and pursue other designations while there is significant down time at work. Also, hire more experience managers, not all are bad but some are just heavily inexperienced and shouldn’t be in there role. Lastly, treat your employees better, this place is heading towards being a well oiled machine where we’re all factory workers, rather than a professional environment. You need to realize that we’re millennials and have nothing but options, this is not the 1950’s where you sit at 1 job for 40+ years and then retire.
pros:
-20+ days of PTO
-A lot of flexibility with your schedule
cons:
- Managers here are hit or miss I’m saying that on the basis that most of us have had every single manager here due to disorganization and restructuring. Some managers really want to see you grow while others don’t mind letting you sit in your role until you burn out and leave.

- A lot of disorganization and misinformation, a lot of having to lie to clients because the firm doesn’t want you to tell them why something is being done to their account.

- I would go on but I rather give advice.
