summary: Lack of technical innovation and deteriorating culture
advice:
Accept that the organization has culture and technical problems that need real change to solve. The meeting on retention where the main take away was "showing people there are opportunities" felt like it was pushing the blame onto people who were thinking about leaving. It came off as extremely tone deaf.

Create and communicate a technical roadmap. Make time for innovation when writing new features. Give people hope they won't be using outdated tech forever. As a large organization, consider specialized roles to support and promote initiatives: tech leads, architects, front-end developers, accessibility leads, scrum masters, QA managers, etc.
pros:
* Co-workers were generally bright, eager to learn, and helpful
* Good social scene (friendly co-workers, social clubs, free beer on Fridays, etc.)
* Development teams had lots of autonomy
* Good pay and great RRSP matching
* Some development managers and product managers were great
* Great work-life balance
cons:
* No technical vision. Technical matters felt like they were directionless. Build times were ever increasing. Some teams lacked oversight/review and pushed code that would not fly on more established teams. No team lead, tech lead, or architect roles.

* Lack of technical innovation. Relentless focus on new features and minimum viable product meant that innovation often fell by the wayside. Many teams continued to use old front-end tech even for green field work, or engage in procedural rather than object-oriented programming. No technical roadmap or strategy to move away from outdated parts of the tech stack was communicated or mandated. Encountered strong push back against moving to a true services architecture.

* Monolithic and legacy code base. Never felt like I had the time or support to break smaller services off from the monolith. Felt trapped in a cycle of "learn new and esoteric part of the monolith" and "accrete new feature onto the monolith".

* Cliques and tone policing. It felt like outspoken and extroverted 'rockstar' developers were rewarded with promotions. Often felt forced to be a 'cheerleader' despite the various issues listed here. Saw from co-workers experiences that sharing actual outlook might result in withholding of promotions or raises.

* Was acquired by Morgan Stanley. We lost sudo access to our machines. "Outside Business Interest" rules required you seek approval for accounts, move securities to particular banks, and report your positions. The sabbatical was taken away despite the fact that many people had been promised it as part of their employment.

* Did not feel like senior management were team players. We were told that, post-acquisition, Morgan Stanley would let the company keep one of its two big annual events: the manager retreat or the Christmas party. Senior management elected to keep their retreat, while everyone else lost the Christmas party.

* Aesthetics felt favoured over functionality. Rolling whiteboards were removed from the office with no consultation of the people that used them daily. MacBooks were rolled out before they were ready and despite being a worse development experience (longer build times, etc.).

* Did not eat their own dog food. Despite making software around implementing equity plans, the company stopped offering regular equity grants to its employees post-acquisition.

* Retention issues. It felt like the best and brightest were constantly leaving. The people I wanted to work with the most always ended up leaving, and ultimately so did I.

advice: It is time to get back on track and start taking up competition. This organization has tremendous potential and we should capitalize on it.
pros: Good company to work for. You could build a good career and work till retirement with satisfaction. This is a employee friendly organization and place to be if you are planning long term career.
cons: Growth and opportunity depends on the team you work in. You compensation and growth depends on the visibility and importance of your project in the organization. This is one of the reasons you get different feedback from different employees.

summary: Great company. Meritocracy. Diverse culture of excellence.
advice: Keep up the good work.
pros: Morgan Stanley is committed to diversity.  They are very supportive of developing new careers.  Access to senior management.  Will help and encourage you to get involved in locally to "give back." An outstanding brand.  A company you are proud to work for.
cons: Not a Con- But setting expectations:  New employees (especially those out of college) need to be prepared to work their way up the ladder.  If you expect to come in and be treated like a Managing Director with direct access to the CEO, you will be dissapointed (And you are maybe a bit dillusional).

advice: Walk the walk, stop talking to the talk.  Bring in new blood from outside industry that can apply commercial change strategy to internal infrastructure, technology and culure.
pros: They project a good public brand, pockets of smart people, reasonable internal events/updates.
cons: Experts at window dressing their core values. Extremely slow and of an outdated mindset regarding infrastructure and technology. Internal processes are all outdated and archaic. Senior/Exec management not dynamic. Although there are senior females the executive leadership is male dominated and old school. Never accts on feedback, prefers to seek the explanation of why rather than see feedback as an opportunity to learn, grow and make meaningful change. Toxic culture veiled in PR spin.

advice: Need to spend more time understanding the rank and file needs and challenges they are dealing with on a day to day basis.  Spend more time grooming managers and rewarding people who are good managers of people and businesses, vs people who are just good deal makers, traders or salespeople.
pros: The brand name of the organization and the reach they have.  Opens up a lot of doors as generally everyone is willing to take a call from Morgan Stanley and do business with them.
cons: High pressure environment, a lot of competitive type-A over achievers as peers and in the last few years the culture has become a lot more political as well.

advice: There should be more effective career mentoring between directors and senior associates and vice presidents.
pros: Great place to start in finance. Tight-knit community. Huge amount of potential is there with the assets and tech resources.
cons: There is a ton of potential given the assets, but the joint venture is taking its toll on some of the better rising stars. Hence a high attrition rate as of late. Many of the best traders and salesman who were with the firm for 3-7 years have departed in the last 12 months. Additionally, with the main operations in Westchester, building up unit cohesion is very difficult. 5:30pm hits and everyone is on their way.

summary: Great place to work, very satisfied...
advice: Mack is doing a great job
pros: the management is great, and working environment is very professional.  everyone is very nice, helpful, and most have the same goal to help the firm grow.  each day is different, as you never know what to expect and the employees are very fun to be around.  makes coming to work each morning very enjoyable.
cons: sometimes difficult to have time off...RFE program is well-thought out, but it can be extremely difficult to obtain the top levels in order to achieve your bonuses.  not much guidance is given aside from self taught / instructional videos you watch online.

advice: Retain smart people. There is no focus on employee retention. Paying people and promoting them is important. Have more internal mobility options.
pros: Meritocracy and the best technology company on wall street. Exciting projects and minimal red tape. Great investment in technology and good collaboration with the business.
cons: Salary is not competitive. Too many senior management people making it hard for star performers to get promoted. Sometimes the work pressure can be a little too much.

advice: Keep doing what your doing
pros: Great people that takes care of you, leadership really cares about your success and will do what they can to get you there
cons: Numbers are high but they are looking for young people and a lot of the older people who have been in the business may seem to feel that they are better than you or they don't want anything to do with you.

advice: Strive to encourage and boast about the behind the scenes staff as much as the front end employees and you'll likely see an increase in employee retention rate.
pros: Good people, nice benefits, great community service involvement.
cons: Did not share the wealth, constantly boasted about Financial Advisors being the top 100 in the nation meanwhile the back office operations areas gave minimal salary increases to it's employees if any.   Also, their in-house technology is approximately 10-12 years behind it's competitors, although when I left they were're preparing for an upgrade.  Very little room for advancement without a license and even with a series 7 it's no guarantee of success.

summary: Morgan Stanley was a great place to work... for some people. Most of the people were great but I also experienced racism
advice: Laying off most of the senior people and outsourcing positions out of NY not only hurt the company but also the local job market. There has to be a better way to balance profit vs. adding to the unemployment statistics.
pros: Pay can be good. Vacation and time off  was good.  Benefits were ok. Opportunity to meet some very talented people.
cons: Management culture change forced many to leave. Heavy work load due to layoffs hurt the morale. Can be very cut throat at times. Also experienced some racism.

summary: Work with the best, get paid well but you will give an awful lot in return for your rewards.
advice: Acknowledge the contributions of even the smallest players - everyone plays a part.
pros: Work with the best in a fast paced industry, as much work as you can take on is as much work as you'll get - plus. If you prove yourself, you will advance.
cons: Not so great for work/life balance. Normal hours is a 50+ hour week and way more during busy seasons. The urgency is always high and people tend to run around with 'their hair on fire'. You get paid well but you earn every cent.

advice: Focus on technology, not politics.
pros:
Lured by good package while joining
Leave policies
cons:
Yearly firing based on eliminating redundancy.
Proclaims itself to use cutting edge/latest technology.
Most of the projects still live in the stone age era. 

College Grads who join here are treated as babies. They will be given preference over lateral hires throughout their career. You could find a 5-10 years experience lateral guys being lead by a 2-3 years Grad, who have no industry experience what so ever. 1 Year Grad is equivalent to 5 years Lateral hires.
Lateral hires will take 3-5 years to get a promotion which a grad will get in 1 year. Firm speaks so much about equal opportunity, but I don't understand how it is encouraged in this case.

Too much politics and favoritism. You need to have higher level contacts to survive.

Not a place for people who are technically strong.

advice: Stop nickel and diming your clients. Incent your people by actually helping clients, not just ripping commissions.
pros: I learned a lot in the process of becoming an Financial Advisor. Taking something so overly complex, and being able to simplify for my clients. I can now do that with my own finances, and happy to help friends and ensure they are not getting ripped on commissions.
cons: Terrible FAA program. Does not set their team up for success, unrealistic expectations. Nearly all advisors solely focused on padding their own pockets and not concerned about fees being charged to clients. It was really eye opening for me and disappointing. I left the industry, but if I had stayed - I would have gone to Fidelity or Betterment, companies that actually care about their clients whether you have $1000 to invest, or 5MM.

summary: Constant learning experience with extensive autonomy
pros: Extensive autonomy and infrastructure support. Wealth management is a wonderful opportunity for the self-motivated. Very diverse perspectives and strategies within the firm. Everyone at the branch is friendly and more than willing to help or give advice when you are starting out.
cons: Extensive national training, but at times can be inefficient and too general/theoretical. There's a fine line between autonomy and chaos. I've seen many stray to the later. Unfortunately, management at the branch level attempts to motivate rookies with fear tactics more often than encouragement. This is obviously not working, considering there is a 80-90% "failure" rate in the industry.

summary: Great if your a IT Fresher, exposure to corporate bureacracy
advice: Think Long-term, Grow slower, and ensure that the systems created are well-understood, and that there are competent staff to suppor tthem.
pros: Great exposure to the myriad of Corporate bureaucracy, and red tape which makes a large corporation inefficient.  Very well respected name, based on their past laurels, acquisitions, and antiquated brand.
cons: The Corporation is so large, that in IT, it sometimes takes days to get the right people responsible for specific data areas.  Ridiculous amount of processes and procedures which keep changing, in hopes that they may possibly  be compliant with governmental regulation, and oversight. Very poor long-term employment prospects, as outsourcing, and onshore consulting companies is the current employment/labor model, as it is easy to release them when a routine corporate staffing re-alignment (lay-off) is scheduled.  There were over 3 of these in phases in 2014 (I'm writing this mid-July 2014).

summary: Solid company not sure about transition with MS
advice: Don’t use tenure as the weighing factor to hiring your higher level positions.
pros: A lot of great people, training, and knowledge prep to increase skill sets. I appreciated being able to work with other teams to learn more about specialized roles.
cons: Merger may be causing headaches. After commission cut-they immediately laid off the tenured employees (extremely quietly). Clients are generally psychotic day traders or people who have no idea what’s going on. I would argue some managers didn’t even know what was going on in reality of markets too. You are way far from them and get no briefings but are expected to answer questions about or regarding such in an instant.

summary: Excellent developers with a fantastic environment
advice: Keep listening to your employees, we really appreciate it!
pros: Incredible co-workers, flexible work hours, huge opportunities to learn how to work in a legacy system and move it into the future. Great social scene in Calgary with employees organizing many different events (chess, mtg, soccer, etc.). Managers are very active on isolating developers from the clients allowing more time for focused development and providing a relatively stress-free environment. Salaries and benefits are competitive. Senior employees are helpful and easy to approach.
cons: Legacy system can be painful to work with and without a large amount of domain knowledge adding large features can be tricky.

summary: High level work for non-lawyers; smart colleagues; substantial training and investment in employees by management
advice: Recognize and appreciate the contributions of all levels of employees to the company; not just those at the very top.  Have the comp structure be more reflective of that concept.
pros: Opportunities for development and increased responsibility; generous benefits, company standards of excellence and respect; diverse work projects and continual opportunities to learn; team mentality, well organized interdisciplinary working groups; great commitment to diversity and inclusion; and to giving back to community;  Legal department has promoted non-lawyers to officer level positions.
cons: Compensation is not keeping up with comparable businesses in banking community - this has been representative of the post 2008 environment of the firm;  changes in upper management more frequent; teams are so lean that workload is generally highly stressful;  but still enjoyable if you are fortunate enough to be part of a caring, well managed team.

summary: Excellent place to work and develop a career
advice: As mentioned above, senior management is a bit out of touch with reality. Instead of doing things the old school way because "that's how it's always been done" I strong suggest they sit down with associates and VPs once a month or quarter and ask them how they feel about the direction of the company and if there is anything they could improve.
pros: The company isn't perfect, but they are trying to adapt to the new age of millennials as best they could. Salary is competitive and every team I have been on has been very warm and encouraging.
cons: Senior management should consult with junior employees on direction of firm.

summary: Not Without Its Politics, but Overall Great Place to Build Your Career
advice: If retention is really a priority, rather than bringing in someone new at a much higher salary than what is being paid to your current employee, reward the individuals who are already exceeding expectations and doing the job at a fraction of the price.
pros: The work life balance is one of the main draws. The people have typically been supportive in the development of your career.
cons: There is definite favoritism in the department and on individual teams. There is not equal recognition for going above and beyond the minimum requirements of your role.

advice: Focus on what it takes to KEEP an employee (appreciation through opportunities, promos, $, etc).   Continue to be clear on the direction and priorities of the firm.
pros: Well-respected name, strong leadership that (typically) is clear about the direction that the firm wants to go.  Pay is on par probably with other banks - I've heard GS is a bit higher.  Benefits are good, HR is responsive, and there are opportunities to be active outside of the office with volunteering etc.
cons: Very political landscape and the promotion process is based purely on circumstance, not hard work.  By circumstance I mean who your manager is, how many other people are in your group at each level, etc. etc. Also in a company that large you do find a lot of people "coasting".  Pay definitely levels off after a few years.

summary: Good pay. But call center job
advice: Schedule time do things other than inbound phone calls. Offer courses n preventing burnout.
pros: Lots of OT avail. Although I barely do any. Lots of upward mobility. Can work from home. But if you are vaccinated, they will likely make you start commuting to office soon. They pay for you to get CEP certification if you would like too. Low pressure environment to work on your sales skills. It is mainly a service job, but extra points are rewarded for sales
cons: Call center job. Have to adhere to a semi strict schedule. Pretty much everyone gets burnt out. But those with enough mental toughness to not burn out, can easily excel and standout. And advance in company quickly

advice: Need to time the time to assess the work load that is put on employees. Otherwise talent looks to leave to have a better work life balance.
pros: Worked with some smart people who were nice. Had a quite a few different managers but only had one that I enjoyed working for. Depending on the manager, you were able to work from different office locations. Health benefits, 401K and bonus were good.
cons: Too many layoffs. People were already scrambling on a daily basis to keep things running. Many superstars jumped ship, because they could. Legacy knowledge was lost. Causes such headaches for those left holding the bag to take on the additional work.

summary: Solid, entry-level position if you are interested in a long-term career in Wealth Management
advice: For those that are motivated and want to progress beyond this position in their career make sure you communicate the different options available.
pros: Client-facing, you learn the business from the ground up and have the chance to network internally to further develop your career. The position gives you the skillset to choose different career avenues within the firm depending on what you'd like to pursue.
cons: Need to be patient to learn the business, and outside of placing trades most of the work is rudimentary and you need to be detail oriented as small missteps can have large, negative implications.

summary: Good Technical Progress... very long to execute
advice: Although management talks about transparency, there could be a lot more of it. More often than not this causes rumours to spread on the floor and insecurity causing un-needed attrition which causes the company to loose very skilled resources. Some of the managers on the floor are not true managers and are more reserved and dont get out of their offices much to talk to resources
pros:
- Good place to learn strict Change Management Process
- Keeping pace with modern technology (although Long)
- Great benefits
- Good compensation
cons:
- Too much disparity between groups making employment experiences varied
- If you like to move fast this is not the place for you. Being a bank holding company Morgan has lots of regulatory requirements making the environment slower paced
-  Some teams (not all) have poor work life balance

summary: Compensation closer to market rate, difficult to get promoted
pros:
Compensation and work/life balance has improved in light of the broader labor shortage and need for the firm to be competitive vs peers. 

Work is rewarding, and the firm is a leader in Wealth Management. Innovative in investment solutions, and the platform is often first call and highly sought after by asset managers looking to pitch or launch new products.
cons:
Difficult to get promoted if your demographic traits don't fit a certain profile given the firm's recent sociopolitical agenda.

While work/life balance has improved, there is still a tremendous need to be super efficient (in other words, take shortcuts) or risk falling behind.

advice: You need to completely tear down and rebuild your management's attitude, or this place will remain to be the place that employees hate to come to every day. And you wonder why turnover rate is so high.
pros: You can wear jeans in the Baltimore office. Oh, and they do allow you to volunteer once a year and still get paid for the day.
cons: This is the most oppressive workplace I have ever worked at - GFC is insanely political and there is absolutely 0 chance for promotion. I have been employed here for three years as entry-level, busting my butt and have not been promoted. The worst part is they have no logical reason. Also, you hardly get a raise, if you even get a raise at all. The management teams are like cliques and you need to do as you're told and not ask any questions at all that they don't like. I can't speak to the other departments within this firm, but as far as Global Financial Crimes goes - stay away.

advice: Remember what gave a franchise in the first place ... the business is too broad and poorly focused.
pros: A low benchmark by peers means it's relatively easy to do well. Pay very well for median performance and even better for great performance. Some charismatic leaders. Leading user of technology. Global standardised accounting protocals are a tribute to the great work by Trevor Harris and Vaughn Harvey.
cons: Highly political, although that's the norm for the industry. Global approach means a lot of boring travel. Research has been emasculated in recent years. Hedge fund clients now run the strategy for the securities division. Poor IBD deal flow makes it harder to get corporate access.

advice: invest in training and technology.  Platforms are very good but they are behind on in these areas.  Turnover needs to come down its expensive.
pros: Morgan Stanley has a great brand and some of the best intellectual capital in the world.  Strong senior management and good communication with the employees for the most part. Very strong investment banking, Prime Brokerage and fixed income departments.
cons: They are very behind on technology and training.  Goals and requirements are very tough for new advisors.  Turnover is very high.  The biggest producers are taken care of the smaller a producer you are the less management watches out for you.

advice: People are no longer promoted at Morgan Stanley based on performance, but rather who they know.  There are too many incompetent managers for this reason.  This is why the company is in so much trouble.  Also, they need to have more titles so employees can get a sense they are moving forward.  It is very hard to get a promotion to VP.  They need titles in between associate and vice president.
pros: - They use good technologies in IT
cons:
- Too many incompetent managers
- It is very hard to get any kind of promotion
- Low compensation

summary: MS: Great place to start a career
advice: None
pros: Good culture, brilliant people, top industry player.  Overall its a great place to start a career you deal wiht really big important client relationships and the managers are very willing to help you learn.  Very much a work hard-play hard atmosphere.  Work very long hours but almost everyone I work with is down for a good time on the weekends.  Almost every person in my analyst class is from a top tier school and is very intelligent, but more importantly, they are fun people to work with and have a real personality.
cons: Large, bureaucratic--you know your place in the chain of command, long hrs

advice: na
pros: Morgan Stanley is a great place to work because it provides a motivated team environment, with ample opportunity for advancement, and lots of access to clients early in your career. The company also offers a good compensation policy and competitive benefits relative to its peers. Employees are self starters and intelligent from junior levels to senior levels. In my experience, the firm provides great access to senior team members. More of a team approach than at many other banks - everyone works together across divisions to achieve the best results for clients.
cons: As in most banking positions, working at Morgan Stanley in investment banking requires long hours and a lack of schedule predictability.

summary: Good place to work but long hours required
advice: If there was a way to make projects more efficient, that would be ideal. But it's nearly impossible given the competitive nature of the business. Hard to give any real feedback here.
pros: Compensation is among the best on Wall Street and the firm has an incredible global platform. Just working for the firm, you can get into a lot of meetings that you wouldn't necessarily otherwise. I have a great financial toolkit after 3 years there, which is saying a lot considering I was a science major in college.
cons: The downsides listed here are not unique to Morgan Stanley - they are applicable to any investment banking analyst position; the hours are long and a lot of it might be "face time", where you are simply sitting at your desk with nothing to do. The work-life balance is really tough to manage....so don't expect to do much outside of the office.

summary: It's a good experience to see how an office operates and I'm learning a lot.
advice: There is no advice I would like to give at this point. Being an intern, what management does doesn't affect me too much.
pros: The people there are extremely friendly. I love the work environment and I would absolutely love to work at a place like this after I graduate. You can work at a fairly relaxed pace.
cons:
Early hours... but good if you're a morning person! 
Sometimes it gets slow as an intern. There are occasions where my boss is not available to speak to since he is talking to clients, so I spend some time sitting around and waiting for him to finish.

summary: Great work experience but not fairly paid
advice: Morgan Stanley promotes the advancement opportunities for in house talent.  However, it does not readily take place and the hard work from analyst and associates are not recognized.  Upper management shouldn't be receiving all the credit through salary boosts and bonuses rather it should be firmwide.
pros: Morgan Stanley provides great work experience that would prepare your for future positions.  There is a definite work life balance so great for someone with a family.
cons: The downside of working at Morgan Stanley, is the salaries are not competitive with employers within the same field.  Upper management are the only employees who are properly compensated.

advice: MSSB is a joint venture. The company is still in transition and very hard searching for its identity.  The management team is doing a good job of moving the company through this transition.  There are many thing that will be address in the future, but for now it is hard to ask for anything more.
pros:
Management has open door policy
Fair compensation, although closely tied to market performance
You get an opportunity to present your ideas
Most position offer a balance between work and personal life
cons:
Too much reliance on off shore
Very strong silo structure, typical for large companies
Minimal information sharing across teams
Often need a push from senior managers to get others to committ
Need to improve overall competency of technology staff

advice:
* Pay the new hires well, and for a longer period of time. Give people a chance to buld a business.
* Senior Management should not have executive roles until they have actually been a wealth advisor 
  and have built a book of business.
* Conduct and maintain a formal level of training for new hires, in all positions.
pros:
* It's rewarding to work with and help clients.
* You can literally build your own business within a business.
* There is a lot to learn to enhance your own peronal wealth building.
* You meet some pretty interesting people with dynamic and varied backgrounds.
cons:
* Success in this business is very difficult.
* The ability to build a business to a level of high compensation takes a lot of time and perserverance..
* The interests of the firm, the client, the shareholder, and the employee are rarely aligned.

summary: Beware of bureaucracy and follow Lord Krishna's advice and don't expect rewards ....
advice:
1. Remove the paper pushers out. That is the only way you will retain good talent.
2. Recognize and reward the India teams "on time". You will lose out on good talent, otherwise.
3. Bad managers need to go. People don't leave the firm, they leave bad managers.
4. Recognize the value of talent from BRICS nations and how India is contributing to the global economy before making a pro-US call. Recognize work life balance not just for US and UK employees but also the Asia counterparts. After all, this is a global firm, aint it?
5. Find the right talent for a job not just fill vacant seats in your new location. You need to grow the team alrite, but with the right talent and the right attitude
pros:
You really need to work hard to get where you want to. There are some smart and dynamic people you will meet along the way -- but man, don't expect them to reward you on time. The word, "on time" is key here. Promotions are important to retain talent and motivate employees. MS fails to understand that.
Designations are important for any employee but you are always told by the senior management that "it is a multi year process to get to the next level". 

Pros: 
1. If you are good worker, you will be recognized (but NOT rewarded).
2. Flexibility for long distance commuters to work from home as needed. In fact their WFH policy is very good
3. Some of the managers are very caring. Be careful which team you get into
4. A lot of the software development happens in house so depending upon the team and team size, you will get to learn a lot of good technologies (Flex, Sencha, Big data tools etc.)
cons:
Cons:
1. In my experience, the Senior management is very partial towards the US and UK employees when they award promotion and rewards. Indian center is seen more as a BPO center. 
2. Managers only want to grow the team brlow them. Some of your peers will not even have half the experience as you do in same designation as you but perform one level lower
3. You are recognized by the number of people who report to you. Senior management should focus on not just hiring, but hiring good talent.
4. Projects should be tracked by managers as well as the upper management. Managers should own up for their team. Finger pointing is not the best way to tackle your subordinates.
5. Senior managements regards proximity as the only barometer for measuring performance.
6. Long working hours for India teams while US teams leave at 5 pm EST.
7. They don't recognize your value till you put down your papers. Exit interview by HR is a joke.
8.  Rewards come to those who either don't work OR are not smart enough but lucky OR  are intelligent enough to work AND have an obsequious eagerness to please the upper management

summary: Formerly an excellent company but has gone downhill
advice: Change your business model so that you have specialized each of sales/marketers, portfolio managers, and service personnel instead of making your advisors do all of these roles at once.  Because advisors have to constantly bring in more business, they neglect their clients portfolios and performance suffers.  Also, make it mandatory to re-assign the over qualified employees.
pros:
Formerly well-managed, could possibly become so again
Good corporate culture with well communicated initiatives
Good benefits
cons:
Frequent changes in structure, products, services which negatively affect customers
Company claims to make optimal use of employees skills and experience but this is not true, if you are in a position beneath your abilities it is almost impossible to become better matched
Be careful if you are hired as a financial advisor because their business model is set up to use you for your contacts and network and then give them to "tenured" advisors.

summary: Great place to start one's career
advice: There are some very nice supervisors at MS. In general, more genuine attention to personal career growths and open dialogue would be nice.
pros: Working with relatively smart people on the institutional side. The culture generally open and cultivating. Training and benefits are good. Overall a good place to start one's career in one of the traditional key business areas.
cons: There tends to be frequent personnel reshuffling especially in front office of key businesses, which tends to redirect career paths. Juniors have very little say in which direction they want to build their career in. Different businesses have very different cultures, and some can be more difficult than others, so be careful what you are getting in to.

advice:
With the heavy emphasis on technology changes and digital, invest in technology resources for the field and those with direct contact with the clients. Need more technology trainers allocated to each complex location. Technology trainers may not be a direct revenue producing position, but better education on new and evolving systems enables better service to the client and higher client satisfaction and retention rates.  
Longer technology test period on new systems and enhancements before going live. Ensure the impact to the field (positive and negatives) are fully understood prior to full rollouts
pros:
Upward mobility 
Excellent culture
Great learning environment with peers that challenge you to think strategically
They take work life balance seriously 
Employees are given ownership of their work and flexibility within reason how it’s completed 
Strong emphasis on ethics
cons:
Stressful at times
Technology system issues
Continuously rolls out new system and technology before the platform is ready. Limited technology training in the field

summary: Your ONLY chance of success as a new Fin'l Advisor is to have a big network of prospects or to join a top team.
advice: Finally acknowledge that the Financial Advisors ARE the company; you, as management, are support.  So do a MUCH better job of supporting the FAs: change the advertising ("World Wise" is NOT what is helping 9 of 10 FAs, who don't have the super-wealthy as clients.  Fidelity and Schwab are eating MS' lunch with their much better advertising for the typical target market), and ... and ... and ... and ... (post a comment with your contact info if you want elaboration; maybe I should charge a consulting fee!)
pros: No experience necessary to be hired for Financial Advisor position.
cons: BEFORE applying to be a Financial Advisor, understand that you will only succeed if you have a great personal network of  highly-qualified prospects or you join a good team.

pros: They paid for my graduate school.  There were lots of brilliant people there.  Also having the name on my resume has definitely helped me.
cons: Way too much internal politics.  Your potential for advancement is largely dependent upon what team you're on and how well connected your team leader is.  What team you're placed on is largely a function of where you went to school. If you didn't go to an ivy league school, you won't get placed on a great team, and then no matter how well you do or how hard you work, you'll never rise up the ranks.  And eventually, you'll get laid off.  They do lots of layoffs.

advice: Make an active effort to retain employees instead of relying on the name/brand of the company. The inability to retain talent is a large problem for this company. Also, when jobs become open, do not look to move someone horizontally, promote people vertically.
pros: Morgan Stanley looks great on a resume and has the resources/breadth to expose its employees to a variety of topics.
cons: Morgan Stanley is generally a bureaucracy and not a meritocracy. Given its long history, it has established requirements for promotion and pay raises, there is very limited ability to reward someone for the work that they have done recently; employees must hope/believe their reward will come later down the road.

summary: Seven Month Background Check, misleading statements.
advice: Fire Management in the Bellevue, WA office. Fire HR at corporate. Compensate me for the false promises and the several months you stole from my life.
pros: The company made this seem like a great career move, decent benefits, okay salary. They promised a trip to New York. They make some enticing promises.

summary: Terrible work life balance, toxis athmosphere, Labor law violations (Budapest office)
advice: I had 3 managers during my time at MS. Two was really great, but the last one makes my team's life a nightmare (3 of 6 already resigned). Be more open to the feedback from team members.
pros: I worked for MS for more than 4 and half year. Its not a place where you can work with cutting edge technologies, but the compensation was great and the team moral was good (before covid).
cons:
My team got a new manager and maybe the covid hit the company heavily. My last year at the firm was a nightmare. I was worked for the Budapest office, be very-very careful when you apply here, situation changed a lot in the last year.

A few highlight from my last year:
-Manager told on a big team status call: "Everybody shall be able to answer calls even in the middle of night, you have to stay home because of covid, you have nothing else to do just work. (nice work-live balance)" 
-Huge amount of overtimes, oncalls in the last year (without any compensation, no extra money, no early leave next day). Somebody in my team even called on new years eve and worked untill 10 PM. Daily 10 hours of work was normal on my last 6 months.
-Managers are constantly lying (I was asked to only speak about overtimes and oncalls when the candidate directly asking it during the interview and always say the minimal information, hired people end up in completely different team, different technology, I had a coworker who resigned on his second day because it was complete different than what they told her during the interview).

-I have asked help from HR about the legal status of uncompensated oncalls and overtimes. I got a follow up email after a month, they said they need more time to answer my question. I resigned a little bit latter, but I didn't get any answer for more than 2 and half month from local HR about a labor law question (that's just ridiculous).

The compensation is still above average, so you can give a try if you want, but ask directly about on calls and overtimes during the interview. Ask follow up questions, and be careful because you can end up in a different team with fully different technology stack then they promise during the interview.

summary: Recently deposed IT staffer tells all
advice: Similar complaints from most of us not in management. Underlings are not idiots (at least not all of them). Pay attention to what's happening right under your noses. All banks are in trouble today because small, isolated groups with a lot of authority decided to make some really dumb bets. Question everything, just like you did when you were younger, and avoid the trouble that complacency so often brings.
pros: Huge, innovative global investment bank with a good reputation. Technology is cutting edge and excellent for an organization that size. Despite market turmoil company is solid and well managed. Growth opportunities exist but usually only for newcomers. Desirable locations for offices to work in.
cons:
Unfortunately many. The biggest downside is lack of security. In my 2 + years there I witnessed severe attrition and laying off. While I can't pretend to know what was going on in each business unit, it did seem that the people who had been with the firm the longest were the first to go. Some well known departments were wiped out and replaced almost entirely. I suspect this is to avoid paying an accruing pension and because of "job performance". The ruthless bankers and managers seemed to be the only ones that survived. Ruthless business I understand, but I've met plenty of successful people who didn't resort to ruthlessness to survive. 
I would also have to complain about some of the middle management. Some of the people chosen to serve in the ranks of middle management were flat out incompetent. My department was re-orged entirely, I was told my job had been outsourced, so I went out and got a better job. Some who decided to stay on got fired instead of a new job as a consultant. 
All in all, it's a big name shop and if you can get in it's a good place to work, but like a lot of other big name companies, be a little leery of what is "promised" at your interview. You will pay dues no matter where you come from, you will probably not make as much as you thought, and after years of dedication you will probably get pinched. Wish I could be more optimistic but I saw several senior bankers in full crisis mode after losing their jobs when they were obviously planning on retiring from the company. I realize times have changed, but Morgan Stanley doesn't even pretend to honor your time spent there, and to me that kind of sucks.

summary: The brand is better than the experience.
advice: Simplify the Firm's business model.  Determine the Firm's core line of business, than purge the Firm of all none core lines of business, and focus on being number one in that chosen line of business.
pros:
The Morgan Stanley brand is well received and respected in the market.
Global footprint provides exposure to a broad array of markets and products.
Best in class in terms of managing data.
Smart co-workers who are always willing to collaborate.
Excellent remote computing capabilities.
Excellent use of collaboration tools.
cons:
The Firm is on a systemic downward death spiral caused inconsistent vision and poor execution.  

Prior to the merger of Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter, Morgan Stanley was one of the most elite firms in Financial Services.  Since the merger the Firm was suffered a perpetual identity crisis.  It oscillates back and forth between wanting to be a retail brokerage Firm or a trading shop.  Unfortunately the oscillations happen at a frequency that never allows the Firm successfully realize the vision of leaders.  As such the Firm is not the best at either.  Currently the Firm is focused on Retail as evidenced by it's acquisition of 51% of Smith Barney.  The merger is at least a year behind schedule and excessively over budget.  From an earnings perspective the Firm has not been able to put together two successive quarters of positive results.  Each earnings report is laden with reasons to justify its inconsistent performance.  The Firm does not seem to know how the grow revenue so it is trying to improve profitability by contracting expenses.  This is being achieved by continuously reducing head count, benefits, salaries and capital investments.  Are these changes working?  No, the stock price is down 18% year to date, moral is down, and our ability to attract top talent is diminishing.  

Prediction: the Firm is acquired within 12-18 months.

summary: Great learning experience...may not be where you stay
advice:
Every other firm I have ever worked for, as well as firms in the area such as Amazon, Microsoft, Capital One, Ameriprise, Boeing---they all use 360 degree ways of giving feedback and receiving feedback from a team.  Here, it's almost like a caste system is created, in that management doesn't allow for the feedback to be given about their Financial Advisors.  Many times support staff are invaluable resources of information, and can see where an advisor could improve relations with clients, become more efficient, participate as more of a team player, all of which would improve the business line.
It's highly irregular for there to be an entire population of employees (Financial Advisors) that can give feedback on another class of employees, but the feedback doesn't go both ways.
Also, flex work schedules are only available to Financial Advisors.  If you are an assistant or support person, you do not have the opportunity to have more flexible schedule in any way, shape or form.
Management at corporate level talks about supporting and promoting from within, changing the culture, but it doesn't really translate down at all.  As long as there is such a huge discrepancy in how employees are treated, they will miss the boat on really connecting with and engaging their top talent for the future.  
Even the work groups, such as Women@MorganStanley, have events that they only send to Financial Advisors, completely cutting out the support staff.
This way of managing people is a huge disadvantage to women, many of whom need a bit more flexibility to reach their potential.
There are far more female support staff than their are female Financial Advisors, and a big reason for that is how they are systematically treated.
I suggest to management that they read Sheryl Sandberg's book Lean In, or Tiffany Dufu's book Drop The Ball.
If Morgan Stanley really wants to be at the forefront of an industry and a movement that is changing the culture and how we work, they need to reevaluate how they are treating their "different" class of employees.
Feedback.
It's good for everyone.
pros: Fantastic opportunity to learn about a broad range of investment products from a major wirehouse, opportunities to learn from many different Financial Advisors how to run a practice
cons:
Typically you must support between 3-5 highly demanding Financial Advisors, and all of their corresponding clients.  The company's way of managing teams is highly irregular.  Most companies allow feedback of all colleagues on a team.  However, here they only "manage" support staff, rather than also allowing for colleagues to provide feedback about Financial Advisors.  However, Advisors are able to give feedback about their support staff.
Management never solicits feedback from support staff about Financial Advisors, so depending on whom you work for, your life could be miserable and management doesn't take steps to bring that in line, nor solicit feedback from others.  Basically, the only time you will work directly with your manager is when you come in for a review annually, where you're told what your current Financial Advisors think of you. 
(Which is the only time you'll ever work with your manager--NO "one-on-ones" quarterly like at other firms, no coaching, no growth opportunities.  As a support staff member, you'll only hear what your Financial Advisors say about you--but they aren't your managers, they aren't trained HR professionals, and you'll only hear what they say about you from your manager.  
Its a very odd dynamic, in that everyone doesn't just all get in the same room and talk about team dynamics at all, and how to improve them.
It's incredibly strange.

advice: With the elevation of Fleming to run asset management and GWM, the Firm has adopted a public stance of being committed to delivering excellence in investment results to clients. Outside of occasional pockets of quality (hedge fund advisory business), I've not seen the evidence of this and, in the long run, the Firm will do better by seriously trying to live up to its advertising.
pros: Firm has a great history and motto - "first class business in a first class way." Relative to the rest of the Street, there is some truth to this. While all major I-banks have lost their way since turning public, the most recent round of preposterously corrupt behavior with absurdly massive fines to match, admissions of criminality, customer abuses, etc., notwithstanding, MS nonetheless has been less tainted than most - often paying fines for example in the hundreds of millions rather than billions. The investment banking advisory business has always been, and remains, first rate, and this is a credit to the firm. PWM in particular once had a proud story before the commoditization of wealth management services, back when the former Private Client group was 300 strong and the only financial advisory group at the Firm. Two M&A delas later (Dean Witter; Smith Barney) that culture is decades past, and PWM long since ceased having any real differentiated value proposition on the investment side. Nonetheless, the hedge fund advisory group is very strong, and this is a key asset class. Supporting professionals providing the soft services - T&E, philanthropy, etc., - generally range from  solid, to excellent.
cons: The Firm is incredibly slow and/or incapable of solving longstanding deficiencies that really give the lie to the group's claim to be a top quality outsourced family office solution. Banking services were terrible when i left, after years of flailing post financial crisis, and the integration of PWM's legacy reporting (on the institutional B/D) w/ the retail old MSDW platform was a decade + running nightmare - and from keeping in touch w/ former clients, it is still a disaster from PWM standpoint, basically a lowest common denominator standpoint.

advice:
Work with individuals on a weekly basis to help them plan, access, and succeed. MS invests much in training and benefits. The 90% failure rate is a statement that much improvement is needed. Matching them with a mentor who reviews their daily activity and help them focus on what will work, how they approach it, and help them find what works could improve the failure rate dramatically. Even a 50% failure rate is too much, driving up recruiting costs and loss opportunity. FA turnover also gives clients a bad image for Morgan Stanley. Unless FAs can acquire large amount of assets under management the pay will not be sufficient.  Spending close daily supervision of activity company training assets are being wasted. More training is needed to help people connect, gain rapport, bring the client on board and manage the relationship. Very little training in this area. Most training is on financial instruments and that is great. If the company spent the same on the soft people skills training failure rates could be dramatically reduced and client satisfaction could also be dramatically improved. 

This is one great company, but you rapidly get the feeling that they hire many and see who sticks. This puts them at risk for robo-advisers in the long run. Over train the soft people skills and then use the team experts and money managers to satisfy client needs. FAs are the front line people and the reason clients are with MS. Focus on the relationship training from day one, map out daily activities, monitor and help FAs in training succeed.
pros: Great company, global leader of wealth management. Benefits and training is constant.
cons: Extremely challenging to succeed. Financial advisers are hired for their networks. MS does little to help you with leads. You must find a way to gain clients through cold calling, buying lead lists, networking and working your networks. Failure rate in the first three years is 90% taking into count of sons and daughters taking over father's and mother's book of business, those that have worked as FAs with other companies and those that are new to the business. Finding someone to partner with on their book of business is important.

pros: The best qualities of Morgan Stanley come from the people you work with and for. Morgan attracts top talent and so you get a chance to work with some of the brightest people, most of which are also good managers that want to help you develop your career and value work life balance.
cons: Compensation stagnates if you stick around for too long. They use a formulation to calculate compensation and it seems like there is no way to get ahead unless you can convince someone very senior to make something happen and that's rare.

cons: Loyal employees tend to suffer from salary compression in the back office functions. I also think the firm can do a better job of reintegrating young mothers back from maternity leave.

advice: Take charge, get rid of the "problems" (no matter how senior) and listen to your staff/direct reports. Try harder to retain talent (the firm's motto for years now) and encourage all to get along. There's no room for pettiness in an organization of this size that wants to succeed.
pros: Decent comp, great experience, good professional development and friendly people.
cons: Management is weak, moral is mediocre at best, culture is weak, turnover is high and bureaucracy tends to get in your way. For me, after any many years, it became a place that was no longer fun to work at.

pros: Marketing teams in Wealth Management are quite lean, and even junior level analysts will have a large amount of responsibility right off the bat. This provides a great opportunity for those just starting their careers to learn about numerous facets of Morgan Stanley's business and also gain valuable face time with senior leadership. Morgan Stanley office culture is collaborative, with a heavy emphasis on mentorship and learning by doing, making it a friendly environment to grow as a professional.
cons: Promotions and performance evaluations only happen once a year (at least as of the time I left the firm), meaning that advancement can be somewhat slow.

advice: It's mostly a great management team. There are always bad managers though. But this team has learned and grown over the years.
pros: They have great benefits. Better than average time off. They convert almost all of the temporary employees they bring in, although it takes time. Terrific career pathing. Although salary banding is not transparent. Management will work with you as an employee so that you can manage work life balance.
cons: Wages are great to start with, but may be slow in growing after. Salary ranges aren't transparent. They've grown quite a bit over the years so that family feeling isn't there as much.

advice: The buddy buddy system is old and dated.  A little effort is not enough, make real change.  Stop the run off by continuously cutting the salary of the work force while the CEO keeps getting more.
pros: Great technology and order entry systems. The platforms give the advisors enough models to accommodate most investor 250K or more in investable assets.
cons: Pay scale is harsh. Typical Wire house model with new trainees. Bring them in and let them burn through calling friends and family. Then pass them through to the "Team Concept" and let the veterans chew them up by taking 30 to 40 % of their earnings while management sits there and does nothing about the ruthless mistreatment. Once they can't make enough to support their lifestyle them let them go and repeat the process.

summary: Good Company That can do Greater
advice: Stop promoting mobility. It's just as hard to get hired internally than it is externally.  There should be raise if hired for a new position. Stop running the Baltimore location as if prison, bage swips, roll counts, etc. Let paperless departments be remote 100%.
pros: Great benefits. 4 wks vacation, unlimited sick time, remote 2 days a week, health insurance excellent.
cons: Promotion process convoluted, if you get hired for another position the move is lateral in pay. They post jobs to appear it's fair competition but the truth is that already have a candidate they've promised the position to.

summary: It used to be a great company with great employees.
advice: The firm has been criticized for the weak risk management since last year.  Please  do something for improving this.
pros: It's a global company with great employees, so you can have lots of opportunities here.  They also quite value the importance of IT and always chase the latest technology, so you won't get bored when staying at the same position.
cons: Sometimes its long working hours drive me crazy.  The bureaucracy also happens in this company all the time.  Based on the current volatile market, the bonus won't be as good as before.

summary: Morgan Stanley is a great place to work.
advice: There really isn't any advice I can provide to the management at the branch in which I worked.  They are doing a fantastic job.
pros: Morgan Stanley honestly was a great experience for me.  The brand name helped when it came to prospecting, and the manager at my branch was very honest about what to expect in this line of work.
cons: The hours are long, but that's how it is if you want to make it in this industry.  Your schedule revolves around your clients, but that is also something that was expected when I came on board.

summary: There were many daily challenges but going to work was fun; you never knew what awaited you. It kept things interesting.
advice: I don't know what to say.  I liked all the management and believe their intentions were good.  But the support the trainees received was next to nothing.  I know much of it had to do with the integration of the platforms keeping everyone so busy.  A CSA for all the trainees, as promised certainly would have been helpful.  I don't think it would have saved our jobs but unkept promises abounded there.  That was rather frustrating, as well as being taught one way by one person and then later (after hours of work) finding out it should have been done a different way.  Getting everyone on the same page as to how things are done I guess is what I'm trying to say.
pros: The lisencing training is excellent if you have the discipline and mind to study hard on your own.  The people and management at our branch genuinely cared about you and did their best to keep things fun yet professional.  People, for the most part got along and if they didn't, the office is so big, it was easy to distance yourself from the ones you wanted to.  The office is so big that there are experts somewhere on every subject and everyone was very giving of their time to teach newbies and answer any questions.  Managers door was always presented as open.  I loved working there but there were definitely cons to it as well.
cons: Due to the merger a few years back, everything still operates on two systems.  Things are getting closer and closer to being on one platform, but the right hand literally had no clue what the left hand was doing most of the time-depending on which platform you were trying to work from; MS or SB.  Because of all this, as great of people as the management were, they just didn't have time for any of the trainees.  They said and acted like their door was always open, and they would often listen, but there would be no follow up on any promises made.  It is exactly as you read in most reviews, if you don't know or have some major assets under your belt or axcess to them right away, you won't meet the extremely high minimum benchmarks they require of you.  They hire a ton, gather as many assets as they can and then fire a ton.

advice: Senior management has to put more effort in talent retention. Stop hiring temps, it's a waste of money and everybody else's time - they are gone within a few months and the rest of staff is left with the same amount of work or someone new to teach.
pros:
-Very knowledgeable people on various levels
-Good exposure to various aspects of the business
-Good benefits
-Nice pantries
-Convenient locations
cons:
-High turnover - a lot of great professionals left in the last couple years
-No good talent retention 
-A lot of shifting people from one group to another puts pressure to adapt to new responsibilities quickly without any extra benefits

advice: Set new Advisors on a team who are willing to mentor and understand hurdles are hard to get in the first year or two
pros: Great company with vast access to products and services to help your clients, forefront of fee based industry
cons: Lack of team opportunities only 2% of individuals survive the first year without getting on a team to help with your hurdles and goals while building a new book of business, very much a hard sale driven atmosphere with a slight "do the right thing for your client" as long are your making your goals, if not then do whatever it take to succeed atmosphere

pros: Work life balance and co-workers were huge advantage.  In the role that I had I was able to have a lot of autonomy and work with many departments across the company.  The people throughout the U.S. that I worked with made the day to day work week great.
cons: There was unfortunately very little opportunity for growth during the time I worked at this company.  No good opportunities for career development.  Many people were being let go and moral was down.  I was lucky enough to ,keep my role but didn't see the ability to move up so moved out instead.

advice: have new employees do the training BEFORE they start working.  it is pointless to have the employees do the training while doing other work.  this was counter productive as you are only paying attention to one thing at a time but doing two things.
pros:
Management is great, a lot to learn here. Fast pace work environment but it was rewarding.
management is very fair and is willing to listen if you have an issue.
cons: extensive training, but it being a financial services company that is expected.  Although you are expected to do the training and take exams afterwards while also doing your daily work.

advice: Management should practice what is being preached. Individual managers shouldn't set policies or form opinions based on their own social circumstances.
pros: The Firm certainly talks about work life balance and taking advantage of it as part of their culture.
cons: In reality, there was very little balance and certain types of managers seemed to frown upon it. If you are a family person and have a manager that is not - it seemed that balancing life and work was a problem. If your manager was in a similar family situation as yourself everything was fine and certainly contributed to a positive work experience.

summary: Smart and talented coworkers who respect your opinions
advice: Keep up the good work but don't make the environment feel too stifling with regards to expense control. Morgan Stanley has a very unique culture among the wall street banks and let us all strive together to keep it that way.
pros: Competitive work environment, good reward for hard work, coworkers are generally helpful and senior management encourages you to voice your opinions.
cons:
Being a large organization there is bureaucracy but not too excessive. Some of the technology seems outdated.
There could be more focus on improving quality control on the software that is developed in house.

advice: Meetings need to have a specific goal, and need to be short and to the point. The general practice is to "overcommunicate" via meetings. This is not efficient.
pros: I joined Morgan Stanley in July 2011 as Executive Director to manage software developers in the Real Time Market Data team. The people are great, very friendly atmosphere and cooperative workplace with smart people.
cons: The cooperation is typically done in the form of meetings, which are sometimes hard to opt out of. In some cases, the meetings to gather requirements were redundant. Several project managers would schedule you to attend meetings for overlapping requirements.

summary: Worst Company to Work For Never Join ICT
advice: nothing, because they can listen with their deaf ear.
pros: Good Colleagues, Good Pay, night drop
cons: Other than pay there is nothing. My advice any techie should not join Morgan Stanley either in Mumbai or Bangalore. No Fix work, You might be hired for java but work on something else and they can fire you anytime. No Job Security. Long Hours. If you don't have good relationship with Manager, you can be fired within a month. Worst company i have ever worked.

summary: A truly professional and prestigious environment.
advice: I would advise for more team-oriented groups to work on deals with clients. The brainstorming will only be able to increase the closing of deals.
pros: Primarily, the company culture is what drove me to become a motivated worked for Morgan Stanley. Albeit having a competitive work environment, I was able to foster my skills with my co-workers to strengthen my industry knowledge.
cons: The only gripe I have with my previous employment at Morgan Stanley is that I was not able to spend enough time with my family. I underestimated the amount of work I would be having to do per week greatly.

pros: With any company, its all about who you work for. I had a great manager. He pushed for you to succeed and created opportunities for you to grow within the firm whether you wanted them or not. He was flexible with vacations and work from home. The maternity leave policy is also one of the best and I was able to extend my time off without and issue.
cons: Salary and bonus' are not great. Sometimes years salary increases are nil. The company is also very political, you have to network all the time and brown nose if you want to advance.

summary: Wasted 5 years of my life here
advice: Treat your employees like human beings. Have training programs for managers. Compensate fairly. Don't tell employees that if they don't like something they should leave.
pros: Big name, easy job
cons: Terrible pay for the industry. Excuses every year when it comes to bonus time. Awful middle managers that have no power or ties to compensation. No training or opportunities for advancement. Layoffs pretty much every year around Christmas time regardless of company performance. A truly soul less company that treats their employees like a number on a sheet. 6 out of the 11 people on my team have quit in the last 2 months. I came in to MS as a bright eyes optimistic analyst and am leaving depressed and hating people and corporate culture.

summary: A company with billions of hopes the world
advice: The company ought to give an opportunity to me to be the part of this company.I want to improve this company exponentially,just give me a chance
pros: This is the company which provide best opportunities to employees.By joining i can judge myself with the global competitive  world. It will be pride for me to be part of this prestigious company
