The culture is not the same in all the teams even though the firm is trying hard to achieve this.
Pay is not uniform in similar job functions and could depend on your past background. (like joining from a very low-income job would not fetch you at-par pay but after few years you may get salary corrections based on your achievements)

pros: I was in Technology 10+ years. Collaborative env, good teamwork in and across teams in general. You can form partnerships across groups in most cases despite the big size of the company. Thx to this, you can get a lot done on your own without needing to escalate to manager, etc. Work life balance was also fine.
cons: Depending on which group you're in, base/bonus increases have been limited in recent years unless you were in a good group with access to bigger portion of the bonus pool.

summary: Job Satisfaction Depends Completely on Office Managment
advice: Offer a better training program, manage advisor expectation, defend and support administrative staff rather thank scapegoating all issues onto the lowest paid employees.
pros: Good Benefits, Average Company Culture
cons: While the corporate culture is well intended, actual culture varies greatly office to office and, at least in Colorado, office culture is reliably bad. Toxic office management can really make or break this role. No diversity at all and no tolerance for individualism. There is very high turnover in the support staff role for a reason.

advice: Meritocracy is not a concept
pros: Used to be the name. Unfortunatly Morgan has lost its cache. The brand advantage has evaporated. Technology is lagging and talent departure is unfotunate.
cons: Managment has lost all connectivity and they have forced out the best managers. There is no meritocracy. In tough times the good ole boy network really kicks in. Most seior managers only care about saving their jobs. No dissent is tolerated and the guys we knew and could count on in tough times are all gone to UBS

summary: Looks Good on Resume but Beware
advice: Build better middle management that actually have people skills. Invest more money into technology esp for programs that can track productivity & quality. Invest more money & resources into operations instead of sales/trading.
pros: 20 days vacation, Liberal Sick policy, Prestigious NAME; Tuition Reimbursement
cons: Mandatory 10 day vacation;  Lack of good management;High turnover; No transparency around promotion requirements; Promotions are granted once a year to the entire company; 401K match is allocated at the end of the year the company's stock fund instead of your fund designations; Unorganized; Terrible technology;

advice: Negative attitude towards corporate office affects working environment. Corporate needs to implement better top-down approach to adress the concerns of Financial Advisors.
pros: Brand recognition, competitive salary and benefits, access to proprietary research and information, company database provides contact information and access to top employees, low-stress working envronment
cons: You are a number. Management saw new recruits at a burden, rather than an asset. was assigned menial tasks, and denied requests to take on projects, Financial Advisors are narrowly focused on their own business- minimal cooperation and social interaction in office.

advice: Don't promote based upon time served.  Pay attention to who is doing the work recognize, promote and pay them.  Be willing to cut people that are not contributing to the group.
pros: Firm has a good reputation.  Merger has created opportunities for creative problem solving.  Firm has good benefits and good research.
cons: Difficult to move up in the organization.  Have to be willing to consider a lateral move.  Not very good at promoting and recognizing employees for work they have done that is above their normal duties.

advice: None.
pros: Great operations, economies of scale in pricing, investment manager access and options, good technology, well respected and known brand
cons:
Beware; If the 4 company values include "do the right thing" and "put the client first" you might ask yourself why those wouldn't be assumed and just the basics for any professional. 
The advisor culture is competitive, cut-throat and selfish. 
The wealth management leadership ONLY values production and profit. 
The resources and operations may be better than other wires and worth the big check to transfer your book there, but only if you know what you are getting into. If you want to build a business, better look elsewhere; unless someone is going to bring you in on the train of privilege (and I would get that in writing if I were you.)

advice: Take a look at yourself in the mirror, might break if you look close enough.
pros: Absolutely nothing positive to say about Etrade or Morgan Stanley.  Abysmal pay, broken promises, no future except if you enjoy taking endless phone calls from miserable clients.  Soon there will be threats and repercussions if you don’t generate enough leads that you don’t get paid on.
cons: I could write a novel as long as War and Peace on the negatives but not going to.  Everything regarding compensation, future promotions, benefits is a lie.  There is nothing positive about working at Etrade.  Now people will read this and still accept a job offer and guaranteed will remember reading this post after of month of torture.  Stay away!!

summary: Challenging and fun place to work
advice:
Developing/maintaining thousands of systems/software tools at the company, many for the same task seems to be a waste on both developers and users side.

Why aren't layoffs communicated better within the company? Or do you think it is better if people learn the bad news from the press? No need to pretend, employees are not fools, and don't like being treated as one.
pros:
Compensation
Challenging tasks
Creativity acknowledged/supported
International teams
Normal working hours
cons:
Sometimes boring.
Lack of freedom: have no word in what project to work on. (Especially coming from the academia this is unusual for me.)
Have to spend lots of time gathering information about undocumented systems.

summary: Mixed bag - has good and bad components; superstar culture, pressure for long hours
advice: If you take with one hand, give back with the other.  Lately pay has been cut and people work longer hours.
pros:
Pay can be good when you've been there a while

In technology, on high end of talent scale
cons:
A little bit of hypocrisy -- sure, there's flex time and whatnot, but in the end, what difference does it make when your colleagues put in (or pretend to put in) long hours?  
Feels more bureacratic by the day
Difficult to move around and learn different technologies, typical corporate environment that way.

advice: Be more selective in hiring, focus on grooming trainees to be the bread winners five years later. Its a marathon business but they make you sprint to your goals.
pros: You will learn a great deal. The array of investment option is almost unlimited. You can truly manage your business.
cons: Meeting goals is challenging. Everything is ok when you are being recruited but unless you feel you can hit the numbers easily, be leery of living on commissions only. Thats the number one reason many brokers dont make, cant pay the bills two years in!!!

advice: During the credit crisis John Mack did a good job of communicating to employees what was happening in the economy and to Morgan Stanley.  He also told employees he understood if they felt they needed to sell their shares of MS stock.
pros:
Great colleagues, lots of flexibility.
Good opportunities to develop skills.
Very professional environment - I was always proud to be part of a team.
cons:
All Wall Street firms are stressful places to work, and Morgan
Stanley is not an exception.  Sometimes you have to work at
times you prefer not to.

summary: Lousy management, cheap, and Poor compensation.. STAY AWAY
advice: Company culture is a disaster, brand is diminishing every daty,  every department is so cheap... sad state of affairs...
pros:
-Good Brand name (still carries some weight in finance)
-Impressive titles handed out (low level managers are given VP titles)
-Respectable name may help in resume
cons:
-Back office roles (operations/IT) are treated like dirt and take crap from everyone.. BEWARE
-Constant cost cutting everywhere: Your managers are constantly trying to find new ways to replace you with cheaper resource
-Training for non-revenue generating role is non-existent ($2000/yr cap for training expense!!?)
-Hardly no bonus (if your not front office, don't expect anything)
-Non-existent meritocracy..  
-Total lack of ambition or motivation from everyone you work with, low morale
-Cheap.. Cheap... Every department is beyond cheap...  never seen anything like it...

summary: Its not like it used to be!
advice: have a little more flexibility, listen to your support staff a little more, they play a huge role in the success of the advisors.  Bonuses would be nice, we have gotten them in the past.
pros:
Vacation time
Benefits 
Non-management people are great.
cons:
No bonuses/mediocre pay
Management does not listen to support staff
changed the hours after the merger and now we only get 30 minutes for lunch and it's unpaid.  i have worked in retail and you got 1 hour unpaid and two 15 minute breaks.
NO, I mean NO Flexibility on hours!!
Favoritism  and nepotism is obvious.

summary: A financial company, with a fair IT division
advice: Be more flexible in terms of IT processes. Put more emphasis on replacing / improving inefficiencies, that affect morale and costs.
pros:
- Well-known, established and recognized international financial company
- Great infrastructure and (usually) well organized processes
- Lots of technologies to learn and to work with, from a software developer's perspective
- You can meet several talented professionals here
- Management usually treats people well
cons:
- Too much time spent on administration
- Lots of legacy systems around, some of them are terribly engineered and awful to work with
- Lengthy and uneasy decision processes

summary: Crowded with less than stellar performers
pros: Flexible work arrangement, friendly environment, no late hours, understanding management, nice life-work balance, culturally the company is pretty well establish and the clashes between legacy Citi and Morgan personnel are not as bad as described.
cons: tough to get promoted, less than stellar co-workers, protected classes feel invincible, compensation is too aligned to the company and unit's performance and not necessarily to the individual's performance.  Benefits are not the greatest, especially health insurance options.  They make even people who have no access to materially non-public information trade via the Morgan Stanley system which is expensive and inflexible.

summary: Great company that offers support in growing business and training to be a great advisor.
pros: Offers a lot of support and resources to excel in growing your business. Focused on being competitive with other financial services companies and consistently improving the CRM systems and ease of working with clients.
cons: Could provide more training for new hires. Difficult to ramp up commission and to be successful when not working with a Senior Partner or Team. Very independent oriented work-place culture.

advice: None
pros: some really nice people and good cafeteria.
cons: Not great for junior people. Working hours were exceptionally long (8-8 was more than normal, often longer) and compensation much lower than the median. Huge mismatch between the pay and the expectations. Lots of stress and high responsibility,  micromanagement, mandatory weekend work all the time despite really low comp. No free food or even drinks like coffee or tea in the office, had to pay for everything.

advice:
Please , scan thru all your middle managers and seriously do something . If not you will lose good employees 
Work life balance needs relook
pros:
Very good company culture . 
Good opportunity to move around firm within . They encourage that 
Sufficient amount of internal training
Senior management v good
cons:
Poor work life balance 
Pay scale below industry average
While senior management is good , middle managers do a poor job . I hope someone is resting this and does something about

pros:
At Morgan I found my colleagues to be very talented and collaborative. I decided to join Morgan because of the people of my team. Since interview i found them to be ground to earth and helpful. Their questions were very work based and not google based.
Morgan spends a lot in the Technical Training which will be very effective upskilling you.
cons:
Weekend deployments [but depends on team]
Infra is completely morganized but then its understandable as its banking and needed for security.

summary: Solid company to work for in finance
pros:
- Everyone is friendly and wants to help you, you can talk to anyone no matter their position and they would be willing to have a conversation with you about your career. 
- Diversity and Inclusion are a big part of the culture
- They want to see you continue your career there. 
- They have a lot of tools and workshops to build on your hard skills and soft skills.
cons:
- High stress, high reward environment
- Benefits are so-so
- Technology tech is older

advice: make people feel more appreciated, more perks, liven up corporate culture,
pros: fortune 500 company; looks good on resume, innovative environment, learn alot, good connections, money can be good
cons: layoffs, instability, long hours, too much change, corporate culture not that great especially with the younger crowds, people stick to themselves, not alot of social events going on, on my floor there was no break room except for a dorm size refrigerator and microwave, and a water cooler which didnt have any cups in it usually

summary: Good days come when the economy is gloomy because clients tend to do nothing
advice: As all the financial institution, it is a very political place. You need to as tough as a cockroach to survive. It is a great name despite a lot of shortfalls. And it is definitely a great place to launch a career.
pros:
Talent people and good name
Interesting work once a while
The biggest corporate clients floating through the bullpen
Relativly stable
cons:
Strict rules for promotions
Senior people are not very accessible
Sometime you will be working at corp. development capacity
Schedule is rather unpredictable

summary: Excellent financial firm to work for
pros: Great IT department to work for, challenging work all around. I've been in the financial industry for over a decade and can tell from colleagues that this is a very strong environment to work in.  Offices in Manhattan are very nice (with some getting recent upgrades!), and technology is kept as up-to-date as possible.  Staff collaborates very well.
cons: Work/Life balance is tough, but if you enjoy doing the work and enjoy the people you work with, you can manage it.

summary: Financial advisors are on their own....
advice: Formulate a plan to grow the wealth management organically, from the grassroots.  The current population of financial advisors is demographically challenged.  New advisors need more support, mentoring and training.  I feel fortunate to have made it on my own....
pros: Brand recognition adds credibility in a very competitive industry.  The firm's reputation in the marketplace is a positive.  The breadth of investment options is appealing to investors.
cons: No real strategy to assist in making financial advisors successful.

summary: Redefining its business and revenue model...
pros: Solid company with a long history of excellence.  A great place for someone to begin their career in one of the world's top financial services.  Tremendous technical platform relative to other financial service companies.
cons: M is  one of the  strongest  financial services companies to exit the recent financial crisis.  The company is adapting to changing market and regulatory conditions, challenging the traditional business model.  The opportunities for growth and new product and technical innovation is very limited.

summary: Wall Street is Still a Boys Club
advice: Rather than just talking about inclusion and meritocracy, practice it.
pros: Super smart colleagues, more office vs home flexibility post pandemic, tight knit firm management culture, more internal mobility than most banks.
cons: Sales and trading is still a boys club at the top pay grades. Traders have alpha status…trading business is a tech endeavor now, this makes no sense. Incredibly hard to make MD even for top performers, losing marketability over time. Loud people get promoted, hard working people are simply used.

summary: One of the best companies on Wall Street to work for!
advice: I really hope James Gorman will do everything in his power to fill the really big shoes of his predecessor
pros:
Great corporate culture
Amazing benefits
"Open–doors" management style
Wide range of internal classes you can take to improve your professional and personal growth
Encouraged rotation after 3 years at one position
cons: At times can be difficult dealing with Human Resources, especially at times of interviewing and salary negotiating. I referred several very qualified people for open position and all of them had difficulties dealing with personalities of HR reps.

advice:
Create an environment where talent is developed and there is a clearer roadmap for Analysts.
Do better job at keeping your word and not just use employees as a pawn or means to an end.
pros:
Great work/life balance
Laid back
Place you can just go in and do your job
Not too much micro managing going on
cons:
No real advancement opportunities
Management does not communicate effectively w/ employees in regards to feedback
Does not actively participate in recruiting best talent - uses temp agency to find candidates
Does not value knowledge,  or coaching & developing analysts

pros: Income is good if you can make your quotas, bonuses also get progressively higher if goals are met.  Other incentives include stock bonus (though very minor) with a five year vesting schedule
cons: You are on your own.  It is the deep end of the pool for new financial advisors.  You get books, time to study, only one chance to pass your series 7, or you are fired asap.  All they want you to do is cold call to increase their assets.

advice: Pay people what they are worth.  Five years with no raise and no bonus = sinking ship.
pros: Bright people, excellent facilities, lots of opportunity to contribute outside the core remit of the job; good exposure to senior management from core locations, as they came to visit often.
cons: Firm not making money, swirling the drain, top talent leaving to find appropriate comp in other firms and especially other countries; overpaid expat managers clueless about local conditions.

summary: Great place to work, great training and great upside!
advice: Continue to help new Financial Advisors get momentum early in production period.
pros: Great training and support. Branch staff are very helpful.  Competitive pay and great upside if you make it. Great name recognition.
cons: Following the training and licensing period there is a set of minimum revenues that need to be achieved in order to maintain employment.  Pretty hard to make these numbers but they are fair considering the investment they have made in each employee.

summary: Love the brand; hate the middle management
advice:
-Stop playing politics and get rid of mediocre middle managers, who are more like line managers at a sweatshop, which this place feels like at times
-Acknowledge employees for real work accomplishments and not being "master cubicle surfers"
pros:
-Incredibly smart people
-Great technology (bleeding edge)
-A lot of work (for those of us who like to work)
-A lot of volunteering opportunities (for those who like to give back)
cons:
-Too much processes
-Mediocre middle management
-Who you know; not what you know
-No work-life balance, but that's expected from a financial services firm

pros:
* Good culture
* Work life balance is respected
* Access to sr. management and an open door policy
* great people to work with
* direction of company seems clear over the last couple of years.
cons:
* Competition for growth is tough , competence is not the only factor that affects growth .... location , team dynamics etc., play a very important role. 
* pay is not above competition .. its at par at best.

advice: Keep reaching out to all employees, encourage more feedback. Spend more time getting to know the people under you and help grow them.
pros: The employees here are excellent, good at what they do, and are willing to offer some guidance. For a big company, they try to give you all possible opportunities to grow.
cons: Being a big firm, compliance is vital so there can be a lot of red tape. Sometimes office politics can get in the way of progress with the old-fashioned mentality that is still at the firm.

advice: My advice to management is to keep doing what they are doing. Pushing employees to do their best. By working your hardest, you are able to achieve greatness.
pros: Amazing atmosphere and employees. Because it is such a big company there are many perks and rewards. Always feeling a need to do and be better.
cons: It is competitive and big. Because it is such a large company sometimes you can get lost within. You need to try and make a name for yourself within your office and start from there.

summary: Connection and relevance are keys at Morgan Stanley
advice: I do not have any advice.  This is a difficult market and situation. Morgan Stanley has weathered other very diffuclt market situations and I am sure will do so again.
pros: Compensation and what was once the best technology group on the street.
cons: Lack of vision and strategy, especially for the IT department.  Layoff of many, many good people and reduction of expenses has created a difficult environment and morale is suffering.  Many good people have left due to the recent and current situation.

advice: Senior management needs to think through decisions before acting. They need to exhaust all reasonable options before making decisions that are detrimental to employee morale and productivity. I think Morgan Stanley would be a great place to work if senior management showed compassion to the people that work for them.
pros: working with intelligent and world-class individuals.
cons: Poor management of people. Disheartening to see people that knowhow to play office politics succeed over people that have truly worked hard to get where they are. Many people exude a sense of entitlement...

advice: Less micromanagement, be a little bolder and, most importantly, stop copying everything from GS's model.
pros: Great team to work for, wonderful people to work with, as well as tons of opportunities for professional growth if you can struggle through the boring stuff in the beginning.
cons: Micromanagement can be a serious problem.  Also, routine is always a killer.  Also, sometimes I wish MS would eliminate a lot of overlapping managerial positions that it currently has because it sucks to be reporting to 15 layers of management on top of you.

advice: Have senior management audited for strengths and weaknesses. Not all ideas are good ideas. Ensuring employee morale is high can help a group maintain top talent.
pros: People are always helping you. Mobility is encouraged. To succeed in this business, you have to be aggressive. Make sure you come prepared.
cons: Like at any company, you can be unfortunate to have an incompetent manager. For the most part, you will need to manage the downside while imagining the upside, and always remember that there is a year end review.

summary: Interesting to see where MS will go . . .
advice: Job descriptions are one thing . . . an employee's full background and scope of experience should be taken into account in allowing for future growth instead of limiting opportunities.
pros: Fantastic franchise and brand recognition.  Opportunities for professional mobility after leaving are tremendous.  Great benefits including health, dental, retirement plans.  Perks including personal discounts on MS products.
cons: Grueling schedule.  Discouraged from taking time off.  Politics and agenda setting are unfortunately rampant especially within the management ranks.  Uncertain future as a premier brand.

advice: Review compensation process
pros:
Senior management is very technical. Some of them still quite hands on
compensation is good in comparison to peers
Working with top notch people because interviews are tough and can take upto 8/9 rounds. Hire from top schools. 
Excellent training program for entry level positions. 
Software infrastructure is best on street resulting in more time spent being productive
cons:
Long hours
Working with brightest also means very competitive
Large percentage of salary is in bonus so its all about results and so people tend to take shortcuts compromising quality

pros: Free coffee and tea. Ability to telecommute depending on the manager.
cons: Managers do not know how to manage and they play favoritism.  It seems consultants outnumber employees.  A lot of functional redundancy and overlap.  People are insecure and a lot of infighting for projects. Strange how the CIO pressures us to reduce our spending, tells us there isn't enough money for better pay and bonuses, tells us our project funding is being cut, along with regular talk of headcount ramp-downs, but managers fly back and forth from NY to London to India. Also, plenty of senior managers hired from the CIO's previous company, who then hired their team members from the company, even though we went through a hiring freeze.

advice: Hire FA Trainees as part of a team to work under a senior advisor. Reduce requirements to a practical level. Branch Managers should be able to answer at least the basic HR questions. Actually care about your employees and not their friends' and families' assets.
pros: Descent base salary. Descent benefits. Nice co-workers. Impressive name to put on a resume. Great for the large institutional investment market.
cons: Management still has not adjusted asset requirements to the new norms of the economy. If you do not have a book already than don't do it. There is very little to no help in creating a book of your own. When the time comes(13 months), if you do not have the assets, you are terminated. Worst experience I have ever had.

summary: If you want to do ibanking, nowhere is great, but MS is better than most
advice: I don't have too much advice for management because we never really interact with them. My advice would be to hire more analysts.
pros:
- Great people, people who do business the right way
- Not an ahole culture
- Groups aren't huge, less hierarchy than most banks
- Tons of recruiters / headhunters reach out to you
cons:
- It's banking after all so not thaaat much fun to be honest
- Pay isn't great given how much you're working
- that's about it

advice: I’m probably not the best person to give advices - they should know it. I think they did, but not sure if there was any improvement since then.
pros: Great colleagues with huge knowledge, lots of internal trainings, lot to learn regarding the infrastructure and solutions. Overall it’s a very great place!
cons: Local management was very poor. There were a lot to improve not sure if it has changed or not. Also there were way too many mandatory meetings and conference calls - it was challenging to focus on actual work.

advice: Pay more attention to what the worker bees are actually saying with regard to timelines for projects.  Get a direct line of communication to them and not just get information filtered through layers of management.
pros: Morgan Stanley offers very unique challenges given the scale of the business.  Generally promotes a decent balance of work and personal life.
cons: Some disconnect between upper mgmt and the working class with regard to strategic direction; most often seen in unrealistic timelines.  Large company so even seemingly simple changes can move like molasses.

summary: Challenging work, growth opportuntiies could be much better
advice: Create a culture where middle and senior management interact more with all employees.
pros:
Challenging work - fulfilling to see the impact of your work.
Work/Life balance was decent.  Work was generally decided for you.
There were not a lot of interruptions and meetings, allowing you to focus and deliver.
Co-workers were generally nice and capable.
cons:
Growth prospects were uncertain - management didn't seem to invest in individual growth.
Compensation was not correlated with performance.
Organization structure was very hierarchical, you rarely interacted with those higher than two levels above you.

advice: Reduce process driven procedures and focus more on developer happiness and take measures which help them use most of their time to be productive.
pros: Good Work if you get a good team. Solid Culture and core values, Tech and Data is best among financial services companies. Good amount of smart and driven geeks reside in Morgan Stanley.
cons: All cons of an MNC and lots of processes, constraints on browsing the internet, contributing back to open source and security constraints as the financial data is very important that social network data.

summary: Great locally, retarded on the corporate level.
advice: You hired smart, competent people to run your offices, so start listening, get out of the way and let them do their jobs!
pros: My co-workers are smart, hard working very caring people, for the most part. Health benefits are good, the office is in a gorgeous location and I really like the management in my branch.
cons: The integration of Morgan Stanley culture with Smith Barney culture is excruciating. The corporate office clearly has no respect or trust in their Branch managers. So much autonomy has been removed that it is difficult to do business.

advice: More forthcoming with business strategy and a clearer definition of what goals are and how success is defined.  More through job of scanning organization for existing top talent.
pros: Ok place to be.  Good environment.  People respectful.  Always changing.  Generally there are opportunities to move up or around if you are able to navigate or elbow your way.
cons: As above, always changing.  Need to be tied to revenues closely if you seek high pay - which makes sense.  Otherwise don't expect a lot of big increases

advice: Work on the culture for the group. It is a shame to see a white shoe firm like MS unable to retain top talent.
pros: Good benefits, excellent colleagues and decent exit opportunities. MS has an excellent brand and at the analyst level placement in private equity is very strong. .
cons: Senior management was terrible. All the associates within my team left within two years. The problem had to do with the sub culture of the LA office. The VP level staff worked the associates and analysts into the ground.

advice: Get involved with your lower associates, be a role model and seem interested in not only your personal needs.
pros: From the short term experience I had, with the small group I worked with, if you like saying you work for a major bank, in a high rise building on the 60th floor, and you get to wear a suit every day, without mentioning, what it is you do or how the atmosphere is when you are at work, this would be recommended.
cons: Such a monotonous and boring routine, no room or trust to handle more demanding tasks.

summary: Good starting position with decent operational exposure
advice: They should increase pay for full-time employees which could help retain some real talent thus driving better efficiency and real cost savings in the future.
pros: Fast past work environment that gives you an opportunity to interact with MS CSRs/ front office out of New York, MS IT department, hedge funds clients, and of course other middle/back office operational groups.
cons: The operations group tries to leverage too many temporary employees to help cut costs. These temps are often ill-trained and ultimately hurt overall performance.

advice: Stop cutting costs and good employees while Gorman continues to be paid handsomely. The consolidation and cost-cutting is having a severe impact on the service level provided to customers, particularly on the retail side.
pros: There are a lot of very intelligent, hard working, professional employees.
cons: Too much time and money spent on senior management initiatives imposed upon employees in lower management as well as subordinates while costs and strong employees continue to be cut. Morale is poor and competitors, let alone smaller (including midsize) shops and hedge funds, tend to pay much better. No place is perfect but general consensus among current employees and former (again, below senior management) is that most places offer a better culture and stronger compensation than MS.

pros: The work schedule was good and the office looked nice.
cons: The office I was in was poorly run.  The manager didn't want to manage the team or even be in the position, but he wanted to all the perks that went with the job.  He would buy personal items and expense them to the company, for example, we did not have a Holiday Party, but he took his family to dinner and said it was the office party.  Advisors would treat the CSA poorly and the manager would do nothing.

summary: Excellent at headquarters, tougher in the field
advice: While I understand the necessity of a strict management structure throughout the branches, a lot of local talent is under utilized.  I understand preference should be given to revenue drivers, but the backbone of the branch system, operations, risk, compliance and support are integral to the success of the sales force and would benefit from more support, opportunities and growth opportunities.
pros: Top notch business culture, continuing educational and growth opportunities at headquarters.
cons: Branch culture is totally different and at times at odds with corporate culture.

advice: Get rid of quintiling process it is effective if your team is diverse in how effective people are .but if you have a strong group people are told they aren't effective even if it isn't true.
pros:
Lateral mobility options
Benefits self starters who want to own their careers
Good bonuses if you are considered to be succeeding in your role.
cons:
Ranking system is flawed. If you're on a strong team you could get ranked poorly even if you're effective at your role.
Very difficult to change roles AND move up in title

summary: It has been a fun 3 years
pros:
Very professional culture. Stress on ownership of modules instead of pushing the envelope. Very smart people around you keep you motivated.
Approachable senior management who actually listen to suggestions.
Enough opportunities to move within organization if you desire a change in role.
cons:
Hours can be long, but this is strictly a one-off thing. I have never personally had any problem with this - if my code breaks, I have to fix it, no matter how long it takes - which I think is fair.
Comp can be slightly on the lower side early in your career.

advice: Demonstrate a stronger commitment to helping each individual in career development and professional growth
pros: Morgan Stanley Research has a great reputation and can open doors on the buy-side or at other sell-side firms.  One gets to work with, and learn from, very competent, professional colleagues. Customer service was very high on the priority list at Morgan, as it should be in Financial Planning.  There were extra efforts to cater to the clients beck and call.  And almost all of these events were covered 100% by the company.  In addition to the events, the Morgan Stanley name provided needed credibility in an unstable investment environment.  At the time of my employment, they and Merrill were the only two large investment firms not owned by a bank.
In addition to client perks and strong health benfits, Morgan Stanley provided matching gifts to msot charitable contributions and promoted community service, both by sponsoring some local events as well as providing specific dollars if you had a viable pet project in your community.  I thought this was great, especially since the DFW market is growing and getting a large number of prospects from other markets on the coasts, where real estate is performing much worse.
cons: Unfortunately, the client catering came at a price, one that was usually too high.  Commission rates were a bit above average, and the constant account fees seemed to nickel and dime clients.  As Finanical Advisors, we were provided a small account to help alleviate some of those fees for our larger clients, but it was never enough to completely respond to the concerns of our entire book.  There was a tiered fee structure that rewarded larger accounts, but the way it was set up, a client could have as much as $249,999 and still be subject to a $150 fee for their account. summary: Acceptance of Mediocrity in a Franchise System
advice:
Talk to regular FAs - not the top 10% of producers, talk to the median producers.

Create a real competency program for CSAs.

Identify the 100 tasks that are completed dozens of times each day by 10,000 FA's and CSA's, then streamline them so they can be done in half the time with fewer 'over the wall' handoffs to other offices, departments and using multiple systems.

Implement a real quality system - read Deming and others quality experts. Right now all you do when a problem is called in is to resolve the problem. How about doing something to keep it from happening again?

The financial services compay that gets this right FIRST will make a lot of money in efficiency, fewer screw-ups to fix, and more satisfied employees and clients.

Be willing to compromise on the age-old "you can run your business any way you want" mantra. 

There is no competitive advantage in a franchise, other than the brand and the processes (which you do not even wish to standardize). So all you have now is a gaggle of FA's and CSA's scrambling to servec clients while BOMS and Regional staff 'oversee' it and try to hire FA's from other firms.
pros: You can run your own business within the company, just stay inside the rules. Extremely flexible - work as har or not as you want, the result is you get paid more (or less).
cons:
Infrastructure is out of date. Internal communication systems are a kluge of emails, wires, faxes, web-based systems and the main CRM and account management system. They do not talk to each other. Network is way overloaded and slow. Information published in intranet is very often way out-of-date and wrong. 

EG - it took more than 2 weeks to get my personal color printer attached to my office computer (we have one old B&W HP Laserjet 4 for 12 people to use). Required two tickets with the IT help desk. This is normal.

New hires take from 2-10 days to get userids and access to the platform. 

The elements of the advisory platform are individually good, but they are not designed to work together well. The FA is the integrator of all the company's services - and this cannot be done efficiently.

There is NO formal training program for non-FA staff....it is all OJT. From what I see they do not even have a list of skills or competencies required to know to be a CSA. If you want a good assistant, you essentially need to hire and train your own. CAS's try to link up with successful FA's and this leads to a competitive spirit between CSAs  - which is a hindrance to knowledge-sharing between them.

All this makes it difficult to run an efficient advisory business. Takes time away that I could be using to better serve my clients.

All this has nothing to do with the MS-SB merger. It was like this before then - but they now havea new excuse for acceptiing mediocrity.

summary: I am proud to work for Morgan Stanley.
advice:
You need to hear from the mid level producers as well as the big producers.  You need to understand how complex our jobs have become and all that you have asked of us.  The administrative support we get is not sufficient in today's environment.  The way things are structured, the bulk of the administrative and operational help goes to a few big producers and the rest of us have to fend for ourselves.  We could be far more productive if we had more highly trained assistants.  Think great legal secretary.

I would really like to be asked to review my complex and regional managers.
pros:
John Mack is a straight shooter so you know where you stand as a corporation.  He is tolerant of errors but expects people to own up to their misjudgements.  Whining is not allowed.  This attitude has been particularly important during the last year when our profession has been under fire.

 Our strategists and analysts have worked hard to help us to help our clients.  We are frequently out of step with what the rest of Wall Street sees and this has worked to our advantage.  

The benefits package is generous and addresses the needs of my family.  The employer match for the retirement plan is generous.  We also have a defined benefit pension plan which is unusual in this day and age.
cons:
Senior management and branch management understand the business and the everyday pressures.  Senior management has provided better tools and IT systems than we have ever had before.  Local management does their best to protect us from the idiocies of regional and complex managers.

Middle management seems to be clueless.  They are too busy protecting their jobs so they do little to stand behind those of us who actually put dollars on the bottom line.  It is difficult to find a line of communication to a higher level if you are having difficulty with middle management.  Middle management is so far removed from the day to day pressures of working with clients that they do more to get in the way than they do to smooth the way in a very difficult global environment.

-there are also large project spanning years
-responsibility chain is clear

I began with approx two week long tasks. Eventually I was charged with large projects, often without anything useful to deliver or demo for a long time to our customers. These often span years. This is a great opportunity to take part in something big and have impact. You also have to support legacy solutions at the same time.
cons:
-fast adapting to requirements -> lots of work
-pre-defined release turnover procedures -> releasing is highly repetitive and a very slow process, often does not exactly fit the current need
-you are responsible for your releases -> means trouble when there is not enough time
-regulatory changes are the highest priority -> code never get's re-factored, designs often sacrifice user experience, readability and performance in order to make higher-ups and regulators happy fast
-stressful work -> same salaries can be obtained elsewhere with significantly lesser stress and no midnight phone-calls and no weekend work
-compensations are complex, base salary might be competitive, but offers no premium compared to the market
-support of multiple trading desks -> customers often use specific terms, often with different definitions between markets
-lot's of legacy mammoth projects which are not possible to get rid of in reasonable time
-one man teams supporting globally distributed users -> "should have been three people, but we cut the budget" so in the end no way to prove your management skills, not doing interviews (no headcount), only manager in responsibility but not in title/compensation and you are the only one who can (and do get) called when there are any issues in any time-zones

pros: Good pay, good perks, great insurance, nice offices with lounge,located at the heart of the Old Montreal. Easy access to VPN and no-laptop hassle.
cons:
Terribly "banking" style. Despite being the SW development team we worked with the pressure of everything that goes wrong with people's money. The work is never done, more bugfix than new projects, lots of legacy, lots of stress. It is fast-paced and you better like that.

Not easy to apply for internal transfer, despite the process being in place.

summary: Horrible Experience working at MS Bangalore Office with managers

advice: Does not try to stay competitive among millennials. A lot of my peers left only after a year or two to go into tech or to work at other companies where they felt valued, got promoted and received salary increases. Management shouldn’t underestimate the importance of treating their employees well. You don’t need to spend a ton of money but just showing that you care about our career ambitions would make us want to stay. I’ve never felt so unimportant and unvalued than I have during my time at Morgan Stanley.
pros: I worked with an amazing team and had a direct boss that was amazing to me. He gave me so many opportunities to grow as an analyst. If you’re in wealth management, your experience will depend on the team you’re with. I loved my direct team but was not fond of management in Palo Alto. You will meet good and hard working people at Morgan Stanley.
cons: Unless you’re a financial advisor... you’re out of luck.  If you’re an analyst or associate you’re not really valued by the firm. They even call us “support staff” to show that we were just there to support.  I was a high performing analyst in a high performing team.  I unfortunately had to deal with individuals that discriminated me based on my age and gender and experienced bullying during my time at Morgan Stanley. I was initially shocked because it’s never happened to me before at any other firm. I brought it up to management and HR multiple times and nothing was done. I wasn’t really listened to all they cared about was performance and not morale. There was also an instance when we lost a member of our team. It’s managements responsibility to hire a new replacement. They never did to cut costs and I was tasked to do the job of 2 people for 10 months which stalled my career significantly and mental well being.  I worked 11 hour days and weekends to make up for it. Again... prioritizing performance and money over morale.

summary: Staffing situation puts pall over entire company
advice: Recognize the people need a positive work culture on top of just cranking through calls.  It's common knowledge that call center jobs are unpleasant and draining - you need to provide something to offset that (and the pay certainly isn't doing it.)
pros:
Well organized resources and prodecures
Schedule flexibility (it's set once you select, but a lot of choices for days/hours to fit your personal needs)
Lots of financial/banking offerings to learn about
Customers are actually nice, despite waiting 2 hours to get through
Opportunity to move into more specialized areas bcs they have a wide breadth of products
Good work/life balance, can choose overtime if you like
Good emphasis on diversity hiring
cons:
Understaffing leads to horrible wait times for customers. In theory this shouldn't be a rep's problem, but because the only mission of the company is to get in-bound calls answered, there is no human interaction. 

There is no fun, no joking, no connecting to co-workers, no meetings, no conversation. Just taking calls while alone in your house. 

Training is brief because they need to get people on the phones, but once you're on a team, nobody will have additional time to help you learn. 
Mood of team leads/managers can be snarky because everyone is under the gun to get the calls answered.

Constant pressure to sell financial consulting, but it's difficult when a customer has been on hold for 2 hours. Morgan Stanley is putting even more pressure on to sell.

It's not that the job is hard - it's just a matter of learning the procedures over time. It's just a hard, hard grind day after day with no friendly or positive interactions.

If you're the type of person who likes to clock in, do the job from home, clock out, not speak to anyone other than customers, and enjoy procedure, this could actually be perfect for you.
