summary: Horrible Pay and Conditions in Wealth Management Capital Markets
advice:
- I've heard a couple managers (ED level) use bigoted slurs that are regarded as homophobic in mainstream professional cultures. They should know better by then. I'm sure 
the you get talent hears this as well and doesn't appreciate it. There is only one female traders and no ethnic minority traders. 


-  it is in Purchase. It is a major pain to ever so anything with clients. Management in fact encourages trading personal NOT to get to know clients or do standard things at other firms such as dinner, drinks, etc. as a trader, you have limited if any 'street coverage'. And in sales, you do not actually get to speak directly with clients, instead must go through a Financial Advisor. Integrate personnel there with the main institutional desk in the city.
pros: Great gym. Free parking onsite.
cons:
This review specifically applies to wealth management trading floor based primarily in Purchase that covers top Financial Advisors' UHNW, middle market and HNW Clients. The division falsely advertises  itself as Capital Markets, that is NOT to be confused with the venerable Global Capital Markets desk in the city that brings deals to the market for major companies. 

Firstly, the horrible compensation ranges say it all:

After ones first three years, compensation  (both base and 'bonus') is far below street avg even within UHNW/how bucket:
- Analyst ( yrs 1-3): $95k-$120k
- Associate ( yrs 3-6): $110k- $160k
- VP ( yrs 6-10): $110-$170k --> you are stuck now and doing exact same work as A2
ED (yrs 10- infinity): $150-$250k 

In the past four months alone, the unit has lost 12 of its stronger performing analysts, associates and younger vps. It even lost its HR Rep in charge of "retaining talent." One would think management would be inquisitive as to this brain drain, especially when they trumpet the wealth management's staff support's "intellectual capital" as a point of strength in helping the firms top individual Clients. But they have not nor do they seem to care. They recruit finance and Econ majors from schools like Harvard, Brown, Georgetown, BC, Nova etc, train them up over a year period, only to lose many by year three. THE ENTIRE ANALYST CLASS OF 2008 IS GONE; all left to greener pastures. 

Over the last four years, there has been 4 different heads of this division. That's right- MDs in charge of managing a 300 person division that produces a half billion in revenue per year just can't seem to stick around. This volatility at the top trickles down to the next rung of management (EDs and newer MDs) where a culture of solo performance, selfishness, complete lack of communication and mendacity permeates the environment. 

Some  examples:
 

- Multiple colleagues have told me, and I've heard it myself, that their manager told them that their performance review nor rating does NOT determine ones compensation. When pressed on what actually determines compensation, no manager has ever explained it. If for example you are a trader at the associate or vp level  and produced $15MM in PnL for the year, you could very well get a 'bonus' of $20-30k pretax, and a low base; very uncompetitive for a 11 hr/day job with a 1 hr commute each way. This has occurred multiple of times to multiple ppl; don't think you'd be an exception. Regardless, no manager has ever explained the discrepancy between performance and pay. One can only infer it is because the division's management is of extremely poor quality and does not advocate senior execs on the divisions value add. 

- stagnate compensation between analyst-vp. Many second year analysts get paid as much if not more than first-third year vice presidents. One third year associate recently left to  lesser competitor and was offered twice their MSWM capital markets total compensation. 

- three star associates who made VP in the last four months left to competitors after they found out their promotion came with a DROP in year on year compensation. They wete doubled at other firms. What kind of management promotes its up and coming officers only to then lower their year on year pay? Bad managers. 

- There is an institutional desk in the city at Broadway and 42nd- where management should encourage relationships and communication to open up, there actually is a policy that says sales staff in Purchase cannot communicate with their colleagues in the city about any market/ job related issue.

- On top of a traders' PnL not being linked to anything comp related, neither are the sales force's sales commission. A sales person may do proactive trades that generate $10mm in gross credits over a year, but the managers do not attribute that work at the end of the year to that persons' efforts. Instead liken it to something that would have happened anyway. Well, what's the point of having a sales force then. 
 

If you don't believe those numbers just do a check on glassdoor but select "Purchase" as location, not nyc. If you decide to join this desk despite this warning, realize you will. E joining a glorified help desk

They are working on fixing these issues as quickly as possible but for now it hinders productivity.

summary: Morgan Stanley is a good company for financial advisors who are self-starters, marketers who bring in clients & assets.
advice: Spending millions on sketchy corporate investments while driving down FA comp does not engender good morale or advisor loyalty.
pros:
Global firm with instant brand recognition
Historically excellent training program
Good benefits including 401(k) and pension
Decent support for marketing efforts
cons:
Almost too-big firm adapts slowly
More of an imitator than innovator
A two-class environment with struggling rookies and highly-comped veterans
High attrition rate among new FAs

summary: Great company, friendly and cool people.  Wall Street culture in general does not value free time though.
pros: The money is good in finance, people can move around the dept after a few years.  Exit opportunities of course are quite good, people recognize the MS brand.
cons: Work-life balance can be awful at times, bonuses are almost completely arbitrary.  People who decide bonuses in a lot of departments don't actually know which analysts are performing the best.

pros: Great research and capital markets.
cons: There is a revolving door of managers and a lack of care towards employees from upper management. Constantly changing technology which leads to never ending issues and talking to someone on the IT desk who just started to learn English.  Checks and balances are a must in this industry but the hoops they have you jump through make it a struggle to conduct business.

advice: Find a way to retain young talent; There is limited upward mobility for young ambitious people; Too many "old - school" wall streeter's still hanging around which is limiting the company's potential
pros: Good pay; Great brand name for the resume; People are typically good, friendly (rare to find on a trading floor)
cons: Extremely political; claim to be a meritocracy, but it is more about kissing the right a**; limited entrepreneurial thought processes; Ignore their younger employees

advice: The training department needs a vast revamping.  In addition, end of year / goal-specific accomplishment bonuses seem to be a thing of the past.
pros: It is a good learning experience for new college grads entering the workforce.  It is a strong company to start a career with.
cons: Depending on the field you start with, it seems to be limit upward mobility of its employees.  Lateral movement within the firm proves to be financially unrewarding as well.

advice: Learn how to lead. Learn how to communicate with your financial advisors so they don't walk around the office treating everyone like complete garbage. Act as if you care if this is reported to you. Get a system that works, technology is important.
pros: Occasional free lunch. Mediocre benefits.
cons: Outdated systems, managers with no answers- often they provide an incorrect answer just to feel like they have supplied you with an answer. Very poor organizational culture.  A large majority of the staff is miserable.  Management doesn't know how to lead and build relationships. There are a few "have's" among the associates and many "Have nots".

advice: My advice to management would be to provide a consistent message in communication to employees.  Sometimes there mixed messages as well as inconsistencies that make employees feel an uncertainty in the direction the company is taking.
pros: Job location is ideal, Management in my department is generally accommodating to schedule changes, work load is manageable, ability to wear multiple hats
cons: Career movement can be cumbersome, additional work/responsibility does not necessarily equate to additional pay

advice: Pay those who perform or you will continue to see the brain drain. Cull the bottom performers, you're not running a charity.
pros:
Great exposure to product lines and markets
Front office willing to spend time and teach
Freedom to take leadership of problems
cons:
Compensation, Compensation, Compensation
No incentives for top performers to go above and beyond
Employees willing only do bare minimum to not get fired
Large number of poor performers due to top talent leaving
Promotions don't guarantee a raise

summary: Good place to start, but not a place to stay.  No bonuses or raises, get out after you get expereience.
advice: Challenge your workers, also dont beat around the bush with bad news.
pros: Easy job to learn and execute.  Young atmosphere, and management is not hard on you.
cons: No room for growth.  They preach mobility when there are none.  In 4 years, they did not even raise my group's salary one time, nor did they pay the "bonus."

summary: Overall positive experience, however very demanding commitment required
advice: Focus on the people in addition to the financials.  Celebrate accomplishments and ensure that those that worked hard on merging MS and SB are aware of Sr managements appreciation of all that they have done and continue to do.
pros: Challenging.  Learn a lot.  Good people to work with.  Intellectually stimulating.
cons: Hard to maintain a work / life balance.  Demanding work commitment.  Long hours and weekends required.

pros: Awesome employees who are kind and helpful. Team is lead by a well humoured and clever guy, positive experience with all employees at Morgan Stanley. HR members have always been polite, welcoming and helpful.
cons: Requires plenty of motivation and interest in the field you are working in. Not necessarily a con, however some people may struggle to adapt to a large international company with thousands of teams working on different parts of the company.

summary: Smart people, prestigious firm, good learning experience
pros: As a junior person, you will learn a lot and be exposed to a wide variety of deals and clients. You can expect to work with extremely smart and ambitious people. Compensation is usually in line with the rest of the street.
cons: Work hours can be long. Always seemed like we were playing second fiddle to Goldman. Financial meltdown hit MS hard and really brought out the worst in people.

advice: 'Our employees are our greatest asset' requires more than lip service.   Continuous staff reductions resulting in increased workloads and low morale in an effort to increase shareholder dividends is not a sustainable long term  strategy.
pros: Benefits are good for this firm.
cons: People are stressed out due to continual layoffs and increased workloads. Low morale.  It helps if to have a 'godfather'  in senior management if you have any plans on staying.

summary: Quality training, decent corporate support, and success is possible through partnerships.
advice: Arrange partnerships with senior advisors and new FAAs. This will reduce employee turnover and increase productivity.
pros: Great people that truly want to help you in any way they can. Substantial support from affiliate organizations and wholesalers (i.e. insurance companies, mutual funds, etc.).
cons: Goals for new advisors to reach are a bit steep in the second year. In order to succeed, you must truly focus on growing fee-based business.

pros: Training is good, and support staff is ok.
cons: Even though is a great training opportunity, their FA Trainee program is extremely short with a vast amount of info that is impossible to assimilate in weeks. They would place FAA on production when you still dont know anything, and expect you to bring the assets necessary in order to make the goals. A sophisticated investor can smell a rookie from miles away.

advice: To have a good relationship with management it is recommended to join a committee with exposure to management.
pros: Morgan Stanley has a great International Environment, with talented, young collegues. There is a strong emphasis on work-life balance, but it depends highly on the position.
cons: Work life balance is not ideal in some positions. Distance between senior management and employees is too wide in most cases. Senior management's communication with employees can be improved.

advice: Do more to retain employees.
pros: Management does a lot to improve your career and look out for your future.  May vary by department, but management is very understanding of the work-life balance aspect.  Will let you work from home and take time off when needed.  Great experience, would highly recommend.
cons: Not the highest paying bank on the street and doesn't give great bonuses to all departments-- even top performers.

summary: Disappointing, uninspiring culture,  few seem to truly care about the work they perform.
advice:
Be realistic in project planning deliverables,  pushing back dates month after month sends a bad message and vibe.

Lots of above average talent is blocked by less than average middle management.  Create visibility opportunities to expose and correct the issue.
pros:
Name brand has goodwill
Good reputation on the Street
Solid financials
cons:
Depressing place to work
Very political
Very inefficient (under utilized resources, idle consultants)

advice: Should try to retain talent by making the path to promotion easier and earlier.  Would cause people to think twice as they evaluate other options
pros: Good place to learn and figure out what you want to do.  Work on interesting, current transactions.  Some people have lots of history of experience
cons: Have to find the right person to work for.  Some people can be very difficult, which impacts work life balance

advice: try to acknowledge more on who actually do the work. Have a clear image of the individual contribution.
pros: nice environment, not that difficult in terms of work load. lots of smart people you can learn from.
cons: lots of time is actually spent on talk to other teams for support/help/clarification. Especially for teams in India, time is not fit. Frequently for a small issue, you need to wait for another day because of time difference.

advice: I got hired as Associate (IT). After one year for the same position with same experience the entry level was VP. I don't think this hiring strategy makes associate employees to stay longer at the firm.
pros:
- Volunteer Pension Fund benefit
- Free cafe, nice office
- Work from home possibilities
- Work/Life balance
cons:
- 1 hour lunch time that should be taken off
- Parking fee

advice: Speak to more people, not just the ones you're close to, so that you get a wholistic view of what's going on and not just have one side.
pros: Good name and place to start career, name opens doors and working with smart people give the opportunity to learn a lot on the job.
cons: Culture can be toxic, competitive in a counter productive way, and management very removed from day to day and unaware of non-quantitative measures

summary: An Incredibly Fast Paced and Intellectual Environment, but
advice: Focus more on diversity of thought and employee satisfaction
pros:
Challenging Work
Incredible talented co-workers 
Diverse projects 
Good technology
cons:
Extreme Focused on bottom line
Employees way down on list of importance.  1st Shareholders, 2nd Clients, 3rd FAs, 4th Employees.
You'll work hard and not get recognized. 
There is an amazing amount of ego in the room 
Much of the work in done in silos
Work life balance can be tough

summary: Great culture and great place to work
advice: Keep the focus on innovation and spend more on tech ology for business enablement. Create a more multi functional and smaller workforce that collaborated across divisions.
pros: Great company to work for in Technology. Strong leadership vision and a culture of innovation. Good business sponsorship of technology projects.
cons: Sometimes feels a little too big and siloed. Has gotten a bit large from the early days and too much acute specialization of roles.

summary: Great Foot in the Door but not much direction
advice: have a better understanding of the job the service associates perform everyday to better manage each associates workload (ie number of advisors each associate suppports) so people are not over worked.
pros: Access to Morgan Stanley platforms and research.  Learn a lot about the wealth management industry.  Good company name on resume well respected.
cons: Everyone is busy, very reactionary job, feel like your an order taker from the financial advisors

summary: Laid back fun environment that gives you opportunity to grow
advice: Pay and advance your high performers. Period.
pros: The culture is pretty strong. Office is young and ppl are welcoming/friendly. You can be successful if you play the game right. Big name helps on the street
cons: Once a year promotion eligibility coupled with stringent “time in role” requirements, leads to the loss of a lot of good talent. Ppl leave for pay bumps at other firms

summary: Salary at Start is Very Important
advice: you're losing good people bc you're not promoting appropriately.  salary and titles within depts should make sense and have level playing field with colleagues.
pros: generally a good place to work.  decent maternity leave and job flexibility.  generally good caliber of competent co-workers
cons: too much is being outsourced so managers in this location are being asked to do more but not getting paid commensurately.  internal promotion is also very difficult.

summary: A good organization for many and a very tough one for others.
advice: Read the reviews that your direct reports are getting from their reports.
pros: Good benefits, collegial atmosphere (for many), internal mobility seems to operate well for many. I’m in a tough group so I can see that many are working on getting out to other groups at the 18 month mark...
cons: Bad management allowed to linger. Favoritism and bad culture hard to expose despite being honest in manager 360 review.

advice: convince upper management to invest in retainment by making the company fun
pros: 401k match, culture is more relaxed then Goldman or Fidelity, paid vacation time off
cons: no employee stock grants, no company parties including Christmas, no bonuses, no incentives to win anything worth anything. really kind of a boring company to work for, hard to move up even with many years experience. lots of the typical big company politics and red tape.

advice: Do not let older employees come into work just to take naps. Force your employees to learn how to use the computer and answer a work cell phone (some of the older people in upper management would literally ask their client associates to turn on their computer, write emails for them, etc)- it can be depressing.
pros: Other than working for a corporate company which people hear and admire, I could not think of any pros.
cons: If you are a young, passionate person run far far away from this position. You will be a glorified assistant and stuck doing administrative tasks all day.

advice: Empower your senior resources and support them as needed vs. staying not being engaged nor available as needed. Manage transition in a more thoughtful manner.
pros: Challenging work and opportunities; company in streamline mode allowing resources to get involved in areas outside prime roles which is a learning opportunity.
cons: Extremely long hours and lack of management support; as company streamlining folks are let go abruptly and not handled in a professional manner.

advice: Continue to train your employees and try to keep them engaged internally. Better communicate the company's direction to those in satellite offices.
pros: High responsibility from day 1, has great on the job training and rewards high achievers. Vacation days arelated good and not a cut throat culture.
cons: Some issues with retention due to workload, also difficult to move internally without having a pre existing connection in the company.

pros: A great environment to learn,  gain technical knowledge and experience working in a multinational organisation setting. I'm glad to have spent my internship year as a finance intern. Sometimes long working hours are offset by the great flexibility in the workplace which is especially important when you're still a student.
cons: Hours can be long and interns are not always given equal amount of responsibility depending on the team/ area they work in.

advice: Need to work on promoting leaders and not managers. Tenure status doesn't necessarily translate into management, so the firm needs to assess candidates as some managers  squash creativity/innovation by imposing only their ideas.
pros: Great people and technology. The company promotes giving back to the community and really cares about their clients.
cons: Depending on who you report to, employee moral can be at its lowest

advice: Employees only see Work-Life Balance in the promotion video. Less workload would significantly drop the fluctuation rate.
pros: Documented processes, improved IT background, good collaboration among colleagues
cons: Overwhelming tasks, hard to keep up with the continuously changing scope of activities, need to cover colleagues while they are on vacation means over 150% workload. Meetings after 9-10 PM Budapest time. Due to the human error in the input files, reports must be rerun 2-3 times before submission.

advice: I had great bosses. Any issues I had were not their doing. They do their best to adjust to shifts that come from up the grapevine.
pros: Great place to start your career and get a feel for wealth management. It is not for everyone, but can yield many rewarding career paths.
cons: The environment is dynamic. Expectations and goals can and will change. It's important to be able to adjust on the fly.

pros: Morgan Stanley has great technology and tools that make the job easier to do. Each complex, branch or team can be unique in the way they function. If you don’t align well at one branch but like the company you could relocate under the umbrella of the firm.
cons: The service professional role is still under valued but this is across the industry. You have to heavily rely on supplemental compensation

advice: You are doing great, need to push across all system to scale and adapt to newer tech
pros:
Excellent Team Culture, Very Open to opinions, implementing new POC's trying out tech, great collaboration, and benefits.
Management has good vision.
cons: Sometimes lot of legacy applications used is not changing , causing newer tech not fit into the grand architecture, and causing a lot of teething problems, as some legacy apps are set in stone.

advice: Create a place where we can grow - just because we are good at our jobs doesn't mean you need to keep you us in that job,
pros: They have good health insurance for you and your family
cons:
1. very hard to get an interview in another business unit when you do the job in another business unit. 
2. no growth 
3. need to know someone to get ahead 
4. hard work doesn't pay off

advice: Focus on developing mid level managers and making sure junior talent is engaged.
pros: Great people, good familial culture, plenty of opportunity to take on new challenges.
cons: Senior management can be disconnected with the people down in the trenches.   This is fairly  standard at a large corporation, but it is a shame since it is really the only thing holding this place back from being a dream organization.

summary: Finding a good boss is more important than a company.
pros: Internal mobility program is the best, you can find another good team in a big company.
cons:
The team culture is based on your ED(executive director). Before you join this company, please have one interview with manager(mostly VP) and his boss(ED level).
If you and your boss cannot find a long term career path for you, please find another team.

advice: let us stop being slaves please
pros: The pay (but if you break it down for the hours we make you work its low)
cons: Too many to list. The work is non stop. Literally non stop, busy from the second you walk in the door until you leave. No times for breaks, always desk lunch cant have time for meetings, just thinking about getting back to the desk and how much time you wasted doing anything just so you can go back to try to finish or you will work later and later and later. its never ending. DO NOT WORK HERE.

summary: Lots of opportunities to learn and take on interesting work
pros: Have greatly enjoyed the colleagues in each of my roles. Smart, generous people. Also have benefited from great roles and opportunities to do important work and learn.
cons: Senior management says they care about diversity but it’s in name only. There is a ceiling for employees, particularly women and people of color. Most won’t go past a certain level and get into their club and be paid equitably.

pros: Fast paced environment where you'll be surrounded by smart and motivated colleagues; entrepreneurial spirit and ability to plot your own path (to a certain degree) without constant oversight from senior management. Good camaraderie across teams.
cons: Trading floor politics and risk of numbers-driven tunnel vision; perception that Singapore office is seen as a satellite and thus not given enough credit for the work that gets done locally. Limited opportunities to move laterally within the organisation.

summary: Morgan Stanley - Top of the Pack
advice: Keep your eye on the big picture and remember if it looks to good to be true, it almost always is.  Keep looking to find the fatal flaw and never think that reward can be achieved with out the need to manage risk.
pros: Great job if you know wealth folks who think your smart
cons: Hard to get started as a new financial advisor.  High failure rate

advice: Talent is self selecting: hire smarter people and more smart people will join. Too many yes-men make office politics too dominant.
pros: The Morgan Stanley name is a pretty strong brand. There is a strong sense of MS pride within the firm.
cons: The compensation for the hours worked is obscene compared to the competitors. Definitely not an intellectually stimulating environment. A monkey can do the job, but you look better in a suit.

advice: please don't hire too many people to do the same job when you can just hire less, save money, and have employees take benefit.
pros: the environment is great.  The benefits and vacation packages are definitely worth it.  Learn a lot of fun stuff.  go
cons: everyday is the same thing over and over again.  i would have so much time on my hands that i didn't know what to do.

summary: Worst company to work for..Sharks is what the business is about..Mgmt = incompetent
advice: Pay more attention to the new hires and less attention to the sharks in the office.  If you want new assets, then you should train the new hires to bring them in.  We all know the old veterans are sitting on their book.
pros:
Flexible work schedule
Great Networking Opportunities
cons:
Mgmt. is incompetent
No training program(its a joke)
The Financial Advisor program is setting you up for failure
Company wants your family and friends' assets and then want to fire you soon after 
Very political in the office (favortism is shown bluntly)

advice: Hiring more staff to even workload, manage teams less militantly and put more emphasis upon making the atmos and work ethic; work-hard, play-hard.
pros: Widely recognised as a leader in the market by rivals and clients alike. There is a great number of very talented individuals one works with too.
cons: The bonus pool is narrowing, there is less opportunity to work and gain professional qualifications and the gap between the super powers is widening.

advice: Improve management in the strategy organization. Develop modern risk-management technology. Improve communication about work process and goals. Define work processes and goals.
pros: Well-known brand in investment banking, good client relationship, history of big deal-making, competitive work environment (good for those who like to compete in a workplace)
cons: Undeveloped risk-management technology, poor mid-level management communication and work organization in strategy and technology, duplication of effort. No coherent firm-wide development plan in risk management technology.

advice: forward thinking; dedicated to taking care of employees; emphasis on building the brand; entry into new lucrative products; shying away from risky and profit-losing businesses
pros: good brand value; strong work experience; smart and competent colleagues; great training; opportunity to launch a career from a global platform; ability to move around the firm
cons: heavy hours and poor work-life balance; tough environment to work for females; demanding bosses that expect perfection; hierarchical and bureaucratic

summary: Overall, a good place to get work experience
advice: Overall ok. This was not the best company I have ever worked for. Alot of dissatisfaction from lower level employees.
pros:
- Learned about work environment
- Gained knowledge about finance industry
- Opportunity to ask questions
- Great mentor ship from boss
cons:
- Lack of opportunity for intern projects
- Mostly filed/copied items
- Did not have the structure, support, or organization of other internship programs I have participated in.

summary: They're only worried about the bottom line.
advice: To start focusing more on what makes the company run everyday instead of what brings in a dollar today.
pros: The products and resources to support clients' needs is great due to the company being as large as it is.
cons: Large producing advisors are the only voice that is heard. If you don't directly add to the bottom line you are seen as expendable.

advice: The software, computers, and technology are slow to work. Also, the interaction between employees and some of the operation associates could be much better.
pros: You have a network of individuals with different ideas and view points. MSSB offers great research reports and investment information/ideas.
cons: The wirehouse setup is an interesting one to work at. The best thing you can do is create relationships with as many people as possible there.

summary: One of the most transparent and professional places to work
advice: May want to rethink strategies at different locations, cannot apply a global strategy to every region
pros:
Working in a very transparent and professional environment
Working with some of the best brains in the world
Amazing infrastructure and support services, letting one focus on responsibilities efficiently
cons:
May lose visibility on account of huge size and large number of employees
Slightly rigid adapting to local environment

advice: Pay the people.. and recogize the people who deserve it.  Not the people who is kissing butt..
pros:
work/life balance
Flexible with working from home 
does promote internal mobility
Meet good people
cons:
low pay- barely any increase or bonus
due to low pay.. good people always leave .. so many turnovers.  People who stay behind suffer bc they are dumped with all the work and training..

summary: Positive and achieved some important milestones. Some great teamwork was accomplished.
advice: Better comminication regarding Pay and a new approach to Compensation and how they calculate it.
pros: Great Culture; Good People and a very professional atmosphere. Projects are very team orientated and employees work very well together.
cons: Pay is stagnant and raises are very poor, sometimes non existant. Communication from senior management can be poor which leads to a lot of disgruntled employees.

summary: Stay Away unless you have a large network of Wealthy Friends and family
advice: wake up and pay attention to your advisers. the days of sitting back and getting paid to do nothing is over.
pros: autonomy to set your own schedule and work the hours that suits you and your situation.
cons: management is looking out for themselves, no leadership, two investment companies got married and there are no connection, technology isn't the best.

advice: Find programs to help people stay
pros: growth! amazing leadership people are great here and met some wonderful friends that are life long, people care and really want you to be there a long time.
cons: Hard to make it in the business! sometimes you seem to feel like there is no support but that is the nature of the business. Hard to figure out what the best way to go when your frustrated.

summary: Great Pay and Benefits, Poor Job and Management
advice: care about your workers more
pros: Great pay and benefits for the company
cons: You will take 30-40 calls per day from customers across the world, with little to no help from most upper management. Company culture is extremely poor with management seeming as if they don't know you nor care about anything about you besides your job. Expected to get licenses, but no help obtaining licenses besides paid for material.

summary: FAA program has very lofty goals
advice: come up with a more reasonable and effective training program and you may have a more successful FAA program leading to a higher success rate.
pros: The starting salary is not bad for a training program. Your benefits start on day one. Offices are nice.
cons: Revenue and asset goals are very high.  training is a bit lacking to properly prepare FA's to succeed. Very high turnover in the program.

advice: Increase pay structure. Make more pay incentives for all departments, especially back office employees.  Moral is not high in certain areas because they don't feel appreciated.
pros: Good brand and name.  Good work life balance.  Development and online university and learning are a plus. Senior management is good.
cons: Not a lot of internal mobility, Need more balance in pay structure. Lack of intelligent people working in certain areas.

summary: Can be good experience depending on your positions
advice: Should really adhere to the preaching of work life balance
pros:
The culture is pretty good
They emphasis a lot of firm mobility and post a lot of jobs internally for people who are looking to transition
A modest benefits package
cons:
They preach work-life benefit but it is hard to really obtain a decent balance there
Can be a bad experience depending on your department 
Some areas have high turnover

advice: Recognize when you have a good employee working underneath you, and all that we do on a daily basis for you!
pros: Easy workload, a lot of downtime, e-mail was very accessible. It wasn't a bad job really at all, just not that challenging for me.
cons: Again, not that challenging, too much downtime, and there was not enough potential for growth. Good employees were not recognized for their efforts.

pros:
- clear carrier path
- safe job
- good salary
- there are smart people (but you have to get lucky to get into a good team)
cons:
- too much distributed team (satelite team)
- many graduate grown up and got used to old techs and since they never seen other hard to change them
- knowledge of economy is more important then technological background
- most in the management good at business logic but terrible with technology

advice: Provide more positive feedback to your employees. Pay attention to those that are working in the ethic that Morgan Stanley would be proud of.
pros: Opportunity to use my assets and move forward.  I have received a lot of positive feedback and compensation equal to my efforts.
cons: Because of the companies size, it can be easy to be over looked. You have to work hard and sometimes to hard to be recognized.

summary: It was a fantastic experience. You work along the smartest people in the industry and the learning curve is steep.
pros: Right when I walked into the door, people were greeting me instantly. Everyone is truly dedicated to their work and this promotes internal competition to constantly keep you thinking on your feet.
cons: My boss didn't provide the amount of work that I had expected. I felt that I kept asking for more work.

advice: Leadership should stop looking for numbers and put more care into customer service and relations - should also put more into training and career development
pros: Good working environment, managers tried their best to help us kids learn and be exposed to different sides of the business
cons:
Easy to get pigeon holed
Not much in terms of career advancement
Work inside a branch is pointless and competitive for no reason

advice: Find a way to get better intern retention, most of us moved on to other opportunities.  Very horizontal structure, but thats just the nature of the business
pros:
Great Networking Opportunity
Awesome People, Laid Back
Can pick up as much responsibility as you want/can handle.  Work as late as you want
cons: Long hours, working for a boss who did not show up much.  Have to cater to bosses needs/less structured than other internships.

advice: try to create a more formalized summer intern program, with better organization and structure so people like myself will want to come back
pros: good pay, good learning and growth opportunities for an intern. convoluted management and leadership, but overall a good place to work and start as an intern
cons: poor communication, rough hours, unreasonable expectations for a college kid interning. rude employees, talked down to, treated like a child, sent to get coffee

advice: i think the management  could be more open to different opinions from others and learn how to treat people fairly
pros:
it is a place that you can be exposed to real financial world 
You can meet some good people and join some great projects
cons:
it is hard to get promotion
pay is a bit below average
culture is just like other investment banks
they made people redundancy if the market is not good

summary: summer intern of tech and data
advice: make a guide book to interns of tech and data about how to set up developing environment quick and accurate, how to acquire license, and how to use in-firm develop tools.
pros: good work environment, colleagues were helpful and friendly. HRs were professional and held us plenty useful seminars.
cons: development environment were out of fashion and complicated. the efficiency of acquiring license of necessary IDEs were too low.

advice: Make sure that wholesalers giving presentations to the branches are offering products that are worth the financial advisor's time and consideration.
pros: Managers were exceptionally nice and supportive of the employees, and financial advisors genuinely cared about their clients, which showed through their work ethic.
cons: There can be some feeling of independence from the corporate headquarters in New York when positioned in a satellite branch, which isn't necessarily a good thing.

advice: Pay attention to morale!!! You're going to lose everybody!!
pros: Vacation time offered is very nice.
cons: Unfortunately the state of the economy affects everyone, and MSSB is no exception. Bonuses have been taken away, layoffs have occurred, and overall morale is down. The company has done nothing to show that it still values its remaining employees. Management has no idea or else they just don't care to realize that they are going to lose the good people they have left.  Unfortunately there is no room for career growth. The only saving grace is the vacation time and short commute.

advice: Continue to encourage a culture that values junior employees -- the analysts do a lot of the gear grinding and it's nice to feel appreciated
pros: Investment banking gets a bad rap, but it's an unparalleled learning experience -- Morgan Stanley has best combination of top performance/respect and nice culture.
cons: Long hours, but that's what you should expect from banking -- in exchange, you get a lot of responsibility and great learning experience.

summary: Morgan Stanley really taught me a lot about software engineering
pros: I loved my team at MS. They were all very helpful and it was not the cut throat wall street environment that I expected. Would love to be hired again!

summary: The Training Program is a Con
advice: Wake up.  If you like watching your margins continue to compress and your market share decline, then keep this bizarre model going.  If you're at all serious about operating in something resembling an ethical fashion, hire sales people to bring in clients and portfolio managers to manage the money.  Stop pimping trainees to serve as your client acquisition department.
pros: MSSB has one of the best brands in the retail brokerage business
cons: Look, becoming a financial advisor a la Morgan Stanley, Merrill, et al is at best a daunting task.  However, ask yourself, how do these firms profit from month after month bringing in FA trainees knowing full good and well that only about 1 in 10 make it five years and only about 2 in 10 even make it to 18 months?  The answer:  Trainees don't cost much.  Getting new clients, even for established FA's is getting harder and harder.  The "financial advisor" profession is way past saturated.  Secondly, the biggest trend in the profession is for FA's at the brokerage firms to either go purely independent as fee-based RIA's, or at least go to a much lower cost/higher payout platforms such as LPL.  Sooooo, what about our trainees?  Well, even the worst trainees are going to bring in one or two or so good accounts before they self-select out due to not making much money or the firm fires them for not hitting sales goals.  And, who gets those good accounts when our trainee leaves MSSB?  You got it, the established brokers get them, NOT struggling new FA's.  Put another way, the training programs are nothing more than client acquisition programs for the established FAs.  Giving these guys the accounts is one of the ways the traditional brokerage firms try to keep them from bolting to greener pastures.  In the meantime, our trainees are back on the street trying to find real jobs.  The only trainees who ever make it are those who have either family members or a big rolodex of close acquaintances who will give them substantial money very soon.  If you are not in that category, remember:  You are expected to bring in a few good accounts reasonably soon and then leave the firm.  In short, the best outcome for the brokerage firms is for trainees to become big producers.  But, that's not the plan.  If it were, do you think the failure rate would be anything approaching 90%?  Really?  No, the second best, and by far the most likely outcome, is for you to bring in a few good accounts and then leave the firm as soon as possible.  It's a very cynical model and is just one example of why the traditional retail brokerage firms are continuing to lose market share to just about everybody else.  Even retail prospects/clients are beginning to ask questions like "Why am I paying so much in fees and commissions?"  "What the heck is my performance and how does it compare to an appropriate benchmark?"  Those are not questions the Morgan Stanleys of the world want to hear.  But, for job seekers, just understand, it's a rigged game.  Morgan Stanley, Merrill, UBS, et al have a perverse, short-term model that is designed for you to fail.  Although they are encouraging FAs to go to fee-based models, it's simply in their DNA to view all prospects/clients as nothing more than a source of revenues.  In fact, all you really have to know is that the only thing... the only thing.... that they grade all FA's on is how much money they make off of every client. so long as they don't break any regulations.

advice: Management needs to acknowledge that rampant cronyism has a deleterious effect on morale, productivity, hiring, retention, and ultimately the firm's stock performance. Serious change is needed to make Morgan Stanley IT a meritocracy.
pros:

cons:
Before you accept a job in Morgan Stanley's IT department, think long and hard about whether it's the best move for you. Here are some important things to know:

1. Morgan Stanley's IT department is extremely political and bureaucratic. In fact, much of your day will likely be spent dealing with non-technical minutia such as PowerPoint presentations, status reports, and status meetings. If you aren't dealing with these minutia or in the midst of a turf battle, then you're probably a very low level peon. Ironically, the low level peons are often the smartest people in Morgan's IT department.

2. If you were hired through a traditional channel, such as a recruiter or the HR department, you're a nobody. Don't expect your career to go anywhere, no matter how technically proficient you are. The people who succeed at Morgan are buddies with senior management. They hang out with management at lunch or after work, and are invited over for barbecues. Can you get into this inner circle? Maybe, but this effort will require your nose to be a glorious shade of brown.

3. Most managers don't care about you or your career. They just want the work done. Why? Because their compensation is a whole lot bigger than yours and their time is usually spent justifying their existence. They will not hesitate to blame you when something goes wrong. Rarely, if ever, have I seen a Morgan Stanley IT manager take responsibly for his employee's actions. To add insult to injury, many of these managers will leave the office each evening well before you do. 

4. If you like cupcakes, then Morgan Stanley is a great place to work. Many employees in one large IT group did not receive bonuses this year. Instead, they were presented with delicious gourmet cupcakes. Mmmmmm.

5. I know of an employee who joined Morgan Stanley IT last year and was not paid his negotiated bonus. While bonuses aren't guaranteed in writing, there is an understanding on Wall Street that the negotiated bonus will be paid. Morgan Stanley violated this sacred agreement.

6. Communication skills are highly valued by management, while tech skills are not. (This wasn't always the case. Ten years ago, Morgan ran a very different IT shop.) You wouldn't believe some of the mediocre talent that gets promoted, simply because they talk the talk. This is a perpetual cycle, because in many cases the managers that handle the promotions aren't great technologists, but are easily bamboozled by their fellow talkers.

7. Presumably, you are at the top of your game. That's why you were hired at Morgan. But you wouldn't know it once you're on board. If you aren't part of the inner circle, you will be given all kinds of absurd reasons why you aren't promoted (e.g. you're not "visible" enough) and your compensation is stagnant or shrinking. You'll be spoken to like you're a child and lectured on things that are completely obvious to you. The idea is to belittle you, so that your manager can keep you in your place - just where you belong.

I believe you can find much better companies to work for, where your skills and effort will be truly appreciated.

On a related note, many functional leaders lack the basic product knowledge so staff (VPs and below) does all the heavy lifting which can be wonderful if you believe in, "If it does not kill you, it makes you stronger."
cons: Most large banks are under severe regulatory scrutiny which has translated into lots of pressure on employees, especially ones in the back office functions like Finance and Risk. MS has been struggling to meet its commitments to the street for a few years and that does not help anyone working there. Front office bankers and some functional leaders are not making as much as they used to and their disgruntlement translates into a pressure cooker environment for all the support staff. Lots of times junior employees in risk functions are asked to cooperate with business and other teams when the regulators expect risk functions to be impartial and diligent. This could be a career limiting move for everyone, especially for those trying to build a long term career without enough leverage. Promotions and salary hikes are awarded based on leverage primarily based on personal affiliations and preferences rather than merit. Don't believe HR or anyone else if they tell you otherwise. HR is the leader of labor cost reduction initiatives and under a lot of resultant pressure.

advice:
- Start looking at companies outside the industry to see how they do things. MS is not 'special'. Technology, and the process of running technology, has moved on enormously. Note, Goldman Sachs is not a role model in this regard. 
- Modern development practices are light years ahead of what MS currently uses, and have a lot to say about how to introduce change into production systems at a reasonable pace and at the minimum of risk. MS senior IT management do not understand how you actually minimise change risk. They simply believe that documentation = proof of testing, and that copious blackouts and sign-off from non-experts lead to system stability.
- Time spent doing TCMs and testing documentation and attending change meetings where non-technical management pretends to know what you're talking about would be far, far more productively spent writing good automated tests. 
- The time spent trying to document that due diligence has occurred takes too much time away from performing that due diligence itself. An audit trail is necessary, but MS goes far, far beyond this.

- Ok salary.

cons:
- Absolutely atrocious development environment. Business units commonly on better spec PCs for using Excel or Outlook than developers get for using heavyweight IDEs. 
- Windows XP.
- 4Gb RAM. That's right, 4. On a developer 'workstation', a.k.a the cheapest dell box money can buy.
- Everything is completely locked down, including developer's own PCs. The simplest tasks become an almighty chore involving multiple layers of non-value adding bureaucracy.  
- IT management is completely divorced from modern software engineering culture. MDs are typically smart, political, completely non-technical, and utterly unequipped to actively lead technical organisations.
- Apps are typically supported by offshored / outsourced vendor teams of poorly trained staff. Devs, intended to be the last line of defence, end up being the first and only port of call for most issues.
- High attrition rate for genuinely talented developers; good developers come in, try to change things, get frustrated when they can't, then move on. 
- If your manager is non-technical, it is a nightmare trying to get some decent tools to do your job. "Why do you need a Resharper license? Jim does just fine without it".
- MS has no idea what motivates developers. Everything revolves around comp and the bestowing of shiny titles. 
- Many MS developers have forgotten what is meant to motivate developers. Everything revolves around comp and the bestowing of shiny titles.

summary: Not a meritocracy, questionable decisions made at sr lvl
advice:
1. Have mgmt provide a rationale for their decision esp when it’s completely contrary to what their team and SMEs recommend.  At least their coworkers can understand why and maybe apply that rationale to future decisions. 
2.  Make it clear to mgmt that completely writing off empls and making a conscious decision not to help them develop (and advising others not to) is completely inappropriate and not the mark of a true leader.  
3.  The right answer to a questionable decision is never “I’m willing to own that decision.”  If it feels wrong, it almost always is.

Also, see the above.
pros: Interesting work, some smart people you can learn a lot from.  The benefits - free access to museums, etc are on par with industry.
cons:
Long hours, more than happy to work you to the bone without compensating that (it’s expected) or even a thanks, penny pinching (e.g. no means to formally recognize an individual or team, no holiday parties, etc), raises and bonuses small/non-competitive.  Also, you need to be very ok with grey areas, doing things you’re uncomfortable with for wrong reasons.

Appearance/politics most important - for example, on a regular basis, mgmt would rather make a wrong decision quickly without accurate info or enough facts and even when better decisions are proposed at the same time by the team or by an individual behind closed doors.  Why? Mgmt would rather appear to be decisive, save face, stand by their decision, and have the team waste time by following that bad approach/decision...inevitably, when it’s beyond clear the bad decision is bad, mgmt proposes a “new” (I.e. original suggestion by the individual/team) decision as their own, doesn’t apologize or admit their mistake (ever) and the team starts all over again.  In spite of that, mgmt still wants the work yesterday and demands the team meet the same deadline (even though they caused several days to be wasted already).  This is almost always announced at 5 or 6pm even though they’d already changed their decision that morning!

Similarly, mgmt is more comfortable with communicating incorrect info both internally and externally for appearance (rather than getting back with an answer - because then it doesn’t appear as if they’re all-knowing) and so they can take the opportunity to “look good” in front of peers and those more senior.

Employees I worked with at the time and former employees I’ve since met have the same gripes.

The department at least new immigrant friendly when hiring new intakes.

cons:
The job title says customer service to justify very low pay, but you do a whole lot more than typical call center duties. There is an insane financial services workload going on and definitely does not justify the 41,000 per annum pay.
There is no clear path if you are looking to change teams and/or apply to internal roles.
Managers do not expect you to take a bathroom break when the call queue is busy, and you can take a leak on your desk for all they care. Taking bathroom breaks when you are not on your set break period can lead to you not receiving a bonus at the end of the year (trust me). You are asked to take calls, document procedures, open investigation tickets. and at the same time answer colleagues questions in the teams chatroom. Your manager can withhold bonus from you if you do not fall head over heels to desperately answer your colleagues questions.
There is just too much micromanaging.
They expect you to take your personal time to catch up read up on new updates, company required trainings, etc.
There's just so much internal bureaucracy going on if looking to advance your career within.
They try to make you take the US FINRA S7 and S63 examination (Canadian equivalent is CSC. FINRA has no use here in Canada beyond this job) yet the difference in pay is next to nothing for the added stress. Expect to take more calls if you English speaking only during busy times (your bilingual teammates can be idle for over an hour, yet you, and not them, are still expected to respond to emails).
Other departments (especially some members in the CSM and RM teams) look down on you and do not consider you worthy of being treated like a human, it doesn't look like the managers can do much about this.
During company events to appreciate customer/client facing teams, nobody recognizes the department and all the work we put in, who cares about a call center right?
Even more archaic processes after the cross over to Morgan Stanley. These processes more stressful and leave you burned out at the end of your shift.
And the pay once again, is very low!
